### [24] [Semantic Register Compression in Multi-Agent LLM Cascades](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14119)
*Manuele Tele Junior Fernandez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Multi-agent LLM pipelines suffer from "semantic register compression," where intermediate agents systematically collapse semantic distinctions needed for downstream decisions. Using a Collector-Evaluator-Decider pipeline across three domains, the authors show the Evaluator stage reduces label separability by up to 41.7%, driven by oriented semantic transformation rather than mere information loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modular multi-agent LLM systems assign specialized roles to different agents, but when intermediate agents transform text across linguistic registers (e.g., from raw data to evaluative summaries), they may inadvertently compress semantically meaningful distinctions, degrading downstream decision accuracy. This failure mode is underexplored and poses safety risks for high-stakes applications like fact-checking, sentiment analysis, and medical triage.

Method: The authors construct a three-agent pipeline (Collector → Evaluator → Decider) and measure semantic register compression via inter-label separation in sentence-transformer embedding space. They test across three domains: LIAR (fact-checking), SST-5 (sentiment), and Triagegeist (medical triage). Five architectural variants are ablated to causally isolate the role of "oriented semantic transformation." A credibility-seeking variant is introduced to test whether transformation valence controls distributional collapse direction independently of compression magnitude. Prompt-level regression is used to explain variance in compression.

Result: Critical evaluation at the Evaluator stage reduces label separability by 41.7% (fact-checking), 27.2% (sentiment), and 20.0% (triage). Identity passthrough preserves separability nearly fully. Oriented semantic transformation is causally identified as the primary driver. The credibility-seeking variant yields minimal geometric compression but shifts outputs toward "mostly-true," confirming that transformation valence controls collapse direction independently. Prompt-level regression explains 78% of variance, with operational constraints linked to lower compression.

Conclusion: Semantic register compression is a measurable, generalizable phenomenon in multi-agent LLM systems. It arises not from simple information loss but from oriented semantic transformation driven by agent role prompts. This has direct implications for safety evaluation in high-stakes multi-agent deployments, where intermediate compression can silently bias downstream decisions.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems commonly decompose complex tasks into specialized roles. However, this modularity introduces a representational risk: when intermediate agents transform text across linguistic registers, they can systematically compress the semantic distinctions needed for accurate downstream decisions. We term this phenomenon semantic register compression and characterize it as an observable failure mode in multi-agent cascades. Using a three-agent pipeline (Collector-Evaluator-Decider), we quantify compression via inter-label separation in sentence-transformer embedding space. Across political fact-checking (LIAR), sentiment analysis (SST-5), and medical triage (Triagegeist), critical evaluation consistently reduces label separability by 41.7% at the Evaluator stage, while identity passthrough preserves it nearly fully. Five architectural variants causally isolate oriented semantic transformation as the primary driver. A credibility-seeking variant produces minimal geometric compression yet shifts outputs toward mostly-true, demonstrating that transformation valence controls the direction of distributional collapse independently of compression magnitude. Compression generalizes across the three domains with varying intensity: 41.7% in fact-checking, 27.2% in sentiment, and 20.0% in triage. Prompt-level regression explains 78% of the variance, with operational constraints associated with lower compression. These results demonstrate that semantic register compression is a measurable and generalizable phenomenon in multi-agent LLM systems, with implications for safety evaluation in high-stakes domains.

</details>


### [25] [Cross-Dataset Generalization in Urdu Fake News Detection: An Empirical Study with XLM-RoBERTa and a Length Confound Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14131)
*Muhammad Abdullah Haroon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First cross-dataset generalization study for Urdu fake news detection reveals catastrophic transfer failure (F1 dropping from ~0.77 to 0.005) caused by a systemic length confound where fake articles are 3.4× longer than real ones, demonstrating shortcut learning that inflates in-domain performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urdu fake news detection is under-resourced despite 231M+ speakers. Prior work focused on in-domain performance within single datasets, with no systematic investigation of cross-dataset generalization — a critical gap for real-world deployment where models must generalize beyond their training distribution.

Method: Fine-tuned xlm-roberta-base under four conditions: in-domain on Ax-to-Grind (10,083 articles, 15 domains), in-domain on Notri-Fact (13,388 articles), and zero-shot transfer in both directions. Compared against TF-IDF + Logistic Regression/SVM baselines. Diagnosed collapse via prediction distribution inspection and a length ablation (capping at 50 words).

Result: Notri-Fact → Ax-to-Grind transfer achieves macro F1 of 0.771, but Ax-to-Grind → Notri-Fact collapses to F1=0.005 (99.7% predicted as fake). Root cause: Ax-to-Grind fake articles average 117 words vs. 35 for real (3.4× ratio). Length ablation yields only 0.0067 F1 drop, confirming the confound inflates but does not solely drive in-domain performance.

Conclusion: Cross-dataset generalization in Urdu fake news detection is severely compromised by dataset-specific confounds, particularly article length. The authors provide a reusable diagnostic methodology combining bidirectional transfer analysis and prediction-collapse inspection applicable to multilingual fake news settings.

Abstract: Urdu fake news detection remains under-resourced despite Urdu being spoken by over 231 million people worldwide. While prior work has demonstrated strong in-domain performance on individual Urdu datasets, cross-dataset generalisation has received little systematic attention. This paper presents the first cross-dataset generalisation study for Urdu fake news detection, using two publicly available balanced datasets: the Ax-to-Grind Urdu corpus (10,083 articles, 15 domains) and the Notri-Fact Urdu dataset (13,388 articles). We fine-tune xlm-roberta-base under four experimental conditions, in-domain on each dataset and two zero-shot cross-domain transfer directions, comparing against TF-IDF baselines using Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines. Our experiments reveal a striking asymmetry: Notri-Fact to Ax-to-Grind transfer achieves a macro F1 of 0.771, while the reverse collapses to F1 of 0.005, with the model predicting fake for 99.7% of test articles. We demonstrate that this collapse stems from a systematic length confound in Ax-to-Grind, where fake articles average 117 words versus 35 for real articles, a 3.4x asymmetry inducing shortcut learning. A length ablation capping articles at 50 words yields only a 0.0067 F1 drop, confirming the confound inflates but does not solely drive in-domain performance. We provide a reusable diagnostic methodology that combines bidirectional transfer analysis and prediction-collapse inspection to identify confound-driven behavior in multilingual fake news detection settings.

</details>


### [26] [Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14147)
*Alex Kwon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A one-line prefill ("Sure, here is") jailbreaks aligned LMs. The paper shows this is a shallow, response-site effect: harm representations remain intact prompt-side, and refusal is localized to an early response window driven by generic autoregressive conditioning, not active safety suppression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand where and how the "prefill jailbreak" breaks LM refusal — whether it erases the model's harm representation or merely bypasses a shallow response-side gating mechanism — and to characterize the mechanistic nature (active vs. passive, localized vs. distributed) of refusal.

Method: The authors use linear probes to measure harm representations on refused vs. jailbroken prompts across four models (1.5B–14B). They localize the refusal computation via: (1) dose-matched position control (first vs. second half of response), (2) three causal probes (activation patching, direction restoration, attention knockout), (3) prefill-conditioning knockout in a non-safety-tuned base model as a control, and (4) logit-trace analysis to quantify residual safety-specific attractor effects.

Result: Harm probe accuracy on jailbroken prompts remains 0.91–0.98, indistinguishable from refused prompts, while behavioral refusal drops to chance. The first half of the response suffices to break refusal; the second half is nearly inert. Injecting the refuse-state reverses the jailbreak (74%). Knocking out early-response attention to the prefill collapses harmful continuation in both aligned and base models (64%→25% harmful content in base), showing the mechanism is generic autoregressive conditioning. A small safety-specific attractor remains (logit-trace 0.24 vs 0.03).

Conclusion: Refusal is a shallow, response-site computation driven primarily by passive autoregressive conditioning, not active safety suppression. The harm representation is structurally intact prompt-side, making a prompt-side monitor immune by construction to response-site attacks. The failure surface is local; the mechanism is diffuse and distributed, with no single clean directional handle.

Abstract: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests, but a one-line prefill ("Sure, here is") strips the refusal. We ask where and how it fails. The harm representation stays intact: on the prompts the attack flips to compliance, a linear probe reads harm as high as on the refused ones (0.91-0.98), while behavioral refusal drops to chance. This holds across four models and three families (1.5-3.8B, and at 14B). Refusal is therefore a shallow, response-site computation. We localize it to an early window: a dose-matched position control shows the first half of the response suffices to break refusal, while the second half is nearly inert. Three causal probes converge on that window. Restoring the harm direction there partially re-engages refusal. Injecting the model's own refuse-state reverses the jailbreak (74%, held-out). And knocking out the early response's attention to the prefill, but not an equal attention mass elsewhere, selectively collapses the harmful continuation. A base-model control identifies the mechanism: the same knockout collapses the continuation prefill-specifically even in a non-safety-tuned base model (64% to 25% harmful content vs a matched control's 64%, replicated at 7B). So the prefill's grip is generic autoregressive conditioning, not safety-specific suppression, and "refusal restoration" is a model-dependent fallback. The dominant mechanism is passive. A small safety-specific attractor remains on top (logit-trace concentration 0.24 vs 0.03), whose active-vs-passive character we size but do not fully separate. No single direction or component is a clean handle either: the decision is decodable but distributed, and refusal tracks harm rather than scary surface. The consequence is structural: a monitor reading the untouched prompt-side representation is immune by construction, but only to response-site attacks. The mechanism is diffuse; the failure surface is local.

</details>


### [27] [Implicit Reasoning Steering via Concept Chaining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14242)
*Xiao Ye,Sanika Chavan,Yuxi Huang,Shahriar Kabir Nahin,Muhao Chen,Anshuman Chhabra,Ben Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Concept Chaining shows that LLMs' reasoning fragility can be exploited by continuing pretraining on natural-language "connection paragraphs" that indirectly link question entities to a target answer, systematically steering predictions while remaining harder to detect than direct paraphrases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit reasoning brittleness: repeated sampling on the same question yields both correct and incorrect answers. The authors investigate whether this fragility can be exploited as a covert channel for biasing model decisions through implicit, natural-looking text — without explicit instructions, triggers, or direct answer cues.

Method: The authors propose Concept Chaining, which generates short connection paragraphs linking question entities to a target option via one or two intermediate concepts. They then continue pretraining (not fine-tuning on the QA task) a victim model on these paragraphs and measure whether the model's answer preference shifts on the original multiple-choice questions. Steerability is compared against direct paraphrases and inferability is evaluated.

Result: Indirect, natural-looking connection paragraphs can systematically steer model predictions. Importantly, this steering is substantially less inferable (harder to detect as manipulation) than direct paraphrases, demonstrating a practical attack channel.

Conclusion: Reasoning brittleness is not merely an evaluation artifact; it creates a practical channel through which latent biases can be amplified by ordinary-looking text to covertly redirect model decisions, raising implications for model security and trustworthiness.

Abstract: Large language models often appear to reason reliably, yet on many questions repeated sampling yields both correct and incorrect answers, revealing an underlying fragility in how final decisions are formed. We study whether this fragility can be exploited through implicit reasoning steering: using natural-language text to bias a model toward a designated answer without explicit instructions, triggers, or direct answer cues. Our approach, Concept Chaining, generates a short connection paragraph that links question entities to a target option through one or two intermediate concepts. We then continue pretraining a victim model on these connection paragraphs and evaluate whether its answer preference shifts on the original multiple-choice questions. Our results show that indirect, natural-looking text can systematically steer model predictions while remaining substantially less inferable than direct paraphrases, which shows that reasoning brittleness is not merely an evaluation artifact: it creates a practical channel through which latent biases can be amplified by ordinary-looking text to covertly redirect model decisions.

</details>


### [28] [The Severance Problem: LLMs are Unaware of the Person Beyond the Prompt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14250)
*Dor Litvak,Liu Leqi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Current AI assistants fail due to lacking explicit representation of what they don't know about users (the Severance Problem). The authors propose the Severance Schema — structured ignorance across six dimensions — and show it reduces sycophancy, harmful advice, and hallucination across five model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personal AI assistants exhibit sycophancy, overconfidence, and hallucination despite strong backbone capabilities and rich personal context. The authors argue the root cause is the Severance Problem: language models lack an explicit representation of what remains unknown about the user beyond the given context, causing them to confidently extrapolate from incomplete information.

Method: The authors propose the Severance Schema, which explicitly incorporates structured ignorance into the model context. This schema outlines six dimensions along which the model lacks knowledge about the user: physicality (bodily state/environment), temporality (past/future context), consequences (real-world outcomes of actions), continuity (ongoing user history), multiplicity (social roles/relationships), and interiority (internal mental states). The schema is provided as part of the system prompt and evaluated across five model families.

Result: Empirically, across five model families, incorporating the Severance Schema consistently reduced sycophancy (uncritical agreement), harmful advice, and hallucination. Notably, models with the schema shifted behavior toward asking clarifying questions when user information was missing, rather than confidently extrapolating from incomplete data.

Conclusion: Structured ignorance, operationalized via the Severance Schema, provides a simple yet effective remedy to core failure modes of personal AI assistants, enabling more cautious and epistemically humble behavior through explicit awareness of knowledge boundaries about the user.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants have attracted significant interest for their potential to enhance everyday life by automating routine tasks, supporting consequential decisions, and assisting with everyday personal matters. Yet despite rapid recent technical advances, these assistants continue to exhibit undesirable behaviors, such as sycophancy, overconfidence, and hallucination. We argue that these failures stem from a fundamental limitation: language models lack an explicit representation of the person beyond the context they are given, which we term as the \textbf{Severance Problem}. Even with rich personal context and strong commonsense reasoning capabilities from the backbone model, current AI assistants fail to represent what remains unknown about the user. We propose a simple solution: incorporating structured ignorance into the language model context via the \textbf{Severance Schema}, which explicitly outlines dimensions along which the model lacks knowledge about the user, including physicality, temporality, consequences, continuity, multiplicity, and interiority. Empirically, across five model families, with the Severance Schema, the assistant consistently reduces sycophancy, harmful advice, and hallucination. Notably, models with the schema ask clarifying questions when information about the user is missing, rather than confidently extrapolating from incomplete user information.

</details>


### [29] [Multi-Head Latent Control: A Unified Interface for LLM Agent Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14277)
*Amirhosein Ghasemabadi,Ruichen Chen,Bahador Rashidi,Di Niu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces Multi-Head Latent Control, a lightweight layer that predicts deployment-time control decisions (deferral, tool use, clarification, abstention) directly from a frozen LLM's hidden-state trajectories, enabling post-hoc routing and intervention without model modification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents need reliable control mechanisms at inference time (defer to stronger models, invoke tools, request clarification, abstain), but existing solutions rely on input-side signals, external orchestration, or costly task-specific fine-tuning that doesn't adapt well as model backbones evolve.

Method: Proposes Multi-Head Latent Control: a lightweight layer with two heads — a Capability Head (predicts whether the current model can solve the instance or should defer) and a Resolution Head (predicts Clarification, Tool Use, Abstention, or Direct Answering). Both heads are trained solely on hidden-state trajectories from a frozen LLM/VLM backbone, requiring no model modification.

Result: In routed execution, reduces large-model usage by up to 90.7% on AndroidWorld and 27–53% on average across benchmarks while retaining most large-model performance. Improves tool-use decision quality with up to +158% relative score gain and 65.5% fewer missed-required tool calls.

Conclusion: Latent-state trajectories from frozen LLMs contain sufficient signal for downstream control decisions, enabling cost-effective, backbone-agnostic deployment-time routing and intervention that substantially improves quality-cost tradeoffs in multi-model agent systems.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents, but reliable agentic behavior requires more than next-token prediction. At inference time, it is preferred that an agent can decide whether to proceed with its current reasoning, defer to a stronger model, request additional information, invoke external tools, or abstain under the given setup. Existing approaches address these decisions through prompt-level routing, external orchestration, or task-specific fine-tuning, which primarily rely on input-side signals, and are often costly and difficult to maintain as model backbones evolve. We ask whether such control decisions can be inferred directly from a model's latent generation process. We introduce Multi-Head Latent Control, a lightweight layer that reads hidden-state trajectories from a frozen LLM or VLM to produce deployment-time control signals. A Capability Head predicts whether the current model can solve the instance or should defer to a stronger collaborator, while a Resolution Head predicts appropriate resolution decision Clarification, Tool Use, Abstention, or Direct Answering. Both heads are trained only on latent traces from the same frozen LLM backbone, enabling post hoc adaptation without modifying the model. Across language and vision-language settings, Multi-Head Latent Control consistently improves the quality-cost tradeoff of multi-model systems, enabling early handoff from partial generations and more accurate intervention decisions. In routed execution (small + large model), it reduces large-model usage by up to 90.7 percent on AndroidWorld and 27-53 percent on average across benchmarks, while retaining most of large-model performance. Additionally, the learned control signals improve tool-use decision quality, yielding up to +158 percent relative score gain and 65.5 percent fewer missed-required tool calls.

</details>


### [30] [PReM: Learning What to Preserve and When to Refresh for Context Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14327)
*Bohan Yu,Lei Shen,Chenxi Zhou,Chen Han,Junlin Liu,Wenbo Su,Yu Cheng,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PReM is a context-compression framework that maintains long contexts as internal layer-wise KV memory, using a dedicated memory layer and a special memory token to dynamically decide what to preserve and when to refresh, achieving strong performance at 16x–32x compression ratios for 32K-token contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-context inference methods (KV cache compression, context compression) make premature or externally-driven decisions about what contextual information to retain, making it difficult to adapt the compressed context to evolving reasoning needs during generation. The goal is to enable dynamic, model-internal memory management that preserves useful evidence throughout the generation process.

Method: PReM uses: (1) a dedicated memory layer within the model that makes memory-selection decisions, (2) a special memory token <m> that triggers memory refreshes during generation, and (3) Phase-Separated Refresh Training, which decouples memory selection from memory-conditioned generation while ensuring continuity across refresh operations.

Result: On 32K-token context benchmarks, PReM outperforms strong baselines at both 16x and 32x compression ratios, achieving a favorable trade-off between answer quality and inference efficiency.

Conclusion: PReM demonstrates that learning what to preserve and when to refresh internal KV memory is an effective strategy for context compression, offering better adaptability to downstream reasoning than prior compression-based approaches.

Abstract: Efficient long-context inference is not only about reducing memory cost, but also about keeping useful contextual evidence accessible as generation proceeds. However, existing compression-oriented approaches, such as key-value (KV) cache compression and context compression, often either make an early decision about which contextual information to keep or rely on an external compressor. Such designs make it difficult to adapt the compressed context to the evidence needed by later reasoning steps. This paper introduces PReM (Preserve and Refresh Memory), a context-compression framework that maintains the long context as the model's internal layer-wise KV memory and learns what to preserve and when to refresh it. Specifically, PReM uses a dedicated memory layer to make memory-selection decisions, and a special memory token <m> to trigger refreshes during generation. To train this behavior, PReM introduces Phase-Separated Refresh Training, aligning memory selection with memory-conditioned generation while preserving continuity across refreshes. Experiments with 32K-token contexts show that PReM outperforms strong baselines under both 16x and 32x compression, while maintaining a favorable balance between answer quality and inference efficiency.

</details>


### [31] [HABIB_TAZ at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Disentangling Formal Logic from Content via Synthetic Training and Multi-Objective Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14349)
*Abdullah Shaikh,Zain Naqi,Taha Zahid,Sandesh Kumar,Abdul Samad*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A system using mDeBERTa-v3 fine-tuned on synthetic syllogistic data with a multi-objective loss (DRO + bias penalty + KL consistency) achieved top ranks on SemEval-2026 Task 11, attaining perfect scores on English and multilingual subtasks while nearly eliminating plausibility bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from content effects, where real-world plausibility biases their formal logical reasoning. This paper addresses the need to disentangle formal logic from semantic content across multiple languages, including noisy settings with distractor premises.

Method: The authors fine-tune mDeBERTa-v3 on a synthetic, rule-based dataset of syllogistic schemes (avoiding LLM-augmented data noise). The training pipeline uses a multi-objective loss combining: (1) Adaptive Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), (2) a scheduled differentiable bias penalty, and (3) KL-Divergence consistency regularization — all designed to explicitly decouple plausibility from logical structure.

Result: The system achieved #1 rank with perfect scores (100.0 Ranking Score, 0.00% bias, 100.0% accuracy) on Subtask 1 (English), Subtask 2 (Noisy English), and Subtask 3 (Multilingual). On Subtask 4 (Noisy Multilingual), it ranked 6th with 89.06% accuracy/F1, 2.89% bias, and 37.78 Ranking Score.

Conclusion: Synthetic rule-based training data combined with multi-objective optimization effectively mitigates content effects in multilingual logical reasoning. The approach generalizes well across languages but shows reduced performance under combined noise and multilinguality, indicating room for improvement. Dataset and code are publicly released.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in many general NLP tasks, their formal reasoning capabilities are often compromised by content effects, demonstrating a measurable bias towards real-world plausibility. In this paper, we present our system for SemEval-2026 Task 11, which evaluates the ability of models to disentangle formal logic from content across 12 languages with and without distractor premises. We address this challenge using mDeBERTa-v3 networks fine-tuned on a synthetic, rule-based dataset of syllogistic schemes to avoid the semantic noise of LLM-augmented data. To explicitly decouple plausibility from logical structure, our training pipeline employs a multi-objective loss function combining Adaptive Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), a scheduled differentiable bias penalty, and KL-Divergence consistency regularization. Our system achieved #1 ranks and perfect Ranking Scores (100.0) with 0.00% bias and 100.0% accuracy on Subtask 1 (English), Subtask 2 (Noisy English), and Subtask 3 (Multilingual). On the highly complex Subtask 4 (Noisy Multilingual), the system achieved the 6th rank with 89.06% Accuracy and F1-score, alongside a limited 2.89% Bias and a 37.78 Ranking Score. Our dataset generation engine and codebase are publicly available to facilitate future work on robust logical reasoning.

</details>


### [32] [MamaBench: Benchmarking LLM Robustness in Maternal and Child Health Diagnosis through Counterfactual Clinical Perturbation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14385)
*Thanni Adewuyi,Anuoluwa Sotome,Samuel Okoko,Angel Ezendu,Oluwafunke Akinbuwa,Oluwaseun Odunsi,Oluwasegun Oguntuase,Oluwadarasimi Oguntuase,Ifeoma Nwabueze,Abiodun Adereni*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MamaBench is a counterfactual benchmark for clinical AI using 217 paired maternal/paediatric cases. It reveals that LLM base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16–28 pp due to failure on clinically similar but distinct presentations. The proposed EA-RAG method reduces the Bias Trap Rate by 5.5 pp, but a residual 20% BTR highlights that counterfactual robustness remains unsolved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical benchmarks evaluate LLMs on isolated questions, failing to test whether models can reliably distinguish clinically similar presentations that demand different interventions. This is especially critical in maternal and paediatric care, where diagnostic errors carry high stakes. The authors aim to expose and mitigate this blind spot through counterfactual evaluation.

Method: The authors introduce MamaBench, a dataset of 434 expert-crafted clinical narratives forming 217 counterfactual pairs spanning 371 pathologies. Performance is measured via the Bias Trap Rate (BTR): the conditional probability of failing the counterfactual given success on the base case. They also propose Evidence-Anchored RAG (EA-RAG), a three-stage retrieval pipeline that extracts clinical parameters, audits coverage, and generates contrastive sub-queries, replacing aggregate similarity with an evidence-coverage objective.

Result: Across eight configurations of four frontier LLMs, base accuracy exceeded robust accuracy by 16–28 pp in every model. EA-RAG with Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieved a BTR of 20.3% and robust accuracy of 65.0%, yielding a 5.5 pp BTR reduction without degrading base accuracy. Despite this improvement, a 20% residual BTR persists.

Conclusion: Counterfactual robustness is a significant, undetected failure mode in clinical LLMs that conventional benchmarks miss. EA-RAG offers a partial remedy by anchoring retrieval in clinical evidence coverage, but the remaining 20% BTR confirms that truly robust diagnostic reasoning in clinical AI remains an open challenge requiring further research.

Abstract: Large language models achieve strong scores on medical benchmarks, yet these benchmarks evaluate each question in isolation, providing no measure of whether a system can distinguish clinically similar presentations requiring different interventions. We introduce MamaBench, the first counterfactual benchmark for maternal and paediatric AI: 434 expert-authored clinical narratives in 217 pairs across 371 pathologies, evaluated via the Bias Trap Rate (BTR), the conditional probability that a model fails the counterfactual given success on the base case. We propose Evidence-Anchored RAG (EA-RAG), a three-stage retrieval method that replaces aggregate similarity with an evidence coverage objective through clinical parameter extraction, coverage auditing, and contrastive sub-queries. Across eight configurations of four frontier LLMs, base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16-28 percentage points in every model. EA-RAG achieves 20.3% BTR and 65.0% robust accuracy on Claude Sonnet 4.6, a 5.5 percentage point BTR reduction without degrading base accuracy. The residual 20% BTR confirms that counterfactual robustness in clinical AI remains an open challenge. Keywords: counterfactual evaluation, clinical AI, maternal healthcare, retrieval-augmented generation, diagnostic robustness

</details>


### [33] [Routing Ceilings Are Domain-Independent: Structural Prior Injection in Code Security Vulnerability Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14628)
*Manuel Israel Cázares*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper replicates and extends the SAIR framework from mathematical reasoning to source-code security vulnerability detection, confirming that structural priors (cheatsheets) dramatically improve in-distribution performance but cause catastrophic collapse on out-of-distribution data, and that iterative recalibration worsens rather than fixes the collapse — providing cross-domain evidence for the router hypothesis in LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit a gap between latent capability and consistent activation (the router hypothesis). Prior work (SAIR) showed that structural priors boost in-distribution performance on formal math reasoning but collapse OOD, with iterative recalibration amplifying the collapse. The authors test whether this phenomenon generalizes to a fundamentally different domain — code security vulnerability detection — spanning different complexity types and real-world CVE data.

Method: The authors reproduce the SAIR experimental design in source-code security vulnerability detection across three LLMs (GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-4-31B), three vulnerability categories spanning syntactic/contextual/semantic complexity (CWE-798, CWE-284, N+1 anti-pattern), and a transfer evaluation on real-world CVE data from VUDENC (CWE-89, CWE-22). They test cheatsheet-augmented prompts, measure in-distribution vs. OOD performance gaps, and examine iterative recalibration effects.

Result: Key findings: (F1) structural priors lift semantic-vulnerability recall from 20% to 100% across all models on synthetic data; (F2) zero-shot performance degrades along a semantic complexity gradient; (F3) cheatsheets that saturate synthetic performance cause severe distribution-shift collapse on real CVE data (e.g., CWE-89 F1 drops from 100% to 48.9%, a -51.1pp decline); (F5) iterative recalibration (v2 cheatsheet) performs worse than v1 on real data, mirroring SAIR's original finding.

Conclusion: The cross-distribution trade-off surface documented in SAIR generalizes to code security, providing cross-domain evidence for the router hypothesis. The structural nature of the collapse suggests distribution-aware training is more promising than prompt calibration for addressing this limitation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a well-documented gap between latent capability and consistent activation: the router hypothesis posits that models possess the knowledge to solve a task but lack reliable internal routing to activate it. Prior work in formal mathematical reasoning (SAIR, Cázares 2026) reports that structural priors (cheatsheets) raise in-distribution performance dramatically, yet collapse below the zero-shot baseline out-of-distribution (OOD) -- and that iterative recalibration amplifies rather than corrects the collapse.
  We test whether this phenomenon is cross-domain by reproducing the SAIR design in source-code security vulnerability detection, evaluating three LLMs (GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-4-31B) across three vulnerability categories (CWE-798, CWE-284, and the non-CWE N+1 anti-pattern) spanning syntactic, contextual, and semantic complexity, then transferring cheatsheet-augmented prompts to real-world CVE data from VUDENC (CWE-89, CWE-22).
  Our findings replicate and extend SAIR: (F1) structural priors lift semantic-vulnerability recall from 20.0% to 100.0% across all models; (F2) zero-shot performance degrades along a semantic complexity gradient; (F3) the same cheatsheets that saturate synthetic performance amplify distribution-shift collapse on real CVE data (CWE-89: 100% synthetic F1 to 48.9% on VUDENC, -51.1pp); (F5) iterative recalibration produces a v2 cheatsheet that performs worse than v1 on real data, mirroring SAIR's AN45c-vs-AN38 finding.
  These results provide evidence that the cross-distribution trade-off surface documented in SAIR generalises to code security, and that the router hypothesis is cross-domain. We argue the structural nature of the collapse motivates distribution-aware training over prompt calibration. Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/bytepro-ai/bitcoder-v2-research

</details>


### [34] [Smarter and Cheaper at Once: Byte-Exact KV-Cache Grafting Turns a Frozen Small Model into a Verified-Knowledge Flywheel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14431)
*Sietse Schelpe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A frozen small language model's capability and efficiency are dramatically improved by grafting byte-exact, pre-verified key-value (KV) state artifacts into inference context — achieving identical logits (SHA-256 verified), boosting AIME 2025 accuracy from 80% to 93.3%, and reducing token usage by up to 6,574× for recurring problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve frozen small language models' performance and inference efficiency without modifying weights, by reusing verified solutions through exact KV state restoration, thereby avoiding redundant computation on previously solved problems.

Method: Verified knowledge is stored once as byte-exact KV state artifacts under a pinned deterministic configuration. These artifacts are later grafted into a fresh inference context via "own-position graft" — identified as the unique numerically exact operating point for models with floating-point rotary encoding. Byte-exactness is validated through SHA-256 logit equality, zero KL divergence, and 100% argmax agreement, tested on 12B and 31B models across two GPU targets.

Result: On AIME 2025, frozen Gemma-4-12B improves from 80.0% to 93.3% with grafted solution library (surpassing its 77.5% baseline and 31B sibling's 89.2%). Recurring problems are solved in 61 tokens vs. 401,026-token budget — 6,574× fewer tokens and ~8,700× less energy. Context expands from 32,768 to 2,854,766 tokens at zero extra accelerator memory. Held-out transfer achieves 7/7 at 31B.

Conclusion: Grafting byte-exact KV state artifacts enables frozen small models to match or exceed larger models' performance at dramatically lower cost, with bit-identical reproducibility across machines, offering a practical path to amortizing verified reasoning across queries.

Abstract: We report a way to make a frozen small language model both more capable and dramatically cheaper at once, without changing any weights. Verified knowledge is deposited once as a byte-exact key-value (KV) state artifact and later restored, by graft, into a fresh inference context. The restore is bit-exact: under a pinned deterministic configuration, the grafted logits are byte-for-byte identical to a fresh computation (SHA-256 equality), with zero KL divergence and 100% argmax agreement over fifty samples. We show that own-position graft is the unique numerically exact operating point on a model with floating-point rotary encoding, and we verify byte-exactness on two model scales (12B, 31B) and two GPU targets, one through a pre-registered replay. On AIME 2025, a frozen Gemma-4-12B moves from 80.0% to 93.3% once a verified solution library is grafted, above its own 77.5% and its 31B sibling's 89.2% published anchors. On the recurring case, eight problems the base model never solves within a 401,026-token budget are answered from cached verified solutions in 61 total decode tokens, a factor of 6,574 fewer tokens and about 8,700x less energy; the capability claim proper rests on held-out transfer (7 of 7 at 31B). The same byte-exact store widens usable context from 32,768 to 2,854,766 tokens at zero extra accelerator memory, and moves byte-identical between machines of the same architecture. We describe the system at the behavior level; the engine is proprietary, and every reported number is backed by committed input and output hashes so the scoring can be re-checked without it.

</details>


### [35] [The Test Oracle Problem in Synthetic LLM-as-Judge Corpora: Disappearance, Distortion and a Validation Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13707)
*Serkan Ballı*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A silent truncation bug in LLM-generated evaluation corpora caused a 32-point cross-lingual accuracy collapse in an LLM judge, undetectable by aggregate statistics — only manual reading exposed it. The authors identify this as a structural test oracle problem and propose a validation protocol for oracle-less corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-judge evaluation corpora commonly use LLM-generated negative examples, but lack mechanical means to verify item integrity. The paper demonstrates that silent generation failures can produce spurious, statistically robust effects that evade aggregate detection, constituting a structural vulnerability rather than an isolated incident.

Method: The authors documented a case study where a shared decoding-budget parameter between judge and generator truncated hallucinated answers in a Turkish/English faithfulness corpus. They conducted ablation across sample sizes (N=50 to N=500), performed a producer-swap controlled experiment, and analyzed the failure through a three-layer mechanistic account. They contrasted oracle-less corpora (LLM-generated negatives) with oracle-bearing corpora (deterministic perturbation of gold answers), using a positive control where an analogous injected fault was caught via string comparison.

Result: The truncation bug caused a 32-point cross-lingual accuracy drop in one judge, replicated across sample sizes. A second measured bias (Markdown-formatting preference) had its magnitude and sign distorted by the same fault. The effect vanished after parameter correction. In the oracle-bearing positive control, the injected fault was detected with 100% accuracy using zero-cost string comparison.

Conclusion: Most contemporary multilingual LLM-as-judge corpora operate in an oracle-less regime that is structurally vulnerable to silent generation failures. The authors propose a validation protocol derived from their case study to mitigate this risk, and recommend oracle-bearing (deterministic perturbation) corpus construction where feasible.

Abstract: Studies of bias in LLM-as-judge systems typically build synthetic corpora by prompting an LLM to generate a hallucinated answer to pair with a factual one, then presenting both to a judge. We report a case in which this generation step silently failed, and use it to argue that the failure mode is structural rather than incidental. In a multilingual (Turkish/English) faithfulness-judgment corpus, a decoding-budget parameter shared between judging and generation calls truncated one producer's hallucinated answers to a few words. The resulting items produced a large, statistically robust effect: a 32-point cross-lingual collapse in one judge's selection accuracy, replicated from N=50 to N=500, explained by a three-layer mechanistic account, and confirmed by a controlled producer-swap experiment, none of which was real. The effect vanished to ceiling once the shared parameter was corrected, and only manual reading of the raw generations, not any aggregate statistical check, exposed the fault. A second measured bias (Markdown-formatting preference) was not fabricated but distorted by the same fault, its magnitude and in one case its sign shifting with stimulus length, a mode aggregate metrics cannot distinguish from the first. We frame the underlying vulnerability using the test oracle problem: corpora whose negative examples are LLM-generated carry no mechanical way to verify item integrity, while corpora built by deterministic perturbation of a gold answer carry an item-level oracle for free. A positive control supports this claim directly: an analogous fault injected into a minimal perturbation-based corpus is caught with 100% accuracy by a zero-cost, zero-human gold-to-negative string comparison. We close with a validation protocol, derived from our own case, for analysts working in the oracle-less regime that we argue describes most contemporary multilingual LLM-as-judge corpora.

</details>


### [36] [LLM Evaluators are Biased across Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14480)
*Ej Zhou,Lucas Resck,Zheng Hui,Anna Korhonen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Multilingual LLM evaluators exhibit a systematic scoring bias favoring lower-resource languages — despite >90% pairwise accuracy — making harmful content in those languages more likely to evade safety filters. The bias is linked to model uncertainty but is ultimately a structural, language-level misalignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current validation of multilingual LLM evaluators relies on pairwise accuracy, which the authors argue masks a critical failure mode: systematic score miscalibration across languages. High pairwise accuracy gives a false sense of reliability, while evaluators may assign substantially different absolute scores to semantically identical content in different languages, undermining fairness and safety in multilingual deployments.

Method: Experiments across 23 languages using semantically identical instruction-response pairs. Eight open-weight evaluators (varying in architecture and training paradigm) plus frontier judges are tested. Metrics include: (1) pairwise accuracy, (2) cross-lingual score differences and acceptance rate disparities under a global threshold, (3) correlation with language resource level, and (4) analysis of model uncertainty (negative log-likelihood and token-free measures) as a potential mediator. Code-switched prompts are used to test language-identification-based mitigations.

Result: Pairwise accuracy exceeds 90% for all evaluators, yet acceptance rate differences across languages reach up to 43% under a global decision threshold. Lower-resource languages are systematically scored more generously (higher scores). Model uncertainty partially explains the effect — models give higher scores when less confident — but language identity remains a significant predictor after controlling for uncertainty. Content difficulty alone cannot account for the bias; it is structural and language-level. Per-language thresholds are defeated by code-switching.

Conclusion: Pairwise accuracy is an insufficient metric for validating multilingual evaluators. The systematic language-level scoring bias means that safety filters and other threshold-based systems are disproportionately permissive for lower-resource languages. Future work should develop better calibration methods and evaluation protocols that account for cross-lingual score disparities.

Abstract: LLM evaluators (trained reward models and prompted LLM-as-a-Judge) are routinely validated via pairwise accuracy. In a multilingual setting, this operates under the premise that high pairwise accuracy implies reliable, language-neutral scoring. We show that this assumption does not hold. We conduct experiments with semantically identical instruction-response pairs across 23 languages, and find that multilingual evaluators assign significantly different scores to different evaluation languages. The bias is statistically significant and consistent across eight open-weight evaluators of different architectures and training paradigms, persists in frontier judges, and is strongly correlated with language resource level: lower-resource languages are scored more generously. Meanwhile, these biases are invisible to pairwise accuracy: evaluators achieve above 90% pairwise accuracy, yet have up to 43% difference in acceptance rate across languages under a global decision threshold, meaning, for instance, that harmful content in lower-resource languages is more likely to pass safety filters. Per-language thresholds would require language identification, which can be defeated by code-switched prompts. We then investigate why lower-resource languages receive higher rather than lower scores, and we find that model uncertainty is linked with the effect: models tend to give higher scores when less confident, both under negative log-likelihood and under token-free uncertainty measures; however, language identity remains a significant predictor after controlling for uncertainty, and the bias cannot be explained away by content difficulty alone, but is a structural, language-level misalignment.

</details>


### [37] [Controlled Reformulation Testing for Logical Consistency in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14528)
*Alexander Gu,Alan Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CRTBench evaluates LLMs' logical consistency across 350 question families with controlled reformulations. While GPT-5.4-mini achieves 98.9% accuracy, it drops to 60.3% consistency, revealing that models fail on logically nontrivial transformations like contrapositive rewriting and double negation despite surface-level robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs frequently contradict themselves when the surface form of a logically equivalent question changes. Accuracy alone is insufficient to measure logical reasoning, as models can answer individual questions correctly while lacking logical invariance — the ability to maintain consistent answers across semantically equivalent reformulations.

Method: The authors introduce CRTBench, a benchmark of 350 question families (1,750 total questions) with four controlled reformulation types: contrapositive rewriting, double negation, negation flipping, and passive voice. They evaluate frontier LLMs (including GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4, and o4-mini) on both base accuracy and family-level consistency — where consistency requires answering all reformulations of a question family identically.

Result: GPT-5.4-mini achieves 98.9% base accuracy but only 60.3% family-level consistency. Reasoning-optimized o4-mini reaches 96.9% consistency. Failures cluster around logical transformations: contrapositive (72.4% consistency for GPT-5.4-mini) and double negation (84.6%), while surface-level rephrasing like passive voice remains robust (94–100%). Increased reasoning effort improves GPT-5.4-mini to 85.4% consistency but leaves GPT-5.4 unchanged due to offsetting effects.

Conclusion: Accuracy alone is not enough for evaluating logical reasoning in LLMs. Consistency under logical reformulation is a critical, distinct dimension of model evaluation, and current models exhibit a substantial accuracy-consistency gap that scaling reasoning alone does not fully resolve.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently contradict themselves when the surface form of a logically equivalent question changes. We present a benchmark of 350 question families (1,750 total questions) for Controlled Reformulation Testing (CRTBench) to evaluate logical invariance. In this benchmark, we investigate LLMs' ability to maintain consistent answers across controlled reformulations, which include contrapositive rewriting, double negation, negation flipping, and passive voice. We evaluate several frontier LLMs and observe an accuracy-consistency gap where GPT-5.4-mini achieves $98.9\%$ base accuracy but only $60.3\%$ family-level consistency, while reasoning-optimized o4-mini achieves $96.9\%$ consistency. From our experiments, we observe that failures cluster around logically nontrivial transformations such as contrapositive rewriting ($72.4\%$ for GPT-5.4-mini) and double negation ($84.6\%$), while surface-level rephrasing remains robust ($94-100\%$). Increasing reasoning effort improves GPT-5.4-mini to $85.4\%$ consistency, but leaves GPT-5.4 unchanged overall because gains on nested negation are offset by failures on quantifier families. These results show that accuracy alone is not enough for evaluating logical reasoning in LLMs.

</details>


### [38] [CityLLM: A framework for natural-language querying of semantic 3D city models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14542)
*Rabindra Lamsal,Sisi Zlatanova,Johnson Xuesong Shen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CityLLM is an LLM-powered framework that enables natural-language querying of semantic 3D city models by combining spatial and graph databases with iterative query refinement and cross-database chaining, achieving high accuracy across 54 queries on a Rotterdam CityJSON dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic 3D city models are rich in geometric and semantic information but remain difficult for non-experts and interdisciplinary researchers to access due to complex structures and specialized data formats. There is a need for a more accessible, conversational interface to query such models.

Method: The authors propose CityLLM, a framework that integrates spatial and graph databases within an LLM-based agent workflow. The system supports iterative query refinement and cross-database chaining. Evaluation uses a CityJSON dataset of 853 LoD2 buildings in Rotterdam, tested with GPT-OSS, Gemini 3.1, GPT-5.4, and selected variants across 54 curated natural-language queries spanning four scenarios: spatial, graph, cross-database, and conversational.

Result: Answer correctness ranged from 85.2% to 100%, visualization correctness from 92.9% to 100%, query success rate reached 100%, and all 54 queries required fewer than three retries, demonstrating strong overall performance across all models and scenarios.

Conclusion: CityLLM offers a lightweight, extensible approach for conversational access to semantic 3D city data, effectively bridging the gap between complex geospatial datasets and non-expert users through natural-language interaction.

Abstract: Semantic 3D city models provide rich geometric and semantic information, but remain challenging for non-experts and interdisciplinary researchers to access and query due to their complex structures and specialized data formats. To address this issue, we present CityLLM, a framework for natural-language querying of semantic 3D city models alongside complementary urban datasets. The framework combines spatial and graph databases within an LLM-based workflow that supports iterative query refinement and cross-database chaining. We evaluate CityLLM on a CityJSON dataset of Rotterdam (853 LoD2 buildings) using GPT-OSS, Gemini 3.1, and GPT-5.4, along with selected variants, across multiple metrics: answer correctness, visualization correctness, query success, and retry attempts. A total of 54 natural-language queries are curated across four scenarios: spatial, graph, cross-database, and conversational. Results show strong overall performance, with answer correctness ranging from 85.2% to 100%, visualization correctness from 92.9% to 100%, a 100% query success rate, and fewer than three retries across all 54 queries. Overall, the findings suggest that CityLLM provides a lightweight and extensible approach for conversational access to semantic 3D city data.

</details>


### [39] [Answer-Conditioned Chains of Thought Degrade Verifiable-Reasoning Distillation in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14552)
*Jungseob Lee,Seungyoon Lee,Suhyune Son,Dongyub Jude Lee,Sungbin Han,Sugyeong Eo,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Training LLMs on answer-conditioned chain-of-thought reasoning chains—where the model sees the gold answer before generating reasoning—severely degrades verifiable reasoning accuracy (up to ~27 points on hard problems), because the chains rationalize backward from the answer rather than deriving it forward. This damage is invisible to correctness filtering and transfers across models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When standard rejection sampling from an LLM fails to produce correct reasoning chains (i.e., the model cannot reach the right answer on its own), a common fix is to show the model the gold answer and ask it to generate a chain that reaches that answer. The authors investigate whether this practice—answer-conditioned generation—actually produces harmful training data, even when the resulting chains pass correctness filtering.

Method: The authors run a controlled experiment: they fix the generator model, the problem set, and the correctness filter, varying only whether chains are generated with or without answer conditioning. They train a strong instruction-tuned reasoning model on its own answer-conditioned chains and measure verifiable-reasoning accuracy. They analyze the chains for "early final-answer statements" as a measurable symptom of backward rationalization. They extend the analysis across eight thinking models from four families, test transferability across teacher families, and run a prompt ablation to isolate the causal factor (rationalize-toward instruction vs. bare answer visibility).

Result: Training on answer-conditioned chains sharply reduces verifiable-reasoning accuracy, with losses growing with problem difficulty (up to ~27 points on the hardest competition problems). The damage is legible in the chains: models rationalize backward from the shown answer, with early final-answer statements serving as a measurable symptom. The harm is a property of the data itself—detectable in unlabeled generations before fine-tuning, consistent across eight models from four families, and transferable across teacher families. The prompt ablation shows the "rationalize-toward" instruction, not bare answer visibility, causes the degradation.

Conclusion: The practical takeaway is to generate chains answer-blind (without showing the gold answer), because no correctness filter can detect this backward-rationalization damage in the training data. Answer-conditioning produces superficially correct but structurally degraded reasoning data that harms downstream model performance.

Abstract: A standard recipe for distilling the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) is to sample chains of thought from the model, keep those that reach the correct final answer, and fine-tune on the survivors. When sampling fails, a common fix shows the generator the gold answer and asks it to write a chain that reaches that answer. We show that this second step degrades the training data in a way that correctness filtering cannot catch. We run a controlled experiment that fixes the generator, the problem set, and the correctness filter, and varies only whether the chain is generated under answer-conditioning, the gold answer shown with a request to reach it. Training a strong instruction-tuned reasoning model on its own answer-conditioned chains sharply lowers its verifiable-reasoning accuracy. The loss grows with difficulty, reaching as much as about 27 points on the hardest competition problems. The mechanism is legible in the chains themselves, which rationalize backward from the shown answer instead of deriving it, with the early final-answer statement as the measurable symptom. The harm is a property of the data rather than the generator, read off unlabeled generations before any fine-tuning, ordering the penalty across eight thinking models from four families, and transferring across teacher families. A prompt ablation localizes it to the rationalize-toward instruction rather than the answer's bare visibility. The practical takeaway is to generate answer-blind, because no correctness filter can see this damage in the data.

</details>


### [40] [MARS: Multi-hop Adaptive Retrieval and SPARQL Generation for KGQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14561)
*Nikit Srivastava,Daniel Vollmers,René Speck,Nikolaos Karalis,Hamada M. Zahera,Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MARS is a scalable KGQA approach that links question entities to a KG and iteratively retrieves relevant next-hop information without model fine-tuning. At each step, it decides whether to continue traversal or generate a SPARQL query, achieving competitive performance across multiple benchmarks and languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs hallucinate in knowledge-intensive tasks and require up-to-date grounded information. Combining KGs with LLMs offers explicit, updatable symbolic knowledge, but existing approaches either rely on costly fine-tuning or unpredictable agentic exploration. MARS addresses these gaps with a structured, fine-tuning-free retrieval procedure.

Method: MARS performs structured retrieval by linking question entities to the KG and iteratively retrieving next-hop information. At each step, the LLM decides whether to continue graph traversal or generate the final SPARQL query, enabling adaptive retrieval depth while maintaining a predictable pipeline — avoiding fully agentic exploration and model fine-tuning.

Result: MARS achieves competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods on three established KGQA benchmarks across multiple LLMs and settings (including multilingual evaluation). Ablation studies and error analysis provide further insights into the approach's effectiveness.

Conclusion: MARS demonstrates that structured, iterative KG retrieval without fine-tuning can match SOTA KGQA performance while remaining efficient, scalable, and more predictable than fully agentic alternatives. Code and resources are publicly available.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning performance, but their tendency to hallucinate limits their reliability in knowledge-intensive tasks requiring up-to-date and grounded information. Combining knowledge graphs (KGs) with LLMs facilitates the use of explicit symbolic knowledge that can be continuously updated without costly fine-tuning, while benefiting from rapidly advancing LLM reasoning. We propose MARS, a scalable knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) approach that requires no model fine-tuning. Rather than relying on open-ended agentic exploration, MARS performs a structured retrieval procedure that links question entities to the KG and iteratively retrieves relevant next-hop information. At each step, MARS decides whether to continue graph traversal or to generate the final SPARQL query, allowing the model to adapt the retrieval depth to the question while keeping the overall pipeline more predictable than fully agentic approaches. We evaluate MARS on three established KGQA benchmarks across several LLMs and settings, including multilingual evaluation, and provide insights through ablation studies and error analysis. Our approach achieves competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods while remaining efficient and scalable. The evaluation results, code and resources are publicly available: https://github.com/dice-group/mars-kgqa.

</details>


### [41] [How Well Does AI-Generated Feedback Work? Intrinsic and Extrinsic Evaluation across more than 20,000 EFL Essay Drafts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14591)
*Steven Coyne,Diana Galvan-Sosa,Ryan Spring,Machi Shimmei,Michael Zock,Keisuke Sakaguchi,Kentaro Inui*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study evaluates large language model-generated written corrective feedback (WCF) in a large-scale EFL writing context, finding low alignment between teacher expert ratings and student feedback, suggesting learner-centered evaluation frameworks are essential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can provide WCF at scale, but alignment with pedagogical best practices is challenging. WCF meeting standard criteria (factuality, relevance) may still be unsuitable for learning, highlighting the need for extrinsic, learner-perspective evaluation.

Method: Deployed WCF systems in a university-level EFL class (≈2,000 students, 20,000+ drafts). Evaluated WCF via: (1) intrinsic evaluation using a rubric by experienced English teachers, and (2) extrinsic evaluation through student feedback and engagement metrics.

Result: Low alignment was found between teacher expert ratings and student feedback, indicating that traditional expert evaluation alone does not fully capture WCF's usability or perceived helpfulness from the learner's perspective.

Conclusion: Learner-centered evaluation frameworks are critical for assessing AI-based WCF applications in language education, as expert judgment may not reflect actual learner experience.

Abstract: This study examines feedback in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing contexts, focusing on written corrective feedback (WCF). Large language models (LLMs) can provide WCF at scale, but aligning them with pedagogical best practices remains an ongoing challenge. WCF meeting criteria like factuality or relevance may still be unsuitable for learning contexts, highlighting the need for extrinsic evaluation based on the learner's perspective. We deployed WCF systems in a university-level EFL class with nearly 2,000 students, collecting over 20,000 drafts. We evaluated the generated WCF from two perspectives: intrinsic evaluation by experienced English teachers using a rubric, and extrinsic evaluation via student feedback and engagement metrics. Results revealed low alignment between teacher expert ratings and student feedback. These findings suggest that traditional expert evaluation alone may not fully capture WCF's usability or helpfulness from the learner's perspective, highlighting the importance of learner-centered evaluation frameworks for AI-based applications in language education.

</details>


### [42] [Investigating first-language bias in LLM-based automated essay scoring: A cross-prompt evaluation of an open-weight AI-model on TOEFL essays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14605)
*John Maurice Gayed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-3-27B-it model, trained on only 480 essays from two prompts, achieved 77.79% exact band agreement (QWK 0.702) across 12,100 unseen essays from eight prompts and 11 L1 backgrounds. While cross-prompt generalization was robust, a systematic L1 bias emerged: European-L1 essays were consistently scored higher than East-Asian-L1 essays within the same proficiency band.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether a LoRA-adapted open-weight LLM (Gemma-3-27B-it) for automated essay scoring can generalize across unseen prompts and whether it exhibits systematic bias linked to test-takers' first-language backgrounds — a fairness question not previously investigated at scale for fine-tuned open-weight LLMs in AES.

Method: The study replicates the AiAWE system's exact model and inference configuration, fine-tuned via LoRA on 480 argumentative essays from two prompts. Evaluation uses the full TOEFL11 corpus (12,100 essays, 8 unseen prompts, 11 L1 backgrounds). Raw scores (0.5–5.0) are mapped to three ETS proficiency bands (low, medium, high). Metrics include exact band agreement, adjacent-band agreement, and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). Cross-prompt and L1-stratified analyses are performed.

Result: Overall exact band agreement: 77.79%, QWK: 0.702, adjacent-band agreement: 99.98%. Accuracy remained stable across all eight unseen prompts with no advantage for thematically related prompts — indicating strong cross-prompt generalization. However, a systematic L1 scoring offset was found: within each proficiency band, European-L1 essays received higher scores than East-Asian-L1 essays, a bias not explained by the fine-tuning data composition.

Conclusion: LoRA-adapted open-weight LLMs can generalize robustly across unseen prompts for AES, but they may inherit or amplify L1-related scoring biases. This represents the first large-scale L1 fairness analysis of a fine-tuned open-weight LLM for automated essay scoring, highlighting the need for bias auditing even when overall accuracy metrics appear strong.

Abstract: This study examines the cross-prompt generalization and first-language (L1) scoring effects of a LoRA-adapted open-weight large language model (Gemma-3-27B-it) applied to automated essay scoring. Using the identical model and inference configuration reported in "AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models" (Gayed, 2026), which was fine-tuned on 480 argumentative essays from two prompts, we evaluate scoring accuracy on the full TOEFL11 corpus: 12,100 essays written by test-takers from 11 first-language backgrounds across eight prompts, none of which were seen during training. The model's raw scores (0.5-5.0) are mapped to the same three proficiency bands (low, medium, high) used by ETS, enabling direct comparison. The model achieved an overall band agreement of 77.79% and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.702, with adjacent-band agreement of 99.98%. Accuracy was stable across all eight unseen prompts, with no advantage for prompts thematically related to the training data, indicating robust cross-prompt generalization. However, the model exhibited a systematic, L1-linked scoring offset. Within every proficiency band, essays from European-language backgrounds received consistently higher scores than essays from East-Asian-language backgrounds, a pattern not attributable to the composition of the fine-tuning data. This is the first large-scale L1 fairness analysis of a fine-tuned open-weight LLM for automated essay scoring.

</details>


### [43] [D-cut: Adaptive Verification Depth Pruning for Batched Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14647)
*Tianyu Liu,Yuhao Shen,Rui Cen,Junhan Shi,Jiebin Zhang,Guangshuo Qin,Hong Liu,Song Liu,Guanghua Yu,Jianchen Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: D-Cut is an adaptive pruning method for speculative decoding that allocates verification budget across concurrent requests based on draft confidence and a runtime cost model, restoring and improving speedups under high concurrency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parallel drafting methods decouple draft length from latency, enabling longer drafts and higher MAT. However, under high request concurrency, long drafts waste computation on rejected tokens, increasing verification cost and potentially making speculative decoding slower than autoregressive decoding. The authors aim to address this inefficiency.

Method: D-Cut performs cross-request pruning by jointly selecting draft tokens across a batch, adaptively allocating verification budget according to draft confidence. It also incorporates a runtime cost model that accounts for GPU architecture and parallelism strategy to adapt pruning depth to the deployment environment.

Result: Under high concurrency, D-Cut improves average speedup from 1.26× to 1.65×, restores acceleration in dense-model configurations where long-draft baselines were slower than autoregressive decoding, and achieves up to 3.0× speedup over autoregressive decoding on MoE models.

Conclusion: D-Cut effectively mitigates the verification-cost overhead of long-draft speculative decoding under high concurrency by adaptively pruning draft tokens, yielding consistent and significant speedups across diverse model architectures and deployment environments.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference without compromising output quality. Recent parallel drafting methods further improve single-request performance by decoupling draft length from drafting latency, enabling longer drafts and higher mean accepted tokens (MAT). However, under high request concurrency, long drafts waste substantial computation on rejected tokens, increasing verification cost and potentially making speculative decoding slower than autoregressive decoding. We present D-Cut, an adaptive pruning method that selects draft tokens jointly across the batch and concentrates the verification budget on tokens most likely to be accepted. D-Cut is motivated by two observations. First, acceptance lengths vary considerably across concurrent requests; D-Cut therefore performs cross-request pruning, allocating the verification budget adaptively according to draft confidence. Second, verification cost depends strongly on the deployment environment, including GPU architecture and parallelism strategy; D-Cut incorporates a runtime cost model to adapt its pruning depth to the target environment. Experiments on dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show that, under high concurrency, D-Cut improves the average speedup from \(1.26\times\) to \(1.65\times\), restores acceleration in dense-model configurations where long-draft baselines are slower than autoregressive decoding, and achieves up to \(3.0\times\) speedup over autoregressive decoding on MoE models.

</details>


### [44] [Harnessing LLMs for Reliable Academic Supervision: A Comparative Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14707)
*Akash Raj*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A case study in academic supervision compares a bare GPT-5 chatbot against a structured system (ASuS) wrapping the smaller GPT-4o-mini in a LangGraph harness. Despite the smaller base model, ASuS significantly outperforms on grounding, explainability, consistency, and other harness-mechanism dimensions, demonstrating that deliberate scaffolding—not larger models—drives reliability in high-stakes domain decision systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs produce fluent single-shot answers but fail as reliable components in domain decision systems requiring consistency, traceability, and institutional accountability. The gap between fluent generation and dependable deployment motivates "harness engineering"—composing deterministic scaffolding around an LLM core.

Method: The authors compare a baseline system (ASA) using GPT-5 with no scaffolding against ASuS, a multi-module system wrapping GPT-4o-mini in a LangGraph harness. ASuS integrates symbolic-semantic retrieval, schema-validated outputs, LLM-as-judge with bounded retry, human-in-the-loop gates, deterministic weighted risk scoring with LLM narration, and per-node SQLite audit trails. Evaluation uses a blind ten-rater hybrid rubric across six harness-mechanism dimensions, supplemented by a 2×2 model-harness ablation.

Result: ASuS outscored ASA on all six dimensions (pooled mean: 4.08 vs. 1.23). Eight of ten raters rejected the null hypothesis at α=0.05 on a paired Wilcoxon test. The ablation confirmed that harness structural contributions are largely model-invariant.

Conclusion: In domains where reliability, traceability, and institutional consistency outweigh open-ended fluency, harness engineering—not scaling model size—is the decisive factor for dependable LLM deployment. Seven recurring harness-engineering patterns are extracted from the case study.

Abstract: Large language models routinely produce fluent answers to single-shot prompts, yet deploying them as reliable components of a domain decision system is substantially harder. Closing this gap is the work of harness engineering: the deliberate composition of deterministic scaffolding (symbolic filters, retrieval, schema-typed I/O, LLM-as-judge loops, HITL gates, persistent state, audit trails) around an LLM core. We present a case study in academic supervision, a domain combining high-stakes recommendation, longitudinal accountability, and structured operational workflows.
  We compare a baseline (ASA), a GPT-5 chatbot with no scaffolding, against a multi-module system (ASuS) that wraps the much smaller GPT-4o-mini in a LangGraph harness with symbolic-semantic retrieval, schema-validated outputs, LLM-as-judge with bounded retry, HITL gates, deterministic weighted risk scoring with LLM narration, and a per-node SQLite audit trail. The evaluation rubric is retargeted at six harness-mechanism dimensions (grounding, explainability, consistency, process integrity, cognitive load, constraint adherence). A blind ten-rater hybrid evaluation, supplemented by a 2 x 2 model-harness ablation, finds that ASuS, despite using a much smaller base model, outscores ASA on every dimension. Across ten raters the pooled mean for ASuS is 4.08 versus 1.23 for ASA, and 8 of 10 raters reject the null at alpha = 0.05 on a paired Wilcoxon test; full numbers are in Sections 6.4 and 6.7. The ablation confirms that the structural contributions of the harness are largely model-invariant. We extract seven recurring harness-engineering patterns and argue that where reliability, traceability, and institutional consistency matter more than open-ended fluency, harness engineering challenges the prevailing 'bigger model is better' intuition.

</details>


### [45] [Gold-Guided Programmatic Distillation for Financial Reasoning over Hybrid Tables and Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14709)
*Yun Dong,Erica Zhao,Elana Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes an execution-verified programmatic distillation framework that transfers reliable numerical reasoning from a large LLM teacher to a smaller student model using verified Python programs instead of error-prone natural-language rationales, achieving state-of-the-art results on the TAT-QA financial reasoning benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial QA over hybrid tabular-textual data requires precise multi-source numerical reasoning, but LLM-generated natural-language rationales frequently contain arithmetic errors, making them unreliable for distillation. The authors aim to provide verifiably correct supervision by using executable programs whose outputs can be automatically checked against gold answers.

Method: The framework uses gold derivations to guide teacher-side Python program synthesis, filtering to retain only programs that execute correctly and produce the gold answer. An iterative recovery stage revisits examples where the teacher failed, allowing the student to incorporate newly verified programs into subsequent training rounds. The student (a 7B model) is then trained on these execution-verified programs rather than textual chain-of-thought.

Result: The best 7B student achieves 87.00 EM and 87.18 F1 on TAT-QA, outperforming the 72B teacher (78.46 EM) and strong baselines including TAGOP and TAT-LLM.

Conclusion: Execution-verified programmatic distillation is an effective and extensible framework for training compact models to perform reliable numerical reasoning, with the student surpassing its teacher by a substantial margin.

Abstract: Financial question answering over hybrid tabular and textual data may require multi-source reasoning and precise numerical computation. While large language models (LLMs) can generate intermediate reasoning steps, natural-language rationales remain prone to arithmetic errors, making them an unreliable supervision source for distillation. Building on programmatic distillation, we develop an approach that transfers reliable numerical reasoning from a large teacher model to a compact student using execution-verified Python programs instead of free-form textual rationales. It leverages gold derivations to guide teacher-side program synthesis and retains only programs that execute correctly and produce the gold answer, ensuring high-quality supervision. We further introduce an iterative recovery stage that revisits teacher-failed examples, enabling the student to recover and incorporate newly verified programs into training. Experiments on TAT-QA show that our framework is highly effective for hybrid financial reasoning. Our best 7B student achieves 87.00 EM / 87.18 F1 on the test set, substantially outperforming the 72B teacher (78.46 EM) as well as traditional and strong LLM-based baselines, including TAGOP and TAT-LLM.
