These results demonstrate that execution-verified programmatic distillation provides an effective and extensible framework for training smaller models to perform reliable numerical reasoning.

</details>


### [46] [CoTu at EXACT 2026: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Transparent Educational QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14735)
*Quoc-Khang Tran,Minh-Thien Nguyen,Phu-An Thai,Xuan-Tung Bui,Truong-Thanh Ma,Nguyen-Khang Pham*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline using a 4B model that emits Z3 encodings for legal reasoning and Python for physics, with self-correction and speculative decoding, achieving a perfect physics score and the highest final-round technical score (13.44/15) in the EXACT 2026 competition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The EXACT 2026 competition requires transparent, explainable question answering using small open-weight models (≤8B), self-hosted, with natural-language explanations — ruling out large proprietary systems and demanding verifiable reasoning at limited scale.

Method: A neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline: a 4B backbone model writes programs instead of direct answers — Z3 SMT encodings for regulation entailment checking and numerical Python for physics problems. Both are wrapped in a shared self-correction loop producing unified explained-JSON output. The system employs answer-type routing, distillation-based task fine-tuning, and a latency-aware serving stack (SGLang with speculative decoding) to stay under the 60-second per-query limit.

Result: Perfect score on the physics task in both automated selection rounds; highest final-round technical score of any team (13.44/15) combining automated evaluation with expert-judged reasoning depth; 3rd place overall when including presentation score.

Conclusion: Grounding answers in symbolic solvers (Z3, Python) yields correct, verifiable deductions at the 4B scale. The residual difficulty lies in premise selection rather than the deduction itself.

Abstract: Transparent educational question answering asks for answers that are not only correct but explainable, and doing so with small models rules out the reasoning power of the largest proprietary systems. The EXACT 2026 competition poses this problem concretely: open-weight language models of at most 8B parameters, self-hosted, with a natural-language explanation for every answer. It pairs two tasks: logical reasoning over university regulations, and multi-step physics problem solving. We describe the system that team \cotu{} developed to address both, a neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline in which a 4B backbone writes a program rather than stating an answer directly: for regulation queries it emits a Z3 encoding whose entailment verdict grounds the deduction, and for physics it emits numerical Python, both wrapped in a shared self-correction loop and a unified explained-JSON output. Answer-type routing, distillation-based task fine-tuning, and a latency-aware serving stack -- SGLang with speculative decoding -- keep the system within the 60-second per-query limit. The system achieved a \textbf{perfect score} on the physics task in both automated selection rounds and obtained the \textbf{highest final-round technical score} of any team -- $13.44/15$, combining automated answer evaluation with expert-judged reasoning depth -- with the equally weighted presentation score included, \cotu{} placed 3rd overall. Grounding answers in a symbolic solver yields correct, verifiable deductions at the 4B scale, and the residual difficulty lies in premise selection rather than the deduction itself.

</details>


### [47] [SEED: Self-Evolving On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14777)
*Jinyang Wu,Shuo Yang,Zhengxi Lu,Fan Zhang,Yuhao Shen,Lang Feng,Haoran Luo,Zheng Lian,Shuai Zhang,Zhengqi Wen,Jianhua Tao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SEED is a self-evolving framework that converts completed agent trajectories into hindsight skills during RL training, then distills skill-induced action probability shifts as dense token-level supervision alongside sparse outcome rewards, improving both performance and sample efficiency on interactive agent tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outcome-based RL for interactive agents suffers from a supervision gap — sparse trajectory-level rewards provide minimal guidance on intermediate decisions, leaving token-level policy learning under-supervised. The authors aim to bridge this gap with auxiliary dense signals derived from the agent's own completed trajectories.

Method: SEED operates in two stages: (1) The policy is fine-tuned to analyze its own completed on-policy trajectories and generate natural-language "hindsight skills" capturing reusable workflows, key observations, and failure-avoidance rules. As the policy updates during RL, skill analysis co-evolves. (2) Sampled actions are re-scored under both ordinary and skill-augmented contexts; the resulting probability shift is converted into a dense token-level distillation signal, jointly optimized with the standard outcome-based RL objective, keeping auxiliary supervision on-policy.

Result: Extensive experiments on both text-based and vision-based agentic tasks demonstrate that SEED consistently improves performance and sample efficiency, with robust generalization to unseen scenarios.

Conclusion: SEED effectively addresses the supervision gap in outcome-based RL for interactive agents by introducing a self-evolving hindsight skill distillation mechanism that provides dense, on-policy auxiliary signals, yielding consistent gains across diverse agentic benchmarks.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained as interactive agents for long-horizon tasks involving multi-turn interaction, tool use, and environment feedback. Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides a practical optimization paradigm, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards offer limited guidance on intermediate decisions, leaving a supervision gap between episode-level outcomes and token-level policy learning. We propose SEED (SElf-Evolving On-Policy Distillation), a self-evolving framework that converts completed on-policy trajectories into training-time hindsight skills and distills their behavioral effect back into the policy model. SEED first fine-tunes the policy to analyze completed trajectories and generate natural-language skills that capture reusable workflows, decisive observations, or failure-avoidance rules. During RL, the current policy both collects trajectories and serves as the analyzer that extracts hindsight skills from them. Policy updates therefore improve subsequent decision making and skill analysis together, allowing hindsight supervision to evolve with the policy. SEED then re-scores the sampled actions under ordinary and skill-augmented contexts, converting the skill-induced probability shift into a dense token-level on-policy distillation signal. This signal is jointly optimized with outcome-based RL, keeping the auxiliary supervision aligned with the current trajectory distribution. Extensive experiments on text-based and vision-based agentic tasks show that SEED consistently improves performance and sample efficiency, exhibiting robust generalization to unseen scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/SEED.

</details>


### [48] [Show Me How You Reason and I'll Tell You Who You Are: Reasoning Graphs for Robust LLM Authorship Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14905)
*Zlata Kikteva,Artur Romazanov,Annette Hautli-Janisz,Ramon Ruiz-Dolz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a graph neural network approach that extracts reasoning structures from texts via argument mining to detect LLM-generated content. It significantly outperforms surface-level baselines under obfuscation attacks and generalizes better to unseen model versions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-generated text detection methods rely on surface-level linguistic features, which are vulnerable to paraphrasing and obfuscation. There is a need for more robust, deeper signals of LLM authorship that persist beyond stylistic manipulation.

Method: The authors extract reasoning graphs from texts using an argument mining pipeline, capturing structural argumentative patterns. A graph neural network (GNN) is then trained on these reasoning graphs to perform LLM authorship detection, compared against a Longformer baseline operating on surface-level features.

Result: The GNN approach outperforms the Longformer baseline by up to 27 percentage points under obfuscation attacks (paraphrasing, backtranslation) and by 19 percentage points on texts from unseen LLM versions.

Conclusion: Reasoning structure, as captured by argument mining and GNNs, provides a more robust and generalizable signal for LLM-generated text detection than surface-level linguistic features, particularly in adversarial and evolving deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Given the current trend to employ large language models (LLMs) in almost any imaginable context, LLM-generated text detection and authorship attribution have become a pressing issue. Prior work has primarily focused on surface-level linguistic features, an approach shown to be susceptible to paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. In this paper, we go beyond the linguistic surface, extracting and analysing reasoning structures in LLM-generated texts with the goal of capturing more complex signals of LLM authorship. We propose a graph neural network approach that leverages reasoning graphs extracted by an argument mining pipeline, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation over a traditional Longformer baseline. Our approach outperforms the baseline by up to 27 percentage points under the obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, and 19 percentage points when evaluated on the texts generated by the unseen model versions, simulating real-world conditions in which new LLM versions are continuously released.

</details>


### [49] [Latent Trajectory Discrimination for AI-Generated Text Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14967)
*Gianluca Bonifazi,Christopher Buratti,Michele Marchetti,Federica Parlapiano,Giulia Quaglieri,Davide Traini,Domenico Ursino,Luca Virgili*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper reformulates AI-generated text detection as distinguishing between latent generation trajectories rather than analyzing static document features. The proposed GTCL framework segments documents into ordered units, encodes them in embedding space, and applies contrastive learning to capture geometric regularities of autoregressive generation, outperforming baselines across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AIGTD methods treat documents as static objects, using aggregate statistics or global embeddings, which ignores the dynamic, sequential nature of autoregressive text generation. The authors argue that modeling how textual representations evolve across a sequence — the latent generation trajectory — provides a more principled and discriminative signal for detection.

Method: GTCL (Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning): (1) segments each document into ordered local units, (2) encodes each unit in an embedding space to form structured, sequence-level trajectory representations, and (3) applies contrastive learning on these trajectories to learn geometric regularities characteristic of autoregressive generation.

Result: GTCL consistently outperforms detection baselines across three different benchmarks and several detection approaches, demonstrating that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics yields robust discriminative signals across different models and domains.

Conclusion: Modeling trajectory differences between human-written and AI-generated text provides a promising and underexplored dynamic direction for AIGTD. The findings suggest that incorporating sequential generation dynamics can improve detection robustness and generalization.

Abstract: Most existing approaches to AI-Generated Text Detection (AIGTD) treat documents as static objects and base their decisions on aggregate statistics or globally compressed embeddings. However, this perspective overlooks the inherently dynamic nature of autoregressive generation, where content evolves progressively through the latent space. In this paper, we reformulate AIGTD as the problem of distinguishing between latent generation trajectories. Instead of relying on static representations, we model how textual representations evolve across the sequence. To this end, we propose Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning (GTCL), a framework that segments the document into ordered local units, encodes each unit in an embedding space, and constructs a structured and sequence-level representation. GTCL then applies contrastive learning to these trajectories to learn geometric regularities associated with the autoregressive generation. Evaluations performed on three different benchmarks and several approaches show that GTCL outperforms detection baselines consistently, which implies that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics provides robust discriminative signals across models and domains. These results suggest that modeling trajectory differences could improve detection and open up a dynamic direction that has been underexplored in previous AIGTD literature.

</details>


### [50] [OmniaBench: Benchmarking General AI Agents Across Diverse Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14989)
*Chengyu Shen,Yujie Fu,Gangtao Xin,Yanheng Hou,Wenlong Fei,Guojie Zhu,Jiawei Li,Hongcheng Gao,Runming He,Zhen Hao Wong,Meiyi Qiang,Hao Liang,Zhao Cao,Hao Jiang,Chong Chen,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OmniaBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating general-purpose AI agents across 90+ domains with 1,431 tasks. It features a hierarchical scenario taxonomy (ToC/ToB/ToE), executable environments, a ten-dimensional capability taxonomy, and eight difficulty factors. Even top models like Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieve only ~57-58% Pass@1, revealing significant gaps in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks are limited in scope—focusing on narrow scenarios, restricted tool ecosystems, or specific interaction formats—making it impossible to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous real-world application settings. There is a need for a broad, diagnostic benchmark that spans diverse domains and supports fine-grained capability analysis.

Method: The authors derive scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, web retrieval, and human refinement to build a hierarchical taxonomy spanning ToC (To Consumer), ToB (To Business), and ToE (To Enterprise) with 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains. Executable environments are constructed from this taxonomy, and tasks are synthesized via four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program, yielding both single-turn and multi-turn interactions. A ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors are introduced for fine-grained evaluation. The full dataset contains 1,431 tasks, with a challenging subset of 644 tasks for cost-efficient evaluation and contamination mitigation.

Result: OmniaBench poses substantial challenges: Claude-Sonnet-5 achieves an Overall Pass@1 of 58.54 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieves 57.14. Analyses reveal clear performance differences across domains and capabilities, with persistent limitations in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction.

Conclusion: OmniaBench serves as a broad and diagnostic benchmark for characterizing the capability boundaries of general agents, exposing critical weaknesses in current frontier models and providing a foundation for systematic progress in agent research.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly evolving from text generators into general agents capable of understanding user requests, invoking external tools, and completing complex tasks through interaction. However, existing agent benchmarks often focus on limited scenarios, tool ecosystems, or interaction formats, making it difficult to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous application settings. We introduce OmniaBench, a benchmark for evaluating general agents across diverse scenarios with explicit state spaces. We derive application-oriented scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, Web retrieval, and human refinement, forming a hierarchical taxonomy that spans ToC, ToB and ToE with 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains. Based on this taxonomy, we construct executable environments and synthesize single-turn and multi-turn tasks through four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program. OmniaBench further introduces a ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors to support fine-grained evaluation and analysis. The resulting dataset contains 1,431 tasks, together with a challenging subset of 644 tasks designed to reduce evaluation cost and mitigate potential contamination of the full set after public release. The bench presents substantial challenges to current frontier models, with even Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieving Overall Pass@1 scores of only 58.54 and 57.14, respectively. Further analyses reveal clear differences across domains and capabilities, as well as persistent limitations in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction. OmniaBench provides a broad and diagnostic benchmark for characterizing the capability boundaries of general agents.

</details>


### [51] [Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15092)
*Haocheng Yang,Licheng Pan,Xiaoxi Li,Zhichao Chen,Zhiheng Zhang,Yuan Lu,Haoxuan Li,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Rubrics on Trial is a query-only framework that iteratively evolves a rubric set from scratch using synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs, with validation checks to filter out non-discriminative, over-specific, and style-only rubrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rubric construction methods rely on human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources but lacks mechanisms to verify that generated rubrics are actually useful — they may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward superficial style, or penalize valid alternatives. The motivation is to create a fully autonomous, query-only framework that produces verifiably useful rubrics without any external annotations or model training.

Method: Rubrics on Trial evolves a rubric set from an empty set using only the query. It generates synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs (one response following the rubric, one not) and subjects each candidate rubric to a validation trial: screening out rubrics that are non-discriminative (cannot distinguish response quality), over-specific (too narrowly tailored), or style-only (reward superficial stylistic features rather than substantive quality). Only validated rubrics are added to the set.

Result: Experiments across five preference benchmark suites show that Rubrics on Trial achieves the best average accuracy and leads on six of seven evaluation sets.

Conclusion: A query-only, validation-driven framework for automatic rubric construction is both feasible and effective, outperforming existing approaches on preference-based LLM evaluation without requiring any external annotations, human-written rubrics, or model training.

Abstract: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a rubric set from an empty set without external annotations or model training. It derives supervision solely from synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs and validates each proposed rubric before adding it, screening out non-discriminative, over-specific, and style-only candidate rubrics. Experiments across five preference benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Rubrics on Trial, which achieves the best average accuracy and leads on six of seven evaluation sets.

</details>


### [52] [Grokipedia vs Wikipedia: An LLM-Based Audit of Political Neutrality along Ideologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15146)
*Filippos Vlahos,Guillaume Bied,Tijl De Bie*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A comparative political bias analysis of Grokipedia (LLM-written) versus Wikipedia, using 1,394 article pairs about politicians across 9 ideology dimensions with 4 LLM judges. All judges, including Grok itself, rated Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias exhibit favorable bias — Grokipedia favors economically right-wing politicians and penalizes socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia shows the opposite pattern.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokipedia was launched in late 2025 as an LLM-generated encyclopedia positioned as an "unbiased alternative" to Wikipedia, which has been criticized for perceived left-wing/liberal bias. The study investigates whether an encyclopedia authored entirely by an LLM (Grok) achieves greater neutrality or merely encodes a different ideological bias, addressing the broader question of how AI-generated knowledge repositories shape political discourse.

Method: The authors conducted a large-scale comparative study analyzing 1,394 matched article pairs from Grokipedia and Wikipedia, all describing members of government. Neutrality was assessed along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions. Four LLMs served as judges: Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. To account for potential judge bias, the study also examined patterns in the LLMs' judgments themselves.

Result: All four LLM judges — including Grok — rated Grokipedia as significantly less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias portrayed politicians favorably overall, but their biases diverged along ideological lines: Grokipedia exhibited favorability toward economically right-wing politicians and penalized socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia showed the reverse, favoring socially liberal politicians.

Conclusion: An LLM-generated encyclopedia does not inherently deliver neutrality; rather, it embeds its own ideological bias, different from but not superior to Wikipedia's. The finding that Grok itself rated Grokipedia as less neutral strengthens the result's credibility and underscores the challenge of achieving truly neutral AI-generated knowledge.

Abstract: Online encyclopedias shape political opinion and, through it, democratic discourse. In late 2025, Grokipedia was released, an encyclopedia written entirely by the LLM Grok. One motivation behind the project was to provide an unbiased alternative to Wikipedia, which has faced accusations of "left-wing" and "liberal" bias. But does an encyclopedia written by an LLM deliver greater neutrality, or does it simply embed a different ideology? We conduct a large-scale political bias study on Grokipedia and Wikipedia, analysing 1,394 article pairs describing members of government for neutrality along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions employing four LLM judges, Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. As the LLMs could themselves be biased, we also investigate patterns in their judgments. We find all LLM-judges, including Grok, to rate Grokipedia less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias are rated as portraying politicians favourably overall, but towards different ideological groups. Grokipedia particularly favours economically right-wing politicians and penalises socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia is rated as favourably biased towards the latter.

</details>


### [53] [Linear representations of grammaticality in neural language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15175)
*Jane Li,Najoung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether neural language models encode grammaticality in their internal representations rather than relying solely on probability-based measures. Using mass-mean probing, the authors find that grammatical vs. ungrammatical sentences are systematically separable in representational space, that this separation is not fully explained by correlated sentence-level factors, and that it generalizes across grammatical phenomena and, to some degree, across languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of grammatical knowledge in NLMs rely on probability comparisons (whether models assign higher probabilities to grammatical strings). This approach is problematic because probability is entangled with many factors beyond grammaticality — lexical frequency, plausibility, world knowledge, etc. The authors argue for a complementary evaluation framework that examines internal representations directly.

Method: The authors employ mass-mean probing, a diagnostic technique that tests whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences form systematically separable clusters in the representational space of pretrained NLMs. They further analyze whether this separability is independent of confounding sentence properties correlated with grammaticality, and test generalization across diverse grammatical phenomena and multiple languages.

Result: Grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations across a wide range of pretrained NLMs, with clear representational separation along the grammaticality dimension. This separation cannot be fully attributed to alternative sentence-level factors. The encoding also generalizes across a broad range of grammatical phenomena and partially across languages, indicating grammaticality forms a coherent representational dimension.

Conclusion: The findings provide new evidence that grammaticality constitutes a coherent representational dimension in contemporary NLMs, contributing to debates on syntactic knowledge in language models. The proposed probing framework offers a complementary method for evaluating grammatical competence that does not depend solely on string probabilities.

Abstract: Whether neural language models (NLMs) possess the ability to distinguish strings on the basis of their grammaticality remains a debated topic in the computational linguistics literature. Existing evidence has largely relied on probability-based measures, testing whether models assign higher probabilities to grammatical than ungrammatical strings. However, probability comparisons have been criticized as a measure for grammatical knowledge based on the assumption that grammaticality is inherently entangled with likelihood. Model-assigned probability is a function of many related sentence properties, such as lexical frequency, plausibility, and world knowledge. In this work, we move beyond probability-based evaluations and investigate whether grammaticality is encoded in the internal representations of NLMs. Using mass-mean probing, we test whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences are systematically separated in representational space. We further examine the extent to which these representations are independent of sentence properties that are correlated with grammaticality, as well as their generalization across grammatical phenomena and languages. Our results provide evidence that grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations of a wide range of pretrained NLMs, yielding clear representational separation on the dimension of grammaticality that cannot be fully explained by alternative sentence-level factors. Moreover, this encoding generalizes across a broad range of grammatical phenomena and to some degree, across languages, suggesting that grammaticality constitutes a coherent representational dimension in contemporary NLMs. These findings contribute new evidence to debates about the nature of syntactic knowledge in language models and offer a complementary framework for evaluating grammatical competence that is not dependent on string probabilities alone.

</details>


### [54] [T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15178)
*Ziyang Cai,Xingyu Zhu,Yihe Dong,Yinghui He,Sanjeev Arora*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: T2MLR introduces targeted middle-layer recurrence in Transformers, where a cached hidden representation from one decoding step is fused into an earlier layer of the next step. This allows latent reasoning states to persist across tokens with minimal overhead, outperforming standard Transformers on reasoning tasks—especially when recurrence is limited to ~20% of layers—and can be retrofitted into existing pretrained models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive decoding in Transformers compresses rich hidden-state computation through a narrow token bottleneck at each step, preventing intermediate reasoning states from persisting across time. Prior solutions that loop over all layers introduce substantial inference overhead. The authors aim to enable persistent latent reasoning with minimal cost.

Method: T2MLR caches a middle-layer hidden representation from the previous token position and fuses it (via a learned gating mechanism) into an earlier layer of the current token's forward pass. The recurrence is applied only to a localized middle-layer block (e.g., 20% of the network), not all layers. The architecture can be trained from scratch or retrofitted into existing pretrained Transformers with brief finetuning.

Result: T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer baselines on natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning. Localized middle-layer recurrence often beats full-layer recurrence. Retrofitting a pretrained 1.7B Transformer with T2MLR and briefly finetuning yields substantial improvements on math reasoning.

Conclusion: Effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers; targeted middle-layer recurrence suffices and can emerge more strongly from this design. The ease of retrofitting lowers the barrier to practical adoption.

Abstract: Transformer reasoning is limited by autoregressive decoding, which repeat edly compresses rich hidden computation through token space and makes it difficult for intermediate reasoning states to persist across time. We in troduce Transformers with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence (T2MLR), a transformers-based latent reasoning architecture that fuses a cached middle layer representation from the previous token directly into an earlier layer of the current token position, enabling abstract intermediate computation to persist across decoding steps with little inference overhead. Across natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning, T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer base lines. Moreover, applying recurrence to only a localized middle-layer block (as little as 20% of the network) often outperforms full-layer recurrence. Im portantly, T2MLR does not require pretraining from scratch: retrofitting the recurrent pathway into an existing pretrained 1.7B Transformer and briefly finetuning substantially improves math reasoning, lowering the barrier to practical adoption. These results suggest that effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers as in previous works, but can instead emerge more strongly from targeted middle-layer recurrence.

</details>


### [55] [Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15200)
*Haran Raajesh,Kulin Shah,Adam Klivans,Philipp Krähenbühl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper formalizes Masked Diffusion Language Model generation as a two-stage action MDP (token prediction + position remasking) and shows that optimizing both terms via policy gradient yields state-of-the-art reasoning results on GSM8K (87.1%) and MBPP (53.4%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning has improved reasoning in autoregressive LLMs, but extending RL to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) is challenging because exact log-likelihood estimation is intractable. Existing methods approximate this by modeling only token predictions while ignoring the order in which masked positions are unmasked, leaving a key aspect of the generative process unoptimized.

Method: The authors formalize MDLM generation as a two-stage action Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each step involves (1) selecting tokens for masked positions, and (2) choosing which positions to remask. Under this formulation, the policy gradient decomposes naturally into a token term and a masking term. The proposed approach jointly optimizes both terms using reinforcement learning.

Result: The method achieves state-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks: 87.1% accuracy on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP, demonstrating the benefit of optimizing both token and masking decisions.

Conclusion: Properly accounting for both token selection and remasking order in MDLM generation, framed as a two-stage MDP, unlocks significant performance gains via RL, enabling MDLMs to compete at a high level on reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has proven effective for improving reasoning in large language models, but extending it to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) remains challenging due to the intractability of the log-likelihood estimation. Existing approaches approximate this log-likelihood by modeling only the token predictions, ignoring the order in which positions are unmasked during generation. We observe that MDLM generation involves two decisions at each step: what tokens to place at each masked position and which positions to remask. We formalize this as a two-stage action MDP, showing that the policy gradient naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term. Combining optimization of both terms leads to state-of-the-art outcomes on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, with scores of 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP.

</details>


### [56] [Expanding the Lexicon of Ge'ez Based African Languages: A Comparative Study of Amharic and Tigrinya](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15209)
*Hailay Kidu Teklehaymanot,Debela Desalegn Yadeta,Wolfgang Nejdl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VEXMLM extends XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords to improve performance on Amharic and Tigrinya, achieving substantial gains over baseline models, with benefits transferring to 17 additional low-resource African languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual PLMs like XLM-R suffer from high OOV rates and excessive subword fragmentation on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages due to Latin-script-centric tokenizer training. This disproportionately harms languages using scripts like Ge'ez (Amharic, Tigrinya) and other African languages.

Method: 1) Train a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic/Tigrinya corpora. 2) Extend XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords. 3) Initialize new embeddings by averaging constituent subword embeddings from the original tokenizer. 4) Two-stage training: continued masked language modeling on the extended vocabulary, then supervised fine-tuning on QA, NER, and sentiment analysis tasks.

Result: On Amharic/Tigrinya QA: VEXMLM achieves 87.0 EM / 90.0 F1 vs. XLM-R (66.0/78.0) and Glot500 (74.0/78.0). On SA: 80.0% accuracy vs. 77.0% (XLM-R) and 46.0% (Glot500). On NER: OOV-token entity accuracy improved from 81.4% to 94.3% averaged over 11 evaluated languages. Gains transfer to 17 additional unaugmented African languages.

Conclusion: Vocabulary extension with script-specific subwords plus embedding initialization via averaging is an effective, transferable strategy for improving multilingual PLM performance on low-resource non-Latin-script languages without requiring full retraining.

Abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models (PLMs) exhibit degraded performance on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages, driven by high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates and excessive subword fragmentation that result from Latin-script-centric tokenizer training. We introduce VEXMLM, a vocabulary-extended variant of XLM-R targeting the two highest-resource Ge'ez-script languages, Amharic and Tigrinya, and further evaluated on 17 additional low-resource African languages (19 total). We train a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic and Tigrinya monolingual corpora, extend XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords derived from this tokenizer, and initialize their embeddings by averaging the embeddings of their constituent subwords under XLM-R's original tokenizer. VEXMLM is trained in two stages: (1) continued masked language modeling over the extended vocabulary on the curated corpora, and (2) supervised fine-tuning on question answering (QA), named entity recognition (NER), and sentiment analysis (SA). On Amharic/Tigrinya QA, VEXMLM achieves 87.0 EM /90.0 F1, versus 66.0 EM/78.0 F1 for XLM-R and 74.0 EM/ 78.0 F1 for Glot500. On SA, VEXMLM reaches 80.0\% accuracy versus 77.0\% (XLM-R) and 46.0\% (Glot500). On NER, VEXMLM raises OOV-token entity accuracy from 81.4\% to 94.3\%, averaged over 11 of the 19 evaluated languages for which OOV analysis was possible. Our contributions are: (i) a vocabulary-extension and embedding-initialization procedure tailored to Ge'ez script; (ii) a two-stage training strategy under which vocabulary and continued-pretraining gains on Amharic/Tigrinya transfer to 17 typologically related, unaugmented African languages; and (iii) an evaluation spanning both intrinsic tokenization metrics (vocabulary coverage, fertility, OOV rate) and extrinsic task performance across all 19 languages.

</details>


### [57] [In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15232)
*Jimmy T. H. Smith,Tarek Dakhran,Alberto Cabrera,Simon S. Lee,Paul Pak,Aditya Tadimeti,Tim Seyde,Maxime Labonne,Alexander Amini,Mathias Lechner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A method to expand a pre-trained model's tokenizer in-place without retraining from scratch, using BPE continuation on multilingual data and a two-stage adaptation process. Applied to an 8B MoE model, it achieves 2.4–2.6× token reduction for Hindi/Vietnamese and up to 4× for Thai, yielding 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedups on-device.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained tokenizers reflect the language distribution of their original corpus. When deployment priorities shift to new languages, those languages suffer from severe token fragmentation (many tokens per word), increasing latency, compute, and energy costs. While cloud models can afford large vocabularies, on-device compact models ship small vocabularies where embedding/LM-head matrices consume significant decode bandwidth. Retraining from scratch for a new tokenizer is prohibitively expensive.

Method: Tokenizer expansion continues the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on a multilingual corpus, ensuring most original tokens remain intact and new tokens have exact decompositions into source tokens. Original embedding rows are copied unchanged; new rows are initialized as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. A two-stage adaptation follows: (1) embedding-only training, then (2) full-model continued pre-training, which recovers source-checkpoint quality. Applied to LFM2-8B-A1B (8B MoE) to produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer.

Result: The expanded 128K tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in ~2.4× and ~2.6× fewer tokens respectively (up to 4.0× on Thai). Combining token reduction with measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary yields an estimated 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedup across reference devices.

Conclusion: Tokenizer expansion is a practical, cost-effective recipe for adapting pre-trained models to new languages without full retraining. The two-stage adaptation preserves model quality while significantly reducing token fragmentation for under-supported languages. The authors release weights, tokenizer, and negative findings that informed the final recipe.

Abstract: A tokenizer fixed at the start of pre-training allocates vocabulary in proportion to the pre-training corpus, reflecting the deployment priorities at that time. When those priorities shift, languages added later are split into many more tokens per word, which can raise latency, compute, and energy consumption for users of those languages. Cloud models can afford a broad vocabulary because the embedding and LM-head matrices are a small fraction of their parameters. On a compact model those matrices are a material share of per-token decode bandwidth, so on-device models ship small vocabularies and accept fragmentation outside a fixed language set. We present tokenizer expansion, an in-place recipe for upgrading a pre-trained model's tokenizer when the model producer controls its design. We continue the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on a multilingual corpus, so most source tokens carry over unchanged as single tokens and every new token has an exact decomposition into source tokens. We copy the carried-over embedding rows unchanged and initialize new rows as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. A two-stage adaptation, embedding-only training then full-model continued pre-training, recovers source-checkpoint quality. We apply the recipe to a continued pre-trained checkpoint of LFM2-8B-A1B, an 8B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model, to help produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer. The expanded tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in roughly $2.4\times$ and $2.6\times$ fewer tokens than the source (up to $4.0\times$ on Thai). Combining these reductions with the measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary, we estimate a $2.2$-$3.7\times$ per-character decode speedup for these languages across our reference devices. We release the model weights and the expanded tokenizer, and report the negative findings that shaped the recipe.

</details>


### [58] [Language Identification via Compositional Data Analysis: A Linear-Time Classifier Based on Log-Ratio Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15238)
*Paul-Andrei Pogăcean,Sanda-Maria Avram*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A deterministic, computationally efficient language identification method using compositional data analysis: character n-gram frequencies are treated as compositional vectors on the simplex, CLR-transformed into Euclidean space where Aitchison geometry applies, with Laplace smoothing for sparsity. Strong accuracy is achieved on six languages, especially for longer texts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language identification methods face a trade-off: neural architectures are accurate but computationally expensive; classical n-gram frequency methods are efficient (linear-time) but rely on distance metrics (e.g., cosine, Euclidean) that are inappropriate for compositional (proportional) data constrained to the simplex. The authors aim to bridge this gap by properly modeling n-gram frequencies as compositional data.

Method: Character unigram and bigram frequency distributions are treated as compositional vectors belonging to the simplex. The centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation is applied to bijectively map these vectors onto the (D-1)-dimensional zero-sum subspace of ℝ^D, where standard Euclidean distance becomes equivalent to Aitchison distance—the natural metric for compositional data. A pipeline integrates CLR-transformed unigram and bigram features with Laplace smoothing to handle zero counts (sparsity). Evaluation is conducted on six languages.

Result: The proposed CLR-based compositional approach achieves robust accuracy across varying text lengths, with particularly strong performance on longer sequences. It provides a competitive alternative to both neural and classical frequency-based methods.

Conclusion: Compositional representations offer a deterministic, interpretable, and computationally efficient alternative for language identification, especially suited for low-resource settings where interpretability and minimal computational overhead are critical.

Abstract: Language identification is commonly addressed using either neural architectures or statistical n-gram models. Neural approaches typically require substantial computational resources, whereas classical frequency-based methods offer efficient linear-time performance, but rely on distance metrics that are not always appropriate for compositional data.
  This work models character and bigram frequency distributions as compositional vectors constrained to the simplex and mapped via the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation bijectively onto the $(D-1)$-dimensional zero-sum subspace of $\mathbb{R}^D$, where Euclidean distances correspond to Aitchison distances. A pipeline is proposed, combining CLR-transformed unigram and bigram features with Laplace smoothing to address sparsity. The method is evaluated on six languages.
  Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves robust accuracy across different text lengths, with strong performance for longer sequences. These findings indicate that compositional representations provide a deterministic and computationally efficient alternative for language identification, particularly in settings where interpretability and low resource consumption are essential.

</details>


### [59] [TikStance: A Multimodal and Hierarchical Dataset for Multi-target Stance Analysis in TikTok Political Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15240)
*Yazhi Zhang,Fuqiang Niu,Bowen Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TikStance is a multimodal, context-aware dataset of 161 TikTok videos and 13,876 hierarchically threaded comments, triple-annotated for stance (Favor/Against/None) toward Trump, Biden, and Harris, enabling research in multimodal stance detection within conversational context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Political discourse has migrated to short-video platforms like TikTok, yet existing datasets fail to jointly preserve audiovisual information and hierarchical conversation structures, limiting computational analysis of how stance manifests across modalities and conversational depth.

Method: The authors collected 161 videos and 13,876 comments spanning September 2023–January 2025, covering three U.S. political figures. Each discussion unit links a host video with metadata to a parent-linked comment tree. Three independent annotators labeled each item using a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None) for both video-to-target and comment-to-target stance. Disagreements were re-annotated, yielding final Krippendorff's α scores of 0.743 (Trump), 0.723 (Biden), and 0.722 (Harris). Descriptive analysis examined stance distributions and conversational depth.

Result: The dataset achieved reliable inter-annotator agreement (α > 0.72 across all subsets). Descriptive analysis revealed target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth, with nested replies constituting 23.3% of all comments.

Conclusion: TikStance, by combining multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level annotations, provides a valuable resource for multimodal stance detection, political communication research, computational social science, and context-aware NLP.

Abstract: Political discourse has increasingly moved to short-video platforms, yet computational analysis of such content remains constrained by the scarcity of datasets that jointly preserve audiovisual information and hierarchical conversations. Here we present TikStance, a multimodal and context-aware dataset comprising 161 videos and 13,876 comments from TikTok, designed for stance detection in political discussions. The dataset covers three major political figures in the 2024 U.S. election cycle--Donald Trump, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris--with content collected between September 2023 and January 2025. Each discussion unit links a host video and its metadata to a parent-linked comment tree, enabling stance analysis within both audiovisual and conversational context. Each item was independently labeled by three annotators using a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None) for video-to-target and comment-to-target stance; items with disagreement were re-annotated, and the final Krippendorff's \(α\) reached 0.743, 0.723, and 0.722 for the Trump, Biden, and Harris subsets, respectively. Descriptive analysis further reveals target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth, with nested replies accounting for 23.3\% of all comments. By combining multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level human annotations, TikStance supports research in multimodal stance detection, political communication, computational social science, and context-aware natural language processing.

</details>


### [60] [Beyond the Leaderboard: Design Lessons for Trustworthy Multimodal VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15241)
*Sushant Gautam,Vajira Thambawita,Michael A. Riegler,Pål Halvorsen,Steven A. Hicks*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Analysis of nine systems from the MediaEval Medico 2025 challenge reveals that while parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pretrained models yields strong QA performance, gains do not reliably translate into faithful clinical reasoning. Methods enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding show more reliable behavior, motivating evaluation beyond lexical overlap and standardized evidence-linked explanations for trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Healthcare multimodal AI systems must integrate visual and textual evidence while maintaining reliability and interpretability. There is a gap between answer-level performance metrics (e.g., lexical overlap) and the actual faithfulness and completeness of clinical reasoning, necessitating systematic analysis of design choices that affect both QA accuracy and explanation quality.

Method: Retrospective case study using the MediaEval Medico 2025 GI endoscopy challenge. The authors analyze design choices across nine documented multimodal QA systems, examining the relationship between parameter-efficient adaptation strategies, structured reasoning enforcement, explicit grounding mechanisms, and the resulting question-answering performance versus explanation quality.

Result: Parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones achieves strong challenge performance on answer-level metrics. However, these gains do not consistently translate into faithful and complete clinical reasoning. Systems enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding exhibit more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types, though the evidence is correlational rather than derived from controlled ablation studies.

Conclusion: The findings advocate for evaluation paradigms that go beyond lexical overlap, incorporating standardized evidence-linked explanations, leakage-aware data governance, and lightweight robustness and calibration checks. These elements collectively support the development of trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI grounded in effective data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation.

Abstract: Healthcare multimodal AI must combine visual and textual evidence while remaining reliable and interpretable. Using MediaEval Medico 2025 as a retrospective GI endoscopy case study, we analyze design choices across nine documented systems for question answering and explanation quality. Parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones provides strong challenge performance, but answer-level gains do not consistently translate into faithful and complete clinical reasoning. Methods enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding show more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types, although the evidence is correlational rather than ablation-based. These results motivate evaluation beyond lexical overlap, standardized evidence-linked explanations, leakage-aware data governance, and lightweight robustness and calibration checks. The findings support trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI based on data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation.

</details>


### [61] [SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15272)
*Yasheng Sun,Zezi Zeng,Yifan Yang,Chong Luo,Wenyi Wang,Ziwei Liu,Jürgen Schmidhuber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciDiagramEdit is a benchmark and agentic framework for instruction-driven scientific figure editing. It mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories paired with authors' revision intents, and uses skill evolution—where an agentic proposer iteratively refines editing skills from execution traces—to progressively improve edit accuracy on held-out data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Editing scientific figures is a routine but time-consuming task in research practice. Automating this under natural-language instruction is challenging because figures are dense infographics combining heterogeneous elements (schematics, plots, photos, captions, arrows) governed by tight visual grammar. Prior work lacks benchmarks and methods that leverage real-world paper revision signals for this task.

Method: SciDiagramEdit mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, grounding each pair in the authors' revision intent. Editing operates on the figure's editable vector source, enabling inspectability and co-editing. To handle diverse instructions, the framework uses agentic skill evolution: an agentic proposer iteratively refines the agent's skill specification over multiple epochs using execution traces, progressively improving edit accuracy.

Result: The skill evolution process progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, demonstrating that natural paper revisions serve as an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.

Conclusion: Natural paper revisions from arXiv provide a viable and effective training signal for automating instruction-driven scientific figure editing. The skill evolution framework successfully adapts to the diversity of editing instructions, and operating on vector source enables user-agent co-editing.

Abstract: Editing the figures in a research paper is a routine and time-consuming part of everyday research practice: authors relabel components, rearrange panels, and restyle visuals as they revise their manuscripts. Automating this editing workflow under a natural-language instruction, however, is challenging, because a scientific figure is a dense infographic in which heterogeneous visual elements such as schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows are composed under a tight visual grammar to advance a specific argument. To address this, we present SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark and skill-evolution framework that learns from natural paper revisions and operates on the figure's editable vector source, where users can inspect and co-edit individual primitives alongside the agent. Our benchmark mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each grounded in the authors' own revision intent. To accommodate the diversity of editing instructions, we adopt agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer continually refines the agent's skill specification from execution traces over multiple epochs. The resulting skill progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, providing evidence that natural paper revisions are an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.

</details>


### [62] [Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15277)
*Patrik Wolf,Thomas Kleine Buening,Andreas Krause,Celestine Mendler-Dünner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether LLMs obey the law of total probability in in-context learning, finding widespread violations. Fine-grained subpopulation estimates aggregated together often outperform direct population-level estimates — a phenomenon dubbed the "macro fallacy." This suggests LLMs possess subpopulation knowledge but fail to propagate it reliably into aggregate estimates, establishing statistical self-consistency as a new reference-free evaluation criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-context learning is widely interpreted as conditional inference, where prompts specify a context and outputs represent conditional distributions. If this interpretation is valid, LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities, particularly the law of total probability (prior-weighted conditional distributions should aggregate into population-level marginals). The authors seek to test whether frontier LLMs actually adhere to this self-consistency principle.

Method: The authors use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. They prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting conditional estimates back into population-level estimates using the law of total probability, and compare these reconstructed estimates against direct population-level estimates across partitions of varying granularity. The protocol is applied across multiple problem domains and state-of-the-art frontier models, with an in-depth study of persona prompting.

Result: Widespread violations of basic consistency properties are observed across problem domains and frontier models. The key finding is the "macro fallacy": estimates reconstructed from fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. This effect persists across variations in tree structure and estimation task and can be partially recovered through implicit prompting.

Conclusion: Models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs, providing a new lens for assessing model reliability beyond accuracy against ground truth.

Abstract: In-context learning is commonly interpreted as a form of conditional inference, in which the prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Applying this protocol across problem domains and state-of-the-art frontier models, we show widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. This effect persists across variations in tree structure and estimation task, and can be partially recovered through implicit prompting. Together, these findings suggest that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

</details>

### [63] [Position: Explainability Research Must Prioritize Foundations over Ad-hoc Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14123)
*Michal Moshkovitz,Suraj Srinivas,Lesia Semenova,Nave Frost,Cyrus Rashtchian,Valentyn Boreiko,Shichang Zhang,Himabindu Lakkaraju,Cynthia Rudin,Jennifer Wortman Vaughan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This position paper critiques the XAI field for focusing on ad-hoc methods without integrating explanations into real-world, actionable workflows. Through literature review and practitioner surveys, it identifies foundational gaps—unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation, and absent feedback pipelines—and proposes a practical checklist to reorient XAI toward human-centered, action-oriented systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite abundant XAI techniques, explanations are rarely used in practice; they are generated and discarded without influencing downstream decisions. The field lacks methodologies for embedding explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems, signaling a need to shift from method proliferation to foundational and structural rigor.

Method: The authors conduct a meta-analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers alongside a survey of XAI practitioners. This dual approach identifies recurring failure patterns: ambiguous problem formulations, poorly specified evaluation criteria, and missing pipelines for explanation-driven feedback loops.

Result: The analysis reveals that cumulative progress in XAI is hindered by three core shortcomings: (1) unclear problem definitions, (2) underspecified evaluation objectives, and (3) absence of actionable feedback mechanisms. These issues persist across top-tier publications and practitioner workflows.

Conclusion: The authors call for a paradigm shift from ad-hoc XAI methods toward foundational clarity. They propose a practical checklist to guide the development of human-centered, action-oriented explanation systems, offering a roadmap for integrating explanations into feedback-driven AI pipelines.

Abstract: Despite the proliferation of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques -- from feature attributions to sparse autoencoders -- explanations rarely influence real-world workflows. In practice, they are often generated and discarded without guiding meaningful action. This gap reflects foundational shortcomings: research has not yet established methodologies for integrating explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems. This position paper argues that the machine learning community must pivot from ad-hoc XAI methods toward addressing foundational & structural challenges, including unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation objectives, and the absence of pipelines for explanation-driven feedback. We support this claim through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of XAI practitioners, revealing recurring issues that limit cumulative progress. We conclude by outlining a practical checklist designed to shift XAI toward a more human-centered, action-oriented paradigm. By emphasizing foundational clarity over the development of ad-hoc methods, we hope to provide a roadmap for integrating explanations into actionable, feedback-driven AI systems.

</details>


### [64] [CARPRT: Class-Aware Zero-Shot Prompt Reweighting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14125)
*Ruijiang Dong,Zesheng Ye,Jianzhong Qi,Lei Feng,Feng Liu,Gang Niu,Masashi Sugiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CARPRT proposes a training-free, class-aware prompt reweighting method for zero-shot VLM classification, assigning per-class weights to prompts based on class-specific relevance rather than using a single shared weighting vector across all classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt ensembling methods use a single weighting vector shared across all classes, implicitly assuming conditional independence between prompts and classes. This assumption fails in practice — e.g., "an aerial view of" suits "airport" but not "apple" — leading to suboptimal zero-shot classification performance.

Method: CARPRT computes class-specific prompt weights in a training-free manner: for each (class, prompt) pair, it averages the image-text relevance scores over all images predicted to belong to that class under that prompt. These estimates are then normalized to produce per-class weighting vectors used during inference.

Result: CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent prompt reweighting methods on standard image classification benchmarks.

Conclusion: Modeling prompt-class dependencies is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and broader VLM applications relying on prompt ensembling.

Abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot image classification by computing the similarity score between an image and textual descriptions, typically formed by inserting a class label (e.g., "cat") into a prompt (e.g., "a photo of a"). Since the score for a given image-class pair is sensitive to the choice of prompt, existing studies ensemble multiple prompts using a weighting vector to aggregate scores across different prompts. Yet, in current strategies, the weighting vector assigned to each prompt is shared across all classes, implicitly assuming that prompts are conditionally independent of classes, which often does not hold in practice, as a prompt like "an aerial view of" might be apt for "airport" but ill-suited for "apple". To address this, we propose class-aware zero-shot prompt reweighting (CARPRT). This scoring scheme adjusts the weighting vector for each class label by capturing the class-specific relevance of different prompts in a training-free manner. For each class label and every available prompt, we quantify their class-specific relevance by averaging image-text relevance scores over images predicted to that class under the given prompt. These estimates are then normalized to derive class-specific weights. Evaluations on standard image classification benchmarks show that CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent reweighting methods, confirming that modeling prompt-class dependencies is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and even broader VLM-based application settings that rely on prompt ensembling. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/CARPRT.

</details>


### [65] [Explainable Geospatial AI for Satellite Ground Station Siting Using LiDAR-Derived Terrain Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14127)
*Shohini Sarkar,Smithi Mahendran,Rishi Chudasama,Varun Mannam,Arav Luthra,Yuvraj Rekhi,Vivek Nadig,Arsh Goenka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning framework using LightGBM with open geospatial data predicts representative clutter height (RCH) with MAE of 1.79m and R²=0.765, outperforming the ITU baseline by over 60%, while maintaining interpretability via SHAP analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ITU-R P.452-18 practice assigns fixed clutter heights per land use class, ignoring within-class variation. This leads to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for LEO ground station siting and spectrum coordination. A globally deployable, data-driven alternative is needed.

Method: RCH is defined as the 75th percentile clutter height. Training labels come from USGS 3DEP LiDAR, and features derive from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. Multiple regressors are evaluated; LightGBM is selected for accuracy, efficiency, and SHAP compatibility. Model evaluation includes standard metrics plus domain-facing criteria: meter-scale error, tolerance band accuracy, over/under-estimation tails, ITU regime agreement, and SHAP-based physical plausibility. International validation uses land-cover matched data.

Result: LightGBM achieves MAE of 1.79m and R²=0.765, reducing absolute error by >60% vs. the ITU baseline. Tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance dominate SHAP feature importance. Non-forest ablations and international validation support global deployability.

Conclusion: Open geospatial data combined with interpretable ML can substantially improve clutter height modeling at global scale without sacrificing deployability or physical interpretability, offering a practical upgrade over static ITU land-use look-up tables for RF planning and spectrum coordination.

Abstract: Representative clutter height (RCH) is a key parameter in radio propagation and interference analysis because it captures the dominant height of local obstructions that drive terminal clutter loss. Current practice often relies on fixed clutter heights assigned to land use classes in Recommendation ITU-R P.452-18, but this misses within class variation and can lead to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for low Earth orbit ground station siting and spectrum coordination. We present an interpretable, globally deployable machine learning framework for predicting RCH from open geospatial data. The model is trained using LiDAR derived labels from the U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program and inference time features from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. We define RCH using a robust 75th percentile clutter height statistic, evaluate multiple regressors, and select LightGBM for its accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility with feature attribution analysis. The final model achieves a mean absolute error of 1.79m and an R^2=0.765, reducing absolute error by more than 60% relative to the ITU baseline. Beyond aggregate fit, we evaluate domain facing criteria relevant to RF planning, including meter scale error, tolerance band accuracy, over and under estimation tails, agreement with ITU clutter height regimes, and SHAP-based physical plausibility. SHAP identifies tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance as the most influential predictors. Studies on segmentation derived features, non-forest ablations, and land-cover matched international validation show that open geospatial data can improve clutter modeling at scale without sacrificing interpretability or deployability.

</details>


### [66] [Certified Domain Consistency for Multi-Domain Retrieval: Label-Free Per-Domain Contamination Control with Conformal Risk Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14157)
*Jayakumar Manoharan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: C3R introduces a drop-in control layer that certifies per-domain contamination budgets in multi-domain retrieval, abstaining when guarantees cannot be met. It uses a two-split scheme with risk-controlling prediction sets to provide finite-sample transfer bounds from inferred to true domains, demonstrating stable certificates across resampled calibrations while outperforming marginal control baselines on worst-domain coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieval over multi-domain corpora often returns wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics fail to detect and that conformal risk control bounds only marginally, systematically under-covering the hardest domains. There is a need for per-domain contamination guarantees rather than aggregate marginal bounds.

Method: C3R is a frozen-stack, reranker-agnostic control layer. It infers a domain posterior without query-time labels, then applies a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets. The finite-sample transfer bound crosses from the inferred domain to the true domain with fully estimable slack, supports heterogeneous per-domain budgets, and can be inverted for deployment. It certifies contamination budgets per domain where feasible, and abstains otherwise rather than silently violating guarantees.

Result: Across 1,000 resampled calibrations, the certificate never violates (stability result), while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw. Soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds, including an independent one from public federal regulations. An LLM-judged downstream probe indicates wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control.

Conclusion: C3R provides reliable per-domain contamination control with formal finite-sample guarantees, outperforming marginal baselines on worst-domain coverage while maintaining practical utility through abstention rather than silent violation.

Abstract: Retrieval over corpora that mix several domains often returns relevant but wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics miss and that conformal risk control bounds only marginally, under-covering the worst domains. This work introduces C3R, a drop-in control layer that, from an inferred domain posterior and no query-time label, certifies a per-domain contamination budget where feasible and otherwise abstains rather than silently violating; on the hardest domains it guarantees a reduction, not a tight bound. The core is a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets, whose finite-sample transfer bound crosses from the inferred to the true domain with fully estimable slack, supports heterogeneous budgets, and inverts for deployment. Population validity rests on this bound and a controlled simulation; across a thousand resampled calibrations the certificate never violates (a stability result) while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw, and soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds including an independent one from public federal regulations, and an LLM-judged downstream probe indicates wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control. The layer is frozen-stack and reranker-agnostic.

</details>


### [67] [QFireNet: A Quantum-Enhanced U-Net for Wildfire Segmentation from Sentinel-2 Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14160)
*Jaiman Munshi,Tanvi Tewary,Sawyer Bloom,Aidan Chu,Chetan Maviti,Kyon Winston-Bey,Harshit Badjatia,Farhan Kittur,Vardhan Madhavarapu,Varun Kota,Joshua Kwon,Nazia Rangwala-Vohra,Franz Klein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes quantum-hybrid U-Net architectures (QB-Net, QuFeX) for wildfire detection from satellite imagery, demonstrating modest improvements over classical U-Net baselines. A key finding is that data mixing across geographically-separated train/test sets significantly boosts performance, with the classical FPN reaching an F1 score of 39.76.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is challenging due to class imbalance, high-dimensional spectral features, and atmospheric interference. The authors hypothesize that quantum machine learning may better model the complex spectral feature space, motivating the development of quantum-hybrid segmentation architectures.

Method: The authors build on U-Net by injecting variational quantum circuits (QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes) into the bottleneck. They compare against a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and explore classical enhancements: parameter compression, alternative loss functions, and uniform data mixing. Cross-dataset transfer validation is performed on the CaBuAr dataset alongside the primary Sen2Fire dataset.

Result: Under matched conditions, QB-Net (F1=31.18) and QuFeX (F1=30.79) outperformed the classical U-Net baseline (F1=28.71). The classical FPN scored 31.13. Data mixing removed domain shift, boosting the classical FPN to F1=39.76. Cross-dataset transfer on CaBuAr validated generalizability.

Conclusion: Quantum machine learning shows potential advantage for wildfire image segmentation, though gains are modest under matched conditions. Data mixing proved critical for addressing domain shift. Further experiments are needed to validate and expand these findings.

Abstract: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is a semantic image segmentation problem that has proven to be difficult due to challenges such as class imbalance, feature complexity, and atmospheric interference. In this paper, we build on the foundational U-Net image segmentation model to develop a quantum-hybrid solution in hopes of more effectively modeling the high-dimensional spectral feature space of the Sen2Fire dataset. We inject a variational quantum circuit in the bottleneck portion of U-Net, specifically the QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes. We test a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) for further comparative analysis of the model, and we also explore classical improvements to the U-Net model and its training process, including a compression of parameters, alternative loss functions, and uniform mixing of input data. Our primary finding is that under matched conditions, both QB-Net (with an $F_1$ score of 31.18) and QuFeX ($F_1 = 30.79$) outperformed the classical U-Net baseline results ($F_1 = 28.71$). Additionally, the classical FPN achieved a comparable score of 31.13. A crucial finding was that data mixing removed a significant domain shift between the geographically-separated train and test sets, which boosted the classical FPN $F_1$ score to 39.76. We validate the architecture's robustness and generalizability to the wildfire detection problem via cross-dataset transfer on the California Burned Areas (CaBuAr) dataset. Overall, we find that quantum machine learning has potential to provide an advantage in the problem of wildfire image segmentation, and further experiments will continue to validate and expand upon this finding.

</details>


### [68] [A Temporal Machine Learning-Based Time-to-Event Model for Predicting ALS Progression and Healthcare Utilization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14190)
*Zongliang Yue,Qi Li,Terry Heiman-Patterson,Frank Bearoff,Zhaohui Qin,Huanmei Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A digital-twin-inspired time-to-event framework integrating ALSFRS-R trajectories with survival modeling enables individualized prediction of functional decline and wheelchair-free survival in ALS, with lower limb function emerging as the strongest predictor of earlier wheelchair access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ALS is heterogeneous and progressive, making it challenging to predict clinically meaningful milestones such as assistive device use. Existing approaches lack individualized, dynamic prediction capabilities that can support proactive care planning.

Method: A harmonized longitudinal dataset was constructed from diagnosis records, ALSFRS-R assessments, ADLs, and demographics. Correlation-based clustering identified functional domains (bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, respiratory).
