When should a user invest in expensive Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) versus lightweight In-Context Learning (ICL)? How does congestion from other users' personalization choices reshape these incentives? And what strategies should platforms adopt when offering multiple personalization algorithms?
  We develop a tractable framework for LLM serving that captures the statistical-economic trade-offs users face. Our analysis yields several surprising insights. First, we show that ICL and SFT dominate in different regimes, determined by an interplay between pretraining coverage and data signal-to-noise ratios, but congestion can flip these rankings. Second, equilibrium resource consumption exhibits pronounced non-monotonicity: improving pretraining precision reduces the congestion, while broader pretraining coverage and harder tasks sometimes increase it. Third, we prove that offering both personalization methods never hurts the platform's maximal profits, despite potentially increasing computational load.
  Experiments with GPT-2 on linear regression tasks validate our theoretical predictions about algorithm performance. Complementing these results, our review of documentation from 21 major AI platforms shows that the share offering both SFT and ICL increased from 9.5% in 2021 to 71.4% in 2025, consistent with our platform-design implications.

</details>


### [90] [Random Logit Scaling: Defending Deep Neural Networks Against Black-Box Score-Based Adversarial Example Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14921)
*Hamid Dashtbani,Mehdi Dousti Gandomani,AmirMahdi Sadeghzadeh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense that confuses black-box score-based attacks by outputting falsified scores from randomly scaled logits, while maintaining model accuracy. Also introduces an adaptive attack that breaks AAA, a state-of-the-art non-randomized black-box defense.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adversarial examples threaten reliable ML deployment, and powerful query-efficient black-box attacks exist. There is a pressing need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses that can counter these attacks without requiring model retraining or significant overhead.

Method: Two contributions: (1) RLS — a plug-and-play post-processing defense that applies random scaling to the logit outputs before producing confidence scores, thereby falsifying score information to mislead score-based black-box attackers while preserving prediction accuracy. (2) An adaptive attack designed specifically to counter AAA, a non-randomized black-box defense that also modifies output logits.

Result: RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks compared to existing randomization-based defenses, while better preserving model accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion. The proposed adaptive attack successfully demonstrates the vulnerability of the AAA defense.

Conclusion: RLS offers an effective, low-effort, plug-and-play defense against score-based black-box adversarial attacks. However, the successful adaptive attack against AAA underscores that defense strategies based on logit manipulation must be rigorously evaluated against adaptive adversaries.

Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly adapted in various domains. However, adversarial examples pose a significant threat to the reliable deployment of these models. In recent years, some powerful adversarial example attacks have been proposed for the fast and query-efficient generation of adversarial examples, even in black-box scenarios, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses. In this work, we present two contributions to the domain of black-box adversarial example attacks and defenses. First, we propose Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense against black-box score-based adversarial example attacks. RLS is a plug-and-play, post-processing defense that can be implemented on top of any existing ML model with minimal effort. The idea behind RLS is to confuse an attacker by outputting falsified scores resulting from randomly scaled logits while maintaining the model accuracy. We show that RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving the accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to state-of-the-art randomization-based defenses. Second, we introduce a novel adaptive attack against AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense against black-box score-based attacks that also modifies output logits to confuse attackers, demonstrating its vulnerability against adaptive attacks.

</details>


### [91] [A Noise-Robust Elicit-to-Optimize Framework for Distortion Riskmetrics via Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14373)
*Yang Liu,Yuhao Liu,Yunran Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework combining adaptive Bayesian inverse RL (for eliciting agents' distortion risk preferences from noisy behavior) with a PPO-based model-free RL algorithm (for optimizing policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics via quantile networks).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IRL methods for preference elicitation often assume rational, noise-free agent behavior and are limited to narrow classes of risk objectives. There is a need for noise-robust preference elicitation under a broad class of distortion riskmetrics, paired with effective policy optimization for those elicited risk preferences in complex environments.

Method: Elicitation: An adaptive Bayesian IRL approach that models agents as taking stochastic, suboptimal actions and infers latent distortion riskmetrics from noisy observations. The method employs a finite set of distinguishing questions and achieves convergence at rate O(exp(-cm + O(√(m log m)))). Optimization: A model-free RL algorithm extending PPO with policy, value, and quantile neural networks. The quantile network estimates the full conditional cost quantile function, enabling numerical evaluation of any distortion riskmetric by expressing it as an integral of the quantile function weighted by the distortion function.

Result: Theoretically, the authors prove existence of a finite distinguishing question set and establish a fast convergence rate for the elicitation algorithm. Empirically, the framework demonstrates high elicitation accuracy and effective policy optimization in complex financial environments.

Conclusion: The proposed elicit-to-optimize framework successfully integrates noise-robust IRL-based preference elicitation with quantile-network-based RL optimization, offering a unified solution for inferring and acting upon agents' distortion risk preferences in realistic, noisy settings.

Abstract: We propose a noise-robust elicit-to-optimize framework that integrates inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and reinforcement learning (RL) for eliciting agents' risk preferences and optimizing policies under a broad class of risk objectives characterized by distortion riskmetrics. On the elicitation side, we propose an adaptive Bayesian IRL method that infers agents' latent risk objectives from their noisy observed decisions, explicitly allowing agents to take stochastic and suboptimal actions. We establish the existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions that identifies the preferred distortion riskmetric within the candidate class and prove that the convergence rate of the algorithm is of order $O(\exp(-cm+O(\sqrt{m\log m})))$ under general settings, where $c>0$ is a constant and $m$ denotes the number of algorithm iterations. On the optimization side, we develop a model-free RL algorithm for optimizing policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics. By representing the objective as an integral of the conditional cost quantile function with respect to the distortion function, the method unifies distortion-riskmetric objectives. We optimize diverse risk objectives by extending the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm with policy, value, and quantile neural networks, where the quantile network estimates the full conditional cost quantile function and enables numerical evaluation of general risk objectives. A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates the framework's elicitation accuracy and effectiveness in complex financial environments.

</details>


### [92] [Integration Matters: Rollout-Based Training for Constrained Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14398)
*Xiaoxuan Liang,Saeid Naderiparizi,Berend Zwartsenberg,Frank Wood*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a fine-tuning framework for constrained generative models that aligns training with sampling by incorporating online rollout-based constraint guidance, differentiating through the noise schedule used in the denoising process to expose the model to trajectory-level constraint violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing constrained generation methods suffer from a training-sampling mismatch: training-time optimization operates on states from the training distribution (different from sampling-time states), while sampling-time correction introduces distribution shift and requires costly per-task tuning. The authors aim to bridge this gap by aligning training directly with the sampling trajectory.

Method: The method fine-tunes a diffusion model by incorporating constraint guidance via online rollout during training. It differentiates through the fixed noise schedule that numerically integrates the denoising process, exposing the model to constraint violations that naturally emerge along the denoising trajectory. This aligns diffusion learning with the actual sampling process.

Result: Experiments across multiple tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves improved constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior constrained generation methods.

Conclusion: Aligning training with the sampling trajectory via online rollout and differentiation through the noise schedule effectively addresses the train-sampling mismatch in constrained generation, yielding better constraint adherence without sacrificing generation quality.

Abstract: Constrained generative models aim to produce samples that satisfy complex feasibility constraints while remaining faithful to the data distribution. Existing constrained generation methods typically enforce constraints either through training-time optimization or sampling-time correction. Training-time optimization approaches optimize on states induced by the training distribution, which can differ substantially from those encountered during sampling. Sampling-time correction methods instead modify the sampling process at inference, introducing distribution shift and requiring expensive tuning, particularly for few-step sampling. We propose a fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance obtained through online rollout into the training process, which aligns training with sampling by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used to numerically integrate the denoising process. This exposes the model to violations that arise along the denoising trajectory and aligns diffusion learning with the sampling process. Experiments across multiple tasks show that our method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior methods.

</details>


### [93] [LATTICE: Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Spatial Omics Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14410)
*Jagan Mohan Reddy Dwarampudi,Veena Kochat,Suresh Satpati,Kunal Rai,Tania Banerjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LATTICE is a graph-based self-supervised framework that integrates five multimodal omics modalities (Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, spatial CUT&Tag) per Visium spot into unified embeddings. Tested on an 11-sample melanoma cohort (54,912 spots), it improved cluster concordance and spatial contiguity over single-modality baselines, though additional chromatin modalities sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived labels, suggesting capture of regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly collect both transcriptomic and epigenomic data, but downstream analysis remains dominated by single-modality pipelines that fail to exploit the complementary information across modalities. There is a need for methods that can learn joint representations capturing transcriptomic, chromatin accessibility, and histone modification states within their spatial context.

Method: LATTICE combines five aligned modality blocks per Visium spot: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT&Tag. It constructs a spatial neighborhood graph and trains a TransformerConv encoder with three self-supervised objectives: (1) masked reconstruction, (2) cross-modal alignment, and (3) spatial smoothness. The framework learns spot-level latent embeddings that harmonize multimodal features within a unified lattice representation.

Result: On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort (54,912 spots), LATTICE showed stable optimization and reproducible embeddings across seeds. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA improved ARI (+0.157), NMI (+0.143), and spatial contiguity (+0.174) relative to Space Ranger clusters. Incorporating additional epigenomic modalities further boosted spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS) but sometimes reduced concordance with RNA-derived reference labels, indicating the embeddings capture chromatin and regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity.

Conclusion: LATTICE provides a practical framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, empirically demonstrating the value of joint transcriptomic-epigenomic modeling. However, the trade-off between capturing regulatory structure and maintaining concordance with RNA-derived labels underscores the need for stronger supervision strategies and broader external benchmarking.

Abstract: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly combine transcriptomic and epigenomic assays, yet downstream analysis is often still performed using single-modality pipelines. We present LATTICE (Latent Alignment of Tissue-level and Transcriptomic Information for Cross-modal Embedding), a graph-based self-supervised framework that learns spot-level representations from harmonized multimodal features. LATTICE integrates five aligned modality blocks per Visium spot: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT\&Tag. These modalities capture spatial transcriptomic measurements, single-cell inferred regulatory activity, and in situ chromatin and histone states within a unified lattice representation. LATTICE constructs a spatial neighborhood graph and trains a TransformerConv encoder using masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness objectives. On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort from an anonymized clinical collaborator comprising 54{,}912 total spots, LATTICE demonstrated stable optimization behavior, reproducible embeddings across analysis seeds, and complete multimodal integration across all samples. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA alone substantially improved concordance with Space Ranger clusters across 11 runs (adjusted Rand index [ARI] +0.157, normalized mutual information [NMI] +0.143, and spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS), although they sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived reference labels, likely because the learned embeddings captured chromatin and regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity alone. These results position LATTICE as a practical and empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, while also highlighting the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking.

</details>


### [94] [Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14418)
*Mohammad Rashid,Hema Yoganarasimhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A large-scale field experiment on an Android app store (5M+ users) shows that increasing ad slots raises revenue up to 43% but reduces conversions up to 5% and engagement up to 2.2%, with substantial heterogeneity across query types. The authors design e-LAAL, an adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts ad load per query, and demonstrate its superiority in a production deployment serving 22.3M users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ad-load design on sponsored search platforms involves a fundamental trade-off: more ad slots boost revenue but may crowd out organic results, harming user experience (conversions, engagement). Static, uniform ad-load policies fail to account for heterogeneity across queries and over time. The authors aim to quantify this trade-off empirically and develop a principled, adaptive solution that optimizes the revenue--user-outcome frontier at scale.

Method: First, a large-scale RCT on an Android app store exposes 5M+ users to 1–6 sponsored slots, estimating causal effects on revenue, conversions, and engagement with heterogeneity analysis across query types and advertiser composition. Second, the authors propose e-LAAL (exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load): a model-free, query-level decision rule combining (1) LAAL, which updates ad-load recommendations using recent empirical outcomes per query, and (2) static exploration arms that ensure support and provide counterfactual benchmarks. A finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee is derived. Finally, e-LAAL is deployed in production on 22.3M users and 77.6M searches.

Result: The RCT shows: +43% max revenue gain from higher ad load; up to −5% total search conversions and −2.2% daily engagement. Gains are concentrated in high-ad-conversion queries; low-conversion queries see little or negative marginal revenue. Advertiser composition (e.g., brand presence) shifts the trade-off within query. In production, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off over static benchmarks, outperforming both uniform and historical query-dependent static policies.

Conclusion: Ad-load optimization should be query-adaptive and dynamic. Uniform policies leave substantial value on the table. e-LAAL provides a theoretically grounded, deployable framework that balances exploration and exploitation to continuously improve platform outcomes, offering a practical blueprint for supply-side optimization in sponsored search.

Abstract: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

</details>


### [95] [HyperShadow: A Benchmark for Detecting 3D Projections of Higher-Dimensional Spatial Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14419)
*Akshay Sasi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HyperShadow is a novel benchmark that challenges models to distinguish native 3D point clouds from "shadows" (projections) of higher-dimensional (4D–6D) rigid objects. Unlike intrinsic dimension estimation (which fails at ~71–73% accuracy), the task requires detecting projection-specific signatures — density folds, radial profiles, and topological changes — which a lightweight point network solves at 96.6% accuracy. A temporal variant using Kabsch alignment residuals achieves near-perfect separation (AUROC 0.982).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing "4D" datasets treat the fourth dimension as time, not space. The authors argue that studying projections from genuinely higher spatial dimensions (R^4 to R^6) into 3D reveals fundamental geometric signatures — density concentrations, self-intersections, topological features — that are undetectable by standard intrinsic dimension estimators. The benchmark serves as a controlled instrument to probe what observable statistics can certify incompatibility with a purely 3D origin.

Method: The authors generate "shadow" point clouds by projecting rigid higher-dimensional objects (convex hulls of random point sets, superellipsoids, procedural shapes) from R^N (N=4–6) into R^3 via random orthographic projections. Native 3D shapes serve as negatives. A 190k-parameter PointNet-style architecture classifies 3D vs. shadow across four corruption tiers (varying noise, occlusion, sparsity). A temporal track uses rigidly rotating objects; the Kabsch algorithm computes optimal 3D rigid alignment between consecutive frames, and the alignment residual — exactly zero for true 3D rotation, strictly positive for higher-D shadows — serves as a zero-parameter witness. Baselines include TwoNN and Levina-Bickel MLE intrinsic dimension estimators.

Result: Intrinsic dimension estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) achieve only 71–73% accuracy, confirming the task is not reducible to dimension estimation. The 190k-parameter point network reaches 96.6% accuracy across corruption tiers and generalizes at 79–91% to unseen object families. On the temporal track, the Kabsch residual witness separates classes at AUROC 0.982, providing a fully interpretable, zero-parameter decision rule.

Conclusion: Detecting higher-dimensional provenance in 3D data relies on geometric signatures — density folds, filled volumes, radial profiles, topology — that intrinsic dimension estimators miss. The Kabsch residual offers a principled, interpretable rigidity witness for temporal sequences. HyperShadow provides a reproducible, seed-controlled benchmark for studying what observable statistics certify dimensional origin.

Abstract: Machine-learning datasets labelled "4D" universally denote three spatial dimensions plus time. We introduce HyperShadow, the first public benchmark in which the fourth, fifth, and sixth dimensions are spatial: the task is to decide whether a 3D point cloud is a native three-dimensional shape or the projection, the "shadow", of a rigid object living in R^N (N = 4-6). We show this task is fundamentally distinct from intrinsic-dimension estimation: a shadow is still at-most-3-dimensional data, and standard estimators (TwoNN, Levina-Bickel MLE) reach only 71-73% accuracy. Detection instead requires projection signatures, density folds, filled volumes with characteristic radial profiles, and topology changes, which a 190k-parameter point network recovers at 96.6% accuracy across four corruption tiers, generalizing at 79-91% to object families never seen in training. On a temporal track of rigidly rotating objects we introduce a zero-parameter rigidity witness: the residual of the optimal rigid 3D alignment (Kabsch) between consecutive frames, which must vanish for any rigid 3D motion but cannot vanish for the shadow of a rigid rotation in R^N. This single interpretable statistic separates the classes at AUROC 0.982. All data are generated reproducibly from seeds; the dataset, models, and code are released publicly. HyperShadow makes no claim about physical reality; it is a controlled instrument for studying which observable statistics can certify incompatibility with a purely three-dimensional explanation.

</details>


### [96] [Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14439)
*Andrew Liao,Hanchen Cui,Karthik Desingh,Aryan Deshwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An active evaluation framework for robot manipulation policies that uses a probabilistic surrogate model to adaptively select test configurations, maximizing information gain about policy performance. Across 2331 real-world evaluations, it reduces required trials by 20-40% compared to random testing while better identifying failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigorous evaluation of generalist robot manipulation policies is fundamentally challenging due to the combinatorial explosion of task factors (object poses, camera viewpoints, etc.) that affect real-world performance. Exhaustive evaluation is intractable, and current narrow test suites miss critical failure modes and misrepresent deployment readiness, while real hardware evaluation is expensive and slow.

Method: The authors formulate policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. They fit a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively select evaluation configurations that maximize information gain about the policy's performance distribution. This enables sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and systematic identification of failure-prone regions.

Result: Across 2331 real-world evaluations spanning 3 tasks with 3 factor variations each, the active evaluation framework saves 20-40% of evaluation trials compared to typical random testing while providing more informative characterization of policy performance.

Conclusion: Active evaluation via sequential experimental design offers a more efficient and thorough alternative to standard random testing for robot manipulation policies, enabling better understanding of policy behavior with fewer real-world trials.

Abstract: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness. We propose an active evaluation framework that addresses this challenge by treating policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. Our approach fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain over the policy's performance distribution, allowing for sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and a systematic identification of failure-prone regions. We conduct 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations and find that our approach typically saves the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.

</details>


### [97] [Depth-Dependent Hidden-State Collapse in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14463)
*Patricia Medina,Hy P. G. Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSAE hidden representations collapse to near-constant values at encoder depth K=5, destroying class-separability and yielding uniform macro F1 scores (0.224688) across all classifiers, regardless of feature augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the behavior and potential failure modes of Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification, specifically examining how encoder depth and feature augmentation affect representation quality and classification performance.

Method: Trained DSAE architectures with encoder depths K=1 through K=5, using both raw spatial coordinates (xyz) and xyz augmented with Product Coefficient features. Evaluated hidden representations using Random Forest, kNN, and a Dummy majority-class baseline, monitoring hidden-state standard deviation and macro F1 scores. Provided a formal proof bounding between-class scatter by total hidden scatter, linking it to hidden-state variance.

Result: At K=5, hidden-state standard deviation collapses to ~10⁻⁵ for both input types, and all three classifiers yield identical macro F1 = 0.224688. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse classification performance nor prevent the depth-induced collapse.

Conclusion: Large-depth representation collapse is a concrete failure mode in DSAE-based LiDAR classification. The theoretical bound demonstrates that near-constant hidden representations cannot preserve class-separating structure, identifying a critical limitation for scaling DSAE depth.

Abstract: We study Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification using spatial coordinates and Product Coefficient feature augmentations. The experiments compare separately trained DSAE architectures at encoder depths $K=1,\ldots,5$ and evaluate the resulting hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline. The main finding is a hidden-state collapse at $K=5$. For both xyz and xyz plus Product Coefficient inputs, the hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of $10^{-5}$, while all three classifiers attain the same macro F1 score of $0.224688$. We prove that between-class hidden scatter is bounded by total hidden scatter, which in turn is controlled by the reported hidden-state variance. Thus a nearly constant hidden representation cannot retain substantial class-separating structure. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the $K=5$ collapse in the present DSAE setting. These results identify large-depth representation collapse as a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification.

</details>


### [98] [Interleaved Noise Injection Improves Clean, Corrupted, and OOD Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14466)
*Matt L. Wiemann,Peter Melchior,Andrew K. Saydjari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Interleaved (on-off) noise injection with gradient-norm stabilization significantly improves model robustness and generalization across clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data, with impulse noise regularizing convolutional architectures and Gaussian noise regularizing attention-based models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard noise injection uses monotonic decay schedules, which limit exploration and risk catastrophic forgetting. The authors investigate whether an interleaved schedule can better leverage noise injection's regularizing properties to escape local minima, improve robustness, and boost performance on both clean and corrupted data without additional computational cost.

Method: An interleaved noise injection schedule that alternates between clean and noisy data phases. Impulse noise is used to approximate Jacobian regularization, while Gaussian noise approximates curvature penalty. A gradient-norm stabilization technique scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes to prevent loss instability during phase switching. The method is stackable with other augmentations and tested on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R across ResNet and ViT architectures.

Result: Substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts. Impulse noise counteracts the locality bias of CNNs (ResNet), while Gaussian noise reduces attention-based models' tendency to latch onto large-scale spurious features. Best results achieved when stacking interleaved noise injection on top of other augmentations. Saliency and attention maps confirm distinct regularization effects per architecture type.

Conclusion: Interleaved noise injection is an effective, zero-cost tool for improving test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data. Its success stems from penalizing architecture-specific failure modes: locality bias in CNNs and spurious large-scale feature reliance in ViTs.

Abstract: Noise injection is a well-known technique in stochastic optimization. We report its surprising effectiveness with an interleaved (on-off-on-off...) rather than the usual monotonic decay schedule. We present a theoretical analysis of noise injection, which confirms that corruption by impulse noise approximates a Jacobian regularization, whereas Gaussian noise acts as a curvature penalty. This regularization behavior has been invoked to explain why noise injection increases model robustness. But the interleaved nature of our proposed schedule produces superior results even for the optimization objective: mixing phases of noisy data permits the optimizer to escape local minima and increase exploration without the risk of catastrophically forgetting the important features from the clean data. To stabilize this training scheme against the rapid changes of the loss when switching between clean and noisy data, we introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes. We compare this method with other common augmentation methods and find substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures, with the best results being achieved by stacking our method on top of other augmentations. Through saliency and attention maps we show that the effect of interleaved noise injection stems from penalizing the failure modes encouraged by the inductive bias of the models: impulse noise works against the locality bias of convolutional (ResNet) architectures, and Gaussian noise reduces the tendency of attention-based models to pick up large-scale spurious features. Interleaved noise injection is therefore an effective tool to improve the test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data at essentially zero computational cost.

</details>


### [99] [Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14506)
*Yuxuan Zhu,Rohan Alur,Daniel Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for billion-parameter LLMs fine-tuned with RLVR, using PAC-Bayes compression bounds and Gumbel-max reparameterization. The proposed Progressive RLVR framework combines RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and quantization, achieving 14,796x compressibility while retaining 84-97% of standard LoRA performance, with bounds exceeding base model accuracy by 9-51%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RLVR is widely used to enhance LLM reasoning, the generalizability of resulting models is poorly understood. Prior generalization bounds for deep learning are either vacuous at scale or inapplicable to the stochastic token-generation process in RLVR-tuned LLMs. The authors aim to provide rigorous, non-vacuous guarantees on generalization for RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale.

Method: The authors adapt PAC-Bayes compression bounds to the RLVR setting, addressing token-generation stochasticity via the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick, which enables differentiable sampling and well-defined posterior distributions over discretized token sequences. They then propose Progressive RLVR, a framework integrating: (1) RLVR with verifiable rewards, (2) on-policy distillation to stabilize training, (3) TinyLoRA (ultra-low-rank adaptation) for extreme parameter efficiency, and (4) model quantization to further compress the posterior. Generalization bounds are computed as the difference between empirical reward and a PAC-Bayes complexity term based on KL divergence between the compressed posterior and a pretrained prior.

Result: Progressive RLVR retains 84-97% of standard LoRA fine-tuning performance while yielding models that are 14,796× more compressible. The resulting non-vacuous generalization bounds are demonstrated across four domains (math, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, Text-to-SQL). These bounds exceed the base model's accuracy by 9-51% and fall within 6-11% of the fine-tuned models' accuracy, confirming that the learned reasoning capabilities generalize beyond the training distribution.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that non-vacuous generalization guarantees are achievable for RLVR fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs. Progressive RLVR provides a practical recipe for obtaining both strong empirical performance and rigorous generalization bounds, bridging the gap between theoretical PAC-Bayes analysis and real-world LLM reasoning tasks. The extreme compressibility (14,796×) suggests RLVR-acquired reasoning skills can be encoded in very few parameters.

Abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the generalizability of the resulting models remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale. Our approach adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds to this setting, and addresses the inherent stochasticity of token generation by applying the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. To operationalize these bounds, we propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization. Progressive RLVR empirically retains 84-97% performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning while producing models that are 14,796x more compressible. We show that this framework yields non-vacuous generalization bounds in four domains: mathematical problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL. Our bounds exceed the accuracy of the base model by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of the accuracy of the fine-tuned models.

</details>


### [100] [Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14516)
*Akhilesh Gogikar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates higher-order Runge-Kutta integrators (specifically Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) with adaptive step control) applied to neural network training under strict compute-matched protocols. Under fair gradient-budget accounting, the adaptive RK variant loses to plain Adam; its "adaptivity" proves illusory (step size pins at maximum). Repairing the method with correct error control yields lower training loss but no test accuracy gain. A secondary finding shows gradient averaging acts as a mild implicit regularizer, but cheaper first-order baselines match or exceed it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work interprets optimizers as discretizations of gradient flows and motivates applying higher-order adaptive ODE integrators (e.g., Runge-Kutta) to neural network training. However, the literature rarely enforces compute-matched comparisons — adaptive methods consume more gradient evaluations per step, creating an unfair advantage. This paper aims to rigorously evaluate whether higher-order adaptive integration provides genuine benefits when all methods receive equal gradient-evaluation budgets.

Method: The authors build a representative Adam variant using the Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) embedded Runge-Kutta pair with FSAL (First Same As Last) reuse and local-error step control. They evaluate under a strict compute-matched protocol: all methods get identical gradient-evaluation budgets. Experiments cover both minibatch and full-batch training. They instrument the method to diagnose adaptivity behavior (step size, error vs. tolerance). They also test a repaired version with a true reject branch and error computed on the applied map, isolate adaptivity via a fixed-step control, and conduct an n=10 seed study comparing gradient averaging against lr-matched Adam, AdamW, RMSprop, and NAdam.

Result: Under compute-matched conditions, the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch settings. Instrumentation reveals the adaptivity is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, step size pins at the growth cap from step one (98–100% of steps), and tolerances spanning 100× yield bit-identical trajectories. The method reduces to fixed-step Adam with averaged gradients at 3–4× cost. The repaired version achieves ~40× lower training loss than tuned Adam in full-batch, with adaptivity manifesting as an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule. However, gains are fragile to initial step size and do not improve test accuracy. The n=10 study confirms gradient averaging as a weak implicit regularizer (beats Adam/AdamW on 10/10 seeds), but RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at one-third the per-step cost.

Conclusion: Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect from gradient averaging, but nothing that cheaper, well-tuned first-order baselines (Adam, AdamW, RMSprop, NAdam) do not already provide. The apparent benefits of adaptive RK methods in prior work are artifacts of unfair compute accounting.

Abstract: Interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations has motivated applying higher-order Runge-Kutta (RK) integrators to neural networks. We build a representative Adam variant (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair, FSAL reuse, local-error step control) and evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol giving every method the same gradient-evaluation budget - an accounting this literature rarely enforces. Under it the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch (RK's best-case) training. Instrumenting it shows the "adaptivity" is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, the step size pins at its growth cap from step one (98-100 percent of steps), and no rtol x hmax x h0 setting makes it act; tolerances spanning 100x give bit-identical trajectories. The method is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost. Repairing it (true reject branch; error on the applied map) reverses the full-batch result - about 40x lower training loss than tuned Adam - and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity (an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule) as the mechanism. But the gain is fragile to the initial step size and does not reach test accuracy. A pre-registered follow-up rules out the obvious explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob only hurts - leaving a trajectory effect, the controller selecting a minimum generalizing 1.3-3.4 points below first-order descent at equal depth. An n=10 study confirms one secondary effect: gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds - yet RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline does not already provide.

</details>


### [101] [A Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning Framework for Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14522)
*Zikun Zhang,Jiayuan Sheng,David D. Yao,Wenpin Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formulates continuous-time RL with discrete states using controlled CTMCs, derives continuous-time PPO/GRPO variants, and applies this framework to fine-tune score-based discrete diffusion models (especially masked diffusion LLMs) with intermediate rewards, introducing trajectory subsampling for computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GRPO-based RL fine-tuning of diffusion models relies only on terminal rewards and ignores intermediate signals along the denoising trajectory. There is also a lack of a principled continuous-time RL formulation for discrete state spaces that can handle reward-driven optimization of discrete diffusion models without requiring differentiable rewards.

Method: The authors model state dynamics as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) and derive policy gradient methods yielding continuous-time PPO and GRPO. For masked diffusion models (MDMs), they exploit analytically tractable probability ratios over the vocabulary simplex. For diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), they propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate per-position probability ratios without computing full trajectory likelihoods.

Result: The framework is validated on low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and on RL post-training of dLLMs for mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, demonstrating effectiveness in both settings.

Conclusion: The continuous-time CTMC-based RL framework provides a unified, principled approach to reward optimization in discrete diffusion models, enabling intermediate reward incorporation and efficient policy optimization. The trajectory subsampling technique makes the approach computationally feasible for large-scale dLLMs.

Abstract: We formulate reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time with discrete state spaces and possibly arbitrary action spaces via a stochastic control approach, where the state dynamics are modeled as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). We consider policy optimization problems and derive the corresponding policy gradient methods, leading to continuous-time variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). As a primary application, we develop a complete continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models. The proposed framework enables reward-driven optimization without requiring differentiability on the reward signals. In contrast to the existing GRPO-based approaches that only rely on terminal rewards, our formulation allows intermediate reward or advantage signals to be incorporated throughout the denoising trajectory. Importantly, when specialized to masked diffusion models (MDMs), our framework encompasses a rich class of policy parameterizations over the vocabulary simplex with analytically tractable probability ratios, providing a unified perspective on exploration and policy optimization in MDMs. For masked diffusion large language models (dLLMs), we further propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate computationally prohibitive trajectory likelihoods, reducing the computational cost of computing per-position probability ratios. We showcase the effectiveness of our methods on both low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of dLLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

</details>


### [102] [xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14530)
*Xiangdong Zhang,Xiaohan Qin,Sunan Zou,Tuo Dai,Xiaoming Shi,Huaijin Wu,Yebin Yang,Zhuo Xia,Shaofeng Zhang,Lin Yao,Yuliang Liu,Yu Cheng,Junchi Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: xHC enables practical scaling of Hyper-Connections beyond N=4 by addressing write-back information bottlenecks and cubic-cost residual mixing via temporal feature augmentation and sparse stream updates, with xHC-Flash further reducing memory traffic for LLM pre-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HC-family methods plateau at N=4 due to two bottlenecks: (1) insufficient write-back information for expanding streams, and (2) residual-mixing generation cost that scales cubically with N. The authors aim to overcome these to unlock meaningful expansion beyond N=4.

Method: xHC introduces two key innovations: (a) temporal feature augmentation to enrich write-back information to all streams, and (b) a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only k=4 out of N=16 streams while maintaining dense read access. xHC-Flash further optimizes memory traffic, reducing per-sublayer traffic from 73.5C to 40C (comparable to mHC at N=4's 34C).

Result: On 18B MoE models, xHC improves average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC with modest training FLOPs overhead. Scaling-law experiments show vanilla and mHC require 1.50× and 1.19× the compute of xHC to reach the same loss. xHC-Flash matches full xHC gains while drastically reducing memory traffic.

Conclusion: xHC and xHC-Flash together make large-N residual-stream expansion both effective and practical for LLM pre-training, establishing residual-stream expansion as a viable scaling axis beyond model width and depth.

Abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of Transformers into $N$ parallel streams, providing a form of memory scaling beyond model width and depth. Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from $N{=}1$ to $N{=}4$ suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at $N{=}4$. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with $N$. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond $N{=}4$. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only $k=4$ of the $N=16$ streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require $1.50\times$ and $1.19\times$ the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-$N$ training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. We therefore introduce xHC-Flash, which reduces the per-sublayer memory traffic from $73.5C$ to $40C$, comparable to the $34C$ required by mHC at $N{=}4$, while retaining the gains of full xHC. Together, xHC and xHC-Flash make large-$N$ residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training.

</details>


### [103] [Muse: Representation Geometry of Muon Beyond Normalized Momentum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14536)
*Da Chang,Qiankun Shi,Lvgang Zhang,Di He,Yaoshuai Ma,Ganzhao Yuan,Yongxiang Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper formalizes the representation choice in Muon-style optimizers as a geometric degree of freedom, introducing a family of optimizers that vary the Frobenius-isometric representation of matrix parameters. The shorter dimension of the representation governs singular-channel support, pullback scaling, and convergence constants. Experiments show balanced non-native representations match native performance, while over-contracting the shorter dimension collapses behavior toward normalized momentum.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map (Newton–Schulz) to matrix momentum, but the representation of the parameter block before orthogonalization is an understudied design choice. The authors aim to formalize this choice as "optimizer geometry" and understand how different Frobenius-isometric representations affect training dynamics, convergence, and empirical performance.

Method: The authors propose a family of Muon-style optimizers that unifies native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations under the same momentum update and Newton–Schulz backend. They analyze each representation as inducing a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry. Theoretical analysis derives how the shorter matrix dimension controls singular-channel capacity, pullback scaling, and constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. A teacher–student model with curvature collapse and Marchenko–Pastur spectral dynamics connects early-stage dissipation to the nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Empirical validation uses LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M pretraining runs plus fixed-momentum diagnostics.

Result: Balanced non-native representations (e.g., nearest-square) can match or approach native representation performance in pretraining. Reducing the shorter dimension weakens scaling and singular-channel support, causing the optimizer to behave increasingly like normalized momentum. The teacher–student analysis links early dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio via Marchenko–Pastur spectral profiles.

Conclusion: Representation choice in Muon-style optimizers is a meaningful geometric hyperparameter. Balanced non-native representations are viable alternatives to the native shape, but aggressively shrinking the shorter dimension degrades the optimizer toward normalized momentum, losing the benefits of structured matrix updates.

Abstract: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, but their updates also depend on the representation of each parameter block before orthogonalization. We study this representation choice as a form of optimizer geometry and introduce {\method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers that shares the same momentum rule and Newton--Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry, in which the shorter matrix dimension determines the number of supported singular channels, the pullback scaling, and the constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. In a teacher--student model, curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko--Pastur spectral profile connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M, together with fixed-momentum diagnostics, show that balanced non-native representations can match the performance of the native representation, whereas reducing the shorter dimension weakens the scaling and singular-channel support, leading to behavior that increasingly resembles normalized momentum.

</details>


### [104] [CASP: Learning-Augmented Offline Approximation with Verifiable Certificates and Bounded-Loss PAC Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14545)
*Haifeng Li,Mo Hai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CASP proposes a framework where machine-learned predictions guide NP-hard optimization by identifying ignorable parts of the search space, but each pruning decision is verified by a polynomial-time sound verifier before acceptance, guaranteeing correctness regardless of prediction quality. The paper develops the learning theory of this design, showing the verifier makes the loss class uniformly bounded (enabling sample-efficient learning), proves impossibility results for unverified commitment, derives closed-form advantages of verifiable confidence filtering over standard min-combination, and demonstrates that predictions remain useful even given LP solutions by breaking ties on degenerate optimal faces. Experiments on five problems confirm theoretical predictions, with verified deployment losing nothing under distribution shift while unverified pruning loses up to 26% of optimality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline NP-hard optimization can be accelerated using ML predictions, but directly committing to a predictor's output forfeits worst-case guarantees — a single bad prediction can ruin solution quality. The authors aim to develop a principled framework that harnesses predictions to prune search spaces while maintaining soundness guarantees through polynomial-time verification, and to provide a formal learning theory characterizing when and why this certificate-augmented approach succeeds where unverified commitment fails.

Method: CASP asks a predictor which parts of the search space can be pruned, but only accepts each answer after a sound polynomial-time verifier checks it against the instance. The predictor outputs certificate parameters; the verifier either confirms the pruning is safe or rejects it. The paper analyzes the induced loss class, proving it is uniformly bounded (enabling $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ sample complexity), contrasts this with unverified commitment which admits no distribution-free rate and has $\Omega(R/\varepsilon^2)$ lower bounds under cost spread $R$. They derive closed-form margins showing that filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates standard min-combination, and prove that symmetric LP policies (whose commitments depend only on verifiable confidence values) provably stall on degenerate optimal faces, motivating prediction-based tie-breaking.

Result: The certificate-augmented loss class is uniformly bounded, yielding sample complexity $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$. Unverified commitment admits no distribution-free learning rate and suffers $\Omega(R/\varepsilon^2)$ lower bounds. Verifiable confidence filtering dominates min-combination with a closed-form margin. Symmetric LP policies provably stall on degenerate optimal faces. Experiments on five NP-hard problems confirm: under distribution shift, unverified pruning loses up to 26% of optimum, while verified deployment of identical predictions loses nothing.

Conclusion: CASP demonstrates that coupling ML predictions with sound polynomial-time verification yields a practical framework for accelerating NP-hard optimization without sacrificing worst-case guarantees. The learning theory shows certificate parameters are efficiently learnable in ways that unverified commitments are not. The approach is robust to distribution shift and remains beneficial even when LP relaxations are available, by resolving degeneracy.

Abstract: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

</details>


### [105] [Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14563)
*Tatthapong Srikitrungruang,Jaesung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PIE-PINN proposes a probabilistic framework using Laplace distributions and B-spline-guided neural networks with hierarchical half-Cauchy priors to robustly estimate heterogeneous elastic properties (Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) from noisy, low-resolution displacement measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement data is severely ill-posed: low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneity, and small measurement errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing methods depend on high-fidelity data and manually tuned loss weights, making them brittle under noise and resolution degradation.

Method: PIE-PINN unifies three components in a probabilistic Laplace-likelihood model: (1) displacement observation residuals, (2) strain-discrepancy residuals, and (3) equilibrium residuals. A B-spline-guided displacement network provides smooth global displacement representation with a neural network correction for local variations. A hierarchical half-Cauchy model adaptively learns displacement residual scales, automatically downweighting severe fitting errors. Training uses alternating maximum-likelihood: weighted residual minimization updates the mean displacement field, and scale updates adjust loss weights.

Result: Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate that PIE-PINN achieves robust recovery of both Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio fields, outperforming conventional inverse methods particularly under high noise and low resolution.

Conclusion: PIE-PINN provides a principled, adaptive framework for inverse elasticity that automatically handles noise and resolution degradation without manual loss-weight tuning, enabled by its probabilistic formulation with heavy-tailed Laplace likelihoods and hierarchical scale modeling.

Abstract: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse elasticity problem because low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneous property variations, and small measurement perturbations or fitting errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing inverse methods often rely on high-fidelity observations and manually prespecified loss weights, limiting their adaptability and making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. We propose a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework for robust estimation of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data. PIE-PINN models displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. To improve robustness, the framework combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global representation of the displacement field, while the neural network correction captures local variations. The hierarchical scale model adaptively downweights severe displacement fitting errors, enabling more robust recovery of the latent mean displacement field. An alternating maximum-likelihood training strategy updates the mean through weighted residual minimization and updates the scales to adjust the loss weights. Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate the robustness of PIE-PINN.

</details>


### [106] [Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14571)
*Dante Lok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gate-zero growth is a function-preserving operator for continual learning that adds residual blocks via zero-initialized gates, inducing rank separation in the functional Jacobian. This ensures old function directions are preserved, new-weight directions are initially flat, and only gate directions contribute first-order variation, yielding controlled function drift O(‖α‖²) and Jacobian leakage O(‖α‖∞). Empirical results on a 300M→857M Transformer show near-zero forgetting, outperforming non-FP baselines by an order of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual learning (CL) suffers from catastrophic forgetting when expanding network capacity. Existing function-preserving (FP) operators like Net2Net allow safe capacity expansion but lack formal analysis of how function drift and Jacobian leakage behave as new parameters are trained. The authors aim to provide a principled, geometrically grounded FP operator with provably controlled departure from the FP locus during subsequent training.

Method: The authors propose gate-zero growth: new residual blocks are added with a zero-initialized scalar gate α=0, ensuring exact function preservation at initialization. Under a transversality condition (new block output not parallel to existing directions), the functional Jacobian exhibits rank separation: old parameter columns are unchanged, new-weight columns are zero (flat), and only gate columns carry first-order functional variation. This yields function drift bounded by O(‖α‖²) and Jacobian leakage bounded by O(‖α‖∞). The framework is shown to subsume LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters as instances of the same local geometry.

Result: On a 300M→857M parameter Transformer expanded from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth achieves near-zero old-domain forgetting (Δ_A < 0.1) under both Isolation (exact preservation) and Freeze-Nothing (joint-frontier) operating points. In contrast, a non-FP control (G_stack, where new blocks are simply stacked without gate-zero initialization) yields an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under identical conditions.

Conclusion: Gate-zero growth provides a theoretically grounded, canonical FP operator for continual learning, with provable bounds on function drift and Jacobian leakage. Its geometric analysis unifies several existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (LoRA, ReZero, zero-init adapters) under a shared local geometry, establishing a principled foundation for safe capacity activation in continual learning.

Abstract: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

</details>


### [107] [Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14576)
*Hyemin Gu,Michael Tyrrell,Tuhin Sahai,Markos A. Katsoulakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a "sublinear-growth principle" for deep residual architectures, establishing that the velocity field of each residual block must satisfy ∥v(x,t)∥ ≤ c∥x∥^q + b with q ∈ [0,1]. This exponent threshold q ≤ 1 is proven both necessary and sufficient for stable training via ODE theory (global forward flow) and optimal control analysis (Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman). The framework provides an arithmetic for certifying stability at the architectural level and demonstrates that a parameter-free modification can reduce Mamba from q=5 to q=1, achieving stable training without layer normalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep residual architectures are typically treated as discretized ODEs, but the conditions under which these continuous-time analogs admit well-posed forward dynamics, stable adjoint sensitivity, and well-controlled training have not been sharply characterized. The authors seek to replace ad hoc architectural trial-and-error (e.g., adding layer normalization) with a principled, certifiable stability criterion grounded in the input-magnitude growth exponent of residual velocity fields.

Method: The method rests on two independent theoretical pillars: (1) classical ODE theory establishes that velocity fields with q ≤ 1 guarantee a global forward flow on [0,T], while q > 1 yields divergence; (2) optimal-control analysis via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation shows that the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so q > 1 leads to blow-up and q ≤ 1 is safe. The authors then develop an arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under five operations composing residual blocks, enabling compositional certification of q_k ≤ 1. A parameter-free modification is applied to the supercritical Mamba block to bring it from q=5 down to q=1.

Result: The q ≤ 1 criterion proves to be a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. The arithmetic of exponents allows efficient certification at the architectural primitive level. The parameter-free modification successfully reduces the Mamba block from q=5 to q=1 without layer normalization. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that q ≤ 1 variants train stably, demonstrating that stability is governed by the input-magnitude exponent rather than the presence or absence of normalization layers.

Conclusion: The sublinear-growth principle (q ≤ 1) defines the correct function space for residual architectures, where forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. This provides a rigorous, certifiable alternative to heuristic stabilization methods like layer normalization, enabling principled design of stable deep neural architectures through compositional exponent arithmetic rather than trial and error.

Abstract: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

</details>


### [108] [Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14607)
*Umid Suleymanov,Ilhama Novruzova,Khalid Mammadov,Natavan Hasanova,Murat Kantarcioglu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First comprehensive study examining how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level, revealing that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated rather than in isolation, and introducing a unified empirical framework for such auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work has extensively studied how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, but the inverse—how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage—remains largely unexplored. This gap is critical for sensitive domains (healthcare, law enforcement, finance) where both fairness and privacy guarantees are mandatory.

Method: The authors adapt the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup-level auditing to uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations mask. They systematically analyze how various fairness-enhancing methods interact with Differential Privacy (DP) across different model architectures, subgroup sizes, and mitigation strategies.

Result: Fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact varies by model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations, meaning certain subgroups bear disproportionate costs.

Conclusion: Fairness, privacy, and utility form a tripartite trade-off that must be evaluated jointly at the subpopulation level. The paper introduces the first unified empirical framework to support such holistic auditing in practice.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

</details>


### [109] [Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14613)
*Jin Dai,Qiuzhen Zhang,Chenyun Dai,Danmei Lan,Can Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AG-SCL proposes a contrastive learning framework for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis that combines angular Gaussian full-covariance modeling, adaptive logit adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation to improve rare arrhythmia detection while maintaining high specificity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-tailed class distributions in ECG data degrade deep learning performance on rare but clinically important arrhythmias. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods address class frequency alone, ignoring direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes.

Method: AG-SCL integrates three components: (1) an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings; (2) Adaptive Logit Adjustment (ALA) that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins; and (3) tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7–25 Hz QRS-dominant band. Evaluated on PTB-XL and a nocturnal ECG dataset (141 subjects, 1317 hours).

Result: On PTB-XL: balanced accuracy 0.838, sensitivity 0.709, specificity 0.968, mAP 0.495, TPR@5%FPR 0.778. On Noc-ECG: balanced accuracy 0.918, sensitivity 0.889, specificity 0.947, mAP 0.488, TPR@5%FPR 0.900. Largest gains in rare/morphologically unstable rhythm classes. Ablations confirmed each component's contribution.

Conclusion: AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity.

Abstract: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets. On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation.
