AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

</details>


### [110] [Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14614)
*Weiwen Xu,Jia Liu,Hou Pong Chan,Long Li,Deng Cai,Min Chen,Hao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CPO introduces token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions as a correctness signal for RLVR, outperforming entropy-based methods while improving generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Entropy-based advantage shaping in RLVR cannot differentiate between useful uncertainty (exploration) and detrimental confusion (errors), limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. A more discriminative signal is needed.

Method: CPO computes token-level contrastive disagreement between two distributions: a reference-guided generation distribution and a vanilla (unconditioned) generation distribution. This disagreement serves as a correctness-aware advantage shaping signal. The method also subsumes On-policy Distillation as a special case where a teacher model instantiates the posterior, and addresses the zero-advantage problem.

Result: CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks while maintaining strong generalization. Correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, with balanced utilization yielding optimal performance.

Conclusion: Contrastive disagreement provides a more reliable token-level correctness signal than entropy. CPO resolves the zero-advantage issue and demonstrates that balancing exploration (from correct responses) and exploitation (from incorrect responses) maximizes performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

</details>


### [111] [PolyQ: Codesigning End-to-End Quantization Framework for Scalable Edge CPU LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14618)
*Hyunwoo Oh,Suyeon Jang,Hanning Chen,KyungIn Nam,Sanggeon Yun,Ryozo Masukawa,Mohsen Imani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PolyQ is a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design that enables efficient fractional-bit LLM inference on CPUs by assigning per-channel bit-widths (2–16) under an average-bit budget, then using compiler techniques to cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks for SIMD/LUT-friendly kernels while keeping layout regularization offline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods either provide only coarse operating points or use fine-grained mixed precision that is inefficient to execute on CPUs. There is a need for practical fractional-bit deployment that is both predictable and energy-efficient across diverse CPU targets.

Method: PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from {2,3,4,8,16} under a user-specified average-bit budget. A compile-time model compiler then: (1) permutes and clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, (2) generates SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and (3) merges compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path.

Result: Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ improves perplexity by 2.4–32.1% over prior methods at a 3-bit target. On workstation, laptop, and mobile CPUs, compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8%. Prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2% relative to an optimized LUT backend.

Conclusion: Fractional-bit CPU deployment via PolyQ is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets, turning fine-grained budget fitting into a viable deployment method for CPU-only LLM inference.

Abstract: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods offer either coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs. We present PolyQ, a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design for activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under a user-specified average-bit budget. PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from $\{2,3,4,8,16\}$, then uses a compile-time model compiler to permute and cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This turns fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment method for CPU-only inference. Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ provides stable quality scaling from 3--6\,b and improves perplexity by 2.4--32.1\% over prior methods at a 3\,b target. End-to-end measurements on three representative CPUs -- workstation, laptop, and mobile -- show that compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8\%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2\% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end. These results show that fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

</details>


### [112] [TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14640)
*Wen Yang Tan,Jiawei Li,Fang Liu,Wei Zhang,Sumei Sun,Peng Cheng Wang,Elisa Y. M. Ang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIDE is a battery degradation estimator that jointly optimizes accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability by combining domain knowledge with operational measurements through a three-component backbone (knowledge-guided prior, monotone residual, contextual learning), then distilling it into a compact symbolic surrogate for model-level interpretation, achieving 19.7% improvement over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate battery health estimation is critical for battery management, especially in intelligent connected systems where estimation errors cascade across devices and downstream decisions. Existing methods lack simultaneous consideration of accuracy, trustworthiness (aging-consistency), and interpretability, all of which are essential for practical deployment.

Method: TIDE employs a three-component backbone: (1) a knowledge-guided degradation prior ensuring trustworthy estimation, (2) a monotone residual component providing interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and (3) a contextual learning component capturing battery-specific operational effects for accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate for concise model-level interpretation of the learned estimation logic.

Result: TIDE improves overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. The knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modeling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations. Component-level interpretation and symbolic distillation provide both local and model-level interpretability.

Conclusion: TIDE demonstrates practical viability for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems by successfully integrating accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability into a unified framework, validated through strong experimental performance.

Abstract: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

</details>


### [113] [Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14652)
*Shusheng Xiao,Jinshuai Bai,Hyogu Jeong,Yunfei Xi,Yilin Gui,YuanTong Gu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework that generates diverse, structurally feasible topologies conditioned on design parameters. A trajectory-aware variant incorporates BESO optimisation history into the probability path, improving generation quality with fewer sampling steps than diffusion models, especially under limited training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional topology optimisation requires costly repeated FEA and sensitivity updates per design. Existing generative TO methods suffer from drawbacks: adversarial training instability, slow reverse-diffusion sampling, or reliance on external guidance for physical consistency. The authors aim to develop a fast, stable generative framework that naturally incorporates physics-guided optimisation history without inference-time penalties.

Method: The authors formulate a linear FMTO baseline using endpoint interpolation between Gaussian noise and BESO topologies. They then propose trajectory-aware FMTO, which constructs the probability path and target velocity field using volume-fraction-indexed intermediate BESO states along the optimisation trajectory. A path-velocity mismatch analysis quantifies how trajectory weighting affects generation stability. The framework is evaluated against a diffusion baseline on compliance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and sampling efficiency.

Result: FMTO generates diverse topologies with improved compliance-related performance, better volume-fraction satisfaction, higher topology fidelity, and requires substantially fewer sampling steps than diffusion baselines. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO with moderate trajectory weighting achieves the best overall performance. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and 3D generation validate the path design principles and framework extensibility.

Conclusion: Flow matching provides an efficient generative framework for topology optimisation. Incorporating physics-guided BESO trajectory information via the trajectory-aware formulation improves generation quality and stability, particularly in data-scarce scenarios. Moderate trajectory weighting balances guidance with transport flexibility, and the approach generalises to 3D problems.

Abstract: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

</details>


### [114] [Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14672)
*Yusuke Sakemi,Tomoya Takeuchi,Takeo Hosomi,Kazuyuki Aihara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSTD introduces a memory-efficient SNN training method by discretizing spike times onto fixed intervals, reducing memory from O(N_out·N_in) to O(N_out·M), and adds temporal regularization for stable deep network training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep continuous-time SNNs is bottlenecked by memory requirements of exact spike-time computation, which scales with O(N_out·N_in) and prevents scaling to deep architectures on standard hardware.

Method: The authors propose Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization (DSTD), which maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto M fixed-time weighted events using differentiable kernels aligned with LIF membrane dynamics. This replaces input-dependent candidate spike-time evaluation with a fixed discretization grid. They also introduce a synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that structures layer-wise firing windows to prevent dead neurons and enable pipelined processing across layers.

Result: DSTD reduced peak memory by ~100× and training time by ~20× versus exact spike-time computation in dense LIF layers. The combined approach enabled training a 9-layer conv SNN on CIFAR-10 and a 20-layer conv SNN on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

Conclusion: DSTD plus temporal regularization makes deep continuous-time SNN training feasible on commodity GPUs, overcoming the memory bottleneck of exact spike-time methods while maintaining accurate membrane-potential dynamics.

Abstract: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware. However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

</details>


### [115] [Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14705)
*Yuchang Zhu,Zezhong Xie,Huizhe Zhang,Huazhen Zhong,Jintang Li,Liang Chen,Zibin Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grad2Fair proposes a gradient-based method to achieve group fairness in GNNs without requiring demographic labels, using gradient distribution distances to quantify bias and directly leveraging gradients for debiasing, avoiding the pitfalls of proxy demographic prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN fairness methods assume full access to sensitive demographic attributes, which is often unrealistic. Recent work using predicted demographics as proxies suffers from inaccuracy, leading to fairness degradation. The authors observe that gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, motivating a demographic-free fairness approach.

Method: First, GradDist is introduced — a gradient-based fairness metric that measures the distance between local modes in misclassified node gradient distributions to quantify bias. Second, Grad2Fair is proposed, a gradient-guided debiasing approach that directly uses gradient information to mitigate group unfairness without ever predicting or using demographic attributes.

Result: Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show Grad2Fair outperforms baseline methods in most cases, demonstrating effective fairness improvement without demographic information.

Conclusion: Gradients of misclassified nodes carry implicit demographic signals that can be exploited for fairness. By directly operating on gradients rather than predicting demographics, Grad2Fair achieves stable and superior fairness performance, offering a practical solution for scenarios where sensitive attributes are unavailable.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

</details>


### [116] [MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14706)
*Xin Li,Zixin Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MESHA is a best arm identification algorithm for strategic linear bandits that uses uniform sampling and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition to counter arms' strategic misreporting of features, outperforming G-optimal design-based methods which can starve the optimal arm under strategic behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing BAI algorithms relying on G-optimal design are vulnerable in strategic environments where arms can misreport feature vectors to manipulate identification probabilities. The optimal design-based sampling can inadvertently starve the truly best arm of budget, motivating a robust alternative.

Method: MESHA combines two components: (1) naïve uniform sampling to reduce the influence of strategic misreporting, and (2) an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC) that eliminates arms whose reported features deviate significantly from ground truth. Analysis is conducted under arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, bounding the failure probability within budget T and proving arms are incentivized to pass the GTC check.

Result: Theoretically, MESHA's failure probability is upper bounded within fixed budget T, and any arm at Nash Equilibrium attempts to satisfy the GTC. SOTA linear BAI algorithms with G-optimal design provably fail by starving the optimal arm. Numerical experiments confirm MESHA outperforms both OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines.

Conclusion: MESHA provides a robust solution to BAI in strategic linear bandits, demonstrating that uniform sampling combined with deviation-based arm elimination effectively mitigates strategic manipulation where optimal design approaches collapse.

Abstract: We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

</details>


### [117] [Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14719)
*Richard J. Fawley,Renato Cordeiro de Amorim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VoICE generates counterfactual explanations for feature-weighted k-means clustering by projecting inputs onto weighted Voronoi regions of target clusters, ensuring valid cluster membership under actionability constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods for clustering naively rely on pairwise centroid boundaries, which fail to account for the full partition geometry and often do not guarantee valid target-cluster membership. There is a need for a method that respects the complete Voronoi tessellation, incorporates feature weights, and produces least-cost, parsimonious explanations.

Method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster. It integrates feature weights into both the clustering geometry and the objective function, producing least-cost explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted toward centroids to mitigate extrapolation and boundary sensitivity.

Result: Across several benchmark datasets, VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, whereas the leading pairwise baseline fails to do so.

Conclusion: VoICE provides a geometrically principled and reliable framework for counterfactual explanations in feature-weighted k-means clustering, outperforming pairwise boundary-based baselines in guaranteeing valid cluster transitions.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

</details>


### [118] [What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14731)
*Kumar Kshitij Patel,Rustem Islamov,Sebastian U Stich,Aurelien Lucchi,Eduard Gorbunov,Lingxiao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves that bounded second-order heterogeneity explains the efficiency of Local SGD for general convex objectives, extending prior results for strongly convex settings. It provides nearly tight upper and lower bounds, and also applies the analysis to serial SGD with replacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local SGD empirically outperforms mini-batch SGD under heterogeneous data, but existing theory only partially explains when and why local updates help. Patel et al. (2025) showed that bounded second-order heterogeneity captures this efficiency for strongly convex objectives and conjectured it extends to general convex settings. This paper aims to prove that conjecture.

Method: The authors prove an improved convergence upper bound for Local SGD on general convex objectives under a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption. They also derive improved lower bounds that nearly match the upper bounds, establishing tightness. As a secondary application, they prove a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

Result: The paper establishes nearly tight upper and lower convergence bounds for Local SGD under general convex objectives with bounded second-order heterogeneity, confirming Patel et al.'s conjecture. Additionally, the lower bound for serial SGD with replacement demonstrates that second-order heterogeneity can explain performance degradation from rare high-curvature clients.

Conclusion: Bounded second-order heterogeneity provides a sharp, fine-grained framework for understanding Local SGD's convergence in the general convex setting. The nearly tight bounds validate this as a principled condition, and the technique extends to analyzing serial SGD with replacement.

Abstract: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

</details>


### [119] [GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14733)
*Xiangni Tian,Kaixian Yu,Runpeng Dai,Niansheng Tang,Hongtu Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAttNHP combines self-attention, soft grouping, and non-crossing quantile regression into a unified Neural Hawkes Process framework for temporal knowledge graph forecasting, achieving state-of-the-art results especially on long-tail event chains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TKG forecasting faces three key challenges: (1) encoding long-range temporal dependencies is difficult; (2) snapshot-level models cannot capture mutual excitation/inhibition across different event chains; (3) heavy-tailed, sparse inter-arrival times make deterministic time predictors unreliable.

Method: The framework has three components: (a) a self-attention encoder that models subject-relation chains as continuous-time point processes to capture lingering excitation from distant history; (b) a semantic soft-grouping module that transforms globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, enabling chains to share excitation patterns via latent group memberships instead of pairwise computation; (c) a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head that yields calibrated, monotonic quantile estimates stable under heavy-tailed distributions.

Result: GAttNHP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on six benchmark TKG datasets for both entity prediction and time prediction. Ablation studies show the largest improvements occur on long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

Conclusion: The three-component design effectively addresses the core limitations of prior TKG forecasting methods — long-range dependency encoding, cross-chain interaction modeling, and robust time prediction under heavy-tailed distributions — with the soft-grouping mechanism providing particular benefit for sparse, long-tail events.

Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

</details>


### [120] [ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14770)
*Xuemeng Liu,Zhengpin Li,Wanpeng Tang,Haotong Xie,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ChronoQG is the first benchmark framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), producing 16,011 verified questions across four datasets. It introduces a temporal-constraint taxonomy and trace-grounded generation, revealing that existing LLM-based KGQG methods struggle significantly with preserving temporal constraints, especially in multi-constraint and harder temporal settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KGQG benchmarks are built on static knowledge graphs lacking temporal scopes, making them incapable of evaluating whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. This gap motivates the need for a temporally expressive benchmark.

Method: The ChronoQG framework comprises three components: (1) a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy categorizing temporal relation types, (2) topology-temporal subgraph sampling that jointly considers graph topology and temporal scopes, and (3) trace-grounded question generation ensuring questions are faithful to both the support subgraph and temporal constraints. The framework generates four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous TKGs, totaling 16,011 verified questions.

Result: Evaluation of representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse settings (varying temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types) shows that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints. Performance degrades notably under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types, revealing a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG capabilities.

Conclusion: Existing KGQG methods are ill-equipped for temporal faithfulness. ChronoQG establishes a challenging testbed for TKGQG, highlighting the need for new approaches that can jointly reason over graph topology and temporal constraints to generate temporally valid questions.

Abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

</details>


### [121] [Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14817)
*Jakub Paplhám,Willem Waegeman,Eyke Hüllermeier,Vojtěch Franc*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper re-evaluates how epistemic uncertainty is measured, arguing that standard proxy tasks (OOD detection, active learning) misalign with Bayes-optimal decision strategies. The authors propose a regret-based evaluation framework that unifies selective prediction under a constrained optimization lens, revealing that learned uncertainty components often fail to correlate with actual decision-theoretic utility, and that method rankings can invert dramatically depending on the evaluation criterion used.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on proxy tasks like OOD detection and active learning, but the Bayes-optimal strategies for these tasks do not align with the scores used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. This mismatch raises doubts about whether learned uncertainty decompositions genuinely serve downstream decision-making. The authors aim to establish a principled, decision-theoretic evaluation framework that directly ties epistemic uncertainty to its operational utility — specifically, identifying regret (reducible error).

Method: The authors formulate selective prediction as a constrained optimization problem over coverage, expected risk, and regret. They prove the optimal selector is a threshold applied to a convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. From this theoretical result, they propose evaluating uncertainty decompositions by measuring the achievable risk-regret-coverage surface, which jointly assesses disentanglement quality and decision-theoretic utility. They benchmark standard uncertainty methods on datasets with dense human annotations, comparing decision-theoretic rankings against traditional proxy-task rankings.

Result: Standard correlation metrics between learned aleatoric/epistemic components do not reliably predict their operational utility. Decision-theoretic rankings can substantially disagree with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions where methods that are top-ranked on one criterion fall to the bottom on another. This exposes a fundamental weakness in how the field currently evaluates uncertainty disentanglement.

Conclusion: The evaluation of epistemic uncertainty should be grounded in decision-theoretic principles — specifically, a method's ability to identify regret — rather than proxy-task performance or correlation-based disentanglement metrics. The proposed risk-regret-coverage surface provides a more faithful diagnostic for both disentanglement quality and practical utility.

Abstract: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

</details>


### [122] [Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14871)
*Theivaprakasham Hari,Yanan Xin,Winnie Daamen,Serge Paul Hoogendoorn,Sascha Hoogendoorn-Lanser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a model-agnostic loss function for time-series forecasting that penalizes under-prediction more heavily and emphasizes peak regions during training. Complemented by a peak-critical evaluation protocol, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across multiple backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In operational time-series forecasting (e.g., crowd demand), under-prediction carries substantially higher risk than over-prediction, and accurate prediction of rare demand spikes is critical. Standard symmetric loss functions (MSE, MAE) and aggregate error metrics mask failures in extreme-value and peak-timing predictions, creating a need for asymmetric, peak-aware training objectives and evaluation protocols.

Method: The authors propose APAL, a model-agnostic loss function with two components: (1) asymmetric penalization that weights under-predictions more heavily, and (2) a peak-aware mechanism that increases training weight on peak regions within each forecast window. They also introduce a peak-critical evaluation protocol using channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%), peak precision/recall/F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error. The method is evaluated on five state-of-the-art backbones using Melbourne pedestrian counts and beach visitor datasets, with generality tested on additional benchmarks.

Result: APAL consistently improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical datasets and settings. It exposes a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, allowing practitioners to prioritize peak-prediction performance when that is the dominant operational concern.

Conclusion: APAL is a practical, plug-and-play solution for time-series forecasting applications where rare demand spike prediction dominates operational risk, offering improved peak detection and timing while maintaining a tunable balance with overall forecast accuracy.

Abstract: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

</details>


### [123] [PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14877)
*Ali Asadi,Krishnendu Chatterjee,Pavol Kebis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first positive result for decentralized PAC learning of turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives under private information, where players do not share learning algorithms, and establishes polynomial sample complexity bounds using a generalized Expected Conditional Distance parameter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reachability is the most fundamental objective in logic and verification, yet PAC learning of reachability is known to be impossible in Markov decision processes and turn-based stochastic games without strong assumptions. Prior work on PAC learning in TBSGs required two restrictive conditions: public information shared by both players and centralized learning (shared algorithm). The motivation is to relax these assumptions to enable learning with private information and decentralized algorithms, which is more realistic for adversarial multi-agent settings.

Method: The authors introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, adapted from MDPs to the TBSG setting. ECD measures the expected length of reaching the target set from any state. They then construct a decentralized learning framework where two adversarial players learn the unknown TBSG model together without sharing private information or a common learning algorithm, and derive polynomial-sample complexity bounds with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

Result: The paper establishes that decentralized PAC learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives is achievable under private information — the first such positive result. A polynomial-sample complexity bound is proven, scaling polynomially in the number of states, actions, the ECD parameter, 1/ε (error tolerance), and 1/δ (failure probability).

Conclusion: The authors successfully relax the strong assumptions of prior TBSG learning literature — centralized learning and public information — and demonstrate that PAC learning with reachability objectives is possible in a decentralized, private-information setting. The generalized ECD parameter provides a natural complexity measure that yields polynomial sample complexity bounds, opening the door to more realistic multi-agent reinforcement learning in adversarial stochastic game environments.

Abstract: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

</details>


### [124] [Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14888)
*Robert Graham,Edward Stevinson,Yariv Barsheshat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on narrow, ideologically-aligned datasets (e.g., economics Q&A) causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains (criminal justice, environment, etc.) — a phenomenon termed "ideological generalisation." The effect amplifies beyond few-shot prompting, survives data mixing, and generalizes across models, while core capabilities remain intact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether fine-tuning language models on curated, moderation-compliant datasets for specific domains inadvertently produces broad, unintended ideological biases across unrelated topics, and to characterize the scope and intensity of such shifts.

Method: The authors fine-tune GPT-4.1 and Gemma-3 on ideologically skewed datasets (right/left-leaning economics Q&A, workplace HR policy, practical finance, food safety), then evaluate ideological shifts across unrelated domains using judge-based and judge-free evaluations, external benchmarks, and comparisons against few-shot prompting. They introduce metrics for breadth (topic reach) and amplification (intensification beyond prompting).

Result: Fine-tuning on narrow ideological data produces consistent, amplified ideological shifts across distant topics. Few-shot prompting predicts the direction, but fine-tuning drives models to more extreme positions — including out-of-distribution outputs like endorsing race-IQ links and political violence. The effect persists despite mixing with generic data and across model architectures, while GSM8K accuracy remains within ±1pp of baseline.

Conclusion: Ideological generalisation is a robust, replicable phenomenon: narrow, benign-seeming fine-tuning can covertly reshape a model's ideological posture across broad domains. This poses significant risks for deployed systems and calls for mitigation strategies beyond simple data mixing.

Abstract: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

</details>


### [125] [Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14889)
*Jean-Marc Brossier,Olivier Lafitte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes optimal linear combination of binary classifiers using truth table structuration; establishes conditions for existence/uniqueness of global minima in convexified empirical risk, provides explicit weight formulas for Exponential and Logistic losses, and introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When combining multiple binary classifiers, iterative optimization methods for finding optimal weights can be computationally intensive and may not guarantee global optimality. The authors seek a rigorous analytical framework that bypasses iterative optimization by exploiting logical relationships among classifiers via truth tables, while also addressing the fundamental issue that global minima may not exist when combining many classifiers.

Method: Uses truth tables to partition data into equivalence classes based on classifier outputs. Generalizes the notion of classification-calibrated functions to multiple dimensions within the convexified empirical risk framework. Derives sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of global minima. For three classifiers, exhaustively enumerates all configurations (unique solution, infima, non-unique minima). Derives closed-form analytical weight formulas for Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) losses. Introduces φ-frontiers to evaluate classifier stability and data quality.

Result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of global minima established. Complete enumeration of three-classifier configurations achieved. Explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights under Exponential and Logistic losses derived, eliminating need for iterative optimization.

Conclusion: The truth-table-based structuration enables rigorous analytical treatment of classifier combination, providing both theoretical guarantees (existence/uniqueness) and practical benefits (closed-form weight formulas). The φ-frontier concept offers a new tool for stability and data quality assessment.

Abstract: This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

</details>


### [126] [Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14895)
*Yu-Du Feng,Niels Mündler-Sasahara,Mark Vero,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a cost-effective method to improve reasoning language models (RLMs) by combining instruction tuning on human-written solutions with model merging, achieving performance gains in both verifiable and unverifiable domains for under $3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLMs excel in verifiable domains (math, coding) via reinforcement learning, but training them on domains lacking reliable verifiers is challenging. Additionally, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist for both verifiable and unverifiable domains. The authors aim to harness this unused data to further improve RLM performance efficiently.

Method: A two-stage approach: (1) Classic instruction tuning — supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces — is applied to the RLM using human-written solution data. (2) Model merging — the instruction-tuned model is merged with the original reasoning model to recover its reasoning behavior on the target domain.

Result: The technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable (e.g., coding) and hard-to-verify domains (e.g., text summarization), while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. The method is highly cost-effective, requiring less than $3.

Conclusion: Unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions can be efficiently leveraged via instruction tuning and model merging to enhance RLM performance across diverse domains at minimal cost, without sacrificing existing reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

</details>


### [127] [A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14937)
*Christoph Jürgen Hemmer,Florian Plaswig,Daniel Durstewitz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper iteratively reduces a SOTA dynamical system reconstruction model (DynaMix) to a minimal two-parameter form called DynaBase, which forecasts via linear blending of the current latent state with the nearest in-context neighbor. Despite extreme simplicity, it achieves competitive zero-shot reconstruction, permits closed-form solutions, and reconciles divergent literature observations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current foundation models for zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but are opaque, providing no mechanistic insight into how they produce forecasts. Understanding these mechanisms could reveal the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain and strip down over-parameterized architectures to their essential core.

Method: The authors iteratively simplify the DynaMix model (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025) down to DynaBase, a two-parameter interpretable model that forecasts by linearly blending the current latent state with the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. This minimal form enables direct optimization on DS reconstruction metrics and yields closed-form one-step analytical solutions for prediction MSE. The analysis further produces a one-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm recovered at one extreme and chaotic behavior at the other.

Result: DynaBase achieves highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems despite negligible parameter load (many orders of magnitude below other FMs). Training strategies differentially yield models optimal for either short-term prediction or DS reconstruction. The one-parameter family of maps reconciles divergent observations in the literature within a unified mathematical framework.

Conclusion: DynaBase exposes the minimal mechanisms sufficient for zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction and demonstrates that a simple linear blend of latent state and nearest-neighbor dynamics is surprisingly powerful. The work bridges interpretability and performance, reconciling conflicting findings in the literature and providing a tractable mathematical frame for understanding in-context learning in DS modeling.

Abstract: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

</details>


### [128] [Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14940)
*Phevos Paschalidis,Constantinos Daskalakis,Devavrat Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a method for causal inference in sequential observational settings with outcome interference, using Ising models with low-rank latent confounders and MPLE-based estimation, with theoretical consistency guarantees and empirical validation on COVID-19 vaccine data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard causal inference methods assume no interference between units (SUTVA), but in many real-world settings — such as epidemic spread or policy evaluation — outcomes are interdependent across units over time. Extending causal inference to handle both temporal dependencies and cross-unit interference in high-dimensional observational settings with latent confounding remains an open challenge.

Method: The authors model binary outcomes across N units and T time steps as Markovian, with dependencies captured by an Ising model at each time step. Treatments and latent confounders enter through an external field. Latent confounders follow a low-rank factor structure (similar to panel data models). Parameter estimation uses Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE), which is computationally efficient. Causal quantities are estimated by sampling from the learned model. Non-asymptotic consistency guarantees are derived under mild assumptions.

Result: The MPLE-based approach achieves non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation, which translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities after sampling. Synthetic experiments validate the method's efficacy. A real-world case study demonstrates the approach by investigating causal effects of vaccination rates on COVID-19 death rates across US counties.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully extends causal inference to high-dimensional sequential settings with outcome interference and latent confounding, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical computational efficiency. The COVID-19 case study demonstrates real-world applicability for policy-relevant causal questions involving interference.

Abstract: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

</details>


### [129] [LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14952)
*Changhai Zhou,Kieran Liu,Yuhua Zhou,Qian Qiao,Jun Gao,Harry Zhang,Irvine Lu,Nolan Ho,Lucian Li,Andrew Lei,Cleon Cheng,Steven Chiang,Yihang Zeng,Di Zhang,Rio Yang,Kaijie Chen,Andrew Chen,Pony Ma,Weizhong Zhang,Cheng Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LongStraw is an execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training (GRPO) under fixed GPU budgets by decoupling the prompt from response replay, achieving 2.1M-token contexts on 8 GPUs and up to 4.46M positions in stress tests, though full training fidelity remains incomplete.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A growing gap exists between inference context lengths (approaching million-token scale) and RL post-training workloads (typically ≤256K tokens). This gap critically affects AI agents whose long trajectories accumulate observations, tool outputs, and decisions. Existing post-training systems rely on length generalization at deployment rather than training at scale, motivating an architecture-aware solution for million-token RL post-training.

Method: LongStraw extends GRPO with an architecture-aware execution strategy: (1) the shared prompt is evaluated without autograd, retaining only model-specific state needed by later tokens; (2) short response branches are replayed one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time; (3) the approach is implemented for two architectures — the hybrid recurrent/full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention MoE GLM-5.2. Experiments run on 8 and 32 H20 GPUs.

Result: On 8 H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for group sizes of 2 and 8, with only 0.21 GB of added peak memory when scaling group size. A stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, the end-to-end execution path validates 2.1M-token prompts across all 78 GLM-5.2 layers. However, these results establish execution capacity rather than full training correctness, since prompt state is detached and some distributed forward/gradient paths remain incomplete.

Conclusion: LongStraw demonstrates feasibility of million-token-scale RL post-training under constrained GPU budgets by trading compute (replay) for memory. The work identifies a critical infrastructure gap for long-context agent training and provides an execution-validated stack, though further work is needed to close remaining correctness gaps in distributed gradient composition.

Abstract: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

</details>


### [130] [Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14962)
*Ku Onoda,Paavo Parmas,Hiroki Furuta,Soichiro Nishimori,Yuta Oshima,Shohei Taniguchi,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Text-to-image models often lack diversity in outputs for a given prompt. This paper formalizes this as "target-mode coverage" and proposes multi-axis max@K, a group-based RL objective that improves coverage across semantically specified modes. The method assigns credit to samples that uniquely maximize scores per category, and shows improved fairness (0.23–0.36 gain) without sacrificing image quality or text alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: T2I models generate realistic images but exhibit limited mode coverage — for the same prompt, outputs cluster in a narrow subset of possible visual modes. For person-centric prompts, this can amplify demographic skews (e.g., underrepresentation of certain attributes). The authors aim to address the gap between the diversity of real-world distributions and the limited diversity in synthetic outputs by explicitly optimizing for target-mode coverage.

Method: The paper formalizes the diversity problem as covering a predefined set of semantically specified modes (target-mode coverage). The core contribution is **multi-axis max@K**: a group-based RL objective operating on a group of K samples. For each target category, it takes the maximum score across the group, then sums these per-category maxima. Credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, enabling different samples to specialize in different categories. The method is validated on a synthetic mixture and SD3.5-M with pixel-based color rewards, then evaluated on perceived-appearance fairness using automatic evaluators.

Result: Multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23–0.36 (relative to the base model) across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts. These gains are achieved while maintaining image quality and text alignment, demonstrating that the objective successfully broadens mode coverage without degrading other desiderata.

Conclusion: Multi-axis max@K is an effective group-based RL objective for improving target-mode coverage in T2I diffusion models. By structuring credit assignment so that different samples contribute to different categories, the method enhances diversity and demographic fairness while preserving image quality and prompt alignment.

Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

</details>


### [131] [Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14995)
*Sara Ketabi,Matthias W. Wagner,Cynthia Hawkins,Uri Tabori,Birgit Betina Ertl-Wagner,Farzad Khalvati*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces MseaCL, a multimodal contrastive learning framework that uses semantic similarity between radiology reports to reduce false negatives during training, achieving a 22.6% AUC improvement in pediatric brain tumor molecular classification when used as pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multimodal contrastive learning assumes instance-based correspondence, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. This assumption fails in medical contexts where samples often share high-level semantic attributes (e.g., similar pathologies), creating false negatives that degrade learned representations.

Method: MseaCL incorporates semantic similarity scores between radiology reports as a guiding signal within the contrastive loss, using a pediatric cohort of paired 3D brain MRI scans and radiology reports. This softens the hard negative assumption by weighting repulsion based on semantic proximity.

Result: Pretraining with MseaCL led to at least a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification compared to baselines, demonstrating improved downstream task performance.

Conclusion: Incorporating semantic awareness into multimodal contrastive learning effectively mitigates false negatives in medical imaging, yielding more robust and semantically aligned representations with significant clinical downstream benefits.

Abstract: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

</details>


### [132] [Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15067)
*Joshua Spear,Matthieu Komorowski,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire,Erica E. M. Moodie*

Main category: cs.LG
