TL;DR: Kernel-WIS is a novel off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that combines the bounded property of weighted importance sampling with the linearity of importance sampling, achieving asymptotic consistency and outperforming baselines, especially under behaviour policy misspecification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) in contextual bandits using only offline data is challenging. Existing estimators face a trade-off: vanilla importance sampling (IS) is unbiased but suffers from high variance, while weighted importance sampling (WIS) is bounded and lower-variance but biased. The authors aim to design an estimator that enjoys the benefits of both — the linearity/unbiasedness of IS and the bounded stability of WIS — to improve robustness under complex conditions like behaviour policy misspecification.

Method: The proposed Kernel-WIS estimator combines weighted importance sampling with kernel smoothing/regularization. It leverages the bounded nature of WIS to control variance while retaining linearity properties akin to vanilla IS. The estimator is constructed to be asymptotically consistent, and its derivation involves integrating kernel methods into the importance weighting framework for contextual bandit off-policy evaluation.

Result: Kernel-WIS is shown to be asymptotically consistent. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that it outperforms strong baselines, including vanilla weighted importance sampling, particularly under complex conditions such as behaviour policy misspecification.

Conclusion: Kernel-WIS successfully bridges the gap between vanilla IS and WIS by combining linearity with boundedness, yielding a robust, asymptotically consistent OPE estimator that excels in challenging scenarios with misspecified behaviour policies.

Abstract: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

</details>


### [133] [An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15077)
*Yao Cheng Li,Ana Larrañaga,Steven L. Brunton,Urban Fasel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This tutorial paper introduces the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method for engineering applications, progressively building from the core algorithm to advanced extensions (weak-form, ensembling, constrained, parametrizable SINDy), and demonstrates its practical utility through case studies on UAV system identification and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineering problems often involve poorly characterized governing equations. While neural network surrogates can model these systems, they require large training datasets (scarce in engineering) and yield physically uninterpretable models. SINDy addresses both limitations—recovering interpretable governing equations from small datasets via sparse regression—but its application to practical engineering remains under-documented.

Method: The paper presents a progressive tutorial on SINDy: (1) the standard SINDy algorithm using sparse regression over candidate nonlinear function libraries; (2) extensions including noise-robust weak-form SINDy, ensembling-based variants, and constrained/parametrizable formulations; (3) two detailed engineering case studies—UAV system identification and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger—with accompanying open-source code.

Result: The tutorial demonstrates that SINDy is simple to implement and flexible enough for advanced engineering identification tasks. The case studies illustrate successful recovery of interpretable governing equations from limited experimental data in realistic engineering systems.

Conclusion: SINDy offers a practical, interpretable alternative to black-box surrogate models for engineering system identification, requiring only small datasets. The authors aim to lower the barrier to adoption by providing a structured tutorial and reproducible codebase, encouraging engineers to adapt SINDy to their own domain-specific problems.

Abstract: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

</details>


### [134] [Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15080)
*Joshua Spear,Rebecca Pope,Neil J Sebire*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper examines whether covariate balance diagnostics can detect hidden confounding or model misspecification in offline RL for treatment recommendations, finding that either existing studies carry high bias risk or current balance metrics are insufficient — in either case, existing work cannot be considered statistically robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline reinforcement learning is increasingly used to derive optimal treatment policies from observational data, but such data are vulnerable to hidden confounding. The authors investigate whether covariate balance diagnostics — a tool borrowed from causal inference — can serve as a post-hoc check for confounding or model misspecification in these studies.

Method: The authors apply covariate balance diagnostics to existing offline RL studies in treatment recommendation settings, systematically evaluating whether balanced covariates across treatment arms can reveal hidden confounding or model misspecification that would otherwise go undetected.

Result: The results present a dilemma: either existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations carry a high risk of hidden bias, or covariate balance metrics are inadequate for evaluating such studies. Either way, current studies cannot be claimed to be statistically robust.

Conclusion: Future research is needed to develop more methodologically robust approaches for applying offline RL to treatment recommendations, particularly around diagnostics that can reliably detect confounding and model misspecification.

Abstract: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

</details>


### [135] [Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15107)
*Sridhar Mahadevan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces LINCS, a categorical framework that recasts machine learning as the repair of non-compositionality — where non-compositionality is defined as the failure of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches in a tangent category setting, rather than as arithmetic loss. It defines Tangent Learning Sketches, the INC endofunctor for iterated tangent lifts, and proves the existence of a final coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a principled categorical foundation for machine learning that moves beyond scalarized loss functions and vector space assumptions, instead framing ML problems purely in terms of compositional structure and its failures. The authors aim to treat non-compositionality as a universal factorization obstruction rather than an arithmetic discrepancy between predictions and targets.

Method: The method introduces Learning Sketches (graphs with commutativity conditions, limit cones, and colimit cocones), defines the base defect as the obstruction to a universal factorization problem, applies the tangent functor T from Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure to lift models to the tangent category, and defines LINCS as the obstruction after tangent lift. The INC endofunctor iterates this process, producing a tower of factorization problems. The Aczel-Mendler theorem is used to prove existence of a final INC coalgebra when a set-based class realization exists.

Result: The paper proves the existence of a final INC coalgebra (νT_INC) under the condition that T_INC admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier, establishing that the iterative tangent unfolding process can reach a coalgebraic fixed point where compositionality constraints stabilize.

Conclusion: ML can be reformulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point in a tower of tangent-lifted factorization problems, with LINCS providing a rigorous categorical semantics for this process. Experimental validation across deep learning, LLMs, and RL is reported as ongoing in companion papers.

Abstract: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

</details>


### [136] [On-Policy Delta Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15161)
*Byeongho Heo,Jaehui Hwang,Sangdoo Yun,Dongyoon Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²) introduces a novel distillation reward called the "delta signal" — the difference between a teacher model and its pre-instruction-tuned base model — to better transfer reasoning capabilities. This method consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation across math, science, and code reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods directly imitate the teacher's output distribution, which provides a noisy and indirect signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. The authors identify that the fundamental design of distillation rewards in on-policy settings is underexplored and seek a more targeted approach to capture reasoning-specific knowledge.

Method: The authors propose the delta signal as an alternative distillation reward, defined as the difference between the teacher model (post-instruction-tuning) and its base model (pre-instruction-tuning). This isolates the changes induced by reasoning-oriented instruction tuning. The resulting method, On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), uses this delta signal for token-level supervision rather than directly imitating the teacher's output distribution.

Result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, science, and code reasoning benchmarks show that OPD² consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation methods, enabling strong reasoning performance with only a short post-training period.

Conclusion: The delta signal is a simple yet effective refinement to on-policy distillation that better transfers reasoning capabilities by focusing on the changes induced by instruction tuning. OPD² represents a meaningful advancement in post-training methodology for reasoning LLMs.

Abstract: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

</details>


### [137] [RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15180)
*Ahmet Demirkaya,Georgios Stratis,Tales Imbiriba,Zachary D. Danziger,Deniz Erdogmus*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a two-stage hybrid neural-physics framework that alternates between RTS smoothing for latent state inference and backpropagation for neural network parameter estimation, enabling learning of missing ODE components from partial observations while retaining interpretable mechanistic structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many dynamical systems modeled by ODEs have partially unknown dynamics and only a subset of state variables are measured. Existing purely data-driven approaches can sacrifice interpretability, while purely mechanistic models may be incomplete. A hybrid framework is needed to learn missing components from data while preserving known physics.

Method: A two-stage iterative framework: (1) State estimation — treat neural network parameters as fixed, use an RTS smoother to infer latent states from partial measurements; (2) Parameter estimation — treat smoothed trajectories as ground truth, update neural network parameters via backpropagation. The two stages alternate until convergence.

Result: The method was evaluated on benchmark systems covering linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. It successfully learned missing ODE components from incomplete measurements, improved latent-state reconstruction, and enhanced long-horizon prediction compared to baselines.

Conclusion: The hybrid neural-physics approach effectively combines mechanistic ODE structure with neural network flexibility, enabling robust learning of unknown dynamics from partial observations while maintaining interpretability and improving both state reconstruction and predictive performance.

Abstract: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to model dynamical systems in physics, biology, neuroscience, and physiology, but in many applications some equations of the dynamics are unknown and only a subset of the state variables are measured. We propose a hybrid neural--physics framework in which the known components of the ODE are kept explicit and the missing components are represented by a neural network. The proposed method consists of two stages where we alternate between state and parameter estimation and iterate until a predetermined criterion is met. Specifically, in the first step, we treat the model parameters as being known and we infer the latent states from the available measurements using a Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother. In the second stage, we treat the smoothed trajectories as being known and use them to estimate the neural networks' parameters through backpropagation. We evaluate the method on benchmark systems spanning linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. Across these settings, the proposed method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements while exploiting and retaining interpretable mechanistic structure and improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.

</details>


### [138] [BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15207)
*Qi Li,Xingyi Yang,Xinchao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BadWAM introduces World-Action Drift Attacks, a class of adversarial perturbations that exploit a core assumption of world-action models—that imagined futures and executed actions are aligned—by either hijacking actions outright or stealthily desynchronizing actions from plausible imagined futures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World-action models (WAMs) are presumed to offer robustness and safety by coupling action generation with future prediction, allowing imagined futures to be checked against intended actions. This paper challenges that assumption, demonstrating that the action-imagination coupling is fragile and can be exploited by adversarial attacks.

Method: The authors propose BadWAM, a unified framework that instantiates two attack types along axes of strength and stealthiness: (1) an action-only adversarial attack that directly drives the model toward task-failing actions, and (2) an imagination-preserving adversarial attack that induces harmful action shifts while regularizing the predicted future to remain close to the clean imagination, thereby evading detection.

Result: On WAM variants, the action-only attack reduces task success rate from 96.5% to 43.1%. The imagination-preserving attack demonstrates that moderate future-preserving regularization maintains strong attack performance while minimizing future imagination drift, exposing a WAM-specific vulnerability.

Conclusion: The coupling between action generation and world prediction in WAMs, often viewed as a safety mechanism, is itself an attack surface. BadWAM reveals a spectrum of WAM-specific failures—from overt hijacking to stealthy desynchronization—and underscores the need for stronger defenses in embodied control systems that rely on world-action models.

Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

</details>


### [139] [Data Driven Block Replacement Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15229)
*Aniruddhan Ganesaraman,VIdyadhar Kulkarni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We develop bandit algorithms to learn the optimal block replacement interval from censored operational data, achieving near-optimal regret bounds, complemented by nonparametric Kaplan-Meier estimation and MDP structural analyses confirming block replacement optimality within its class.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In block replacement of N identical machines, the cost-minimizing interval k* depends on the unknown lifetime distribution. Practitioners need data-driven methods to learn k* online from censored failure histories without prior distributional knowledge.

Method: Problem is cast as a stochastic multi-armed bandit with arms k ∈ {1,...,K}. Two algorithm families: (1) Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms with nested observation exploitation achieving O((K−k*)log T) regret; (2) A Kaplan-Meier renewal algorithm that nonparametrically estimates the lifetime distribution from censored data. Additionally, two average-cost MDP formulations analyze structural properties: a time-elapsed MDP proving block replacement optimality within its policy class, and an age-vector MDP establishing monotone threshold structure under IFR distributions.

Result: LCB algorithms achieve O(K log T) regret matching the Lai-Robbins lower bound; correlated variants achieve O((K−k*)log T) with only O(1) pulls of suboptimal arms k < k*. The Kaplan-Meier algorithm attains almost-sure policy consistency with near-zero incremental regret empirically. The time-elapsed MDP confirms block replacement optimality within its class for any lifetime distribution; the age-vector MDP proves a monotone threshold under IFR and provides a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm theoretical regret orderings and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

Conclusion: Block replacement interval optimization can be effectively learned online with strong theoretical guarantees. The nested observation structure enables significant regret reduction, nonparametric estimation provides a complementary practical approach, and the MDP analyses supply structural validation and cost benchmarks for the block replacement policy class.

Abstract: We develop data-driven algorithms for maintaining $N$ independent identical machines under a \textit{block replacement policy}, in which each machine is replaced upon failure and all machines are jointly replaced at regular intervals of length $k$. The goal is to learn the cost-minimizing interval $k^*$ from operational data when the lifetime distribution is unknown. At each decision epoch, the operator selects $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}$, observes the resulting failure history (a mixture of complete and right-censored lifetimes) and incurs a per-unit-time cost governed by the renewal function. We formulate this as a stochastic multi-armed bandit and propose Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms achieving $O(K \log T)$ regret, matching the Lai--Robbins lower bound. Exploiting a nested observation property unique to block replacement, correlated variants attain $O((K-k^*)\log T)$ regret and require only $O(1)$ direct pulls of suboptimal arms $k < k^*$. A complementary Kaplan--Meier renewal algorithm estimates the lifetime distribution nonparametrically from censored data, achieving almost-sure policy consistency and empirically near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. We additionally analyze two average-cost MDPs: a time-elapsed formulation establishing that block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution, and an age-vector formulation proving a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions and providing a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical ordering and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

</details>


### [140] [Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15242)
*Hector J. Garcia,Nick Clayton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces mutable sketches using KP-trees to solve embedding staleness in two-stage recommendation systems, enabling real-time embedding updates without model retraining, with proven monotonic error reduction guarantees and significant efficiency gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In two-stage recommender systems, user embeddings become stale between retraining cycles—when a user rates new items, their embedding remains unchanged, leading to degraded recommendation quality. Existing methods like FunkSVD and eALS lack guarantees on how new observations improve predictions.

Method: The authors propose mutable sketches that store user preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation). A low-rank projection is fitted once, and embeddings are recomputed on-the-fly as new ratings arrive. The method uses norm-proportional sampling for sparse regimes and uniform sampling for dense matrices.

Result: On the KuaiRec dataset, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE while reading only 1.8% of the data, compared to ALS achieving 0.822 RMSE at 100% data read. Per-batch updates are 8x faster. New users receive personalized recommendations in under 1 ms after their first rating without retraining. Norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density).

Conclusion: Mutable sketches with KP-trees provide a provably sound solution to embedding staleness, offering monotonic prediction error tightening (Theorem 1), substantial computational efficiency, and near-instant cold-start personalization, outperforming traditional ALS while requiring only a fraction of the data.

Abstract: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

</details>


### [141] [Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15258)
*Arthur G. Bubolz,Abreu Quevedo,Giancarlo Lucca,Rafael A. Berri,Eduardo Borges,Bruno L. Dalmazo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study combining on-chain data, financial metrics, and Twitter sentiment to classify Bitcoin market sentiment using XGBoost (F1≈0.84), with SHAP providing interpretability of feature contributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing Bitcoin adoption as a decentralized digital asset necessitates better understanding of its market behavior. Existing models predominantly focus on price prediction rather than explaining market sentiment, leaving a gap in interpretable sentiment analysis that leverages both blockchain-native and social media data sources.

Method: The approach integrates three data streams — blockchain on-chain transactions, historical Bitcoin price data, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications — into a normalized dataset. Multiple machine learning models are evaluated via cross-validation, with XGBoost (Gradient Boosting) selected as the best performer. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is applied post-hoc to quantify each on-chain feature's contribution to model predictions.

Result: XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of approximately 0.84 for sentiment classification. SHAP analysis demonstrated that on-chain features contribute meaningful and interpretable predictive signals, validating the efficacy of combining blockchain and social media data for market sentiment analysis.

Conclusion: Combining on-chain, financial, and social media data yields actionable and transparent insights into Bitcoin market sentiment. The SHAP-enhanced XGBoost framework supports data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and opens avenues for future improvements using deep learning techniques.

Abstract: The growing use of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset and investment tool has sparked strong interest in understanding its market behavior. This study presents a new approach to analyze Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain and financial data with social media posts. Unlike models that aim to predict prices, this work focuses on explaining market sentiment using blockchain transactions, historical price data of Bitcoin, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. The method merges sentiment trends with on-chain and financial metrics, normalized into a dataset for detailed market analysis. Multiple machine learning models were tested using cross-validation, with Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) emerging as the most reliable model for classifying sentiment, achieving an average F1-score of about 0.84. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a game theory-based method for model interpretability, was used to quantify the contribution of on-chain features to the model's predictions, improving transparency. The results indicate that this data combination yields meaningful predictive signals and insights, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and future improvements with deep learning.

</details>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [142] [Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161)
*Junpeng Hou,XianXing Zhang,Sai Xiao,Derek Cheng,Darren Reger,Olafur Gudmundsson,Mehdi Ben Ayed,Zhiqing Rao,Huizhong Duan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Pinterest deploys a causal deep learning system that learns when to trigger shopping content retrieval, cutting shopping triggers by up to 85% while maintaining key shopping sessions and improving overall engagement (+0.26% sessions, +1.10% saves), with a reliable offline replay method for policy evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shopping content in Pinterest's recommendation pipeline should be shown only when helpful, not distracting. The core problem is deciding when to invoke expensive shopping candidate generators in early retrieval — framed as a causal decision: the cost of triggering vs. the incremental benefit (uplift) of showing commerce content.

Method: A deep multi-task model jointly predicts outcomes and uplift for multiple events using doubly-robust pseudo-outcomes combined with calibrated outcome losses for stable single-robust uplift learning. Training data comes from randomized logging for counterfactual coverage. A linear-time offline replay method selects thresholds and forecasts policy impact. The model runs in parallel with remote retrieval calls to avoid latency regression.

Result: Shopping triggers reduced by up to 85% while key shopping sessions remained neutral. Total sessions improved by +0.26%, Pin saves by +1.10%, with significant infrastructure savings. Offline replay showed extremely high consistency with online results.

Conclusion: The work provides a practical, production-grade recipe for optimizing early-retrieval decisions in cascading recommenders using deep causal learning with reliable offline evaluation, applicable beyond shopping to any content domain.

Abstract: Pinterest is where people turn inspiration into action as users browse ideas, then take steps toward realization, often by discovering shoppable content. To support this journey, we must distribute commerce content when it helps, not when it distracts. We frame this as a causal decision of triggering shopping candidate generators in early retrieval and deploy a production system at Pinterest that learns personalized and contextualized triggering policies. A deep multi-task model jointly predicts outcomes and uplift of multiple events, trained with a doubly-robust pseudo-outcome alongside calibrated outcome losses for stable, single-robust uplift learning. A randomized data logging supplies counterfactual coverage, and the model is evaluated by both regular and reverse metrics for full assessment. A linear-time offline replay is designed to select thresholds and forecast policy impact with extremely high consistency with online results. For productionization, the model runs in parallel with remote retrieval calls without end-to-end latency regression. At web scale, we cut shopping triggers by up to 85% while holding key shopping sessions neutral, improving important total sessions (+0.26%) and Pin saves (+1.10%), with significant infrastructure savings. By unifying deep causal learning with reliable offline replay and demonstrating production-grade deployment, this work provides a generally practical recipe for early-retrieval optimizations in modern cascading recommenders beyond shopping, aligning exploration and cost with user intent at scale.

</details>


### [143] [Long-History User Transformers for Real-Time Ad Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14331)
*Viacheslav Ovchinnikov,Georgii Smirnov,Nikolai Savushkin,Veronika Ivanova,Maksim Kuzin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A production advertising system decouples user history encoding from real-time inference: a heavy offline transformer pre-trains on interaction logs to produce compact, cacheable user representations, while a lightweight online model combines them with recent events for fast CTR prediction, achieving significant ranking and revenue gains without added latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long user interaction histories are highly informative for CTR prediction but cannot be processed by large sequence encoders under strict serving latency constraints (a few hundred milliseconds). The authors seek to leverage full interaction histories without sacrificing inference speed.

Method: A two-stage architecture: (1) an offline high-capacity transformer pre-trained autoregressively on large-scale logs with a dual objective (feedback prediction + next-item prediction), encoding the full cross-surface history into a compact cached representation; (2) a lightweight runtime model that fuses this cached representation with recent events and request context. The full pipeline is fine-tuned end-to-end for CTR prediction on the target surface.

Result: Offline, the split design recovers 72–80% of the quality of an undeployable full-history runtime transformer. In production A/B tests, primary ranking metric improves +2.77% (search ads) and +2.1% (Yandex Ad Network), with revenue gains of +2.26% and +0.43%, respectively, at no additional latency.

Conclusion: Decoupling history encoding from real-time inference via an offline pre-trained transformer and cached representations is a practical, effective strategy for injecting long-term user history into low-latency CTR prediction, delivering substantial business gains while respecting strict serving constraints.

Abstract: Long interaction histories are among the most informative inputs for click-through rate (CTR) prediction, yet in online advertising they collide with a hard serving constraint: ads must be scored within a few hundred milliseconds to enter the auction, which rules out running a large sequence encoder at request time. We describe how a production advertising system resolves this conflict by decoupling history encoding from real-time inference. A high-capacity offline transformer asynchronously encodes the user's full cross-surface interaction history into a compact representation cached in a feature store, while a lightweight runtime model combines this cached representation with the user's most recent events and the request context at serving time. The offline encoder is pre-trained autoregressively on large-scale interaction logs with a dual objective - feedback prediction and next-item prediction - and the two-stage architecture is then fine-tuned for CTR prediction on the target advertising surface. Offline, the split design recovers 72-80% of the quality of a full-history runtime transformer that would be too expensive to deploy, and the cached representation is robust enough to staleness to permit inexpensive refresh policies. In production A/B experiments, the system improves the primary ranking metric by +2.77% in search advertising and +2.1% on the Yandex Advertising Network, with revenue gains of +2.26% and +0.43% respectively - without increasing serving latency.

</details>


### [144] [Impact of Expert-Following Strategies in Financial Asset Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14556)
*Ryuki Unno,Koshi Watanabe,Keigo Sakurai,Keisuke Maeda,Takahiro Ogawa,Miki Haseyama*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes Expert-Following Strategies, a framework that identifies top investors by historical ROI and recommends assets based on ROI-weighted purchase frequency, achieving simultaneous improvements in both profitability (ROI) and relevance (nDCG) over market-average baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing recommendation strategies in finance optimize either return (ROI) or preference relevance (nDCG) individually, leading to an inherent trade-off. The authors aim to bridge this gap by simultaneously maximizing both objectives.

Method: The Expert-Following Strategies framework operates in two stages: (1) identifying top-performing investors ranked by historical ROI, and (2) recommending assets those experts purchased, scored by ROI-weighted purchase frequency. The approach leverages real-world transaction histories and is evaluated across four different thresholds.

Result: The proposed strategy achieves statistically significant improvements over the market-average baseline in both ROI and nDCG simultaneously across all four evaluation thresholds.

Conclusion: Expert-Following Strategies successfully resolves the ROI-nDCG trade-off by mimicking top investors, demonstrating that a single unified framework can deliver both profitable and preference-aligned financial recommendations.

Abstract: Financial institutions hold rich transaction histories, yet delivering recommendations that simultaneously maximize investment returns and ensure preference alignment remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches, namely return-based and preference-based strategies, each optimize a single objective, resulting in a fundamental trade-off between profitability (ROI) and relevance (nDCG). In this paper, we propose the Expert-Following Strategies: a framework that identifies top-performing investors based on their historical ROI and recommends the assets they purchased, scored by ROI-weighted purchase frequency. Our experiments using real-world transaction histories show that our strategy achieves statistically significant improvement over the market-average baseline in both ROI and nDCG simultaneously across all four thresholds.

</details>


### [145] [LLM-Based Re-Ranking for Real Estate Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14835)
*Nkateko Ntimane,Rafel Guedes,Tiago Cunha,Pedro Nogueira*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: QuintoAndar developed an LLM-based re-ranker for conversational real-estate search that reorders candidates using multi-turn dialog context. Evaluated on a 960K-pair dataset and via a production A/B test, it delivered +5.3% CTR and +4.8% scheduled visits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional faceted search is insufficient for housing discovery, where user intent is multi-dimensional, context-dependent, and evolves across conversations. Users increasingly expect to express needs through open, multi-turn dialog rather than rigid filters, creating a need for conversational recommendation systems that can interpret nuanced, context-rich intent.

Method: An LLM-based re-ranker is integrated into a conversational recommendation system. It reorders retrieved housing candidates according to the full conversational context. A large-scale offline evaluation dataset of 960,000 query-item pairs was constructed using both synthetic and production queries, annotated via an LLM-as-a-Judge framework with human validation. The approach was evaluated offline and through an online production A/B test.

Result: Offline and online evaluations showed consistent ranking quality improvements. The production A/B test yielded a statistically significant +5.3% increase in click-through rate and +4.8% increase in scheduled visits.

Conclusion: Integrating conversational context into housing recommendations via LLM-based re-ranking provides measurable, significant gains in user engagement and conversion, validating the approach for real-world deployment at scale.

Abstract: QuintoAndar Group operates the leading housing marketplace in Latin America for both rentals and sales. The platform replaces traditionally paper-heavy workflows with a fully digital experience, making housing transactions faster and more accessible to tenants, buyers, and landlords in the region. Finding the ideal home in such a vast catalog is inherently difficult. At the same time, the widespread adoption of conversational assistants is reshaping user expectations: people increasingly want to express their needs through open, multi-turn dialog rather than rigid filter menus and faceted search. This shift is particularly pronounced in housing, where intent is multi-dimensional, context-dependent, and rarely reducible to a small set of structured constraints. To meet these expectations, we propose a Large Language Model (LLM) based re-ranker that augments a conversational recommendation system by reordering retrieved candidates according to the nuanced, context-rich intent expressed across the user's conversation. We additionally construct a large-scale offline evaluation dataset for conversational real-estate search, containing 960,000 query-item pairs constructed from both synthetic and production queries and annotated using an LLM-as-a-Judge framework with human validation. We validate our approach both offline, on this proprietary dataset, and online, through a production A/B test. Both evaluations show consistent improvements in ranking quality, including a statistically significant increase in production of +5.3% in click-through rate and +4.8% in scheduled visits, demonstrating the value of integrating conversational context into housing recommendations.

</details>


### [146] [Does generative AI supersede supervised XMLC? A Benchmark Study on Automated Subject Indexing with German Scientific Literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14882)
*Maximilian Kähler,Katja Konermann,Lisa Kluge,Markus Schumacher*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks automated subject indexing for German scientific literature at the German National Library using supervised Extreme Multi-Label Classification (XMLC) methods, classical lexical matching, and LLM-based generative approaches. While XMLC methods excel in overall binary relevance, LLM-based methods outperform on graded relevance and long-tail vocabulary terms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated subject indexing with a large controlled vocabulary is challenging, especially for reliably suggesting terms from the long tail. The authors aim to determine whether supervised XMLC methods or emerging LLM-based generative approaches are more effective for this real-world library task.

Method: The authors benchmark several approaches on German scientific literature from the DNB: (1) specialised supervised XMLC methods using transformer-based dense features, (2) a classical lexical matching baseline, and (3) three custom LLM-based generative methods. Evaluation uses both binary relevance against previously indexed material and graded relevance ratings from professional subject librarians.

Result: Supervised XMLC algorithms with transformer-based dense features achieve the best overall binary relevance metrics. However, LLM-based generative methods yield better results for graded relevance and for performance on the long tail of the subject vocabulary.

Conclusion: LLM-based generative methods are a promising alternative to XMLC for automated subject indexing, particularly when graded relevance and coverage of rare subject terms are prioritised, suggesting potential for productive deployment in library settings.

Abstract: With a large controlled vocabulary as the label set, the task of automated subject indexing in a library can be understood as a multi-label classification task. If the set of subject terms is large, the problem fits the Extreme Multi-Label Classification (XMLC) objective. In this study, we apply a selection of specialised supervised XMLC methods to the test case of subject indexing contemporary German scientific literature, collected at the German National Library (DNB). We contrast these results by including a classical lexical matching baseline and three of our own recently developed LLM-based methods into the benchmark. Algorithms are evaluated and compared in several metrics. This includes binary relevance comparisons with previously indexed material, as well as graded relevance ratings by professional subject librarians. A challenge for all methods is to reliably make suggestions from the long tail of the subject vocabulary. We find that supervised XMLC algorithms relying on transformer-based dense features give best results in terms of overall binary relevance metrics. However, focusing on graded relevance and performance in the long tail of our subject vocabulary, the LLM-based generative methods give better results, making them a promising alternative for future productive use.

</details>


### [147] [CoSimRec: Measuring Coordinated-Content Penetration in Recommender Feedback Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15114)
*Nan Li,Jiahong Shao,Jiuyang Lyu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: CoSimRec is an offline agent-based framework for evaluating how coordinated inauthentic activity propagates through recommender systems in a closed feedback loop. It introduces the Algorithmic Penetration Rate (APR) metric family and demonstrates that popularity-based and feedback-sensitive recommenders significantly amplify coordinated attacks, while synchronization-aware ranking mitigates this effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current robustness evaluations of recommender systems focus narrowly on static target-rank changes and fail to capture the dynamic feedback loop between coordinated interactions, algorithmic ranking updates, and non-bot user responses. This gap obscures the real-world amplification effects of coordinated activity.

Method: CoSimRec is an offline, agent-based evaluation framework that simulates coordinated accounts, dynamic ranking, non-bot user responses, and ranking interventions within a shared closed-loop process. The framework introduces the Algorithmic Penetration Rate (APR) metric family, which measures target content share of non-bot exposure/engagement, lift against matched no-attack baselines, and exposure gained per coordinated interaction. Evaluations span three datasets (MIND, MovieLens, LastFM), five recommender types, ten-seed inference for primary APR analysis, and population-scale experiments up to 1000 users.

Result: Random recommenders show no statistically supported positive penetration. Popularity-based and feedback-sensitive recommenders produce significant positive APR-Lift across all six dataset–recommender pairings, reaching 0.4505 on LastFM. Synchronization-aware ranking reduces APR in every corresponding defense setting.

Conclusion: Coordinated attacks are substantially amplified by non-random, popularity-driven, and feedback-sensitive ranking algorithms through recommendation feedback loops. Defensive strategies like synchronization-aware ranking can effectively mitigate this amplification, underscoring the need for closed-loop evaluation frameworks when assessing recommender system robustness.

Abstract: Recommender systems increasingly shape which content reaches users, making it important to understand whether coordinated activity is amplified beyond the accounts that initiate it. Existing robustness evaluations largely focus on static target-rank changes and do not capture how coordinated interactions, recommendation, and user response evolve within a feedback loop. To address this gap, we propose CoSimRec, an offline agent-based evaluation framework that models coordinated accounts, dynamic ranking, non-bot responses, and ranking interventions in a shared closed-loop process. CoSimRec introduces the Algorithmic Penetration Rate (APR) metric family to measure target content's share of non-bot exposure and engagement, lift against matched no-attack baselines, and exposure gained per coordinated interaction. We evaluate CoSimRec on MIND, MovieLens, and LastFM using random, popularity-based, feedback-sensitive, MF, and BPR-MF recommenders, with ten-seed inference for the primary APR analysis and population-scale experiments of up to 1000 users. Random controls show no statistically supported positive penetration, whereas popularity-based and feedback-sensitive ranking produce significant positive APR-Lift in all six master-worker dataset--recommender settings, reaching 0.4505 on LastFM; synchronization-aware ranking reduces APR in every corresponding defense setting.

</details>


### [148] [Bridge Evidence: Static Retrieval Utility Does Not Predict Causal Utility in Multi-Step Agentic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15253)
*Debayan Mukhopadhyay,Utshab Kumar Ghosh,Shubham Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Static document relevance (whether a document answers a question) and causal usefulness in agentic search (whether a document enables future retrieval steps) are nearly independent. The paper introduces Counterfactual Trajectory Utility (CTU) to measure the latter and identifies "bridge documents" — documents that appear useless to a static reader but are causally critical for steering the agent's subsequent queries via discriminative entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current retrieval evaluation assumes static usefulness: a document is valuable if it directly improves answer quality. This assumption fails when a language model acts as a search agent issuing multiple queries and reasoning across turns. A document's value may lie not in what it says about the current question, but in what it enables the agent to do next. The paper aims to measure this gap between static relevance and causal trajectory utility rather than merely arguing it exists.

Method: Using a ReAct-style agent on HotpotQA, the authors replay 1000 development questions. For every document the agent reads, they delete it and re-run the remainder of the trajectory from that point (counterfactual ablation). CTU is computed from three deltas: final answer quality, next-query retrieval quality, and turn count. CTU is cross-compared against Static RAG Utility (SRU) across 23,322 document observations. A second experiment uses Observable Entity Relevance (OER) to trace whether entities from useful documents appear in the agent's next query.

Result: CTU and SRU are nearly statistically independent (Spearman ρ = -0.026). Approximately one-third of documents read are "bridge documents": causally load-bearing yet appearing useless to a static reader. This pattern holds when SRU is replaced with BM25/cross-encoder proxies (27.2% bridge cell on an evenly spread axis). Discriminative entities from bridge documents appear in the agent's next query 4.02× more often than entities from non-relevant documents (6.1% vs 1.5%, n=227,139).

Conclusion: Static relevance and causal usefulness are fundamentally different quantities in agentic retrieval. Optimizing for static relevance does not deliver causal usefulness. Bridge documents earn their keep by providing discriminative entities that redirect the agent's search trajectory, revealing a mechanistic explanation for the observed independence.

Abstract: Retrieval systems are trained and evaluated on a static idea of usefulness: hand a document and a question to a reader model, see whether the answer improves, and score the document accordingly. The idea holds up when a document is read on its own. It breaks when a language model works as a search agent, issuing several queries and reasoning across turns, because a document can matter for what it lets the agent do next rather than for what it says about the current question.
  We measure that gap rather than argue it. Using a ReAct style agent over HotpotQA, we replay 1000 development questions and, for every document the agent read, delete it and re-run the rest of the trajectory from that point. Comparing the original run against its counterfactual gives a Counterfactual Trajectory Utility (CTU) score from three deltas: final answer quality, next query retrieval quality, and turn count. Crossing CTU against Static RAG Utility (SRU) over 23,322 document observations, the two are close to statistically independent (Spearman rho = -0.026). Roughly a third of the documents the agent reads are causally load bearing while looking useless to a static reader; we call these bridge documents. The pattern survives when the reader based axis is swapped for a BM25 and cross encoder proxy, giving a bridge cell of 27.2% on an evenly spread axis.
  A second experiment pins down the mechanism. Using the Observable Entity Relevance (OER) measure from prior work, entities that discriminate relevant from non-relevant candidates appear in the agent's next query 4.02 times more often than entities found only in non-relevant documents (6.1% vs 1.5%, n = 227,139). A bridge document earns its keep by handing the agent a discriminative entity that redirects the search. Static relevance and causal usefulness are different quantities in agentic retrieval, and optimizing the first does not deliver the second.

</details>

### [149] [Intelligent Three Level Learning Architecture for Autonomous UAV Swarms in Search and Rescue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14093)
*Oleksii Bychkov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A three-level hierarchical learning architecture for autonomous UAV swarms in SAR, integrating Hebbian neuroplasticity, MARL with GNNs/behavior trees, and MAML with BDI reasoning/digital twins. Formalized via 22 architectural contracts providing six guarantee classes, with Swarm Meta-Cognition enabling cognitive strategy switching. A main integration theorem proves guarantee preservation when contracts are satisfied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hierarchical RL approaches suffer from five fundamental limitations: they apply a single learning paradigm across all hierarchy levels, lack formal guarantees across safety/liveness/optimality dimensions, and fail to provide mechanisms for cognitive self-monitoring and strategy switching. The paper aims to bridge the gap between abstract optimization theory and concrete SAR operational scenarios.

Method: A three-level biologically-inspired architecture: (1) Hebbian neuroplasticity for individual agent adaptation (reflexes), (2) multi-agent RL with graph neural networks and behavior trees for tactical coordination (skills), (3) model-agnostic meta-learning with BDI reasoning and a digital twin for strategic decision-making (reasoning). Formalized through 22 architectural contracts across six components, with five constructive progress functions for SAR task types. Five additional dynamic contracts extend the framework for active learning scenarios.

Result: The main integration theorem establishes that when all contracts are satisfied, the hybrid neuro-symbolic system preserves all six guarantee classes (safety, budget correctness, optimality, liveness, starvation freedom, inter-level consistency). The dynamic extension adds three further guarantees: cognitive resilience, graceful degradation, and monotonic meta-improvement. Swarm Meta-Cognition emerges as a compositional property from the structured interaction of all three levels.

Conclusion: The proposed architecture addresses all five identified limitations of existing hierarchical RL approaches and provides a formally-grounded, cognitively-adaptive framework for autonomous UAV swarm operations in search and rescue missions.

Abstract: This paper presents a novel three level hierarchical learning architecture for autonomous UAV swarms performing search and rescue operations. Unlike conventional approaches that apply a single learning paradigm across all hierarchy levels, the proposed architecture integrates three qualitatively different learning mechanisms corresponding to the biological hierarchy of reflexes, skills, and reasoning such as Hebbian neuroplasticity for individual agent adaptation, multi agent reinforcement learning with graph neural networks and behavior trees for tactical coordination, and model agnostic meta learning with BDI reasoning and a digital twin for strategic decision making.
  The architecture is formalized through twenty two architectural contracts organized across six components such as BDI, Behavior Trees, GNN, MARL, Neuroplasticity, Meta Learning that collectively provide six classes of formal guarantees such as safety, budget correctness, optimality, liveness, starvation freedom, and inter level consistency.
  We introduce Swarm Meta Cognition as a compositional property arising from the structured interaction of all three levels, enabling the swarm to monitor its own cognitive state and switch between cognitive strategies. Five constructive progress functions for SAR task types bridge the gap between abstract optimization theory and concrete operational scenarios.
  The main integration theorem establishes that when all contracts are satisfied, the hybrid neuro-symbolic system preserves all six guarantee classes. For the dynamic case with active learning, five new contracts extend the framework with three additional guarantees such as cognitive resilience, graceful degradation, and monotonic meta improvement. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the architecture addresses five fundamental limitations of existing hierarchical RL approaches.

</details>


### [150] [HG-RAG: Hierarchy-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14095)
*Pranav Yadav*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HG-RAG is a hierarchical knowledge graph traversal framework for RAG that resolves entity anchors from queries and expands context through parent, lateral, and child nodes, outperforming flat retrieval baselines on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks while reducing hallucination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG systems retrieve context from flat document stores, which are inadequate for queries requiring hierarchical or relational reasoning across structured knowledge. This motivates a graph-based approach that can traverse structured relationships.

Method: HG-RAG constructs a hierarchical knowledge graph and uses a retrieval pipeline that: (1) resolves a named entity anchor from the query, (2) expands context upward through parent nodes, (3) expands laterally through relational neighbors, and (4) expands downward through child nodes as needed. Evaluation spans three world scales (18-800 nodes) with four query types: local fact, hierarchical, neighborhood, and multi-hop.

Result: HG-RAG consistently outperforms the dense retrieval baseline on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks. It also reduces hallucination and maintains locality coherence compared to the flat baseline.

Conclusion: Hierarchy-guided graph traversal provides structured, multi-directional context that enables LLMs to handle complex reasoning tasks more effectively than flat RAG retrieval, offering a promising direction for structured knowledge integration in RAG pipelines.

Abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has proven to be a widely successful process at improving the quality of outputs from a Large Language Model (LLM) for wider context. However, RAG systems typically retrieve context from flat document stores, which struggles when queries require hierarchical or relational reasoning across structured knowledge. I present HG-RAG (Hierarchy-Guided RAG), a framework that performs graph-traversal over a hierarchical knowledge graph to deliver structured context to a language model. My retrieval pipeline resolves a named entity anchor from the query, then expands context upward through parent nodes, laterally through relational neighbors, and downward through child nodes when needed. I evaluate HG-RAG against a dense retrieval baseline across three world scales (18-800 nodes) with four query types: local fact, hierarchical, neighborhood, and multi-hop. Results show HG-RAG consistently outperforms the flat baseline on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks, while reducing hallucination and maintaining locality coherence.

</details>


### [151] [IMEX Interaction-Based Model Explanation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14096)
*Emiliano Massi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IMEX is an explainability framework that identifies important features and their interactions in predictive models using Static Correlation Power (PCS) for individual contributions and Interaction Correlation Power (PCI) for non-additive effects. The PCS component is experimentally validated against INVASE on three synthetic datasets, showing IMEX can recover relevant structures under non-linear, conditional, and multicollinear conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Black-box predictive models lack transparency, making accurate predictions difficult to interpret and validate — especially in critical contexts where understanding the reasons behind decisions is essential. There is a need for methods that not only identify important features but also capture higher-order interactions without imposing cardinality limitations.

Method: The IMEX (Interaction-Based Model Explanation) framework employs two complementary metrics: PCS (Static Correlation Power) for quantifying individual feature contributions, and PCI (Interaction Correlation Power) for capturing non-additive interaction effects among features. The method imposes no restrictions on interaction order, enabling analysis of feature subsets with cardinality greater than two. The PCS component is experimentally validated through comparison with INVASE on three synthetic datasets with known structures.

Result: Experimental validation on three synthetic datasets demonstrates that IMEX (specifically its PCS component) can successfully recover relevant feature-level structures even in the presence of non-linear relationships, conditional dependencies, and multicollinearity between input features and prediction targets. Comparison is made against the INVASE baseline.

Conclusion: IMEX provides a promising direction for explainable predictive modeling by enabling interpretability maps of predictions through feature importance and interaction analysis. The PCS metric is validated as effective for identifying relevant features under challenging data conditions, with PCI offering additional capability for uncovering higher-order interactions.

Abstract: In predictive modeling, the ability to explain why a model produces a given target prediction has become increasingly important [5, 10]. Black-box models do not provide a transparent description of the internal mechanisms that generate the prediction, making even accurate predictions difficult to interpret and validate. In critical contexts, predictive accuracy alone is not a sufficient validation metric if the reasons underlying model decisions remain unexplained. The IMEX (Interaction-Based Model Explanation) approach represents a methodological direction within explainable predictive modeling. IMEX is designed to identify which variables contribute most to the target prediction and which interactions among variables are significant in determining the target. The method does not impose limitations on higher-order interaction analysis, allowing the investigation of feature subsets with cardinality greater than two. Beyond the identification of feature importance, IMEX enables the exploration of interaction patterns that may be consistent with latent mechanisms influencing the outcome. Through the application of the IMEX algorithm, it is possible to construct an interpretability map of the predictions. The IMEX framework is built on two complementary metrics: Static Correlation Power (PCS), which quantifies the contribution of individual features, and Interaction Correlation Power (PCI), which captures non-additive effects among features. In the present work, the PCS component is experimentally validated through a comparison with INVASE [18] on three synthetic datasets with known structures. The results indicate that IMEX can recover relevant feature-level structures in the presence of non-linear, conditional, and multicollinear relationships between input features and prediction targets.

</details>


### [152] [RegNetAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Network Regulatory Driver Identification in Cancer Genomics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14097)
*Jose A. Bird*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RegNetAgents is a multi-agent AI framework that identifies cancer gene regulators by integrating bulk tumor (TCGA) and single-cell (GREmLN) regulatory networks, with candidates ranked by cross-network evidence consistency and significantly enriched for known cancer genes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identifying regulatory candidates across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks is challenging due to the lack of unified, interpretable frameworks that can integrate bulk and single-cell-derived networks while incorporating clinical annotations. Existing approaches typically focus on network inference rather than downstream candidate prioritization and biological interpretation.

Method: A multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow that performs: (1) dual-network classification across TCGA-derived and GREmLN single-cell ARACNe networks for a given focal gene, (2) cancer gene filtering via OncoKB annotations, (3) mode-of-action (MoA) assignment for tumor-derived regulatory relationships, and (4) candidate ranking by evidence consistency (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only). The system is accessible through a unified Python API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client.

Result: Across 11 BRCA and 12 COAD focal genes, TCGA-derived candidates showed strong OncoKB enrichment (Stouffer Z = 6.69 BRCA, 6.95 COAD); GREmLN-derived candidates were also significantly enriched (Z = 5.51 BRCA, 7.06 COAD; all p < 0.0001). No enrichment was observed in housekeeping or non-driver controls, confirming signal specificity.

Conclusion: RegNetAgents provides an interpretable, structured AI framework for cross-network regulatory candidate identification, bridging bulk and single-cell regulatory data with clinical cancer annotations to support biological hypothesis generation in cancer genomics.

Abstract: We introduce RegNetAgents, an AI-oriented multi-agent framework for structured, query-driven regulatory candidate identification across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks. The system enables unified analysis of bulk tumor and single-cell-derived ARACNe networks by integrating TCGA-derived cancer networks with large-scale single-cell regulatory networks from the GREmLN project. For a given focal gene, the framework performs dual-network classification, cancer gene filtering using OncoKB annotations, and mode-of-action (MoA) assignment for tumor-derived regulatory relationships. Candidates are ranked by evidence consistency across networks (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only). The system is implemented as a multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow, accessible through a unified Python API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client, operating as a downstream analytical layer over precomputed regulatory networks rather than a network inference method. Across eleven breast cancer (BRCA) and twelve colorectal cancer (COAD) focal genes, RegNetAgents identifies candidate regulators significantly enriched for OncoKB-annotated cancer genes. TCGA-derived candidates show strong enrichment (Stouffer Z = 6.69 for BRCA and 6.95 for COAD), while GREmLN-derived candidates also demonstrate significant enrichment (Z = 5.51 for BRCA and 7.06 for COAD; all p < 0.0001). No enrichment is observed in housekeeping or non-driver control gene sets, supporting signal specificity. An extended module enables structured evaluation of oncogenic potential, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability, supporting end-to-end interpretation from candidate identification to biological hypothesis generation. RegNetAgents establishes an interpretable AI framework for cross-network regulatory candidate identification in cancer genomics.

</details>


### [153] [DialogueVPR: Towards Conversational Visual Place Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14115)
*Yukun Song,Changwei Wang,Xingtian Pei,Shibiao Xu,Wenhao Xu,Shunpeng Chen,Yu Zhang,Ke Zhang,Rongtao Xu,Xuxiang Feng,Pengyang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), shifting language-guided geo-localization from static one-shot retrieval to interactive dialogue-driven reasoning, with a new benchmark DlgQuest-Cities and a GRPO-trained intelligent questioner (DQ-pilot) that significantly outperforms baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-guided geo-localization methods use a static, one-shot retrieval paradigm that cannot handle the ambiguity and incompleteness of real-world natural language descriptions. The authors argue for a reasoning-based retrieval paradigm where localization becomes an interactive dialogue process.

Method: Introduces DlgQuest-Cities, a large-scale dialogue benchmark, and a unified reasoning framework with a cross-modal multi-level retriever and an intelligent questioner called DQ-pilot. DQ-pilot is trained via a curriculum: supervised fine-tuning on DQ-cities-20k, then reinforcement refinement on DQ-cities-10k using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Two metrics guide training: Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) for curriculum sampling and Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) reward for measuring retrieval improvement per question.

Result: The reasoning-based interactive approach significantly outperforms baseline methods on the DlgQuest-Cities benchmark.

Conclusion: Dialogue-driven reasoning retrieval is a promising new paradigm for language-guided geo-localization, overcoming the limitations of static one-shot methods by interactively resolving ambiguity through intelligent questioning.

Abstract: Inspired by how humans communicate spatial information, language-guided geo-localization has gained significant traction for its intuitive and practical value. Despite this progress, most methods still rely on a static, one-shot retrieval paradigm, which fails to handle the ambiguity and incompleteness inherent in real-world natural language descriptions. We propose a paradigm shift to reasoning retrieval and introduce Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), which casts localization as an interactive, dialogue-driven reasoning process. To support this new task, we present DlgQuest-Cities, the first large-scale dialogue-based benchmark for place recognition, and a unified reasoning framework that couples a cross-modal multi-level retriever with an intelligent questioner, DQ-pilot. DQ-pilot is trained in a curriculum: supervised fine-tuning on a curated DQ-cities-20k subset followed by reinforcement refinement on a harder DQ-cities-10k split via GRPO. Two task-aligned metrics guide learning: a Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) for curriculum sampling and a Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) reward that directly measures retrieval improvement induced by a question. Experiments show this reasoning-based approach significantly outperforms baselines. The code and model are available at https://github.com/Graysonggg/DlgPR.

</details>


### [154] [Orchestrating Power Grid Studies with Multi-Agent AI and MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14158)
*Jérôme Picault,Clément Goubet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This position paper proposes integrating Agentic AI with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to assist Transmission System Operators in power-grid studies, introducing pypowsybl-mcp as a testbed interface between LLM-based agents and numerical grid simulation tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Power-grid studies at TSOs are complex, tool-heavy, and require extensive human expertise. The authors aim to explore how LLM-based AI agents, connected to simulation tools via standardized protocols, can streamline study workflows, reduce manual overhead, and maintain auditability under human supervision.

Method: The paper introduces pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface that exposes selected capabilities of the pypowsybl power-system simulator to AI agents via standardized tool calls. It outlines principles for human-in-the-loop oversight, multi-agent workflow design, and proposes an evaluation strategy blending technical metrics with practitioner feedback.

Result: As a position paper, it presents no experimental results but delivers a conceptual architecture and a functional MCP interface (pypowsybl-mcp) enabling agents to set up simulations, execute analyses, and retrieve results through structured tool calls, establishing a testbed for future empirical evaluation.

Conclusion: MCP-based tool integration represents a promising step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments, positioning standardized agent-tool communication as a practical pathway for introducing AI assistance into mission-critical power-system operations.

Abstract: This position paper explores how Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) can support power-grid studies in a Transmission System Operator (TSO) context. We focus on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision. We identify key industrial requirements for agent assisted grid studies and introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface exposing selected capabilities of our simulation tool, pypowsybl to AI agents. This first step provides a testbed to study how agents can setup simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls. We also discuss principles for human-in-the-loop, multi-agent workflows and outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback. The paper positions MCP-based tool integration as a step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments.

</details>


### [155] [Interpretable Language Model for Closed-Loop Type 1 Diabetes Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14126)
*Maya Sarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-T1D combines RL-trained insulin controllers with fine-tuned LLMs (LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B) to create a transparent, explainable artificial pancreas system for Type 1 Diabetes, achieving 73.5% Time-in-Range on the UVA/Padova simulator with formal safety guarantees against hallucinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement Learning-based Artificial Pancreas Systems for T1D are effective but operate as "black boxes," undermining trust among patients and clinicians. There is a need for controllers that are both high-performing and capable of providing human-understandable explanations for their decisions.

Method: An expert RL system is first trained for insulin delivery control. Its decision-making knowledge is then distilled into two 8B-parameter LLMs (LLaMA 3.1 and Qwen3) via fine-tuning.
