The resulting LLM controllers are evaluated on the FDA-approved UVA/Padova T1D simulator, with formal safety verification applied to detect and mitigate hallucinations.

Result: The LLM-based controllers surpass the original RL system's performance, achieving 73.5% Time-in-Range (a key glycemic control metric). Strict formal verification methods ensure safety by guarding against hallucinated outputs.

Conclusion: Distilling RL policies into LLMs yields a controller that combines strong glycemic control with interpretable, natural-language reasoning, offering a more trustworthy and transparent approach to automated insulin delivery for T1D management.

Abstract: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is a chronic, life-threatening autoimmune condition characterized by the complete destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. While Artificial Pancreas Systems (APS) powered by Reinforcement Learning (RL) have shown promise in automating insulin delivery, their ``black-box'' nature makes it hard for patients and doctors to trust them fully. This paper presents LLM-T1D, a promising approach that combines the precision of RL with the clear, human-like reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) to create a more transparent and reliable insulin pump controller. By training an expert RL system and distilling its knowledge into fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1 8B and Qwen3 8B models, we developed a controller that not only surpasses the RL system's performance but also explains its decisions in plain, understandable language. Tested on the FDA-approved UVA/Padova T1D simulator, the LLM controllers deliver excellent blood sugar control (73.5% Time in Range) while maintaining strict formal safety verification against hallucinations.

</details>


### [156] [ReasFlow: Assisting Reasoning-Centric Scientific Discovery in Applied Mathematics via a Knowledge-Based Multi-Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14178)
*Yutong He,Daibo Li,Guohong Li,Jiahe Geng,Zhengyang Huang,Can Ren,Zekun Zhang,Yifan Liu,Shuchen Zhu,Hengrui Zhang,Boao Kong,Ming Sun,Shu Li,Chenyi Li,Jiang Hu,Kun Yuan,Zaiwen Wen,Pingwen Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReasFlow is an autonomous agent system for theory-driven scientific discovery that treats the human as Principal Investigator and the AI as a graduate student, featuring internal verification and self-improving knowledge retrieval, and it outperforms open baselines on generating complete research papers from minimal prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated research systems focus on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery—particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and domain knowledge synthesis—largely underexplored. Key gaps include difficulty verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient autonomous frontier exploration, and scarce procedural heuristics in the literature.

Method: ReasFlow is an end-to-end autonomous agent system using a collaborative human-AI paradigm (human as PI, agent as graduate student). It comprises: (i) an internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors before human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that surfaces declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation.

Result: ReasFlow autonomously generated five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts. It consistently achieved the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric.

Conclusion: ReasFlow successfully bridges the gap in autonomous theory-driven scientific discovery, demonstrating that a human-in-the-loop PI–graduate-student paradigm with robust internal verification and proactive knowledge retrieval can produce high-quality, rigorous research outputs. The system is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models have fueled autonomous AI agents capable of tackling complex scientific tasks, yet existing automated research systems remain predominantly focused on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery, particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge, largely underexplored. Key challenges include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for autonomous frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature. We introduce ReasFlow, an end-to-end autonomous agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that operationalizes a collaborative paradigm where the human expert acts as Principal Investigator while the agent executes rigorous derivations as a capable graduate student. ReasFlow incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors prior to human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that proactively surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics, substantially reducing expert intervention. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single system. Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform, providing a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research. Github repo: https://github.com/ReasLab/ReasFlow.git.

</details>


### [157] [Human AI Construction of Bayesian Networks for Operational Decision Support -- A Virtual Survey Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14141)
*Kumar Rahul,Shovan Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel methodology that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) with a panel of AI agents embodying specific personas to estimate Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) probabilities, bridging the gap between pure expert judgment and data-driven learning. A trimmed-mean rule filters response noise. The approach is demonstrated via a six-step BBN framework modeling customer intention to consult a doctor in alternative healthcare, revealing that subjective norms have a stronger causal effect than self-efficacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building BBN structures and estimating parameters is inherently difficult, forcing an unsatisfying trade-off between subjective expert judgment and the need for large datasets. The authors seek a middle ground that leverages AI to simulate expert-like probability estimation with reduced cost and bias.

Method: The methodology employs a panel of LLM-based AI agents, each assigned distinct personas and contextual framing, to elicit probability estimates for BBN parameters. A trimmed-mean aggregation rule mitigates outlier noise. These estimates feed into a structured six-step BBN framework for modeling and causal analysis.

Result: Applied to alternative healthcare consultation intention, the BBN model shows that although self-efficacy appears prominent, its actual causal impact is small. Subjective norms exert a substantially stronger causal influence. The optimal intervention strategy combines boosting both self-confidence and community norms simultaneously.

Conclusion: LLM-driven probability elicitation via persona-based AI panels is a viable bridge between expert judgment and data-driven BBN construction. The case study underscores that apparent factors (self-efficacy) may mask true causal drivers (subjective norms), highlighting the value of the BBN framework for strategic decision-making.

Abstract: Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs) are powerful tools for decision-making under uncertainty. However, building their structures and estimating parameters are difficult. Currently, researchers must choose between relying on expert judgement or using large datasets to learn the structure and parameters of the network. We propose a new methodology using Large Language Models to bridge the gap between expert opinion and data-driven learning. This approach uses a panel of AI agents to estimate probabilities based on specific personas and context. We then apply a trimmed-mean rule to remove noise from these responses. We develop a six step BBN framework and illustrate it to model customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system. The model reveals that while self efficacy appears to be a major factor, its actual causal impact is small. In contrast, subjective norms have a much stronger effect in modelling customers' intention. The most effective strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms simultaneously.

</details>


### [158] [Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14256)
*Genglin Liu,Muye Zhang,Krishnamurthy Viswanathan,Nichole J. Hansen,Blaž Bratanič,Nathan L Clement,Shalini Ghosh,Ariel Fuxman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an automated, multi-agent red-teaming framework that iteratively synthesizes adversarial multimodal examples to probe MLLM safety vulnerabilities, and uses these examples via test-time retrieval to reduce the False Negative Rate from 41.2% to 24.5% without human labeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs deployed for content safety/moderation are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases, but traditional active learning and manual annotation cannot scale to handle the volume and complexity of novel multimodal threats.

Method: An agentic red-teaming framework employing a multi-agent architecture with: (1) a high-reasoning Architect agent that proposes novel hypotheses, (2) an advanced image generator, and (3) a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters. The system iteratively synthesizes difficult adversarial examples through hypothesis generation and mutation of past attempts, then uses these examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time Retrieval.

Result: The framework autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases. On a public image safety benchmark, the approach reduces the False Negative Rate from 41.2% to 24.5% without any human labeling.

Conclusion: Automated, agentic red-teaming with iterative synthesis and test-time retrieval of adversarial demonstrations can substantially improve MLLM safety robustness at scale, eliminating the dependency on costly human annotation.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed for nuanced content safety and moderation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation fail to scale against the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats. In this paper, we propose an automated, agentic red-teaming framework that systematically synthesizes difficult examples using an iterative strategy that proposes novel hypotheses as well as mutating on past attempts. Leveraging a multi-agent architecture that consists of a high-reasoning Architect agent, an advanced image generator, and a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters, our system autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases without any human intervention. By employing these carefully synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time Retrieval, we substantially improve the target model's robustness, reducing the False Negative Rate (FNR) from 41.2% to 24.5% in a public image safety benchmark without relying on any human labeling.

</details>


### [159] [Capability from Access Structure, Not Scale: Lower Bounds and Pre-Registered Tests for Hybrid Sequence Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14144)
*Wenhui Chen,Jianlin Chen,Ziyao Lin,Chi Man Vong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH): while neural network representations converge with scale (Platonic Representation Hypothesis), capability convergence requires specific architectural ingredients — namely, a hybrid architecture combining a compressive O(1)-state channel and a scalable verbatim-index channel. The authors identify three information-theoretic "walls" and demonstrate through pre-registered experiments that crossing them requires paying each wall's price, making capability strictly super-additive under composition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests representations converge across models with scale, but this does not guarantee that capabilities also converge. The authors seek to delineate the boundary conditions under which capability convergence does or does not occur, grounding the analysis in fundamental resource constraints (information-theoretic lower bounds, circuit complexity) rather than empirical trends alone.

Method: The paper combines theoretical lower bounds with pre-registered small-scale experiments. Three resource walls are formally named and analyzed: the Shannon wall (information-theoretic, barring any o(Nb)-state architecture), the horizon wall (barring fixed-window models), and the circuit wall (barring fixed-depth attention-only composition, conditional on TC0 ≠ NC1). Under an explicit separability assumption, the hybrid architecture is shown to cross all three walls. Pre-registered experiments test specific predictions: a "scissors gap" in exact-retrieval error, a state-tracking bifurcation boundary, and a conjunction witness task requiring an irreducibly two-channel solution.

Result: Three pre-registered predictions were confirmed: (1) the scissors gap was measured — exact-retrieval error 0.994 vs. 0.000 when a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer; (2) the state-tracking bifurcation landed at the registered boundary; (3) the conjunction witness showed an irreducibly two-channel solution. One prediction failed with reversed direction and is reported transparently.

Conclusion: Representational convergence is an emergent byproduct of scale alone, but capability convergence requires deliberate architectural investment — specifically, access to both compressive and verbatim-index channels. The access-completeness principle is grounded in information-theoretic lower bounds and experimental evidence, while the broader field-level convergence trend remains an economics-motivated conjecture.

Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that as models scale, representations of heterogeneous networks converge toward a shared model of reality. We propose its sequel and boundary, the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH): under a fixed per-token inference budget, representational convergence does not entail capability convergence. Capability instead converges toward a class, the access-complete hybrid: any architecture holding both a compressive O(1)-state channel and a scalable verbatim-index channel. We anchor it on a witness task, the Newton's-apple problem in an infinite stream, and name three resource walls: a Shannon wall barring any o(Nb)-state architecture, a horizon wall barring any fixed window, and a circuit wall barring fixed-depth attention-only composition (conditional on TC0 != NC1). Under an explicit separability assumption a hybrid crosses all three by paying each wall's price, so capability is strictly super-additive under composition. We separate what we prove from what we conjecture: the access-completeness principle rests on information-theoretic lower bounds and pre-registered experiments, while the field-level convergence trend is an economics-motivated conjecture. We report the first pre-registered small-scale tests under criteria frozen before the data: the predicted scissors gap is measured (exact-retrieval error 0.994 vs. 0.000 once a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer), the state-tracking bifurcation lands at the registered boundary, and a conjunction witness shows an irreducibly two-channel solution; one prediction failed with its direction reversed and is reported as such. Representational convergence is given freely by scale; capability convergence must be purchased by access structure.

</details>


### [160] [AI Agents Do Not Fail Alone:The Context Fails First](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14275)
*Fouad Bousetouane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Context engineering quality is an independent, measurable leading indicator of AI agent reliability. Using a multi-juror scoring harness across seven criteria, the authors show that context scores predict behavioral outcomes like hallucination resistance, instruction following, and tool misuse — establishing context measurement as a validated preflight signal for agent governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Context engineering — the accumulated instructions, tools, memory, knowledge, guardrails, and inputs shaping agent behavior — is central to reliable AI agents but remains largely unmeasured. Agent failures (hallucination, tool misuse, constraint violations, injection vulnerability, token waste) are often rooted in weak context, yet no validated, non-circular method exists to quantify context quality as a predictor of downstream behavior. The authors aim to fill this gap by validating context quality as an independent leading indicator of agent reliability.

Method: The authors implement ProofAgent-Harness, an open-source evaluation infrastructure employing multi-juror, consensus-based scoring. The harness rates agent context across seven criteria: (1) role clarity, (2) guardrail coverage, (3) instruction consistency, (4) tool schema quality, (5) grounding sufficiency, (6) injection hardening, and (7) token efficiency. Critically, the context score is isolated from behavioral metrics and release decisions to avoid circular validation. A controlled study is conducted across regulated agent domains, holding frontier LLM agents fixed while systematically varying only their operating context, then measuring how context-quality criteria predict corresponding behavioral outcomes.

Result: Context-quality criteria consistently predict their corresponding behavioral outcomes: grounding sufficiency predicts hallucination resistance, guardrail coverage predicts manipulation resistance, instruction consistency predicts instruction following, and tool-schema quality predicts tool-use reliability. These correlations hold across controlled variations in operating context with fixed LLM agents.

Conclusion: Context measurement is a validated preflight signal for agent reliability, and context engineering should be treated as an auditable, governable layer in AI agent evaluation. The work positions context quality alongside model capability as a distinct axis of agent trustworthiness.

Abstract: Context engineering has become central to building reliable AI agents, yet it remains largely unmeasured. Agents do not fail in isolation: their behavior is shaped by the instructions, tools, memory, retrieved knowledge, guardrails, and untrusted inputs accumulated in their context. When this context is weak, agents drift, hallucinate, misuse tools, ignore constraints, become vulnerable to injection, and waste tokens. This paper validates context-engineering quality as an independent leading indicator of agent reliability. We implement the measurement in ProofAgent-Harness, an open-source infrastructure for AI agent evaluation that uses multi-juror, consensus-based scoring. The harness assesses context across seven criteria: role clarity, guardrail coverage, instruction consistency, tool schema quality, grounding sufficiency, injection hardening, and token efficiency. Crucially, the context score is isolated from behavioral metrics and release decisions, enabling a non-circular validation. Through a controlled context-quality study across regulated agent domains, holding frontier LLM agents fixed and varying only their operating context, we show that context-quality criteria consistently predict their corresponding behavioral outcomes. Grounding sufficiency predicts hallucination resistance, guardrail coverage predicts manipulation resistance, instruction consistency predicts instruction following, and tool-schema quality predicts tool use. These findings establish context measurement as a validated preflight signal for agent reliability and position context engineering as an auditable layer of agent evaluation and governance.

</details>


### [161] [ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14145)
*Weiting Liu,Jieyi Bi,Wanqi Zhou,Jianfeng Feng,Yining Ma,Ai Han,Wenlian Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ToolAnchor addresses the "behavioral inertia" problem where LLM agents default to familiar tools despite new ones being available. It uses teacher-model-generated counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes successful interventions through agentic post-training, enabling effective toolset expansion without full retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-augmented LLM agents are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets and struggle to incorporate new tools when task requirements change. Retraining from scratch is impractical. The core obstacle is "behavioral inertia" — agents fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns even when superior new tools are available, causing them to fail on tasks that the new tools could otherwise solve.

Method: ToolAnchor operates in three stages: (1) A teacher model hypothesizes counterfactual anchor contexts — alternative reasoning prompts injected at critical decision points — designed to disrupt behavioral inertia. (2) These counterfactual contexts are verified by running student agent rollouts to confirm they recover previously failed trajectories. (3) Successful interventions are internalized into the agent through agentic post-training, effectively teaching the agent to adopt the new tools without full retraining.

Result: Extensive evaluations across three diverse benchmarks — GAIA (general AI assistant), BrowseComp (textual search), and VDR-Bench (visual search) — demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently achieves competitive performance when operating with expanded toolsets compared to baselines.

Conclusion: ToolAnchor bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic tool adaptation, offering a scalable path for agentic reinforcement learning. By overcoming behavioral inertia through counterfactual intervention and internalization, the framework enables practical toolset expansion without the cost of retraining from scratch.

Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [162] [SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14494)
*Yiming Zhang,Koji Tsuda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAGA addresses "type-blind grounding" in interactive KBQA agents by introducing schema-constrained property exploration. It maintains bidirectional type state to filter semantically incompatible properties early, presents schema-annotated graph patterns, and handles missing schema information permissively. SAGA achieves state-of-the-art F1 on all nine benchmark settings and top exact-match on eight, while reducing empty-result queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interactive LLM agents for semantic parsing in KBQA suffer from "type-blind grounding": they select properties based only on lexical relevance and instance-level observations, ignoring entity types, property domains/ranges, and expected answer types. This enlarges the search space and produces semantically incompatible triple patterns that yield empty results. The core motivation is to make grounding schema-aware to prevent such failures.

Method: SAGA is a training-free framework that augments agentic text-to-SPARQL generation with schema-constrained grounding. Key components: (1) persistent bidirectional type state tracking entity and property types throughout query construction; (2) filtering known-incompatible property candidates at construction time using domain/range constraints; (3) presenting remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format for the agent; (4) permissive handling of missing schema information via empirical evidence and trace-local observations.

Result: Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves highest F1 on all nine settings and highest exact-match accuracy on eight. It also reduces empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings, demonstrating that schema-aware grounding directly mitigates the type-blind failure mode.

Conclusion: Schema awareness is critical for interactive KBQA agents. By constraining property exploration with type information, SAGA substantially improves grounding accuracy, reduces wasted queries, and sets new state-of-the-art results without requiring additional training.

Abstract: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

</details>


### [163] [Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14553)
*Artan Markaj,Raphael Höfer,Felix Gehlhoff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL) is a middleware that uses an LLM grounded in OWL ontologies to parse natural-language goals into persistent, first-class intention objects, detect conflicts at registration time, and explain them before execution, shifting assurance from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution checking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In modern industrial environments with multiple autonomous subsystems sharing physical resources, high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded. No running component can verify whether it still aligns with original human intent, and goal conflicts are only discovered after causing failures. This motivates a need for persistent, inspectable intention representations and pre-execution conflict detection.

Method: The IAL is a domain-agnostic middleware with three components: (1) an LLM grounded in a formal OWL ontology that parses natural-language goals into structured, persistent intention objects; (2) a consistency monitor that detects conflicts between intentions at registration time, before execution; and (3) a transparency module that explains detected conflicts in natural language.

Result: In a proof-of-concept experiment, two autonomous agents registered conflicting production and energy intentions. The IAL successfully flagged and explained the conflict before it reached the execution layer.

Conclusion: The IAL demonstrates a viable mechanism to shift behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking, enabling early detection and resolution of goal conflicts.

Abstract: Modern industrial environments increasingly run many autonomous subsystems at once - schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets - each pursuing its own goals while sharing the same physical resources. Because high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, no running component can tell whether it is still doing what was actually intended, and goal conflicts surface only after they have caused a missed target or a shutdown. We propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domainagnostic middleware that represents intentions as first-class, persistent, and explainable runtime objects: a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses naturallanguage goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time, before execution, and a transparency module explains them in natural language. We report a first proof of concept in which two autonomous agents register conflicting production and energy intentions, and the IAL flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer. The result is a mechanism that shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

</details>


### [164] [Enhancing Small Language Models Reasoning through Knowledge Graph Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14149)
*Dimitrios Kelesis,Konstantinos Bougiatiotis,Georgios Paliouras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic agentic framework that augments small language models (SLMs) with tool-based symbolic fact extraction and expert relational graph convolutional network (RGCN) hints to improve multi-hop reasoning on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. While RGCN hints yield 1.5–2x gains, performance is limited by extraction errors and compounding deductive failures, with a notable "distraction effect" where noisy self-generated facts degrade outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs achieve strong zero-shot reasoning but are costly and environmentally taxing. SLMs offer a sustainable alternative but struggle with complex, multi-hop logical reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap using a neuro-symbolic agentic approach that combines SLMs with structured symbolic tools.

Method: The framework transforms SLMs (Gemma 3 1B/4B, Llama 3.2 3B) into minimalist agents equipped with two tools: (1) extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction from text, and (2) get_hint for obtaining expert reasoning signals from a pre-trained Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). Evaluation is conducted on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark under two settings: an Oracle scenario using ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge.

Result: RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5–2x performance improvement over story-only baselines. However, the system faces two key bottlenecks: (1) an extraction bottleneck where erroneous self-extracted triplets limit downstream reasoning, and (2) sequential deductive fragility where early extraction errors compound across multi-hop chains. Additionally, a "distraction effect" is observed in certain architectures, where noisy self-generated facts degrade performance even when expert hints are available.

Conclusion: The work characterizes the fundamental challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems, highlighting extraction fidelity and error propagation as critical constraints. The authors propose iterative verification as a promising direction for improving neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. Our approach transforms the SLM into a minimalist agent utilizing two specialized tool calls: extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction and get_hint for expert reasoning via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). We evaluate these models across two configurations, both in an Oracle scenario with ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge. Our results reveal that while RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5 - 2x performance gain over story-only baselines, the system is constrained by the extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early extraction errors compound over multi-hop chains. Furthermore, we identify a "distraction effect" in specific architectures where noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite the presence of expert hints. This work characterizes the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and provides a roadmap for iterative verification in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

</details>


### [165] [SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15257)
*Yuyao Zhang,Junjie Gao,Zhengxian Wu,Jiaming Fan,Jin Zhang,Shihan Ma,Yao Yao,Weiran Qi,Chuyan Jin,Guiyu Ma,Xingzhong Xu,Kai Yang,Ji-Rong Wen,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchOS is a multi-agent framework that externalizes search progress into explicit shared state (Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, Failure Memory) and uses pipeline-parallel scheduling with a Search Tool Middleware Harness to prevent repetitive search loops, outperforming baselines on WideSearch and GISA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based search agents suffer from losing track of task progress as interaction histories grow, leading to repetitive search loops, wasted budgets, and degraded output quality. Existing single- and multi-agent systems lack explicit, persistent mechanisms to track what has been searched, what evidence has been gathered, and what has failed.

Method: SearchOS formulates open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations. It introduces Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM) to externalize state into four components: Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. A pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism overlaps sub-agent execution and refills freed slots with tasks targeting coverage gaps. A Search Tool Middleware Harness intercepts model-tool interactions to record evidence and react to stalls/budget exhaustion, complemented by a hierarchical skill system (strategy and access skills) to avoid repeating failed search patterns.

Result: SearchOS achieves leading performance across all metrics on the WideSearch and GISA benchmarks compared to both single-agent and multi-agent baselines.

Conclusion: By making search progress explicit, persistent, and shared across agents, SearchOS enables robust information-seeking collaboration and overcomes the fragility of implicit progress tracking in existing systems.

Abstract: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

</details>


### [166] [Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301)
*Shahin Hossain,Tukhbita Afroz Nawmi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops and validates the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four types of GenAI reliance—Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic—among undergraduates. Confirmatory factor analysis with 382 students supports a five-factor structure with strong psychometric properties, including scalar invariance across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GenAI reliance measures were developed inductively, focused on discrete problem-solving tasks, and validated with homogeneous samples. There is a need for a theoretically grounded, psychometrically robust instrument that captures how—not just whether—undergraduates rely on GenAI in academic writing, with implications for learning, academic integrity, and equity.

Method: The scale was developed from a theoretical typology of four reliance types. Validation followed the multisource framework of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing. A survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution was administered, along with interviews of 14 purposively sampled students. Confirmatory factor analysis compared six competing models; reliability was assessed via omega coefficients; measurement invariance was tested across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors; and Rasch analysis evaluated response format functioning.

Result: A five-factor structure emerged: Strategic Reliance split into two facets (Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation), alongside Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic factors (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Subscale reliability ranged from ω = .75–.88. Scalar invariance held across all tested groups. Rasch analysis recommended a five-point response format. Strategic reliance correlated positively with AI literacy, and reliance types differentiated students across multiple writing process and outcome variables.

Conclusion: The GenAI-RTS provides a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated tool for identifying undergraduate GenAI reliance profiles, supporting research, writing assessment, and AI literacy interventions in higher education.

Abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in undergraduate academic writing, how students rely on these tools, rather than simply whether they use them, has become a central question for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity. Existing measures of reliance were developed inductively, focused on discrete problem-solving tasks, and validated mainly with homogeneous samples. This study developed and validated the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four theoretically derived types of GenAI reliance: Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic. Validation followed the multisource framework of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, drawing on a survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution and interviews with 14 purposively sampled students. Confirmatory factor analyses of six competing models supported a five-factor structure in which Strategic Reliance comprises two facets, Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation, alongside Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic factors (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Subscale reliability was acceptable to good (omega = .75-.88), and scalar measurement invariance held across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors, to our knowledge the first such evidence for a GenAI reliance instrument. Rasch analysis indicated that a five-point response format would improve category functioning. Strategic reliance was positively associated with AI literacy, and the reliance types differentiated students across multiple writing process and outcome variables. The GenAI-RTS offers researchers and educators a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated instrument for identifying undergraduate reliance profiles and supporting research, assessment, and AI literacy intervention.

</details>


### [167] [MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14159)
*Yue Huang,Wenjie Wang,Han Bao,Yuchen Ma,Xiaonan Luo,Yi Nian,Haomin Zhuang,Zheyuan Liu,Yue Zhao,Xiangliang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemoHarness is an adaptive framework that learns from execution experience to optimize agent harnesses across six editable control dimensions, using a dual-layer experience bank for case-specific adaptation without test-time labels or feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic improvement methods for LLM-based agents focus narrowly on prompts, pipelines, or workflows, while the broader agent harness (context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, output handling) remains statically configured. There is a need for a method that adapts the full harness based on execution experience rather than relying on a single global configuration.

Method: MemoHarness decomposes the agent harness into six control dimensions (context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, output handling). It builds a dual-layer experience bank storing per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns. At test time, it retrieves relevant experience to adapt the harness for each case, requiring no labels, feedback, or additional search. The framework learns from its own prior executions.

Result: Across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness outperforms fixed harness baselines. It demonstrates selective transfer capability to unseen benchmark suites and base models. The additional context overhead remains cost-competitive when retrieved experience is cacheable.

Conclusion: Execution experience is a practical substrate for building adaptive agent harnesses that outperform static configurations. Broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution are deferred to future work.

Abstract: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

</details>


### [168] [Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14673)
*Leanne Tan,Rohan Jaggi,Shaun Khoo,Roy Ka-Wei Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Kaleidoscope is an integrated evaluation workflow that combines persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and reliability-gated LLM judging, enabling automated scoring only when human-LLM agreement exceeds a configurable threshold. A three-week pilot across four organizational use cases demonstrates its practicality for real-world AI deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world AI deployment faces an evaluation bottleneck: public benchmarks fail to capture application-specific users, contexts, and policies, while human review is costly and difficult to scale. This is especially acute in the public sector, where applications must satisfy stringent local policy and governance requirements.

Method: Kaleidoscope integrates three components: (1) persona-based test case generation tailored to specific use contexts, (2) application-specific contextualized rubrics for scoring, and (3) a reliability-gated mechanism where LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with human annotations exceeds a pre-configured threshold. Human reviewers provide labeled annotations that serve as both ground truth and a gating signal.

Result: A three-week pilot deployment across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs (spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions) provided early evidence of the workflow's effectiveness, highlighting useful features for end-to-end reliable automated scoring.

Conclusion: Kaleidoscope offers a practical, inspectable, and iterative evaluation workflow for product teams, bridging the gap between generic benchmarks and context-specific deployment requirements while balancing automation with human oversight through reliability gating.

Abstract: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

</details>


### [169] [When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14169)
*Javier Aguilar Martín*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-synthesized Code World Models can achieve near-perfect transition accuracy yet fail catastrophically in planning because the tiny fraction of errors corresponds to pivotal game dynamics. The paper formalizes this "verified-vs-correct gap," derives a quantitative danger law, shows the failure stems from rule translation rather than inference, and extends the finding to imperfect-information settings with a coverage bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current practice accepts LLM-synthesized Code World Models (CWMs) based on high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. The authors argue this is fundamentally the wrong evaluation criterion for planning, since a model can be nearly perfect on random samples while systematically misrepresenting the rare but decision-critical dynamics that determine planning success.

Method: The paper proceeds through four linked contributions: (1) an end-to-end synthesis pipeline demonstrating the verified-vs-correct gap where a CWM passes a 100% sampling gate but loses at play due to missing pivotal dynamics; (2) derivation of a quantitative law, danger = play_cost × (1−rarity)^N, with an exact gate-miss factor and empirically bounded play cost; (3) experiments across GPT-5.x models and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples) showing LLM synthesis operates as rule translation rather than rule inference; (4) extension to imperfect-information CWMs, proving a coverage bound (N ≳ b^{d_max}) for belief-inference functions and constructing Beacon, a hand-crafted verified-but-wrong inference function.

Result: (1) A CWM with 100% transition accuracy and ≥98% state-accuracy on the planner's search distribution still loses systematically, with a play cost of 0.091 (95% CI [0.065, 0.117], n=4800). (2) The danger law holds with exact gate-miss and empirically bounded play-cost factors. (3) No model or data regime induced rule inference; the omitted rule was never recovered. (4) The coverage bound explains why shallow games (e.g., Kuhn poker) show no gap, while Beacon demonstrates that verified-but-wrong belief inference loses every game.

Conclusion: Adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the planner's search distribution or by direct play outcomes, not by prediction accuracy on randomly sampled transitions. The verified-vs-correct gap is systematic, quantifiable, and irreparable by scaling data alone when the underlying mechanism is translation rather than inference.

Abstract: Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

</details>


### [170] [Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15202)
*Hoang-Loc Cao,Van Pham,Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,Phuc Ho,Veronica Whitford,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A self-evolving annotation framework for depression datasets that combines LLM-assisted labeling with expert verification, using dual-memory architecture to align annotations with DSM-5-TR criteria while producing audit-ready evidence trails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Annotation quality in mental health datasets is compromised by labels lacking structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable DSM-5-TR alignment, which undermines both transparency and downstream model interpretability in XAI systems for depression research.

Method: A three-stage annotation framework: (1) candidate evidence selection from textual records, (2) criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and (3) case-level synthesis producing diagnostic and severity labels. The system employs a dual-memory architecture — Example Memory and Reflection Memory — to internalize expert feedback and iteratively refine future annotations without retraining. All outputs include evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories for auditability.

Result: A pilot study with expert-reviewed samples demonstrated improved annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort. Evaluation of the dual-memory mechanism across multiple feedback cycles is deferred to future work.

Conclusion: The proposed framework offers a promising direction for building DSM-5-TR-aligned, explainable depression datasets, though rigorous multi-cycle evaluation of the memory architecture remains necessary to validate its self-evolving claims and generalizability.

Abstract: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in building reliable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems for mental health research. In depression-related datasets, labels are often assigned without structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable alignment with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), limiting both transparency and downstream model interpretability. We propose a self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that combines large language model (LLM)-assisted labeling with expert verification. The framework is intended to support the construction of explainable, DSM-5-TR-aligned datasets rather than to perform clinical diagnosis. It operates in three stages: candidate evidence selection from textual records, criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and case-level synthesis that produces label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture, composed of Example Memory and Reflection Memory, is designed to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve future annotations without retraining. We describe this mechanism and leave its evaluation across multiple feedback cycles to future work. In addition to final labels, the framework exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories, enabling comprehensive auditability. In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the proposed approach improves annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort.

</details>


### [171] [RxBrain: Embodied Cognition Foundation Model with Joint Language-Visual Reasoning and Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14187)
*Haotian Liang,Mingkang Chen,Yufei Huang,Yuchun Guo,Xiaomeng Zhu,Xiangli Shi,Kaixuan Wang,Yunxuan Mao,Weijie Zhou,Ling Chen,Shirong Zeng,Yueyu Long,Yuchen Si,Yajuan Zhu,Xingyu Zhou,Minghui Wang,Wanjia He,Xin Yang,Lingzhu Xiang,Zhiqing Liu,Bohan Ma,Xiran Huang,Tianshuo Yang,Zhiheng Liu,Xuantang Xiong,Zisheng Lu,Ping Luo,Yao Mu,Han Hu,Zhengyou Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RxBrain is an embodied cognition foundation model that jointly reasons over language and visual imagination in a single planning sequence, using a unified Mixture-of-Transformers architecture to couple task-level reasoning with world state prediction for embodied planning and robot action generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing models treat high-level task reasoning (via VLMs) and physical state prediction (via world models) separately, lacking a unified framework that connects abstract planning with grounded physical states essential for embodied cognition.

Method: RxBrain uses a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting language, image, and video understanding and generation. It represents embodied plans as joint text-visual sequences where language handles task decomposition and logic, while visual imagination provides world state prediction and subgoal grounding. An automatic pipeline converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps aligned with state transitions. RxBrain-Bench is introduced to evaluate joint textual-visual planning representation.

Result: RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. When extended to continuous robot action generation, it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining.

Conclusion: RxBrain demonstrates that jointly modeling language-based planning and visual imagination within a single foundation model is a viable and promising initial step toward embodied cognition foundation models, bridging abstract reasoning with physical state grounding.

Abstract: Embodied cognition requires agents to connect high-level task reasoning with the physical states to be achieved. We introduce Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model with joint language-visual reasoning and imagination. Unlike vision-language models that emphasize scene understanding and textual decision making, or generative world models that mainly predict future visual states, RxBrain represents embodied plans in a single planning sequence where language and visual imagination play complementary roles. Language provides the abstract structure of a plan, including task decomposition, planning primitives, constraints, temporal order, and decision logic, while visual imagination grounds this structure through world state prediction and joint subgoal planning, associating each planning step with intermediate and final physical states. RxBrain adopts a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports language, image, and video understanding and generation within one model. To train this capability, we build an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps and aligning them with visual state transitions. We further introduce RxBrain-Bench to evaluate whether models can represent embodied plans through joint textual and visual components rather than separate understanding or generation. Experiments show that RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, and produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. We also extend RxBrain to continuous robot action generation, where it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining. These results provide an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

</details>


### [172] [Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15176)
*Patrick Phuoc Do,Chau M. Ta,Chaoli Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark study evaluating six MLLMs on scientific visualization literacy using the standardized SciVis literacy assessment test (49 items, 18 visualizations, 8 techniques, 11 task types). Gemini outperforms humans on average, while open-source models fall below. Performance is uneven: models excel at illustration and spatial tasks but struggle with texture-based visualizations and quantitative estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLM vision evaluations are chart-centric and fail to probe understanding of scientific visualizations (SciVis). There is a need to systematically assess whether MLLMs possess scientific visualization literacy — the ability to interpret domain-specific visualizations like volume renderings, flow fields, and tensor glyphs — beyond simple charts and plots.

Method: The authors benchmark six MLLMs — three closed-source (Gemini, GPT-4, Claude) and three open-source — using the scientific visualization literacy assessment test (a validated instrument originally designed for humans). The test contains 49 items across 18 scientific visualizations spanning 8 visualization techniques and 11 task types. Model performance is compared against human baseline data from 485 participants under a closed-world evaluation protocol.

Result: Gemini is the top-performing model, exceeding the human mean. All open-source models score below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven: models perform best on scientific illustration, search tasks, and spatial understanding; they perform worst on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation tasks. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation.

Conclusion: SciVis literacy constitutes a necessary and distinct benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems, orthogonal to existing chart-centric evaluations. The observed performance gaps highlight critical weaknesses in current MLLMs that must be addressed for reliable deployment in scientific contexts.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

</details>


### [173] [How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14197)
*Jason Miklian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI answer engines frequently hallucinate when answering questions about conflicts, with error rates inversely correlated with the richness of retrievable records. Thin records enable Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)-based information warfare, which is already occurring across sources these engines rely on.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether LLM hallucinations follow discernible patterns when asked about peace and conflict issues, and to understand the implications for the global conflict information environment, particularly the structural vulnerabilities created by sparse documentation.

Method: The authors queried five leading AI answer engines with a set of questions about 28 conflicts, producing 5,460 answers which were scored against documented evidence for accuracy. They further analyzed 1,048 websites serving as sources for these LLMs to detect GEO-based manipulation and state-partisan digital capture.

Result: Hallucination rates — including invention, misattribution, and miscounting — increase as the retrievable documentary record around a conflict becomes thinner. Thin records create structural exposure to misinformation via GEO. Analysis of source websites confirmed that GEO optimization is already underway, and state-partisan digital capture, while incipient, is growing rapidly.

Conclusion: The findings underscore the rise of GEO information warfare and its threat to conflict scholarship. The authors advocate for a return to deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI cannot replicate, and call for further research into this rapidly evolving space.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment? To answer, we first asked a battery of questions about 28 conflicts to five leading answer engines and scored their 5,460 answers against documented evidence. We found that the thinner the retrievable record around a given conflict, the more the engines invent, misattribute, and miscount. Thin records don't just encourage hallucination, but create structural exposure to mis- and disinformation, because they are the easiest records to warp through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to bias engine responses. Through an analysis of 1,048 websites that the AI LLMs pulled conflict facts from, we found that GEO source optimization is already happening, and while state-partisan digital capture remains incipient it is rapidly growing. We explain what these findings mean for scholarship with the rise of GEO information warfare, and for policy argue for a return to the deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate, closing with a discussion of future research opportunities and challenges in this fast-moving space.

</details>


### [174] [Align AI to Dynamic Human-AI Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14240)
*Valerie Chen,Cleotilde Gonzalez,Anita Williams Woolley,Michael Lee,Tongshuang Wu,Vincent Conitzer,Aarti Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that current AI alignment approaches, which rely on static human preference representations, fail to capture the dynamic, co-evolving nature of real human-AI interaction. It proposes shifting toward interactive, complementary alignment grounded in interdisciplinary insights from social sciences, and outlines a research agenda for building systems that align through interaction rather than mere emulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing alignment methods use static representations of human preferences and focus on emulating human behavior, which cannot capture the dynamic, context-dependent, and co-evolving nature of real-world human-AI interactions. The authors identify a fundamental gap between static alignment paradigms and the trajectory-level reality where human and model behavior mutually influence each other over time.

Method: The authors formalize the gap by contrasting static alignment approaches with a trajectory-level perspective of co-evolving human-model behavior. They ground their argument using insights from an interdisciplinary workshop and draw on lessons from social-science accounts of human-human collaboration. They then analyze how human-AI systems amplify interaction dynamics, introducing new asymmetries that complicate uncertainty reasoning and create novel coordination challenges.

Result: The paper does not present empirical results; it is a position/agenda paper. Its contribution is a conceptual framework identifying that human-AI interactions introduce amplified dynamics and new asymmetries beyond those in human-human collaboration, making alignment a fundamentally interactive rather than static problem.

Conclusion: The authors conclude by calling for a research agenda that shifts from static, emulative alignment toward interactive, complementary alignment. This requires an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning with social and decision sciences to develop AI systems capable of aligning with humans through ongoing interaction.

Abstract: Current alignment approaches typically focus on emulating human behavior using static representations of human preferences, failing to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions. In this paper, we argue for a shift from static and emulative to interactive and complementary alignment, where preferences emerge through interaction and alignment is defined not by satisfying preferences alone. We first formalize this gap by contrasting existing alignment with a trajectory-level view in which human and model behavior co-evolve over time. Because these interaction dynamics have not been adequately captured within existing ML formulations, we ground this perspective in insights from an interdisciplinary workshop. We draw on lessons from social-science accounts of human-human collaboration and then argue that human-AI systems amplify these dynamics, introducing new asymmetries that make reasoning about uncertainty harder and introduce new coordination challenges. Based on these lessons and new challenges, we conclude by outlining a research agenda for developing AI systems that align with humans in interaction, requiring an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning and the social and decision sciences.

</details>


### [175] [teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15254)
*Qiwei Li,Jorge Ortiz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: teLLMe is an exploratory causal analysis system that combines causal structure learning (PC algorithm), stability checks, and LLM-based natural language querying to help traffic analysts answer causal questions from observational dashcam video data, outputting structured "Causal Cards" with effect estimates and explicit uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traffic agencies collect large volumes of observational video-derived data, but answering causal questions (e.g., "How would rain change traffic density?") is difficult because these data lack experimental interventions. Existing tools do not bridge the gap between natural-language causal queries and rigorous causal inference on observational traffic data.

Method: teLLMe starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations. It employs the PC algorithm for causal structure learning with bootstrap-based stability checks, DoWhy and linear regression for effect estimation, and a schema-aware LLM to map natural-language queries to structured causal queries specifying treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. Results are presented as a "Causal Card."

Result: Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events demonstrate that teLLMe surfaces plausible causal relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while explicitly communicating uncertainty and modeling assumptions.

Conclusion: teLLMe is designed as a hypothesis generation and expert reasoning tool rather than a source of definitive causal claims, enabling transparent exploratory causal analysis on observational traffic datasets.

Abstract: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims.

</details>


### [176] [The Steering Budget: Examples beat Knobs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14246)
*Raj Kumar Rajendran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Training data imposes a budget on how far generative model properties can be steered. Knobs (prompts, guidance scales) can only access part of this range, while example-based steering can reach the full budget. The paper provides a method to audit training data to measure this budget and construct example sets that achieve complete coverage, enabling both greater reach and expressiveness (including targets that cannot be described verbally).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models exhibit a saturation point where further adjustment of steering knobs (prompts, guidance scales, property tags) fails to move a target property. The authors argue this ceiling is not a model deficiency but a fundamental constraint imposed by the training data distribution, and that a significant portion of the property's movable range is only accessible through example-based conditioning rather than knob-based controls.

Method: 1) Theoretical framing of the training data as setting a "budget" that partitions a property's movable range into a knob-accessible part and an example-only-accessible part. 2) A cheap auditing procedure on the training data to quantify this budget and determine the split. 3) A recipe for constructing example sets from the model's learned manifold (not via retraining) that can steer properties across the full budget. 4) Empirical verification through falsifiable claims tested in two domains: image generation and crystal-structure generation.

Result: The paper verifies that: (a) a property's movable range is indeed split into knob-accessible and example-only regions as predicted by the training data budget; (b) example-based steering reaches the full budget, including regions knobs cannot access; (c) example-based steering enables targeting properties that resist verbal specification. These claims hold across both image and crystal-structure generation domains.

Conclusion: The ceiling on property steering in generative models is a training-data budget, not a model flaw. Example-based conditioning unlocks the full range of achievable property values, including those inexpressible through language. The audit and example-construction recipe allows practitioners to determine in advance whether knobs suffice or examples are needed.

Abstract: Generative models are steered with knobs -- prompts, guidance scales, property tags. Turn one as hard as you like and, past a point, it stops moving the property you care about. We find that ceiling is not a shortcoming of the model but a budget, set by the training data before the model is trained: a property's movable range splits in two -- the part a knob can reach, and a second, significant part that only examples -- concrete instances of what you want more of -- can reach. That second part is usually much larger, but not always, and the same budget says so in advance.
  Reaching that second part takes a different move: instead of turning a knob, you show the model examples, composed from what it already learned rather than added to its training. A cheap audit of the training data measures the budget; we give a recipe for building the example set that reaches all of it.
  This buys two things a knob can't. Reach: it moves a property across the whole budget, not just the part a knob reaches.
