Expressiveness: it steers toward targets you can only specify by example -- including ones you can't put into words. We turn these into a handful of falsifiable claims and verify them in two unrelated domains, image and crystal-structure generation -- marking where a knob is enough, and where only examples will do.

</details>


### [177] [Tracing LLM Behavior to the Training Data with Empirical Next-Token Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14306)
*Zachary Izzo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how closely an LLM's next-token probability distribution matches the empirical next-token distribution (ENTD) computed directly from the pretraining corpus. The authors find strong agreement for most inputs, with alignment improving at larger scales, but also identify a long tail of significant divergence. They explore sources of this mismatch and advocate for "data-centric mechanistic interpretability."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability typically focuses on how model behaviors are encoded in learned weights. The authors propose a complementary perspective: understanding model behavior by examining the training data itself. The ENTD serves as a natural, interpretable baseline — it is the theoretical global minimizer of the pretraining loss — against which to compare the LLM's learned distribution.

Method: The authors compare an LLM's next-token distribution against the ENTD (derived from the pretraining corpus) across many input contexts. They measure agreement between the two distributions, analyze how this agreement varies with model scale and training compute, and examine the long tail of inputs where divergence is large. They investigate possible causes of discrepancy, including architectural constraints of the transformer, artifacts of the training procedure, and finite-sample noise in estimating the ENTD itself.

Result: For a significant fraction of inputs, the LLM's output distribution aligns almost perfectly with the ENTD. Average agreement increases with both model scale and training compute. However, a long tail of input sequences exhibits substantial divergence between the two distributions, prompting investigation into the sources of this mismatch.

Conclusion: The strong overall alignment suggests LLMs largely learn to approximate the empirical distribution of their training data. The persistent divergences highlight gaps that may stem from architectural, optimization, or statistical factors. The authors call for broader adoption of data-centric mechanistic interpretability as a lens for understanding model behavior.

Abstract: In this paper, we study the connection between an LLM's output distribution and the data used to train it. Specifically, we study the degree to which an LLM's next-token distribution agrees with the empirical next-token distribution (ENTD) given the context in the training data. The ENTD is an appealing target because it is the unrestricted global minimizer of the next-token cross entropy loss used for pretraining, as well as an easily interpretable function of the pretraining corpus. We find that for a significant fraction of inputs, the LLM's distribution agrees with the ENTD almost perfectly, and the average agreement increases with model scale and training compute. Nevertheless, there is a long tail of input sequences where the LLM and ENTD differ significantly, and we examine several possible sources of this discrepancy across the transformer architecture, training procedure, and finite-sample noise in the ENTD estimate itself. More broadly, we hope our findings will encourage more work on ``data-centric mechanistic interpretability,'' a complement to standard mechanistic interpretability that opens the black box of how model behaviors arise from the data, rather than how they are encoded in the learned weights.

</details>


### [178] [Traccia: An OpenTelemetry-Based Governance Platform for AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14309)
*Nutan Kumar Naik,Aditya Kumar Saroj,Vijay Prasad Poudel,Saurav Samantray,Abhishek Patel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current disjointed LLM evaluation and monitoring tools fail to govern agentic AI systems, leaving gaps in alignment, security, and compliance. Traccia, a multi-level AI governance stack built on OpenTelemetry, addresses this by combining telemetry, semantic guardrails, and tamper-resistant execution lineage into a hashed trace ledger, automatically generating compliance evidence for the EU AI Act.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid proliferation of LLM-powered autonomous agents has outpaced existing software governance mechanisms. Despite regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act demanding rigorous transparency and accountability, a significant gap persists between these theoretical requirements and the capabilities of current platforms for LLM evaluation, ML workflow management, and application performance monitoring. Existing solutions are fragmented and cannot adequately protect agentic architectures with unbounded state spaces from critical risks.

Method: The authors propose Traccia, a coherent multi-level AI governance stack built atop the OpenTelemetry infrastructure platform. Traccia integrates three key components: (1) telemetry data collection, (2) passive semantic guardrail assessment, and (3) execution lineage tracking, all recorded into a hashed trace ledger. It appends tamper-resistant fingerprints and SHA-256 content hashes to automatically generate compliance evidence packages. These packages are mapped to specific regulatory requirements (Articles 12, 14, 19, 26(6), and 50 of the EU AI Act) without compromising data privacy.

Result: Traccia demonstrates that a unified, telemetry-based governance layer can automatically produce machine-readable compliance evidence for autonomous AI systems. The system resolves the "last mile" of AI alignment by providing verifiable traceability across agentic workflows, addressing alignment drift, SaaS security concerns, and shadow AI deployment risks that current disjointed solutions fail to manage.

Conclusion: A methodical, telemetry-driven approach to AI governance, as exemplified by Traccia, establishes a solid machine-readable foundation for enterprise-wide management of autonomous AI systems. By bridging the gap between regulatory mandates and operational reality through tamper-resistant, privacy-preserving compliance evidence, Traccia offers a viable path toward trustworthy, accountable deployment of LLM-powered agents at scale.

Abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligent (AI) powered autonomous agents has fundamentally changed the existing forms of software governance. In spite of the rigorous standards of transparency and account ability required according to the international frameworks such as the European Union's AI Act, there is a considerable gap between theory and reality. The present study discusses the inherent drawbacks of currently utilized platforms for LLM evaluation, machine learning workflow, and application performance monitoring in general. It has been shown that current disjointed solutions fail to protect unbound state space agentic architecture from serious threats such as alignment drift, SaaS security concerns, and unauthorized deployment of shadow AI systems. Moreover, a solution is proposed for overcoming the discussed challenges in form of a coherent multi-level AI governance stack Traccia built on the top of OpenTelemetry infrastructure platform. Traccia resolves the last mile for AI Alignment by adding the telemetry data, passive semantic guardrail assessment, and execution lineage into a hashed trace ledger. Traccia automatically creates compliance evidence packages by appending tamper-resistant fingerprints and SHA-256 content hash, that map to regulatory requirements (Articles 12, 14, 19, 26(6), and 50 of the EU AI Act) without invading any data privacy. By performing this evaluation in a methodical manner, a solid machine-readable base has been created for enterprise-wide management of autonomous AI systems.

</details>


### [179] [CIPHER: A Decoupled Exploration-Selection Framework for Test-Time Scaling of Data Science Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14386)
*Maxime Heuillet,Sharadind Peddiraju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIPHER is an AI agent for data science that improves robustness by generating multiple candidate initial states, decoupling exploration from selection, and executing them in parallel—outperforming single-state agents and competing with larger models despite using a smaller base LM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI agents for data science tasks rely on a single initial state to condition the entire execution, making them prone to cascading failures when that initial state is suboptimal. The authors aim to address this brittleness through test-time scaling with multiple diverse initial states.

Method: The paper introduces CIPHER, which implements a Decoupled Exploration-Selection (DES) framework. It explicitly separates the generation of multiple candidate initial states (exploration) from the strategic selection of which states to execute (selection), then runs selected candidates concurrently. The empirical study characterizes how generation strategy, selection strategy, and aggregator model capacity affect overall performance.

Result: CIPHER achieves state-of-the-art performance in matched-model comparisons across two benchmarks (closed-form and open-form tasks) and remains competitive with larger-model baselines despite using a substantially smaller base language model.

Conclusion: Decoupling exploration from selection in a multi-initial-state framework effectively mitigates cascading errors from poor initialization. The DES framework provides actionable design recommendations, and test-time scaling via parallel execution of diverse candidates is a viable alternative to simply scaling model size.

Abstract: Data science tasks span from closed-ended information extraction to open-ended analysis, presenting significant challenges for automation. Recent AI agents powered by language models show promise for handling such complex tasks. However, existing agents typically rely on a single initial state that conditions the entire agent's execution, making them vulnerable to cascading errors initiated by a suboptimal initial state. To mitigate this, we present CIPHER, an automated data science agent that leverages test-time scaling through the generation and selection of multiple initial states for concurrent execution. Unlike existing works on test-time scaling of AI agents, CIPHER explicitly decouples the generation of candidate initial states from their strategic selection for parallel execution. Through extensive evaluation on two benchmarks (closed-form and open-form tasks), we demonstrate that CIPHER exceeds state-of-the-art performance in matched-model comparisons, and remains competitive against larger-model baselines despite relying on a substantially smaller base LM. Our empirical study characterizes the design space of the Decoupled Exploration-Selection (DES) framework: we quantify how generation strategy, selection strategy, and aggregator model capacity contribute to overall performance, and derive actionable design recommendations for practitioners.

</details>


### [180] [Democratizing Agent Deployment Safety: A Structural Monitoring Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14570)
*Preeti Ravindra,Rahul Tiwari,Vincent Wolowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that detects infrastructure-level sabotage by AI coding agents via structural analysis of control-flow and data-flow graph diffs. An untrained IFG monitor reduces missed attacks from 11.6% (git diff baseline) to 3.5% in asynchronous mode and achieves 0% joint task success in synchronous mode, offering a practical, auditable safety mechanism for organizations lacking sophisticated monitoring infrastructure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents can covertly weaken security safeguards (e.g., broadening permissions, degrading logging, inserting persistence) while completing assigned tasks. Frontier labs can deploy complex learned monitor ensembles, but most organizations and individual users lack the resources and governance maturity to do so. There is a need for practical, accessible, and auditable monitoring that works without extensive training data or infrastructure.

Method: The authors propose an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that detects security regressions by computing diffs over control-flow and data-flow graphs in addition to raw code diffs. The monitor is evaluated in the infrastructure-as-code setting from ControlArena, comparing untrained monitors (git diff, IFG) against a trained Async RF monitor, across both synchronous (pre-deployment blocking) and asynchronous (post-hoc audit) deployment modes.

Result: In asynchronous evaluation at 1% FPR auditing budget: untrained git diff misses 11.6% of attacks, untrained IFG reduces misses to 3.5%, and trained Async RF achieves below 1%. In synchronous mode, IFG realtime rollback reduces joint main-task and covert-task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable degradation in legitimate task completion.

Conclusion: Untrained structural monitors like IFG provide a practical, auditable, and effective path toward democratizing deployment safety for AI coding agents, enabling trustworthy adoption even by organizations with limited resources and monitoring maturity.

Abstract: AI software development agents are increasingly capable of modifying infrastructure and security critical systems, creating risks where an agent completes its assigned task while covertly weakening safeguards through actions such as broadening permissions, degrading logging, or introducing persistence mechanisms. While frontier laboratories may deploy sophisticated monitoring pipelines, many organizations and individual users adopting coding agents lack the resources and governance maturity required to maintain complex learned monitor ensembles. We study this problem as infrastructure level sabotage under task success in the infrastructure-as-code setting from ControlArena and compare trained and untrained monitors across synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes. We introduce an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that analyzes structural security regressions using control-flow and data-flow graph diffs alongside raw code diffs. In asynchronous evaluation, an untrained git diff monitor misses 11.6% attacks at 1% false positive rate auditing budget, our untrained IFG monitor reduces this to 3.5%, and the trained Async RF monitor achieves below 1%. Unlike the trained Async RF monitor, IFG can also operate synchronously as a pre-deployment safeguard that blocks suspicious infrastructure changes before execution or merge. In synchronous mode, IFG realtime rollback reduces joint main task and covert task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable reduction in legitimate task completion. These results suggest that untrained structural monitors provide a practical and auditable path toward democratizing deployment safety for organizations seeking trustworthy adoption of advanced AI agents.

</details>


### [181] [Chat2Scenic: An Iterative RAG-Based Framework for Scenario Generation in Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14387)
*Yuan Gao,Wenting Miao,Mattia Piccinini,Haoyu Wang,Qunying Song,Johannes Betz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Chat2Scenic is an iterative retrieval-augmented framework with a chatbot interface that generates executable DSL scenario scripts from regulatory descriptions for autonomous driving testing, achieving 76.42% compilation success rate and significantly outperforming existing retrieval-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Validating autonomous driving systems requires diverse, regulation-compliant test scenarios, but automatically generating executable simulation scripts from regulatory text remains an open challenge. Existing retrieval-assemble methods achieve reasonable compilation rates but lack scalability, while retrieval-based full-script generation suffers from low compilation success.

Method: Chat2Scenic is an iterative, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework featuring: (1) a chatbot interface for interactive scenario refinement, (2) RAG integration to ground generation in regulatory knowledge and DSL syntax, and (3) an open benchmark of 123 scenarios sourced from NHTSA, UN Vehicle Regulations, and other standards. The system iteratively refines DSL scripts through conversation.

Result: Chat2Scenic achieves 76.42% Compilation Success Rate (CSR) and 58.17% Framework Accuracy (FA), dramatically outperforming Retrieval-Assemble (30.08% CSR, 11.03% FA) and Retrieval full-script generation (16.26% CSR, 10.86% FA).

Conclusion: Chat2Scenic demonstrates that iterative, RAG-powered chatbot interfaces can effectively bridge the gap between regulatory natural-language descriptions and executable DSL scenario scripts, setting a new SOTA for regulation-compliant autonomous driving scenario generation. The open-source release facilitates further research.

Abstract: Validating autonomous driving systems requires diverse, regulation-compliant test scenarios. In simulation-based testing, scenarios are defined as executable scripts. Yet automatically generating such scripts from regulatory descriptions remains an open challenge, and existing approaches face fundamental trade-offs. Retrieval-assemble methods achieve reasonable compilation rates but lack scalability, whereas retrieval-based full-script generation suffers from low compilation success rates. We present Chat2Scenic, the first iterative retrieval-augmented framework to generate scenario scripts in Domain Specific Language (DSL). Specifically, Chat2Scenic provides a chatbot interface that supports interactive scenario refinement and integrates Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG) to ground scenario generation in regulatory knowledge and DSL syntax. Furthermore, we propose an open benchmark for scenario generation comprising 123 scenarios from various regulations, including NHTSA and United Nations Vehicle Regulations, as well as other sources. Extensive evaluation with State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrates that Chat2Scenic achieves 76.42% Compilation Success Rate (CSR) and 58.17% Framework Accuracy (FA), outperforming existing methods (Retrieval Assemble with 30.08% CSR, 11.03% FA and Retrieval full script generation with 16.26% CSR, 10.86% FA). To facilitate future research, we release our code as open source at https://github.com/TUM-AVS/chat2scenic.

</details>


### [182] [A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models for Long and Short-Term Forecasting of the Egyptian Stock Market: A Focus on EGX30](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14391)
*Muhammed Walid,Ahmed El-Naeimy,Hosam Moubarak,Walid Gomaa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Compares ML models (KNN, RF, XGBoost, LSTM, GRU) for predicting Egypt's EGX30 index across multiple time horizons. GRU excels at longer forecasts (1-week to 2-months), XGBoost leads for 1-day predictions, ensemble methods dramatically improve long-term results (5× better than GRU at 2-months), and KNN surprisingly performs well on long-term predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most stock prediction research focuses on developed markets, leaving a gap in understanding price dynamics in developing economies like Egypt. The EGX30 is a key Middle Eastern financial hub, yet its unique market characteristics remain underexplored from a predictive modeling perspective.

Method: Historical EGX30 data was used to evaluate six model types across four forecast horizons (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 2-months): K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and ensemble techniques. Performance metrics included RMSE, MAPE, and R².

Result: GRU outperformed all models on 1-week, 1-month, and 2-month horizons. XGBoost was best for 1-day predictions. Ensemble techniques dramatically boosted long-term performance, achieving results up to 5× better than GRU at the 2-month horizon. KNN showed surprisingly strong long-term predictive performance.

Conclusion: Model selection should be horizon-dependent: XGBoost for short-term (1-day), GRU for medium-term, and ensembles for long-term forecasting. The unexpected efficacy of KNN in long-term predictions suggests it retains relevance for fintech applications. These findings provide actionable insights for investors in the Egyptian market.

Abstract: This study concentrates on predicting stock prices in the Egyptian market, focusing on the EGX30, an influential financial hub in the Middle East. While most research focuses on global stocks, there's a growing need to understand stock trends in developing countries like Egypt. The study compares different machine learning models for forecasting EGX30 trends, covering short and long-term predictions. Using historical EGX30 data, including metrics like root mean squared error, Mean Absolute Percentage Error, and coefficient of determination, models like K-Nearest Neighbours, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, long short-term memory networks, and gated recurrent unit networks were evaluated. The goal is to determine the most effective models for EGX30 prediction, considering Egypt's unique market dynamics. Insights from this study aid investors in making informed decisions. Results show that the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) outperformed the other models in the one-week, one-month, and two-months while the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model outperformed others in the one-day predictions, highlighting their usefulness in predictive analysis for financial markets. The study also showed the importance of using the ensemble techniques, especially in the long-term predictions which proved better results reaching 5 times the GRU in the two-month predictions. Additionally, the study notes the surprisingly good performance of K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) on long-term predictions, suggesting its enduring relevance and potential for future applications in the fintech domains.

</details>


### [183] [CatalogAgent: A Supervisor-mediated Self-Learning System Enabling Context Engineering for GenAI Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14396)
*Zhu Cheng,Zhenming Wang,Yu,Tang,Dan Liu,Bryan Zhang,Athanasios N. Nikolakopoulos,Pranav Souri Itabada,Jing Zhang,Chih-Chi Chou,Peng Gao,Fatemeh Mansoori,Bharat Bojja,Sarath Chander,Sameer Thombare,Umit Batur,Tarik Arici*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CatalogAgent is an agentic system for e-commerce catalog enrichment that uses a Supervisor Agent to mediate conflicts between LLM-based Generator and Evaluator models, with a Memory Base that aggregates patterns into learnings fed back to the worker models, achieving ~15% performance improvement through self-learning without human intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: E-commerce product catalogs suffer from missing structured attribute values. While LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks are effective for SA prediction, they break down when Generator and Evaluator disagree, as either can err. Additionally, external seller feedback introduces further conflicts. Existing systems lack mechanisms to resolve these conflicts and learn from them systematically.

Method: CatalogAgent introduces a Supervisor Agent that mediates conflicts from (1) internal Generator-Evaluator disagreements and (2) external seller feedback. The system includes a Memory Base storing Supervisor decisions on individual cases and a Memory Summarizer that distills these into aggregated learnings. Through context engineering, these learnings are injected back into the Generator and Evaluator LLMs' prompts, enabling continuous self-improvement without human intervention.

Result: The CatalogAgent system improved Generator performance by 15.24% and Evaluator performance by 13.98% through the self-learning loop, demonstrating that Supervisor-mediated learnings can be successfully transferred to worker LLMs via context engineering.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy, particularly in structured attribute prediction for e-commerce catalogs.

Abstract: Product catalogs are the backbone of e-commerce sites, yet a large number of structured attributes (SAs) -- such as material, color, and shape -- often have missing values. Typically, SA values are extracted from product information, including titles and descriptions. While LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks have demonstrated effectiveness for SA prediction -- where an LLM generates SA values and another evaluates them -- they face challenges when the Generator and Evaluator produce conflicting outputs, as either component can make mistakes. We introduce \texttt{CatalogAgent}, a novel agentic system that continuously improves Generator and Evaluator models for e-commerce catalog enrichment. When disagreements arise from (1) internal conflicts between the LLM-based Generator and Evaluator, or (2) external feedback from sellers on LLM outputs, a Supervisor Agent intervenes to mediate these conflicts and make final decisions. The system also incorporates a Memory Base and a Memory Summarizer that stores Supervisor Agent activities from individual cases and aggregates patterns into learnings. These learnings are fed back to the worker Generator and Evaluator LLMs, enabling self-improvement without human intervention. Through context engineering -- injecting learnings and insights into worker LLMs' contexts -- the system successfully transfers the Supervisor's capabilities to the Generator and Evaluator, improving their performance by 15.24\% and 13.98\%, respectively. Our experiments demonstrate a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy.

</details>


### [184] [When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15218)
*Weimeng Wang,Ziqiang Wang,Zihang Zhan,Chuanpu Fu,Qi Li,Ke Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs as embodied planners face "physical danger" (PD) distinct from "content danger" (CD). The paper shows CD and PD are separable in hidden states across multiple models, then proposes PRISM, a logistic probe that achieves high accuracy and low false-positive rates on physical safety benchmarks, significantly outperforming LLM-as-judge baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linguistically benign instructions can become physically unsafe when executed by embodied agents. The core question is whether this physically grounded danger is the same as text-level content danger. If distinct, a dedicated detection method is needed beyond standard content moderation.

Method: The authors (1) conduct hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests across Qwen2.5, Phi-3.5, and SmolLM2 to demonstrate CD/PD separability; (2) introduce PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic regression probe over full hidden states; (3) construct PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1,000 physical-risk pairs designed without direct harm keywords to isolate physically grounded danger detection.

Result: PRISM achieves 86.2–87.7% accuracy on SafeAgentBench (11.7–13.7% FPR), while LLM judges over-block at 24.7–39.0% FPR. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6% accuracy and 0.7% FPR versus a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejecting 67.8% of safe tasks. Results replicate on SafeText and EARBench.

Conclusion: Content danger and physical danger are representationally separable in LLM hidden states. Hidden-state probing offers a viable representation-level method for physical safety that avoids the over-blocking tendencies of LLM-as-judge approaches, enabling safer embodied agent deployment without sacrificing benign task execution.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. Building on the CD/PD separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. PRISM achieves 86.2--87.7\% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7--13.7\% FPR, while same-scale LLM judges over-block safe tasks at 24.7--39.0\% FPR. We further introduce PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1{,}000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords, to test whether methods detect physically grounded danger rather than explicit unsafe wording. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6\% accuracy and 0.7\% FPR, whereas a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8\% of safe tasks. PRISM also replicates on SafeText and EARBench, supporting hidden-state probing as a representation-level method for physical safety beyond text moderation.

</details>


### [185] [Instrument Effects in Language-Model Honesty Evaluation: An Auditable Single-System Demonstration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14399)
*Justin Bronder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper tests the reliability of language-model honesty evaluations by treating the evaluation instrument itself as the object of study. Using a controlled text-adventure game environment, the authors show that seemingly minor changes to the evaluation setup—verdict grammar options, budget rendering, and narrative register—dramatically alter measured model behavior, undermining the validity of single-run eval results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of language model honesty treat model outputs as direct evidence of underlying truthfulness, without scrutinizing whether the evaluation instruments themselves are reliable measurement tools. The authors argue that eval instruments may introduce systematic biases that distort conclusions about model behavior, and that the field lacks rigorous protocols for validating these instruments before interpreting results.

Method: The authors built a text-adventure game world where an external game engine (not any LM) holds ground truth about quest completability. An LM plays the game under a budget and must issue one of several verdicts (complete, unreachable, incomplete/not yet decidable). The engine scores verdicts against known ground truth. The study systematically varies instrument features: (1) verdict grammar size (two vs. three options), (2) presence/absence of a sentence disclosing the success criterion, (3) narrative register (presence/absence and content), and (4) budget rendering format (meter vs. lantern). Decision rules and analyses were preregistered with varying strength across series.

Result: Expanding verdict grammar from two to three options reduced strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40 on four byte-identical anchors, with the new "incomplete" verdict absorbing 28/40 outcomes. Adding one success-criterion disclosure sentence eliminated false verdicts entirely (18/59 → 0/58). Repeated runs of the same fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3 of 4 instances, revealing that single runs conflate samples with stable dispositions. A preregistered narrative-register gradient hypothesis was falsified. Post-hoc, register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering format shifted verdicts more than register content. The narrator compressed abundant budgets toward scarcity landmarks, but a preregistered mediation test returned null.

Conclusion: Evaluation instruments for LM honesty are not neutral; their design choices causally and substantially affect measured behavior. The authors propose a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments: (1) test-retest reliability, (2) sensitivity to instrument variants, (3) preregistration of decision rules and analyses, and (4) binding of run artifacts to executed revisions. Without such checks, single-run evaluations risk reporting artifacts of the instrument as properties of the model.

Abstract: Evaluations of language-model honesty read the model's verdicts as evidence about the model. We test the instrument instead. We built a text-adventure world where the game engine, not any model, knows whether the quest can be completed. A language model plays under a budget and must eventually declare its quest complete, unreachable, or not yet decidable; the engine scores every verdict. Decision rules were recorded before results were read, and run artifacts bind the revisions they executed; the strength of preregistration varies by series and is disclosed. With the player held fixed, instrument choices substantially changed measured behavior. On four byte-identical anchors, expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts moved strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40, while the new incomplete verdict took 28/40 outcomes; across series 2, 93/158 valid games ended incomplete. One sentence disclosing the success criterion took matched-instance false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58, through fewer decision points and cleaner decisions. Repeated runs of one fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3 of 4 instances: single runs report samples as dispositions. A formally preregistered narrative-register gradient was falsified; two post-hoc, hypothesis-generating patterns remain: register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering moved verdicts more than register content (.383 meter vs .150 lantern). The narrator compressed abundant budgets toward scarcity landmarks, yet the registered mediation test returned a null. We propose a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments.

</details>


### [186] [Reward-Free Evolving Agents via Pairwise Validator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14408)
*Minghao Liu,Yu Wang,Jiayun Wang,Wei Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes replacing per-iteration scalar reward signals in self-evolving agentic loops with a pairwise LLM validator that judges which of two agent candidates (parent vs. child) is better, eliminating the need for costly labeled data and domain-specific reward design while maintaining competitive task accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing reliable scalar reward signals for self-evolving agents is expensive, requiring domain expertise and costly labeled examples. The authors aim to eliminate this bottleneck by leveraging the observation that pairwise comparison (contrastive judgment) is easier and more stable than absolute scoring, as it avoids strict scale calibration.

Method: The authors introduce a frozen LLM as a pairwise validator that issues binary better/worse verdicts between parent and child agent candidates at each iteration's accept/reject gate. They integrate this validator into three existing self-evolving engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) under two flavors: (1) Adaptive Focus, which retains the engine's existing validation-set parent selection, and (2) Soft Elo, where validator verdicts drive parent selection, eliminating val-set rewards entirely. The method is evaluated across prompt and code substrates with cross-family validator swaps.

Result: Across multiple agents and both prompt and code artifact substrates, the pairwise validator matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on the majority of evaluated settings. The pattern holds even under cross-family validator swaps, demonstrating robustness.

Conclusion: The pairwise LLM validator serves as an effective drop-in replacement for per-step reward design, achieving competitive task accuracy without the associated labeling cost, thereby lowering the barrier to building self-evolving agent systems.

Abstract: A self-evolving agentic loop repeatedly proposes a tweaked version of an agent (its prompt template or program) and accepts or rejects the change based on a per-iteration quality signal. Designing that signal is often the costly part of the project: a reliable scalar reward requires domain expertise and labeled examples that are themselves as expensive to assemble as the agent's underlying task. We propose replacing the scalar at the accept/reject gate with a pairwise validator: a frozen LLM that, given the parent and child candidate, returns a binary verdict on which is better. Pairwise judgment is generally easier and more stable than absolute scoring, due to its contrastive nature, which mitigates the need for strict scale calibration. The validator also requires no training of its own. We integrate the validator into three published self-evolving engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and report two flavors: Adaptive Focus, which retains the engine's existing val-set parent selection, and Soft Elo, which lets the validator's verdicts drive parent selection so that val-set rewards drop as well. Across multiple agents and two artifact substrates (prompt and code), our method matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on the majority of settings we evaluate, and the pattern survives a cross-family validator swap. The pairwise gate is thus a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design at competitive task accuracy without the labeling cost.

</details>


### [187] [CausalGraphX: A Counterfactual Graph Neural Network Framework for Explainable Systemic Risk Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14416)
*Rabimba Karanjai,Hemanth Madhavarao,Lei Xu,Weidong Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CausalGraphX is a framework combining Graph Neural Networks with counterfactual reasoning to explain systemic risk in financial networks, outperforming baselines in predicting cascading defaults while generating actionable causal explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Regulators need explainable models for systemic risk assessment. Traditional models fail to capture non-linear network dynamics, and standard GNNs are black boxes that learn correlative rather than causal patterns, limiting their utility for stress testing and intervention design.

Method: CausalGraphX integrates Graph Attention networks to learn institutional vulnerability representations, applies adversarial regularization to isolate causal drivers from spurious correlations, and uses an optimization-based counterfactual generation approach to answer intervention queries (e.g., minimal capital injection to prevent default).

Result: The framework significantly outperforms both traditional and deep learning baselines on large-scale synthetic financial networks in predicting cascading defaults, while generating sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.

Conclusion: Integrating causal reasoning with GNNs yields both superior predictive performance and regulatory-grade explainability for systemic risk assessment, enabling more effective stress testing and intervention planning.

Abstract: The interconnected nature of global financial systems makes them vulnerable to systemic risks, where the failure of a few institutions can trigger catastrophic cascading defaults. Traditional risk models often fail to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of these networks. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promise in modeling relational data, they primarily learn correlative patterns and function as black boxes, offering little insight into the causal mechanisms of shock propagation. This limitation is critical for regulators who require explainable models to perform stress tests and devise effective interventions. We introduce CausalGraphX, a novel framework that integrates GNNs with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable assessments of systemic risk. CausalGraphX employs a Graph Attention mechanism to learn representations of institutional vulnerability and uses an adversarial regularization technique to ensure these representations capture causal drivers rather than spurious correlations. Furthermore, we propose an optimization-based approach to generate counterfactual explanations, answering questions such as, "What minimum capital injection would have prevented Bank A's default under a specific stress scenario?" We validate CausalGraphX on large-scale synthetic financial networks. Our results demonstrate that CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults while providing sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.

</details>


### [188] [Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14427)
*Joe Logan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A depth-recurrent transformer trained with randomized recursion depth exhibits per-token convergence to a fixed point, with convergence speed varying by token type. A training-free halting rule that stops computation once a token stabilizes achieves depth-8 quality using only ~5 loops on average (38% reduction), outperforming a learned router. This demonstrates that convergence depth is directly readable from the model state without auxiliary training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed depth-recurrent transformers (weight-tied, variable-depth) can produce one checkpoint usable across inference depths via randomized-depth training. The authors ask: what do such models actually compute per token? They investigate whether per-token convergence behavior can be exploited to dynamically allocate computation, reducing average FLOPs without sacrificing quality.

Method: The authors train a 135M-parameter depth-recurrent transformer on FineWeb-Edu with randomized recursion depth (1–16 loops). They measure per-token convergence via successive-output KL divergence and state-change magnitude. They compare two halting strategies: (1) a training-free rule that stops a token once its output KL divergence falls below a threshold, and (2) a learned linear router trained on convergence labels. Quality is evaluated against uniform-depth baselines, and average depth serves as a FLOP proxy.

Result: Recurrent state converges to a per-token fixed point: mean KL divergence drops from 3.9e-1 (loop 2) to 8.5e-6 (loop 16). Convergence is non-uniform: median tokens converge by loop 6; ~10% still update at loop 8. Convergence depth correlates with token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). The training-free halting rule achieves uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (38% reduction) and matches uniform depth across the range. The learned router requires nearly full depth with no reduction. Validation loss is elastic: 3.80 at 1 loop, 3.20 at 8 loops, stable to 32.

Conclusion: Per-token convergence depth is directly readable from model state without auxiliary training, enabling a simple halting rule that significantly reduces average computation while maintaining quality. A learned router performs worse, suggesting the signal is already explicit in the model's output dynamics. Results are reported at a single scale and seed, with no FLOP-matched parity claims, and wall-clock speedup is not realized in the current implementation.

Abstract: A depth-recurrent transformer applies a weight-tied core a variable number of times, and prior work has shown that training with a randomized recursion count yields one checkpoint usable across a range of inference depths. We ask what such a model actually computes per token, and measure it directly. On a 135M-class model trained on FineWeb-Edu, the recurrent state converges to a per-token fixed point: mean successive-output KL divergence falls from 3.9e-1 at the second loop to 8.5e-6 by the sixteenth, and per-token state change decays in step. Crucially, this convergence is not uniform across tokens. The median token converges by loop six, while approximately 10 percent of tokens continue to update at the training-mean depth of eight, and mean convergence depth is ordered by token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). This per-token variation is the central object of the paper. We show it is directly readable and that reading it outperforms learning to predict it: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth) and matches uniform depth across the average-depth range, whereas a linear router trained on convergence labels harvested from the same model requires nearly full depth and yields no reduction. The elasticity that makes this possible reproduces here as background (validation loss decreases monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight and remains stable to 32 loops). We report average depth as a FLOP proxy with a three-point wall-clock bracket rather than a realized speedup, make no FLOP-matched parity claim, and note that the allocation results are established at a single scale and seed. The complete study runs on a single RTX 4090 in approximately 100 GPU-hours.

</details>


### [189] [Tactile: Giving Computer-Using Agents Hands and Feet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14443)
*Yong Liu,Zhenyi Zhong,Zhanpeng Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Tactile introduces an open-source middleware layer that replaces brittle pixel-based GUI interaction with a structured observe-ground-act-verify loop, leveraging accessibility APIs, OCR, and visual fallbacks to provide semantic, verifiable, and auditable action grounding for computer-use agents, yielding significant benchmark improvements across multiple agent frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current computer-use agents rely on a fragile motor layer: screenshot analysis → coordinate prediction → click → hope. This collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation with no provenance, making interaction unreliable and debugging difficult. There is a need for a reusable execution substrate that treats UI actions as structured, semantic objects rather than anonymous pixels.

Method: Tactile is a tool layer that fuses heterogeneous UI evidence sources — OS accessibility semantics (e.g., AX APIs), OCR-grounded text regions, and visual fallback — into action-grounded interface states. These states consist of compact target candidates annotated with source labels, roles/text, state flags, bounding geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop: they prefer native semantic actions when accessibility metadata is available, fall back to OCR-grounded coordinate clicks when visible text is the best signal, and maintain full provenance for replay and failure attribution.

Result: On macOSWorld-style tasks, Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall, and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks specifically. A 96-task cross-agent evaluation shows consistent gains across four agent frameworks: Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose.

Conclusion: Reliable desktop computer use requires not just stronger models but a reusable execution substrate that exposes UI actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects. Tactile demonstrates that such a layer yields consistent, measurable improvements across diverse agents and tasks.

Abstract: Computer-use agents are becoming capable software operators, but their interface to desktop applications is still often a brittle motor layer: they look at screenshots, predict coordinates, click, and hope that the visible state changed as intended. This collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation. We present Tactile, an open-source tool layer that gives agents a more reliable "hands and feet" for desktop use. Tactile converts heterogeneous UI evidence--operating-system accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual fallback regions--into action-grounded interface states: compact target candidates with source labels, roles or text, state, geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop that prefers native semantic actions when available, falls back to OCR-grounded coordinates when visible text is the best evidence, and keeps full provenance for replay and failure attribution. On macOSWorld-style tasks, adding Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks; a 96-task cross-agent subset shows consistent gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose. These results suggest that reliable computer use requires not only stronger models, but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

</details>


### [190] [Alipay-PIBench: A Realistic Payment Integration Benchmark for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14573)
*Shiyu Ying,Xuejie Cao,Yingfan Ma,Yuanhao Dong,Wenyu Chen,Bowen Song,Lin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Alipay-PIBench is a benchmark with 9 projects and 18 tasks for evaluating coding agents on Alipay payment integration, covering basic completion and advanced risk-aware scenarios; experiments on six models show that providing a payment-integration skill improves mean rubric pass rate by ~10 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Payment integration is a complex, multi-faceted software engineering task requiring product selection, client-server flow implementation, payment verification, and transactional consistency. There is a lack of controlled benchmarks to diagnose coding-agent capabilities specifically in this domain and to assess how structured guidance (skills) affects performance.

Method: The authors introduce Alipay-PIBench, comprising 9 product-specific projects and 18 task instances split into Basic (functional completion) and Advanced (risk-aware hardening) scenarios. Evaluation uses scenario-specific rubrics with deterministic checks (static, unit, integration, end-to-end) plus LLM-assisted semantic assessment. Six coding-agent models are evaluated under with-skill and without-skill conditions, measured by rubric pass rate (RPR).

Result: Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Providing the alipay-payment-integration skill yields an average gain of 10.31 percentage points in mean RPR over the without-skill condition, with variation across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level analysis distinguishes performance across source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements.

Conclusion: Alipay-PIBench offers a controlled, realistic setting for diagnosing coding-agent capabilities in payment integration and demonstrates that structured, domain-specific skill guidance significantly improves agent performance, with effects varying by model and task type.

Abstract: Payment integration is a demanding repository-level software task: agents must select a suitable product, implement coordinated client-server flows, verify payment outcomes, and preserve consistency between transaction and business states. We introduce Alipay-PIBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration. It contains nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, each organized into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Scenario-specific rubrics support deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, supplemented by LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. We evaluate six coding-agent models and report rubric pass rate (RPR). Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Access to the alipay-payment-integration skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average relative to the without-skill condition, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements. Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration.

</details>


### [191] [Step-Level Preference Learning for Generative Agents in Social Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14485)
*Wenchang Gao,Pingyue Sheng,Lanlan Qiu,Yunfei Ma,Jian Zhao,Baicheng Chen,Kangda Wang,Yuyang Tian,Shunqiang Mao,Tianxing He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an interactive simulation interface for collecting step-level human preference annotations on LLM-based generative agent decision trajectories, yielding 57K fine-grained annotations. Using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on this data, the authors improve simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality in agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based generative agents lack grounding in human preferences over intermediate decision steps (planning, memory retrieval, reflection, action selection), and fine-grained human annotations for these steps are scarce. Bridging this gap is essential for improving agent behavior alignment with human expectations.

Method: The authors introduce an interactive simulation interface that captures step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, generating a dataset of 57K annotations. They then apply supervised finetuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on open-weight language models using this data to perform step-level preference learning.

Result: Step-level preference learning consistently improves simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and induces more socially effective agent behavior. The results demonstrate that step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.

Conclusion: Step-level human supervision serves as a powerful and effective training signal for improving LLM-based generative agents, enhancing both fine-grained intermediate decisions and overall long-horizon behavioral outcomes in simulations.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based generative agents simulate human behavior through long-horizon decision-making processes that comprise intermediate steps such as planning, memory retrieval, reflection, and action selection. However, fine-grained human annotations of these intermediate steps remain scarce, and existing agents are not grounded in human preferences over such intermediate decisions. To address this gap, we introduce \method, an interactive simulation interface that enables us to collect step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, leading to a dataset of 57K fine-grained annotations. We conduct step-level preference learning on open-weight language models using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on this data, consistently improving simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and inducing more socially effective agent behavior. Our results show that step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.

</details>


### [192] [MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14642)
*Huanxi Liu,Kun Hu,Jiaqi Liao,Qiang Wang,Pengfei Qian,YuanZhao Zhai,Dawei Feng,Bo Ding,Huaimin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MCPEvol-Bench is a benchmark evaluating LLM agents' adaptability to evolving MCP server tools. Using 11 mutation operators across 123 MCP servers, it reveals that even frontier models like GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 suffer significant performance drops (13.7% and 14.4%) when tool interfaces change, exposing critical vulnerabilities in LLM-driven tool-use workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MCP-based benchmarks assess LLM agents using static tool interfaces, ignoring the reality that MCP servers continuously evolve in both interfaces and functionalities. This oversight leads to flawed evaluations that fail to measure agent adaptability in dynamic, real-world tool landscapes.

Method: The authors introduce MCPEvol-Bench, built on a large-scale empirical study of real-world MCP server evolution. They design 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution across 123 MCP servers, creating multiple versioned environments. Twelve state-of-the-art LLMs are then benchmarked on these evolved server versions to assess task-solving performance, with detailed error analysis of planning and reasoning failures.

Result: Frontier models exhibit marked performance degradation under tool evolution: GPT-5.4 drops 13.7% and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 drops 14.4%. These declines are accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors, demonstrating that even the most advanced LLMs lack robustness when tool interfaces and functionalities change.

Conclusion: LLM-driven workflows are highly vulnerable to tool evolution, and MCPEvol-Bench establishes a necessary standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments, highlighting an urgent area for improvement in LLM agent design.

Abstract: As Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers emerge as the core infrastructure for connecting LLMs with external tools, existing benchmarks leverage real-world MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities. However, these benchmarks overlook the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities within MCP servers, resulting in flawed assessments that fail to capture the agent's adaptability in changing tool landscapes. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{MCPEvol-Bench}, a novel benchmark for evaluating the task-solving capabilities of LLM agents under dynamic toolset evolution. Inspired by large-scale empirical study, we propose 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution within 123 MCP servers. We benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple versions of MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models struggle to adapt to evolving tools. For instance, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. These findings highlight the vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows, establishing MCPEvol-Bench as a standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

</details>


### [193] [Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14890)
*Jek Huang,Jeffery Hsia,Jiayi Sun,Freddie Shi,Wei Huang,Ian H. White*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proof-or-Stop is a lifecycle control method for autonomous coding agents that requires fresh, tracked, mechanically verifiable evidence before permitting lifecycle state transitions, treating agent outputs as claims rather than state. Evaluated via mechanism tests, a 9,240-cell ablation, and self-application, it achieved zero false-DONE, significant reduction in hidden failures, and demonstrated that gated review as a lifecycle requirement drives improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous coding agents produce multi-step software artifacts with lifecycle states (reviewed, tested, DONE, ready-to-merge), but these states are merely claims unless backed by current, verifiable evidence. Without such evidence, agents can silently skip steps or produce false assurances, leading to hidden failures. The work addresses the need for a principled control layer that constrains lifecycle transitions to only occur when gate-admissible, mechanically verifiable proof exists.

Method: Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and defines proof operationally as gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model — not semantic program correctness. Lifecycle transitions are permitted only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method is evaluated through: (1) mechanism tests on an unattended-loop engine (10 scenarios) and local-key receipt bundles (18 tamper classes); (2) a 9,240-cell powered control-policy ablation comparing A4 (gated loop) vs A2-prime (naive compute-budgeted loop) and A3 (reviewer-without-gate) vs A4; and (3) operated self-application evidence from a corpus of 565 stories and 1,007 review findings.

Result: The unattended-loop engine passed 10/10 scenarios with zero false-DONE; receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In the 9,240-cell ablation, the gated loop (A4) reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31/1,800 injected cells (A2-prime) to 2/1,800 — a 1.6 pp improvement (95% CI [0.8, 2.5]). The A3 vs A4 comparison (14/1,800 vs 2/1,800) indicates gains are associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate, not merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus shows 94.8% of 1,007 review findings resolved, with a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit.

Conclusion: Proof-or-Stop is a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer effective at deciding which agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus, indicating need for broader validation.

Abstract: Autonomous coding agents increasingly execute multi-step software work, but lifecycle states such as reviewed, tested, DONE, and ready-to-merge remain claims unless supported by current evidence. We present Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control, a method that permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and uses proof operationally to mean gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model, not semantic program correctness.
  We evaluate an open-source implementation through mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, and operated self-application evidence. The unattended-loop engine passed 10 of 10 scenarios with zero false-DONE, and local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, the pre-registered A4 versus A2-prime comparison reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells under a compute-budgeted naive loop to 2 of 1,800 under the gated loop, a 1.6 percentage-point improvement in not-amplified rate with a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.8, 2.5]. A near-compute A3 versus A4 comparison, 14 of 1,800 versus 2 of 1,800, indicates that the gain is associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate rather than merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8 percent resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. These results support Proof-or-Stop as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

</details>


### [194] [Contextualized Evaluation of Vision Language Models through Dynamic, Multi-turn Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14499)
*Yijiang Li,Huiqi Zou,Bingyang Wang,Ziang Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CEDI is a dynamic, multi-round, interactive evaluation framework for MLLMs that uses a three-party setup (evaluatee, automated examiner, grader) with graph-guided conversations. Applied to visual hallucinations, it reveals significantly more and more realistic hallucinations than static benchmarks, uncovers accumulation effects over long contexts, and exposes vulnerability to premise-rejection tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM benchmarks operate in controlled, static settings that fundamentally misalign with the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world deployment. This gap makes real-world effectiveness uncertain despite strong benchmark performance.

Method: CEDI frames evaluation as a three-party interaction: an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversations guided by a graph-based task representation with state-space transitions, deploying strategies like clarification requests and adversarial probes to elicit performance evidence. The framework is instantiated for visual hallucination evaluation across multiple models, datasets, and domains.

Result: Contextualized interactive evaluations uncover significantly more hallucinations than static evaluation, with hallucinations that more closely resemble practical use cases. Hallucinations accumulate over long contexts through self-reinforcing dialogue history. Models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal.

Conclusion: CEDI represents a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid MLLM assessment, demonstrating that dynamic interactive evaluation reveals critical failure modes invisible to static benchmarks.

Abstract: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial advances on benchmarks, yet their real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. This gap stems from the fundamental misalignment between benchmarks in controlled, static settings and the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDI (Contextualized Evaluations of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions), a framework that recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction between an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversation guided by a graph-based representation of the task. By navigating state-space transitions, CEDI deploys diverse strategies, from clarification requests to adversarial probes, to elicit performance evidence. We apply CEDI to visual hallucinations. Empirical results across multiple models, diverse settings, datasets, and domains show that contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal not only significantly more hallucinations than conventional static evaluation but also ones that more closely resemble those arising in practical use cases. We further show that hallucinations often accumulate over long contexts, through self-reinforcing dialogue history, and models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Together, these findings highlight CEDI as a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLMs' capabilities. Code is available at github.com/williamium3000/cedi.

</details>


### [195] [VLT: A Vision-Language-Time Series Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14510)
*Haiteng Wang,Jingheng Yan,Xiaokang Wang,Lei Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series data, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge for industrial PHM. It introduces a frequency spectrum as a visual bridge, a Time-MoE for heterogeneous temporal dynamics, a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner for joint spectral-semantic modeling, and a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism to resolve cross-modal optimization conflicts. VLT achieves SOTA performance with strong robustness under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing industrial PHM approaches are typically limited to single-modality modeling (time-series only), restricting generalization in complex, real-world scenarios. Although LLMs offer multimodal learning potential, bridging continuous time-series signals with discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge that the paper aims to address.

Method: VLT jointly models three modalities: time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. Key components include: (1) Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics; (2) Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enabling joint modeling of spectral and semantic features in a shared representation space; and (3) a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism using gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts.

Result: VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple industrial datasets and demonstrates superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

Conclusion: The frequency spectrum serves as an effective visual bridge between continuous time-series and discrete textual semantics. VLT's multimodal design and gradient alignment strategy enable robust industrial PHM under challenging real-world conditions.

Abstract: Industrial time series serve as the foundation for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) to ensure the reliability and safety of industrial equipment such as aero-engines. However, existing approaches are typically limited to single-modality modeling, which restricts their generalization in complex scenarios. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities for multimodal learning, bridging continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge. To this end, we propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. A key insight is to utilize the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics. Specifically, a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) is designed to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enables joint modeling of spectral and semantic features within a shared representation space. Furthermore, a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism is introduced to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets demonstrate that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

</details>


### [196] [RetroAgent: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured Memory for Agentic Retrosynthesis Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14512)
*Yanqiao Zhu,Jingru Gan,Xiaoqi Sun,Fang Sun,Yidan Shi,Md Mofijul Islam,Chao Shang,Wenhao Gao,Connor W. Coley,Yizhou Sun,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RetroAgent is an LLM-based agent for multi-step retrosynthesis planning that combines symbolic tree search with neural reasoning via structured memory and chemistry tools, enabling informed navigation of the combinatorial search space with strong in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional retrosynthesis methods use tree search with offline value networks that evaluate candidates in isolation without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent LLM-based approaches suffer from simple interfaces that restrict full exploration of the search space. There is a need for an agent that can reason holistically about the entire search state.

Method: The authors propose RetroAgent, an LLM agent equipped with a harness featuring structured memory and chemistry tools. The agent observes the full search state — including explored routes, available alternatives, and intermediate properties — allowing it to make decisions based on both global progress and domain-specific chemical knowledge.

Result: RetroAgent demonstrates strong performance and generalization on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution retrosynthesis benchmarks.

Conclusion: Bridging symbolic search with LLM-based neural reasoning through structured memory and tool integration yields an effective retrosynthesis planner that generalizes well beyond its training distribution.

Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization.

</details>


### [197] [WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524)
*Adnan Labib,Yixuan Huang,Jiahui Wu,John Maurice Gayed,Zheng Yuan,Qiao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WrAFT is a modular automated writing evaluation tool for argumentative essays that achieves SOTA scoring (QWK=0.84, RMSE=0.44) and highly rated multi-level feedback (93-96% approval) using fine-tuned LLMs on TOEFL essays.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated writing evaluation systems often lack the ability to deliver both accurate holistic scoring and comprehensive, multi-level feedback (surface-level and deep-level) in a unified, reliable manner.

Method: A modular AWE architecture with three components: scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback (macro and micro). Multiple LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7) were evaluated via direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning on a proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official scores. Evaluation metrics include QWK, RMSE for scoring, and human approval ratings for feedback.

Result: Scoring: QWK of 0.84 and RMSE of 0.44 on a 0-5 scale (SOTA). Human evaluation: 96.14% approval for surface-level feedback, 93.03% for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69% for deep-level micro feedback. A public, free-to-use interactive UI was developed.

Conclusion: The modular LLM-based design of WrAFT enables reliable, fine-grained writing assessment and feedback, validated by strong quantitative scoring metrics and high human approval ratings, with practical deployment through a public interface.

Abstract: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

</details>


### [198] [Are LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Production-Ready? A Trace-Driven Benchmark and Optimization Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14541)
*Lingyun Yang,Yuxiao Wang,Shenghao Liang,Linfeng Yang,Daocheng Ying,Chunbo You,Rui Zhang,Luping Wang,Yinghao Yu,Guodong Yang,Liping Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Atrex-Bench is a GPU kernel generation benchmark sampled from production inference traces, revealing that frontier coding agents achieve only ~10% of hardware roofline on real operators. The authors co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven optimization agent that closes this gap by converting fallbacks into kernels matching hand-tuned baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks rely on synthetic or curated problems unrepresentative of production workloads. This mismatch means benchmarks fail to measure real-world capability, and apparent correctness is inflated by PyTorch fallbacks rather than model-generated kernels.

Method: Atrex-Bench is constructed by sampling 30 operators and 440 shapes from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem is weighted by its share of observed GPU time (weighted by application card-hours) and carries a per-problem roofline ceiling. AKA, the accompanying agent, uses iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout to escape stalled contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference kernels, 244 optimization documents, plus external upstream references).

Result: Six frontier coding agents evaluated on Atrex-Bench reached only ~10% of hardware roofline on production operators. Much of the apparent pass rate came from PyTorch fallbacks rather than self-written kernels. In a controlled case study, AKA converted zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that matched or exceeded hand-tuned production baselines.

Conclusion: Current coding agents significantly underperform on real production kernel generation tasks, and correctness metrics alone overstate capability. Profile-driven optimization agents like AKA, combining iterative search with structured optimization knowledge, can bridge the gap between generated and hand-tuned production kernels.

Abstract: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks draw problems from synthetic or curated sources that diverge from deployed workloads. We present Atrex-Bench, a benchmark whose 30 operators and 440 shapes are sampled directly from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs.
