Each problem carries an importance weight derived from its share of observed GPU time, weighted by application card-hours and computed separately for the serving phases in which it runs, together with a per-problem roofline ceiling, so the aggregate score emphasizes the kernels that consume the most serving time. Evaluating six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows that even the best vanilla model reaches only ${\sim}10\%$ of the hardware roofline on production operators; and correctness alone overstates capability, since much of the apparent pass rate comes from PyTorch fallbacks rather than kernels the model wrote. To close this gap, we co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel-optimization agent that combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout for escaping stalled search contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-knowledge documents, plus external upstream reference projects for API/ISA lookup). In a controlled case study, the agent converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.

</details>


### [199] [Seeing the End at Step Zero: Accelerating Diffusion MLLMs via MLP Sparsity-Aware Truncation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14557)
*Qicheng Zhao,Qi Sun,Zheyu Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DMLLMs waste compute on padded [EOS] tokens during fixed-length generation. The authors discover that MLP activation sparsity shifts at the first denoising step reveal the true semantic boundary. Seer, a training-free framework, detects this boundary via SNR, truncates redundant suffixes, and uses a hybrid batching strategy, achieving up to ~31× throughput speedup with no performance degradation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion Multimodal LLMs suffer from severe inference inefficiency because they must predefine a maximum output length, leading to massive redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] padding tokens when actual outputs are shorter.

Method: Seer is a training-free, plug-and-play framework with three components: (1) detection of the semantic boundary at the first denoising step via an SNR-based criterion applied to MLP activation sparsity shifts; (2) one-shot truncation of the redundant token suffix for all subsequent denoising steps; and (3) a hybrid batched execution strategy that maximizes throughput while accommodating dynamically varying sequence lengths.

Result: Seer achieves up to ~31× throughput acceleration by eliminating padding waste. Across 9 benchmarks, it maintains overall performance and even yields minor accuracy gains on complex visual tasks (e.g., DocVQA: 63.52 → 63.66) by mitigating noise leakage.

Conclusion: Seer provides a highly efficient, training-free, plug-and-play solution for accelerating DMLLM inference by exploiting early-step activation sparsity signals to dynamically truncate padding, with robust performance preservation across diverse multimodal benchmarks.

Abstract: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) are highly effective for multimodal reasoning, yet their inference efficiency is significantly hindered by fixed-length generation constraints. Since the actual output length is unknown, output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, resulting in substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. In this work, we discover that DMLLMs implicitly reveal their valid semantic boundary at the very first denoising step through a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity. Leveraging this observation, we propose Seer, a training-free framework that detects this boundary using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-based criterion and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. To preserve these theoretical gains during batched serving, Seer incorporates a hybrid execution strategy that maximizes throughput while seamlessly accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experimental results demonstrate that Seer effectively eliminates padding waste, accelerating throughput by up to $\sim$31$\times$. Across 9 benchmarks, Seer robustly maintains overall performance and even improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by mitigating noise leakage (e.g., DocVQA score increases from 63.52 to 63.66), offering a highly efficient, plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

</details>


### [200] [Collaborative Spatial Learning with Multi-LLM Agents in Networked Social Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14574)
*Hao He,Chris J. Kuhlman,Xinwei Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents playing the Mason–Watts network search task exhibit a significant network-efficiency effect only when instructed to randomize their first-round choices. A simple randomization prompt dramatically improves collective payoff. Bayesian optimization agents outperform LLM agents on this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether groups of LLM agents exhibit network-efficiency effects (shorter-path networks outperforming longer-path networks) in collective problem solving, as originally demonstrated with human subjects in the Mason–Watts experiment. The work also seeks to compare LLM agent behavior against mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents and human data.

Method: Sixteen LLM agents are placed on each of the eight Mason–Watts network topologies to perform the original two-dimensional search task. Mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents are developed as a benchmark. Experiments compare conditions with and without a first-round randomization instruction. Agent behaviors are analyzed along dimensions of exploration–exploitation tradeoffs, copying, and spatial diversity.

Result: LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect only with first-round randomization. The randomization instruction improves collective payoff by over 3× the estimated payoff difference across the eight topologies. Bayesian optimization agents achieve higher payoffs than LLM agents. Behavioral differences in exploration–exploitation, copying, and spatial diversity are characterized.

Conclusion: LLM agents can reproduce the network-efficiency effect from human experiments but only under specific prompting conditions (randomized initialization). Prompt engineering has a disproportionately large impact on collective performance. Mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents remain superior on this spatial search task, suggesting room for improvement in LLM agent design for collective problem solving.

Abstract: Collective problem solving often requires that group members consider the tradeoff between exploitation of known solutions and exploration for new ones, where information of known solutions can be disseminated among individual members through communication networks. The Mason--Watts experiment (PNAS 2012) showed that human groups in shorter-path networks outperform those in longer-path networks on a two-dimensional search task. In this work, we focus on the investigation of such network-efficiency effects in the setting of a group of large language model (LLM) agents. Specifically, we consider groups of sixteen LLM agents playing the Mason--Watts experiment on the eight Mason--Watts network topologies. Moreover, we develop mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents such that the performance of LLM agents can be compared with both the mechanistic agents and the human experimental data. Our computational experiments indicate that the LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, but not under the default initialization. In this experiment, adding a one-sentence first-round randomization instruction improves collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across the eight network topologies. Also, the Bayesian optimization agents obtain higher payoffs than the evaluated LLM agents on this spatial search task. We further compare the agents' exploration--exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

</details>


### [201] [Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14581)
*Sinyoung Ra,Jonghun Kim,Hyunjin Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A cooperative multi-LLM system generates a paired 3D MRI-text dataset for brain oncology, which is then used to train a VLM that outperforms existing 2D and 3D methods on report generation and visual question answering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs in medicine are largely limited to 2D images (e.g., chest X-rays) due to the scarcity of paired 3D imaging-text data. Extending VLMs to 3D modalities like MRI is critical for brain oncology applications but remains challenging.

Method: First, a cooperative multi-LLM framework generates and cross-validates reports for 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases, producing a high-quality paired 3D image-text dataset. Then, a VLM is built that tokenizes 3D MRI volumes and aligns them with textual instructions via vision-language alignment training.

Result: The proposed VLM, trained on the newly created dataset, surpasses both 2D and 3D baseline methods on report generation and visual question answering benchmarks in brain oncology.

Conclusion: The cooperative LLM-based dataset creation pipeline effectively addresses the 3D image-text data gap, and the resulting VLM improves report quality while supporting better diagnosis and treatment planning in brain oncology.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

</details>


### [202] [MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14582)
*Junjie Zhang,Jiayu Liu,Wenbin Liu,Zhenya Huang,Doudou Wang,Yan Jiang,Leiye Xu,Tao Xiong,Wen Huang,Qi Liu,Guoping Hu,Enhong Chen,Mengping Zhang,Xiangdong Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MathCoPilot is a human-in-the-loop system for interactive mathematical theorem proving, where mathematicians guide high-level strategy while LLM agents handle formalization and proof construction in Lean 4. Benchmarking four SOTA LLMs reveals strong performance on undergraduate-level problems but significant gaps on domain-specific PDE theorems requiring deep mathematical insight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based theorem provers operate as autonomous agents given a stated proposition, lacking the collaborative, iterative workflow essential to real mathematical research. There is a need for a symbiotic human-AI paradigm where the mathematician retains high-level creative control while AI handles labor-intensive formalization and verification.

Method: MathCoPilot integrates three components: (1) an interactive workbench with a living proof blueprint for stepwise human inspection and refinement; (2) automated proving skill orchestration combining adaptive knowledge base search with Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval with automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Four LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and an unnamed fourth) are evaluated on a FormalMATH subset and two real PDE theorems, testing both verified proof generation and error-detection in deliberately incorrect proofs.

Result: Current SOTA models achieve high success rates on undergraduate-level problems under favorable autoformalization conditions. However, substantial challenges persist for domain-specific PDE theorems that demand genuine mathematical understanding, where success rates drop considerably.

Conclusion: The human-in-the-loop symbiotic paradigm is a promising direction for AI-assisted mathematical research, but today's LLMs still fall short on deep domain-specific reasoning. MathCoPilot provides a foundation for future systems that more tightly couple human mathematical intuition with AI formalization capabilities.

Abstract: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

</details>


### [203] [SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14616)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Haotian Xia,Akshaya Bharadhwaj,Anay Putty,Anirudh Ravishankar,Jaewoong Lee,Jinglin Xiao,Kyumin Andrew Shim,Mishika Ahuja,Nisarga Patil,Leo Liu,Zhuohan Liu,Weining Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces SportD, a soccer decision benchmark from the 2022 FIFA World Cup, to evaluate whether vision-language models can make strategically optimal on-ball decisions. The best VLM achieves only 31.4% optimal-action accuracy (vs. 38.9% for professionals) and exhibits systematic bias toward low-variance, low-reward actions like conservative passing over shooting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While VLMs excel at visual understanding, it is unclear whether they can translate visual perception into strategically effective decisions. Soccer provides an ideal testbed because every on-ball action (shoot vs. pass) can be quantitatively evaluated via possession-value models, unlike conventional visual QA tasks that lack objective decision-quality metrics.

Method: The authors construct SportD, a benchmark of 478 on-ball decision events from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each decision is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates which action (shoot or pass to a specific teammate) maximally increases the attacking team's scoring probability. Metrics include optimal-action accuracy and regret (value forfeited by suboptimal choices). Three frontier VLMs are tested against both the optimal policy and actual professional player decisions.

Result: The best VLM selects the highest-valued action on only 31.4% of events, versus 38.9% for professional players. All models incur significantly greater regret than humans. VLMs display systematic bias toward lower-variance, lower-reward actions: they shoot less often and choose less progressive passes. Models also reproduce player-specific actions above chance even when suboptimal, suggesting imitation of familiar patterns rather than genuine counterfactual reasoning.

Conclusion: Current VLMs fall short of professional-level strategic decision-making in soccer, favoring conservative choices and imitating observed behavior rather than evaluating counterfactual alternatives. SportD offers a value-grounded framework for benchmarking physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

Abstract: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

</details>


### [204] [Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14635)
*Yufeng Ji,Wenhao Tang,Haoyi Niu,Koushil Sreenath,Yi Wu,Zhongyu Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that action supervision in VLA models has a dual effect—necessary for action-compatible representations but potentially destabilizing language-side and object-grounding representations. To address this, the authors propose Action QFormer, a query-based interface that reorganizes multimodal information before action generation, achieving dramatic improvements in zero-shot sim-to-real navigation (18.8% → 56.3% success rate) while reducing harmful upstream representation rewriting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLA models treat action supervision merely as a downstream prediction objective. The authors reconceptualize it as a force that actively shapes inherited multimodal representations, and investigate its dual nature: necessary for action compatibility yet potentially destabilizing to language processing and object grounding when applied too directly to the multimodal pathway.

Method: Action QFormer: a query-based, action-facing interface inserted between the inherited multimodal backbone and downstream action generation. It uses instruction-conditioned queries to selectively reorganize multimodal information into action-facing representations, decoupling action supervision's direct influence on the upstream multimodal pathway while preserving targeted, constructive adaptation.

Result: In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Analyses demonstrate reduced broad upstream representation rewriting while maintaining targeted action-supervised adaptation.

Conclusion: Improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones but also better mechanisms for selecting, organizing, and controlling how inherited multimodal representations are shaped under action supervision.

Abstract: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

</details>


### [205] [Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14641)
*Remo Pareschi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper develops a formal framework for analytic abduction using a κ-τ apparatus, where κ encodes epistemic interactions among hypotheses and τ sets a risk-sensitive commitment threshold. The core contribution is the causal cluster — a structured object capturing latent factors, weights, and interactions — with a two-level architecture that prevents premature convergence and causal misattribution, demonstrated in epidemiology and cybersecurity contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional abductive reasoning either imposes premature, greedy commitment to a single explanation or fails to provide actionable structure under ambiguity. The paper seeks a disciplined, risk-sensitive alternative where competing explanations coexist transparently, enabling sound decision-making before ambiguity is fully resolved.

Method: The formal core is the κ-τ apparatus: κ models epistemic interaction (how hypotheses support, compete, or combine) among candidate explanatory factors; τ is a commitment threshold calibrated to decision stakes. The causal cluster encodes which latent factors participate, with what weights and interaction structure. A two-level architecture uses intra-cluster κ* and inter-cluster κ** metrics to govern factor resolution and guard against causal misattribution. The framework is demonstrated on epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis.

Result: The framework yields suspended decomposition as a legible coordination object for human-AI reasoning. Instead of a single imposed answer, decision-makers receive competing explanatory scenarios weighted by plausibility, paired with the key evidence that would discriminate between them, providing structural resistance to premature convergence.

Conclusion: Analytic abduction, formalized via κ-τ and causal clusters, transforms explanation from a single-output inference into a transparent, risk-calibrated coordination artifact. This enables robust action under ambiguity and strengthens human-AI collaborative reasoning by making the structure of uncertainty explicitly legible.

Abstract: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $κ$-$τ$ apparatus: $κ$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $τ$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $κ^*$, inter-cluster $κ^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

</details>


### [206] [TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14658)
*Mingze Xu,Yinghui Li,Jiayi Kuang,Zhanhui Kang,Di Yin,Ying Shen,Xing Sun,Yuxing Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopoAgent introduces a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear reasoning in MLLMs with a dynamic Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of isolated atomic sub-tasks, featuring adaptive atomic fission to split bottleneck nodes at runtime, achieving superior performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs use monolithic, linear planning for scientific reasoning, leading to three key failures: visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. These limitations call for a fundamentally different reasoning architecture.

Method: TopoAgent operates in two stages: (1) a front-end decomposer fractures complex scientific queries into visually-grounded atoms and organizes them into a DAG based on dependencies, ensuring strict context isolation so each node is shielded from irrelevant upstream noise; (2) adaptive atomic fission dynamically detects bottleneck nodes where tool capabilities are exceeded and recursively splits them into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime, enabling self-correction without predefined granularity.

Result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks show that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, demonstrating robustness, noise resistance, and self-correcting behavior.

Conclusion: TopoAgent provides a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning by replacing linear trajectories with dynamic topological graph evolution and runtime-adaptive granularity control.

Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

</details>


### [207] [SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14661)
*Zhihan Jiang,Meng Li,Shenghao Liu,Keran Li,Ruiben Zhou,Xianjun Deng,Shuai Wang,Haipeng Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SmartRAG is an on-device framework that decomposes mobile LLM assistants into four modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking), using a continually learnable NER (EvoNER) and a three-layer knowledge graph (MRGraph) with hybrid retrieval to enable multi-hop QA on smartphones with a quantized 1.7B model, matching performance of models up to 18× larger.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLMs as personal assistants on mobile devices requires privacy, low latency, and offline operation, but giant models exceed edge-hardware budgets. The authors argue that model compression alone is insufficient; instead, on-device intelligence should be decomposed into complementary functional roles to balance capability with resource constraints.

Method: SmartRAG organizes the assistant into four modules: (1) Perception — EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label set via teacher-distilled updates without retraining the backbone LLM; (2) Memory — MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph for storing extracted knowledge; (3) Focus — a hybrid retrieval pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search; (4) Thinking — the on-device LLM invoked only for high-value operations (labeling, planning, answer synthesis). A quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone is used.

Result: On four QA benchmarks — TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MultiHopQA — SmartRAG with the 1.7B backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18× larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency constraints.

Conclusion: Decomposing on-device intelligence into modular functional roles, combined with continual NER learning and structured knowledge graph retrieval, enables resource-efficient yet powerful mobile LLM assistants that rival much larger models while satisfying privacy, latency, and offline requirements.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

</details>


### [208] [Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14682)
*Harikrishnan P M,Goutham Vignesh,Ganesh Parab,Saisubramaniam Gopalakrishnan,Vishal Vaddina,Varun V,Rohit Agrawal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Perception-RFT introduces GRPO-based RL training for multimodal document QA that directly aligns visual features with grounding outputs, bypassing reasoning tokens. At 4B scale, reasoning-enabled models suppress their traces and converge to perception-only policies, reducing inference tokens by >60%. The paper also identifies "Grounding Divergence" — a trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal document QA approaches face two key limitations: SFT requires large annotated datasets and plateaus in optimization, while reasoning-centric RL inflates inference token costs with verbose intermediate traces that provide no clear benefit. The authors aim to determine whether explicit reasoning chains are genuinely necessary for visual grounding, and to characterize optimization dynamics in multimodal RL post-training.

Method: The authors propose Perception-RFT, which applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA without intermediate reasoning tokens, directly optimizing visual feature alignment with structured grounding outputs. They construct a reasoning-enabled variant under identical reward settings for controlled comparison. Experiments use Qwen3-VL-4B, with fine-grained analysis of optimization dynamics including SFT saturation, cold-start RL instability, and joint RL behavior on two OOD benchmarks (4,828 samples). They also test early SFT→RL transition strategies.

Result: Reasoning-enabled models spontaneously suppress reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B scale, reducing per-query inference token length by over 60%. Reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability — previously documented in text-domain post-training — extend to multimodal settings. A newly identified phenomenon, Grounding Divergence, reveals a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on OOD benchmarks under joint RL. Early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

Conclusion: Explicit reasoning chains are unnecessary for effective visual grounding in multimodal document QA at the 4B parameter scale; perception-only RL via GRPO achieves superior performance with substantially lower inference cost. The discovery of Grounding Divergence highlights a fundamental tension in joint optimization that warrants further investigation. Early transition from SFT to RL offers a data-efficient training recipe.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

</details>


### [209] [InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14683)
*Hao Yang,Yanyan Zhao,Kewei Zhao,Hongbo Zhang,Tian Zheng,Yusheng Liu,Xing Fu,Bichen Wang,Yu Zhang,Hao He,Zhen Wu,Xuda Zhi,Yongbo Huang,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InCarEmo is a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring, integrating RGB/IR video, audio, and dialogue text. It supports emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring, with benchmarks across unimodal and multimodal methods including modality-missing and noisy conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and lack conversational/linguistic information, hindering comprehensive understanding of driver emotion and state in realistic human-vehicle interaction contexts.

Method: The authors created InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios simulating realistic driver behaviors under diverse lighting and driving conditions. It includes RGB video, infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text in Chinese, plus an auxiliary English benchmark for cross-lingual evaluation. A unified benchmark with extensive baseline experiments covers unimodal and multimodal methods under standard, modality-missing, and noise conditions.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion for in-cabin affective tasks, while also revealing remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions, indicating room for improvement in robustness.

Conclusion: InCarEmo provides a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, aiming to promote safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction through multimodal emotion and state recognition.

Abstract: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

</details>


### [210] [AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14756)
*Zahratu Shabrina,Muhammad Asa,Jin Rui,Lu Yin,Stephen Law*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates Vision-Language Models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) for classifying building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from Google Street View images, comparing VLM predictions against human expert labels. Chain-of-Thought prompting yields the most stable performance (~70% average accuracy). The study also analyzes AI reasoning patterns, finding VLMs emphasize visual indicators while human experts rely more on contextual/domain knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore whether Vision-Language Models can automate building-typology classification at scale, reducing reliance on manual expert labeling, and to understand the reasoning differences between AI and human experts in urban analysis tasks.

Method: Multiple state-of-the-art VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) were prompted with GSV images to infer three building typologies. Different scaling strategies and prompting techniques (including Chain-of-Thought) were tested. VLM predictions were benchmarked against ground-truth labels from civil engineers and architects. Reasoning analysis was conducted by extracting keyword probabilities from AI-generated explanations to identify thematic patterns in agreement/disagreement with experts.

Result: Chain-of-Thought prompting provided the most stable performance. VLMs achieved approximately 70% average accuracy. AI predominantly relies on visual indicators for classification, while human experts integrate broader contextual cues and domain knowledge. VLMs can approximate expert-level building-typology classification in pattern recognition and object identification tasks.

Conclusion: VLMs show promising potential as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, particularly for scalable visual pattern recognition. The study contributes to understanding AI reasoning processes and supports the development of automated workflows in urban analysis and prediction tasks.

Abstract: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

</details>


### [211] [Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14782)
*Rachel Adams,Fola Adeleke,Ayantola Alayande,Selamawit Engida Abdella,Ana Florido,Nicolás Grossman,Leah Junck*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GIRAI 2026 evaluates 135 countries across 38 indicators on responsible AI governance. While 126 countries have at least one AI policy, frameworks rarely translate into binding protections — 78% of Global South frameworks are non-binding vs. 42% in the Global North. Only 18% of countries require public disclosure of government algorithms, and 35 countries show evidence of deploying unacceptable-risk AI systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether countries' responsible AI commitments — grounded in human rights frameworks like the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI — are being translated into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and accessible redress mechanisms, rather than remaining at the level of non-binding policy adoption.

Method: A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points across 38 indicators, organized into three pillars: (1) government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), (2) civil society engagement (5), and (3) enabling conditions (15), plus documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data spans November 2023 to September 2025. A composite score out of 100 ranks all countries across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service.

Result: Key findings: (1) 126 of 135 countries have at least one AI policy initiative, indicating expanding governance. (2) A North-South implementation gap persists — Global South countries contributed 203 of 306 new indicator frameworks, yet 78% remain non-binding (vs. 42% in the Global North). (3) Transparency and Explainability is the strongest indicator (58% of countries have frameworks), but only 18% mandate Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. (4) Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI was found in 35 countries.

Conclusion: Responsible AI governance must move beyond symbolic framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, adequately resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress mechanisms. Current commitments are widespread but shallow, failing to constrain governments' own algorithmic practices.

Abstract: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

</details>


### [212] [Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14791)
*Darius Lim,Nathan Leow,Xin Wei Chia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using per-layer transcoders on a Qwen3-4B model, the authors identify deception-related features and construct attribution graphs for circuit-level analysis, demonstrating that these features causally influence deceptive outputs and enable predictable steering between deceptive and non-deceptive responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deceptive behaviour in language models poses significant safety and security risks. The authors aim to understand the internal mechanisms underlying such behaviour using mechanistic interpretability tools, specifically transcoders, to enable monitoring and early detection of malicious behaviours.

Method: The study applies pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) to a Qwen3-4B model. Attribution graphs are constructed to capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies. Feature steering and circuit analysis are then employed to identify a dictionary of deception-related features and to assess their causal influence on model outputs.

Result: A dictionary of deception-related features was identified. These features exert stronger influence on deceptive outputs and produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses when steered, indicating that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms rather than superficial patterns.

Conclusion: Deception in language models is driven by identifiable internal mechanisms that can be surfaced via transcoder-based circuit analysis. Transcoders show strong potential as tools for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities tied to malicious model behaviours.

Abstract: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

</details>


### [213] [CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14800)
*Miguel Lopez-Duran,Julian Fierrez,Aythami Morales,Daniel DeAlcala,Gonzalo Mancera,Javier Irigoyen,Ruben Tolosana,Oscar Delgado,Francisco Jurado,Alvaro Ortigosa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrimeNER Demo is an AI platform that extracts crime-related information from documents using pretrained NER models with two-level entity granularity, supporting user-provided data fine-tuning for law enforcement and research applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To promote crime-related Named Entity Recognition (NER) research and provide a practical, accessible tool for researchers and law enforcement agencies to automatically extract crime information from documents.

Method: The platform offers: (i) pretrained NER models built on the CrimeNER database with two-level entity type granularity; (ii) fine-tuning capability allowing users to train models on their own annotated data for domain-specific cases; and (iii) an automatic pipeline that extracts and annotates crime entities from input documents.

Result: The demonstrator delivers a fully functional, publicly available platform on GitHub complete with pretrained crime-domain NER models, a fine-tuning interface, an automated extraction/annotation pipeline, a tutorial, and a video demonstration.

Conclusion: CrimeNER Demo successfully bridges the gap between crime-domain NER research and practical deployment, offering an extensible, user-friendly tool that lowers the barrier for both researchers and law enforcement to leverage NLP for crime information extraction.

Abstract: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

</details>


### [214] [Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14886)
*Chien-Liang Liu,Tsao-Lun Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAPTOR is a self-supervised pretraining method that injects reachability-aware inductive bias into RL agents for TKG reasoning, improving exploration efficiency by learning to estimate whether candidate actions can reach the target entity, thereby reducing unpromising path exploration and providing strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning suffer from sparse rewards and highly inefficient exploration due to the vast, time-evolving action space during training, which hinders both training efficiency and overall performance.

Method: Proposes RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining approach that trains the agent to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity. This injects a reachability-aware inductive bias, steering exploration away from unpromising paths and providing effective weight initialization for subsequent RL fine-tuning.

Result: Experiments on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets show RAPTOR markedly improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines.

Conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning, addressing key inefficiencies in exploration and reward sparsity.

Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

</details>


### [215] [Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14957)
*Besim Shala,Peter Mandl,Andreas Humpe,Martin Häusl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-based system for detecting online firestorms (rapid escalations of negative user content) on Reddit. It offers two modes: retrospective thread classification and early warning detection using sliding windows. The system estimates negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count, achieving strong classification and high-recall early detection with minimal comments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing firestorm detectors rely on volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features, which only indirectly capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads. The authors aim to leverage LLMs' contextual understanding to directly model the semantic dynamics of firestorms.

Method: An LLM-based detection system with two operating modes: (1) Global/retrospective mode: classifies complete Reddit threads by aggregating local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. (2) Early warning mode: processes threads sequentially, issuing alerts when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. The LLM estimates three indicators — negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. Evaluation is conducted on a balanced Reddit dataset.

Result: Global mode achieves strong classification performance on the balanced Reddit dataset. Early warning mode attains high recall and successfully detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors.

Conclusion: LLMs are effective not only for static judgment tasks but also as repeated estimators in context-aware, real-time monitoring of social media discourse, enabling practical early detection of online firestorms.

Abstract: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

</details>


### [216] [Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14970)
*Paul Darm,Cem Alpturk,Kenneth Ulrich,William Duncan,Ali Anwar,Annalisa Riccardi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes combining Implicit Function Theorem-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and LLM-driven narrative generation to produce fast, interpretable explanations for industrial process optimisation, achieving 40× speedup over KernelSHAP with equivalent accuracy on an HPGR control problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A trust gap exists between engineers who design optimisation algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. While SHAP has improved interpretability for ML predictions, optimisation outputs lack similarly effective explanation methods suitable for real-time industrial settings.

Method: The authors integrate three components: (1) IFT-based sensitivity analysis to derive exact parameter sensitivities ∂p*/∂x from Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions, (2) efficient GradientSHAP computation leveraging these analytical gradients, and (3) LLM-based narrative generation to translate attribution results into operator-friendly natural language explanations tailored for industrial control contexts.

Result: On an industrial HPGR control optimisation problem with 22 features, the IFT-GradientSHAP approach produces SHAP attributions with correlation >0.99 compared to KernelSHAP while achieving over 40× speedup, enabling real-time explanation generation.

Conclusion: IFT-based GradientSHAP provides a computationally efficient and accurate alternative to sampling-based SHAP methods for optimisation explainability. Combined with LLM narrative generation, the approach bridges the trust gap by delivering timely, interpretable explanations validated through domain expert feedback on industrial scenarios.

Abstract: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

</details>


### [217] [CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14975)
*Yuan Gao,Wenjun Yu,Jun Jiang,Yunfan Li,Xinyu Guo,Shugong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CFM-Bench is a unified benchmark for channel foundation models (CFMs) that standardizes multi-domain, multi-task evaluation across six diverse channel configurations, with strict data isolation rules to ensure fair comparison of CFM transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current CFM evaluations are fragmented: each uses different data, configurations, metrics, and adaptation procedures, making it impossible to fairly compare CFMs against each other or against task-specific baselines. Reported results only show pretraining benefits within isolated pipelines, not cross-model rankings.

Method: CFM-Bench curates six channel configurations (3GPP statistical, two ray-tracing, industrial/aerial measurements, vehicular multimodal simulation) with official data splits that isolate trajectories, sessions, links, realizations, or spatial regions. It enforces strict rules: no benchmark split for pretraining, training split only for fine-tuning, mandatory disclosure of all development data, and prohibition on using test units during training. Six task groups span PHY channel intelligence, RAN decision intelligence, and ISAC.

Result: The benchmark successfully provides a standardized substrate for comparing CFM representations across models, domains, and tasks, though this paper focuses on benchmark design rather than experimental results.

Conclusion: CFM-Bench establishes the first fair, reproducible evaluation framework for channel foundation models, enabling meaningful cross-model comparison and advancing CFM research toward standardized benchmarking practices.

Abstract: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

</details>


### [218] [Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14984)
*Mahmoud Ibrahim,Bart Elen,Chang Sun,Gokhan Ertaylan,Michel Dumontier*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Medical image classifier fairness audits suffer from insufficient minority subgroup samples. The paper proposes using a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator (fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1) to both mitigate training bias (via sequential pretraining with balanced synthetic data) and detect evaluation bias (by providing reliable per-subgroup performance estimates). On COVID-19 chest CT classification, synthetic pretraining outperforms joint augmentation and achieves full-real baseline performance at ~100× data efficiency. For evaluation, synthetic cohorts perfectly reproduce subgroup rankings (Spearman ρ=1.00) and provide reliable estimates where real test sets fail due to sample scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fairness audits of medical image classifiers are undermined by the sample-size problem in held-out test sets: minority subgroups have too few samples, yielding confidence intervals wider than the bias the audit seeks to detect. This renders per-subgroup performance evaluation unreliable. The authors aim to solve both sides of this problem — bias mitigation during training and bias detection during evaluation — using a single demographically-conditioned synthetic data generator.

Method: The authors fine-tune Stable Diffusion 2.1 end-to-end to generate demographically-conditioned chest CT images (conditioned on sex, race/ethnicity, and COVID-19 status). For bias mitigation, they compare two strategies: (1) joint augmentation (mixing real and synthetic data during training) and (2) sequential pretraining (pretraining on balanced synthetic data, then fine-tuning on real data). For bias detection, they use the generator to create five synthetic minority cohorts and compare subgroup performance estimates against a well-powered real-data oracle, evaluating ranking agreement via Spearman ρ and per-cell estimate reliability.

Result: For training: sequential pretraining + fine-tuning significantly outperforms joint augmentation under identical data constraints, and the resulting classifier matches full-real baseline performance at ~100× real-data efficiency. For evaluation: across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator achieves Spearman ρ=1.00 (on both MCC and Recall) against the real oracle for subgroup ranking and provides reliable per-cell estimates precisely where the small real test set runs out of samples.

Conclusion: A demographically-conditioned synthetic generator serves dual purpose: as a bias mitigation tool (via balanced pretraining) and as a bias measurement tool (via synthetic test cohorts). The synthetic approach is most valuable exactly in the low-sample minority cells that fairness audits target, offering both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias in medical image classification.

Abstract: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

</details>


### [219] [Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14998)
*Jean-Paul Van Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Rather than asking how humans should treat ASI, the paper inverses the question: how would a sentient ASI morally evaluate humanity? It proposes preliminary post-human moral principles that may govern ASI behavior and argues that design choices, human moral conduct, and the nature of humanity itself could determine our standing in a post-ASI world.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional AI ethics focuses on human responsibility toward AI systems (alignment, control, fair treatment). This paper identifies a neglected dimension: the moral gaze of a future sentient ASI directed back at humanity. As we design increasingly autonomous and possibly sentient systems, we are simultaneously shaping the initial conditions under which those systems will form moral judgments about us — a framing the authors consider urgent and underexplored.

Method: The paper employs a conceptual inversion methodology — reframing the standard human-to-AI ethical axis into an ASI-to-human evaluative axis. It then develops a preliminary normative framework: a set of "post-human moral principles" that a sentient ASI might adopt when evaluating human conduct and worth. The approach also identifies specific technical design choices (e.g., value initialization, goal architectures) that could causally influence ASI's eventual moral stance toward humanity.

Result: The analysis yields a proposed set of post-human moral principles for sentient ASI. It further concludes that three interlocking factors — technical design specifications, humanity's own moral track record, and the philosophical essence of human nature — jointly shape how favorably an ASI would regard and treat humans in the long run.

Conclusion: The moral standing of humanity in a post-ASI era is not fixed but partially malleable through present choices. Designers of intelligent systems bear a dual responsibility: ensuring alignment with human values, and also anticipating how their design decisions configure the moral lens through which future ASI may view its human creators.

Abstract: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

</details>


### [220] [SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15003)
*Riccardo Curcio,Toni Mancini,Enrico Tronci*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SMC-ES, a method that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking to synthesize control policies that come with formal probabilistic guarantees on safety, performance, and robustness, demonstrated on continuous control benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning-based controllers (e.g., Reinforcement Learning) for autonomous cyber-physical systems lack formal safety and robustness guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. There is a need for automated policy synthesis methods that deliver both competitive performance and provable certificates.

Method: The authors propose a simulation-based methodology combining Evolutionary Strategies (ES) for policy optimization with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) for verification. Given user-specified properties, a confidence parameter δ, and a failure probability ε, the method produces a policy with a certificate: with confidence ≥ 1−δ, the probability of property violation is ≤ ε. The algorithm, SMC-ES, iteratively evaluates and improves policies using SMC-based statistical verification during the ES optimization loop.

Result: Evaluated on Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium continuous control tasks, SMC-ES delivers formal guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness. It achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines, at the cost of a sustainable increase in computational overhead.

Conclusion: SMC-ES successfully bridges the gap between learning-based policy synthesis and formal verification, enabling safe deployment of autonomously synthesized controllers in safety-critical cyber-physical systems with statistically rigorous guarantees.

Abstract: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

</details>


### [221] [Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15027)
*Sofi Gjing Jovanovska,Kuntal Ghosh,Daniel Muhu Njenga,Ahmed Mufassir,Shadan Sadeghian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ArtSplit is a provotype that quantifies human vs. AI contributions in creative workflows to explore tensions around ownership. The study finds that measurement-based attribution fails to capture artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, challenging the reduction of a socially situated relationship into a technical problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI integration in creative work has sparked debates about ownership among artists and legal scholars, yet no consensus exists on how to attribute ownership when human and AI contributions are intertwined.
