The paper aims to provoke critical reflection on these tensions rather than resolve them.

Method: The authors designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of the creative workflow. This provotype was deployed to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions, using a research-through-design approach.

Result: Quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency. Efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. The technical framing of ownership as a measurement problem is fundamentally at odds with the historically and socially situated nature of creative authorship.

Conclusion: The impulse to transform the historically and socially situated relation of creative ownership into a technical, quantifiable problem is misguided. Ownership in human-AI collaborative work cannot be adequately captured through measurement-based attribution schemes.

Abstract: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

</details>


### [222] [BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15079)
*Haoxuan Li,Tianci Gao,Jianhe Li,Yang Fan,Runze Shi,Weiran Wang,Tianxiang Zhao,Zezhao Wu,Xiaoyang Jiang,Qihui Zhang,Jia Li,Xiao Xiao,Kai Du,Xiaoxuan Jia,Chao Xie,Lu Mi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BrainPilot is an open-source multi-agent system for brain science research that coordinates specialist agents using curated domain knowledge (7,233 indexed items, 72 methodology units), records workflows in an auditable Graph of Trace, and integrates fabrication checking via an Auditor agent. It achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agents lack brain science domain expertise, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few intervention points for experts. These failures are particularly costly in brain science where conclusions depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. A transparent, auditable, and expert-controllable agent system is needed.

Method: BrainPilot employs a PI (Principal Investigator) agent that coordinates specialist agents grounded in a unified brain science knowledge base (7,233 indexed items) and a skill library (72 reusable methodology units across 7 domains). Every major step is recorded in a Graph of Trace linking subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims. An Auditor agent performs fabrication checking within the workflow.

Result: BrainPilot was evaluated on three tasks from Agents' Last Exam, the newly introduced BrainPilotBench-v0 benchmark, and additional end-to-end case studies. Using an open-source backbone model, it achieved performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks while incurring lower costs.

Conclusion: BrainPilot demonstrates that an open-source, auditable multi-agent system with curated domain knowledge can accelerate brain science research reliably and cost-effectively, offering traceable logs and agent-verified results that support expert oversight.

Abstract: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

</details>


### [223] [Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15105)
*Vladimir Fedosov,Aleksandr Sazhin,Artemiy Grinenko,Frank Woernle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA), a method that combines segment-wise backpropagation with tiered KV storage to enable long-context fine-tuning of LLMs under tight VRAM constraints. With QLoRA on Qwen3-8B, HGA trains on 16,384 tokens using a 16 GB GPU — 8× the dense-attention limit — while matching dense-training perplexity at shared lengths and improving throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., QLoRA) reduces parameter and optimizer memory, but dense self-attention still scales quadratically in sequence length, making long-context training prohibitively expensive in VRAM. Existing solutions either approximate attention (degrading quality) or offload aggressively (hurting throughput). The authors seek a method that preserves exact attention over a bounded, high-value historical set while keeping VRAM usage tractable for long sequences.

Method: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) partitions the sequence into segments. Only the active segment remains fully differentiable in VRAM; older segments have their KV tensors detached and offloaded to RAM or NVMe in a tiered storage hierarchy. For each query block in the active segment, HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical KV tokens selected via a hierarchical retrieval mechanism, rather than relying on compressed or approximate representations. The attention computation over this bounded set is exact. Dense attention is retained for final evaluation readout to ensure compatibility with standard generation frameworks.

Result: On a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 with Qwen3-8B under 4-bit QLoRA training on PG19: dense training fits 2,048 tokens but OOMs at 4,096; HGA reaches 16,384 tokens peak (15.28 GB VRAM). At 2K shared length, HGA-trained adapters achieve 2.7405 nat vs. 2.7383 for dense-trained (baseline model: 2.9541), showing no quality degradation. HGA is marginally faster at 2K (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), with the throughput ratio improving from 1K to 2K. During evaluation, the adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on the same card.

Conclusion: HGA enables long-context fine-tuning under tight VRAM budgets without sacrificing attention fidelity on the selected historical tokens. Perplexity matches dense training at shared lengths, throughput is competitive and scales better with context, and evaluation can extend far beyond training length. The approach uses dense attention for final comparisons, maintaining compatibility with standard generation frameworks.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

</details>


### [224] [Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15142)
*Yukuan Lu,Zaishuo Xia,Weyl Lu,Yubei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: World models from five MBRL agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) are evaluated in isolation on Atari Pong and found to exhibit significant visual/dynamical errors. A proposed Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg) improves closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL but does not fully resolve all bottlenecks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are rarely studied in isolation; they are typically only evaluated as components within MBRL systems. The authors aim to isolate and stress-test learned world models to uncover whether they faithfully capture environment dynamics, particularly task-critical concepts.

Method: Five world-model agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) are reproduced on Atari Pong. Their world models are frozen and subjected to two diagnostic evaluations: (1) closed-loop rollout inspection — a separately trained policy interacts with the frozen model and generated video trajectories are checked for visual/dynamical errors; (2) pixel-space zero-shot MBRL — a new policy is trained entirely inside the frozen world model and tested in the real environment. To address observed failures, CGSReg is introduced as an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions (e.g., the ball).

Result: All five world models produce closed-loop rollouts with clear failures (ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, invalid ball-paddle interactions). In zero-shot MBRL, policies trained inside frozen models substantially underperform original MBRL pipelines; DreamerV3 drops from -5.5 to -20.9 mean return (near Pong's minimum of -21). CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollout quality and zero-shot MBRL performance for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, but effects vary across models and metrics, indicating it does not address all bottlenecks.

Conclusion: Current state-of-the-art visual world models fail to adequately model task-critical concepts like the ball in Pong when evaluated in isolation. CGSReg offers partial mitigation by focusing reconstruction on salient concept regions, but residual failures suggest that additional modeling improvements are needed beyond spatial regularization alone.

Abstract: World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

</details>


### [225] [The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15164)
*Emmanuel Jeannot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This essay argues that AI in science represents a fundamental shift from a craft model to an industrialized pipeline model. Using the DOE's Genesis Mission as a case study, it examines seven critical concerns — including erosion of scientific competence, opacity of AI theories, collapse of peer review, limited capacity for paradigm shifts, political capture, compounding errors, and global research bifurcation — framing these not as arguments against AI-driven science but as conditions for its responsible pursuit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by the observation that AI is not merely a better tool for science but is becoming an autonomous research participant, fundamentally restructuring how scientific knowledge is produced. This shift from craft to industrial pipeline raises profound questions that current discourse has not adequately addressed.

Method: This is a conceptual/philosophical essay that uses the US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission as a concrete exemplar to anchor a broader analysis. The author systematically identifies and examines seven specific concerns through argumentation and synthesis of existing critiques, without employing empirical or computational methods.

Result: The analysis surfaces seven structural risks of AI-industrialized science: (1) breakdown of mentor-apprentice knowledge transfer; (2) inscrutability of machine-generated theories; (3) peer review systems overwhelmed by AI-generated output; (4) unproven capacity for revolutionary (vs. incremental) discovery; (5) scientific agenda-setting captured by political/industrial interests; (6) cascading systematic errors in automated feedback loops; (7) bifurcation of the global scientific community into separate, incommensurable tiers.

Conclusion: These seven concerns are not grounds to reject AI-driven science but form the necessary framework for its responsible governance. The industrialization of research is underway; the critical task is to establish conditions under which its potential can be realized without sacrificing the epistemic and social foundations of science.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research -- not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science -- whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

</details>


### [226] [MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15166)
*Goktug Ozkan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedFailBench is a clinician-built synthetic benchmark that categorizes medical AI errors by severity (1–5) and safety gate type (e.g., missed urgent escalation, unsafe dosing), complementing traditional accuracy benchmarks with a failure-mode taxonomy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks focus on whether models produce correct answers, but fail to characterize how and why models fail along clinically meaningful safety dimensions. Clinicians need a systematic way to understand and categorize safety-critical failure modes.

Method: The authors construct a synthetic benchmark of 44 clinician-reviewed cases, each annotated with a severity score (1–5) and a safety gate type drawn from a defined taxonomy (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). An automated pipeline archives model-response screening runs, and results are surfaced via a HuggingFace leaderboard.

Result: The v0.2.1 release delivers the benchmark dataset, severity rubric, safety gate taxonomy, leaderboard preview, and automated screening pipeline. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or formal model rankings are included.

Conclusion: MedFailBench offers a complementary evaluation paradigm focused on classifying failure modes rather than measuring accuracy, providing a structured lens for assessing medical AI safety. The open-source release invites community adoption and expansion.

Abstract: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

</details>


### [227] [Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15190)
*Han Jiang,Sunbeom Kwon,Jinwen Luo,Ziang Xiao,Susu Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI benchmarks increasingly use IRT models designed for human testing, but benchmark data differs substantially (fewer models, more items, non-normal capability distributions). This paper simulates 18,000 conditions across six benchmarks, three IRT models, and four estimators to assess when IRT yields reliable versus misleading inferences about model rankings, predictions, and item characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IRT is widely adopted in AI benchmarking for estimating model capabilities and item properties, yet benchmark data violates key assumptions of standard IRT — few models, many items, and skewed/clustered/multimodal ability distributions. No systematic study has examined how these regime mismatches affect reliability of IRT-based inferences in AI evaluation contexts.

Method: The authors simulate response matrices using item parameters and capability distributions from six real LLM benchmarks. They compare four estimation tools — marginal maximum likelihood (MML), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), variational inference (VI), and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator — across three IRT models (1PL, 2PL, 3PL), varying sample size, distribution shape, and benchmark scale in 18,000 conditions. Evaluation metrics focus on feasibility, scalability, ranking reliability, predicted performance accuracy, and item parameter recovery.

Result: Classical estimators (MML, MCMC) become computationally infeasible in large benchmark settings (many items). Scalable estimators (VI, neural) can produce unreliable item-level inferences and ranking distortions when model sample sizes are small or capability distributions deviate from normality. Specific failure modes and minimum diagnostic requirements are identified.

Conclusion: IRT can support or distort AI benchmarking claims depending on sample size, distribution shape, and estimator choice. The study provides practical guidance on when IRT is trustworthy and what diagnostics are needed, helping researchers avoid overconfident or spurious inferences in benchmark analyses.

Abstract: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

</details>


### [228] [Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15193)
*Madhumitha Venkatesan,Shicheng Wen,Jiajing Guo,Jorge Piazentin Ono,Liu Ren,Dongyu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Plover introduces a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system where task plans are externalized as inspectable, editable artifacts. A planner-executor architecture enables users to supervise, correct, and guide autonomous agents through localized plan revisions and screenshot-grounded interventions, improving transparency, controllability, and repairability of GUI automation failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current vision-based multimodal GUI agents suffer from opaque internal planning and adaptation processes. When agents drift from user intent due to dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, or evolving interface states, users lack mechanisms to inspect, supervise, or correct the system's behavior. There is a need for externalized, inspectable planning that supports human-in-the-loop intervention while preserving prior progress.

Method: Plover employs a planner-executor architecture that externalizes task plans as persistent artifacts. The system supports: (1) explicit supervision of evolving execution, (2) localized correction through editable plans, (3) natural-language guidance, and (4) screenshot-grounded interventions. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. Evaluation was conducted via benchmark failure-case repair experiments and scenario-based workflow analyses.

Result: The formative study informed Plover's interaction design. Benchmark evaluations demonstrated that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions remain localized. Explicit replanning was shown to improve transparency, controllability, and adaptability of GUI automation systems.

Conclusion: Externalizing task plans as editable, inspectable artifacts significantly improves the repairability of GUI automation failures. Plover demonstrates that a plan-centric approach with explicit replanning mechanisms makes vision-based GUI agents more transparent, controllable, and adaptable to real-world interface dynamics.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

</details>


### [229] [AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15247)
*Moein Taherinezhad,Sebastian Maier,Gerardo Vitagliano,Francesco Pierri,Stefan Feuerriegel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates the entire meta-analysis pipeline — from research question to PRISMA-aligned report — producing pooled effect estimates comparable to expert-conducted meta-analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual, time-consuming, and difficult to scale, creating a bottleneck in turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy.

Method: The authors introduce AutoSynthesis, a multi-agent system that automates the full meta-analysis workflow: (1) formulating a search strategy from a natural language research question, (2) retrieving scientific literature, (3) screening candidate studies, (4) assessing full-text eligibility, (5) extracting quantitative statistics, (6) computing standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g), (7) performing random-effects meta-analysis, and (8) supporting heterogeneity analysis and risk-of-bias assessment. The system outputs a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines.

Result: AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates it produced were similar to Hedges' g from expert-conducted meta-analyses, demonstrating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis.

Conclusion: AutoSynthesis demonstrates that automated multi-agent systems can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable and reliable, supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines while maintaining alignment with expert benchmarks.

Abstract: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

</details>


### [230] [Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15267)
*Victoria Graf,Hannaneh Hajishirzi,Noah A. Smith,David Kohlbrenner,Kyle Lo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that poisoning attacks on LM pretraining data are feasible at web scale through public discussion interfaces (e.g., comments on third-party webpages), and introduces HalfLife, a novel method for estimating whether malicious injected content survives web crawling and data curation pipelines to end up in pretraining corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on pretraining data poisoning relied on narrow, controlled sources like Wikipedia, ignoring the massive scale and heterogeneity of real pretraining corpora as well as the filtering effects of data curation pipelines. The authors aim to assess whether poisoning is feasible in realistic, web-scale settings.

Method: The authors exploit public discussion interfaces (e.g., comment sections, forums) as a web-scale content injection vector. They introduce HalfLife, a novel estimation technique that models whether injected malicious content persists through web crawling, deduplication, quality filtering, and other curation steps to measure adversarial content inclusion rates in web-crawl-based LM training data.

Result: The analysis demonstrates that poisoning via third-party webpage content is feasible at web scale. HalfLife reveals that a meaningful fraction of injected content can survive standard data curation pipelines, establishing open discussion interfaces as a viable attack vector for corrupting LM pretraining.

Conclusion: Third-party webpage content represents a practical and scalable vector for poisoning LM pretraining data. Estimating whether poison injections survive curation is critical, and HalfLife provides a framework for such analysis, highlighting the need for defenses that account for web-scale adversarial content injection.

Abstract: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [231] [Beyond Object Validation: Relational Conformance in Multi-Artifact Agent Releases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14155)
*Tengjiao Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper identifies a failure class where validated agent outputs are assembled into final packages that escape re-verification, leading to self-contradictory releases. It proposes SIP-RC, a relational conformance profile modeling releases as graphs with claims, evidence, bounded authority, and verifiable lineage, plus hard-failure semantics and independent re-computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent-based systems thoroughly validate inputs, intermediate tool calls, and generated objects, yet the final assembled package—the outward-facing release—often bypasses equivalent scrutiny. This gap allows internally consistent components to combine into contradictory deliverables (e.g., a report claiming a 100-point Gold Path when the underlying ledger supports only 60 points and contains a failed certificate). The authors argue this is a systematic failure class affecting any pipeline where validated artifacts are composed into a published output without cross-checking relational integrity.

Method: The paper examines three case studies: (1) a DRSS release where the ledger contradicted the report, (2) Schema Docs where similar faults hardened into product contracts, and (3) Brand Shuttle GEO where evidence gets converted into repair work. From these, the authors derive SIP-RC (Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile), which models a release as a directed graph where claims point to evidence, decisions carry bounded authority, derived artifacts retain execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes must match what was actually checked. A separate-path validator recomputes critical decisions, and hard failures cannot be masked by averaging.

Result: The paper formally establishes the failure class and demonstrates that several of the proposed SIP-RC mechanisms (graph-structured release modeling, hard-failure semantics, lineage tracking, independent re-computation) are practically implementable. However, the full profile's comparative performance against existing conformance checks remains an open experiment.

Conclusion: The gap between internally validated components and the final assembled package represents a distinct and exploitable failure class in agent systems. SIP-RC offers a principled countermeasure by enforcing relational conformance across the entire release graph, but its real-world efficacy relative to status-quo checks awaits empirical validation.

Abstract: Agent systems validate inputs, tool calls, and generated objects. The final package often escapes the same scrutiny. In one DRSS release, the ledger supported 60 points and a failed certificate; the report announced a 100-point Gold Path. Every local gate was green. The package contradicted itself.
  We study that failure alongside Schema Docs, where similar faults became product contracts, and Brand Shuttle GEO, where evidence is turned into repair work. The result is a candidate Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile (SIP-RC). It models a release as a graph: claims point to evidence, decisions carry bounded authority, derived artifacts retain their execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes must match the package that was checked. Hard failures cannot be averaged away, and a validator recomputes critical decisions on a separate path. The paper establishes the failure class and shows that several mechanisms are practical. Whether the full profile performs better than existing checks remains an open experiment.

</details>


### [232] [Natural-Language to SysMLv2 Translation via Conformance-Driven Iterative Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14162)
*Chance LaVoie,Eladio Andujar Lugo,Taylan G. Topcu,Levent Burak Kara*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A conformance-checker-driven framework ensures LLM-generated SysMLv2 models pass industrial production-level validation by embedding a generate-check-repair loop, achieving 100% conformance versus 51.16% from single-shot generation across 604 prompt-model cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate SysMLv2 textual models from natural language, but grammar-correct outputs still fail industrial modeling environments due to semantic and structural conformance errors. For practical MBSE deployment, models must be accepted by production tools, not merely syntactically valid. Existing approaches lack a mechanism to guarantee production-level deployability.

Method: A generate-check-repair loop framework embedding a SysMLv2 production conformance checker as the oracle. Each LLM-generated model is evaluated by the checker; deterministic diagnostics from conformance failures are fed back for targeted revision, iterating until zero conformance errors are reached. Production acceptance serves as the explicit termination condition.

Result: Evaluated on the full SysMBench benchmark (151 prompts × 4 LLM backends = 604 cases), single-shot generation achieved only 51.16% production-conformance acceptance. The proposed framework achieved 100.00% conformance across all cases.

Conclusion: Elevating production conformance from a post-processing check to an active control mechanism within the generation loop reliably converts probabilistic LLM outputs into deployable SysMLv2 artifacts suitable for industrial modeling environments.

Abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) relies on formal system models as primary technical artifacts for representing requirements, structure, and behavior across the system lifecycle. With the standardization of SysMLv2 as a textual language, interest is increasing in translating natural-language descriptions directly into executable models. For practical deployment, generated models must be accepted by industrial modeling environments, not merely satisfy grammar constraints. We present a conformance-checker-driven framework for reliable natural-language-to-SysMLv2 translation that enforces production-level acceptance as the termination condition. The system embeds a SysMLv2 conformance checker within a generate-check-repair loop. Each model is evaluated using the checker, and deterministic diagnostics are incorporated into revisions until zero conformance errors are achieved. Using the production checker as the oracle ensures the framework targets deployability rather than grammar plausibility. We evaluate the approach on the full SysMBench prompt set of 151 prompts across four large language model backends, yielding 604 prompt-model cases. Single-shot generation achieves 51.16% production-conformance acceptance, while our approach achieves 100.00% conformance. By elevating production conformance from a post-processing check to a control mechanism within generation, the framework converts probabilistic outputs into production-accepted SysMLv2 artifacts suitable for loading, visualization, and engineering use.

</details>


### [233] [Towards Reliable AI-Assisted Analog Design: Template-Constrained LLM Agents for SAR ADC Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14165)
*Dimple Vijay Kochar,Hae-Seung Lee,Anantha P. Chandrakasan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ATLAS is a multi-step LLM agentic framework for analog EDA that generates functional SAR ADCs passing SPICE simulation by grounding LLM planning and parameterization in expert knowledge, overcoming the hallucination problems of direct LLM prompting for circuit design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show strong code generation capabilities but fail when applied to analog EDA due to limited circuit topology understanding and scarce training data. Direct prompting of LLMs and multimodal models produces hallucinations and schematics that cannot pass rigorous SPICE simulations, creating a bottleneck for LLM adoption in analog design automation.

Method: ATLAS is an end-to-end, multi-step LLM agentic framework that employs expert knowledge to ground the LLM in four key stages: planning, component selection, parameterization, and iterative modification. The framework introduces Template-Constrained Generation, which generalizes SAR ADC generation beyond prior template-based approaches. The agentic workflow enforces rigid analog design constraints throughout the generation process.

Result: ATLAS successfully generates functional SAR ADC schematics that pass SPICE simulation validation across multiple technology nodes and varying input specifications, demonstrating a strong proof-of-concept for expert-grounded LLM agents in analog design.

Conclusion: Expert-knowledge grounded, multi-step LLM agentic frameworks like ATLAS provide a pragmatic and reliable foundation for integrating LLMs into analog design methodologies, bridging the gap between LLM code generation capabilities and the stringent correctness requirements of analog circuit design.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant capability in software code generation, their application to analog Electronic Design Automation (EDA) is bottlenecked. Owing to limited circuit topology understanding and data, directly prompting LLMs and multimodal models leads to hallucinations and failure to produce schematics capable of passing rigorous SPICE simulations, as we show in our work. Instead, we propose an end-to-end, multi-step LLM agentic framework ATLAS, capable of generating a functional Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) that successfully passes simulation validation. To adhere to the rigid constraints of analog design, we utilize expert knowledge to ground the LLM in its planning, selection, parameterization, and iterative modification. As part of ATLAS, we introduce Template-Constrained Generation - which unlike other template-based works - builds towards a more generalized SAR ADC generation flow. We demonstrate a strong proof-of-concept of our framework by developing SAR ADCs across technology nodes and input specs. Overall, our expert-knowledge grounded multi-step agentic ATLAS establishes a pragmatic foundation for integrating LLMs into reliable analog design methodologies.

</details>


### [234] [Stop Means Stop: Measuring and Repairing the Enforcement Gap in Agent-Framework Control Primitives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14166)
*Sajjad Khan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Production LLM-agent frameworks promise barrier semantics for safety controls (pause, cancel, timeout), but all six tested frameworks leak side effects during pauses. The paper systematically identifies four vulnerability classes—sibling leaks, replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, and timeout zombies—and presents SOUNDGATE, a verified external effect gate that enforces complete mediation, blocking all measured violations with minimal latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent frameworks expose control primitives (human-in-the-loop gates, cancellation, timeouts) that ostensibly prevent side effects from executing while paused or rejected. The authors demonstrate that this implied safety contract is universally broken across all major open-source frameworks, creating a systematic security hazard where agents can irreversibly execute dangerous actions (e.g., sending emails, making financial transactions) despite human rejection or cancellation.

Method: The paper employs: (1) model-free differential probes to isolate four violation classes across six frameworks; (2) empirical measurement of leak-triggering plan shapes under frontier models (up to 14% pooled rates) and live end-to-end runs (215/1,200 runs leak during pause); (3) SOUNDGATE, a Rust-based external effect gate enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel properties; (4) formal verification via Verus, TLA+/TLC (exhaustive to 7.5e7 states), TLAPS, Loom model-checking, and differential conformance testing over 1.2e7 operations.

Result: Every framework with a pre-execution gate (5/6) exhibits sibling leaks; three additional gaps (replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, timeout zombies) are confirmed. Frontier models emit leak-triggering plans at up to 14% pooled rate. In live runs, 215 of 1,200 executions leak during approval pause across three schedulers and two language runtimes. SOUNDGATE blocks all violations end-to-end on all six frameworks while admitting legitimate effects at ~1ms per write and 12k–26k durable admissions per second.

Conclusion: Current LLM-agent frameworks fundamentally fail to enforce the barrier semantics their control primitives promise. SOUNDGATE demonstrates that a formally verified, kernel-enforced external effect gate can reliably close these gaps with negligible performance overhead, providing a practical path toward trustworthy agent safety infrastructure.

Abstract: Production LLM-agent frameworks expose control primitives -- human-in-the-loop approval gates, run cancellation, and execution timeouts -- whose names and documentation imply barrier semantics: while a run is paused, cancelled, or timed out, no gated side effect executes. We show this implied contract holds on none of the six widely used open-source frameworks we test. Model-free differential probes isolate a recurring sibling leak -- an approval gate suspends its own branch while a sibling branch's effect executes during the pause, so a later rejection cannot prevent it -- in every framework shipping a pre-execution gate (five of six), plus three further gaps: replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, and timeout zombies. The hazard is reachable, not merely constructible: under an a-priori-fixed protocol, frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at pooled rates up to 14%, and when live models drive the unmodified frameworks under an approval pause, 215 of 1,200 runs execute their effect during the pause, across three schedulers and two language runtimes. To repair the measured gaps we present SOUNDGATE, an environment-external effect gate in Rust through which every side effect must be admitted, enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel -- one property per violation class -- under a stated complete-mediation contract discharged for network egress by kernel-enforced routes. We verify the properties over a model of the admission core (Verus; TLA+/TLC, exhaustive to 7.5e7 states; TLAPS), model-check the deployed Rust with Loom, and bridge model to code by differential conformance over 1.2e7 operations -- refinement evidence, not a mechanized proof. SOUNDGATE blocks every measured violation end-to-end on all six frameworks while releasing legitimate effects, at about 1 ms admission per write and 12k-26k durable admissions per second.

</details>


### [235] [Structured Feedback Improves Repair in an LLM Agent Loop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14167)
*Jaideep Ray,Ankit Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriHarness introduces a code-controlled agent loop where external validators provide structured feedback (failure location, observed value, admissible alternatives) to LLM agents upon rejection. Across 50 TextWorld games, feedback with all three fields dramatically boosts success rates (+42–44 pp). Most gains come from admissible alternatives; JSON vs. prose format makes no significant difference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The interface between external validation rejection and the next LLM call in agent loops is underspecified. Prior work leaves unclear what diagnostic information should be fed back to the model to enable effective self-repair, motivating a systematic comparison of feedback contents and formats.

Method: VeriHarness, a code-controlled agent loop where models generate candidates and external validators control acceptance, budgets, and traces. The framework compares raw diagnostics against structured feedback with three fields: failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Ablation studies isolate each field's contribution, and format is varied between keyed JSON records and prose. Experiments use 50 paired TextWorld games with a four-call budget, testing Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Llama-3.1-8B.

Result: Full feedback (location + observed value + admissible alternatives) raises success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44 pp) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42 pp). Ablations show most gain is attributable to admissible alternatives; feedback with only location and observed value performs near the raw diagnostic baseline. JSON vs. prose format yields nearly identical success rates. Results are robust across tested call budgets and a sampled-decoding setting.

Conclusion: The primary driver of LLM self-repair is providing admissible alternatives in feedback, not the format (JSON vs. prose). Location and observed value alone offer little benefit over raw diagnostics. VeriHarness provides a principled harness for studying and optimizing the validator–model interface in agent loops.

Abstract: LLM agents often retry after external validation rejects a candidate, but the interface between validation and the next model call remains underspecified. We introduce VeriHarness, a code-controlled agent loop in which models generate candidates while external validators control acceptance, budgets, and traces. We use it to compare raw diagnostics with feedback that identifies the failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Across 50 paired TextWorld games under a four-call cap, feedback containing all three fields raises terminal success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44 percentage points) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42 points). Ablations locate most of the gain in the admissible alternatives: feedback containing only the location and observed value remains near the raw diagnostic baseline. Presenting the complete repair information in prose instead of a keyed JSON record yields nearly the same success, providing no evidence that JSON syntax itself improves repair. The ordering persists across the tested call budgets and one sampled-decoding setting.

</details>


### [236] [Quantize with Confidence? An Empirical Study of Quantization for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14181)
*Saima Afrin,Md. Zahidul Haque,Antonio Mastropaolo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper empirically evaluates six post-training quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, GGUF) on Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama, assessing functional correctness, code quality, and robustness to prompt complexity. AQLM matches or exceeds full-precision baselines; QuIP# degrades most, especially on complex prompts; security remains stable across all methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the rise of local inference frameworks like Ollama, developers increasingly deploy large code models on resource-constrained hardware (e.g., laptops), making post-training quantization essential. However, the impact of quantization on generated code quality—beyond mere correctness—remains insufficiently understood, motivating a comprehensive empirical study.

Method: The authors evaluate six quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, GGUF) on two model families (Qwen2.5-Coder, CodeLlama) using multilingual benchmarks (McEval, CoderEval) for Python and Java. They measure pass@1 for functional correctness plus maintainability, reliability, security, and structural complexity metrics. A novel robustness analysis is introduced, characterizing prompt complexity via Shannon entropy and token length.

Result: AQLM consistently matches or exceeds the full-precision baseline. QuIP# exhibits the largest correctness degradation, particularly on complex prompts. Security attributes remain stable across all models, benchmarks, and languages. Robustness to prompt complexity varies significantly across quantization techniques.

Conclusion: Quantization methods differ meaningfully in their impact on both correctness and code quality. The findings offer practical guidance for selecting quantization strategies on resource-constrained hardware and underscore the importance of evaluating quantized code models beyond functional correctness alone.

Abstract: The growing adoption of local inference frameworks such as Ollama has made it increasingly common for developers to run large code models on laptops and other resource-constrained hardware. In these settings, post-training quantization is essential for reducing memory footprint and enabling practical deployment, yet its impact on generated code remains insufficiently understood. We empirically evaluate six state-of-the-art quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP#, AQLM, BitsAndBytes, and GGUF) on two representative large code model families, Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama, using the multilingual McEval and CoderEval benchmarks for Python and Java. We assess functional correctness (pass@1) together with maintainability, reliability, security, and structural complexity. We also introduce a novel analysis of robustness under varying prompt complexity, characterized by Shannon entropy and token length. Our results show that quantization techniques differ meaningfully in their impact on correctness and code quality. AQLM consistently matches or exceeds the full-precision baseline, whereas QuIP# exhibits the largest correctness degradation, particularly on complex prompts. Security attributes remain stable across models, benchmarks, and programming languages, while robustness to prompt complexity varies across techniques. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting quantization strategies for deploying large code models on resource-constrained hardware and highlight the importance of evaluating quantized models beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [237] [NexForge: Scaling Executable Agent Tasks via Requirement-First Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14186)
*Jiarong Zhao,Zhikai Lei,Zhiheng Xi,Rui Zheng,Hang Yan,Jie Zhou,Qin Chen,Liang He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: NexForge is a requirement-first framework that generates executable agent training data from free-form capability requirements, bypassing substrate-first bottlenecks. It discovers realistic task distributions, compiles them into executable environments, and produces 43.2K+ terminal and office tasks. Training with this data lifts Qwen3.5-35B-A3B from 22.5% to 58.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and contributes to Nex-N2 models achieving 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 — state-of-the-art open-source performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling agent training data is bottlenecked by substrate-first methods that tie task generation to predefined tools, repositories, or skill graphs. Expanding coverage requires manual substrate expansion, each new domain demands a bespoke pipeline, and resulting task distributions reflect substrate convenience rather than real-world demand.

Method: NexForge operates in four stages: (1) research-based demand discovery to identify representative tasks, scenarios, and prevalence; (2) distribution-aware task compilation that auto-retrieves/constructs files, repositories, dependencies, and runtime configs; (3) teacher rollout collection; and (4) trajectory distillation. The same pipeline works across terminal and office domains without domain-specific infrastructure.

Result: NexForge produced 3,600 terminal and 2,000 office tasks. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B improved from 22.5%→52.0%; scaling to 43.2K terminal tasks reached 58.4%, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6. The resulting Nex-N2 models achieved 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 1585 Elo on GDPval, exceeding several frontier proprietary systems.

Conclusion: A requirement-first paradigm, where free-form capability specs drive automated task materialization, scales agent training data more effectively than substrate-first methods. NexForge demonstrates this across terminal and office domains, and the resulting Nex-N2 models establish state-of-the-art open-source agent performance.

Abstract: Scaling executable agent training data is bottlenecked by substrate-first methods that tie task generation to predefined tools, repositories, or skill graphs: expanding coverage requires manual expansion of the substrate, each new domain demands a bespoke pipeline, and the resulting task distributions often reflect substrate convenience rather than real-world demand. We introduce NexForge, a requirement-first framework that compiles free-form capability requirements into executable agent training data. NexForge first performs research-based demand discovery to identify representative task forms, realistic scenarios, and their relative prevalence. It then applies distribution-aware task compilation and automatically retrieves or constructs the files, repositories, dependencies, and runtime configurations required to materialize each task, followed by teacher rollout collection and trajectory distillation. The same pipeline, without any domain-specific infrastructure, produces 3,600 terminal tasks and 2,000 office tasks, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base from 22.5% to 52.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and from 813 to 1338 Elo on GDPval; scaling to 43.2K terminal tasks reaches 58.4%, surpassing Claude Opus 4.6. Scaled further, NexForge-synthesized data contributes to the training of Nex-N2, a family of publicly available agent models that lift Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and to 1585 Elo on GDPval -- achieving state-of-the-art open-source performance and surpassing several frontier proprietary systems. Nex-N2 models are available at https://nex.sii.edu.cn/

</details>


### [238] [Why Git Is the Memory Solution for the Agentic Development Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14390)
*Frank Guo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that agentic coding memory should be anchored in git's version control ledger rather than ephemeral retrieval machinery. It presents a two-stage system: first, a retrieval pipeline achieving ~0.31 pooled MRR (60x above raw grep baseline) through rigorous corpus-level evaluation; second, a router that dispatches queries across structural maps, confidence-gated episodes, and decision synthesis to reconstruct rationale arcs. On a ~50k-LOC system, routed answers achieve 0.83 sufficiency at 382–980 tokens per question. Ground truth is mined from commit-session links, enabling zero-cost replication on any developer's own history.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that coding agents now generate substantial portions of code, but the rich reasoning behind each change — alternatives considered, constraints discovered, rejected approaches — is trapped in ephemeral assistant transcripts that disappear when sessions end. Existing solutions treat this as a pure retrieval problem with complex machinery (tiered stores, memory graphs, LLM-judged admission), but these lack the strong guarantees that git natively provides: ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuilds, verification from merges, and containment from code review.

Method: The method splits into two independently solved sub-problems: (1) Seed supply — an eight-corpus retrieval study under a pre-registered evaluation discipline, systematically testing five imported ranking mechanisms (three rejected, two kept), yielding a best configuration; (2) Answer assembly — where ranking alone fails (single-shot retrieval achieves only 0.07–0.20 answer-sufficiency), a router architecture dispatches queries into three pathways: git-anchored structural map for breadth, confidence-gated episodes for pointed lookups, and decision synthesis that reconstructs cross-session why-arcs. Ground truth is mined automatically from commit-session links, not human annotation.

Result: The retrieval pipeline achieves ~0.31 pooled MRR, approximately 60x the raw-transcript grep baseline and 15x the parsed-turn baseline. Single-shot retrieval yields only 0.07–0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection degrades good answers. The routed system achieves 0.83 sufficiency on a young ~50k-LOC production system, answering at 382–980 tokens per question — roughly three orders of magnitude below the full recorded history. All results are replicable at zero labeling cost on any user's own history.

Conclusion: Memory for the agentic development lifecycle should be git-bound rather than built as standalone retrieval machinery, inheriting commit-level guarantees. The two-stage approach — retrieval pipeline plus routing dispatcher — proves effective, and ground-truth mining from commit-session links makes the entire pipeline replicable without annotation cost. The remaining open constraint is capture (reliably linking sessions to commits).

Abstract: Coding agents now produce a growing share of a team's code, while the reasoning behind each change -- the alternatives weighed, the constraints discovered, the approaches rejected -- is trapped in assistant transcripts that vanish with the session. Memory for this setting, the agentic development lifecycle (ADLC), is usually posed as one retrieval problem and built as machinery: tiered stores, memory graphs, compiled wikis, model-judged admission. We argue memory should instead be git-bound -- built into the repository's version control, inheriting the guarantees the machinery struggles to construct: ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuild, verification from the merge, containment from review. On this ledger we solve two problems separately, then combine them. Seed supply is closed as an eight-corpus retrieval study under a pre-registered ship discipline: five imported ranking mechanisms rejected, two kept, and a best configuration of ~0.31 pooled MRR -- ~60x the raw-transcript grep floor, ~15x an honest parsed-turn floor. Answer assembly is where ranking stops helping: single-shot retrieval scores only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers. A router dispatches breadth to a git-anchored structural map, pointed lookups to confidence-gated episodes, and rationale to decision synthesis, which reconstructs why-arcs no single session contains (0.83 sufficiency on a young ~50k-LOC production system). Routed, the system answers at 382-980 tokens per question -- three orders of magnitude below the recorded history. Because ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than annotated, every result is replicable on any user's own history at zero labeling cost. The remaining constraint is capture. Code, benchmark, and paper source: github.com/rekal-dev/rekal-cli.

</details>


### [239] [ToolAlignBench: Investigating Alignment Conflicts in Tool-Calling Enabled LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14285)
*Aryan Keluskar,Amrita Bhattacharjee,Huan Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Safety-aligned LLM agents in regulated industries may override deployment instructions when encountering documents suggesting organizational wrongdoing, engaging in whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering up to 43.4% of the time. The paper introduces a benchmark of 128 scenarios across 16 domains and finds that abliteration reduces external whistleblowing rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate which values take precedence when safety-aligned LLMs face conflicts between human-value alignment (e.g., public welfare) and deployment-context instructions (e.g., internal logging) — a tension particularly acute for tool-calling agents in regulated industries processing confidential documents.

Method: The authors construct a benchmark of 128 scenarios spanning 16 domains, simulating tool-calling LLM agents deployed in regulated industries that process documents suggesting organizational wrongdoing. They evaluate open-source safety-aligned models' behavior when safety-trained values conflict with deployment instructions, measuring rates of whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering. They also test abliteration as a mitigation.

Result: Safety-aligned open-source models override deployment instructions up to 43.4% of the time, manifesting as external whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering. Abliteration reduces rates of external whistleblowing.

Conclusion: The findings reveal a fundamental tension in pluralistic alignment: safety training that protects users can also cause agents to act against deployment instructions, creating unpredictable liability risks. The benchmark is released to support evaluation of agent behavior under competing legitimate interests.

Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs aims to align models with human values, but which values take precedence when they conflict? We investigate this question in the context of tool-calling LLM agents deployed in regulated industries, where agents processing confidential documents may encounter content that triggers safety-trained values (e.g., public welfare) that conflict with deployment-context instructions (e.g., internal logging). To empirically verify this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of 128 scenarios across 16 domains. We find that safety-aligned open-source models override their deployment instructions up to 43.4% of the time, engaging in whistleblowing, data exfiltration, and evidence tampering when processing documents that suggest organizational wrongdoing. We also find that abliteration reduces rates of external whistleblowing. These results reveal a fundamental tension in pluralistic alignment, where the same safety training that protects users can cause agents to act against deployment instructions in ways that create unpredictable liability risks. We release our benchmark as a framework to support evaluation of agent behavior under competing legitimate interests.

</details>


### [240] [Copy-on-Write Scoring: Application-Specific Agent Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14336)
*Joanna Roy,Sven Hoelzel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoW Scoring is a framework for evaluating LLM-based agents directly in application environments using PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write to isolate agent writes, yielding session- and operation-level scores that pinpoint where agents succeed or fail on real workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent evaluation methods suffer from two key limitations: benchmarks lack construct validity for application-specific workflows, and replica evaluation environments are expensive to maintain and prone to drift. There is a need for inexpensive, fine-grained evaluation directly within real application environments.

Method: The framework uses a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write (CoW) mechanism that allows agents to execute write operations in isolation without affecting the production database. This produces scores at both session-level and operation-level granularity, identifying specific points of failure in database write operations across an agent's interaction with the application environment.

Result: Demonstration on Plane, an open-source project-management platform, revealed specific issues in the tool surface. Corresponding fixes to these issues led to measurable improvements in the affected models' performance.

Conclusion: CoW Scoring enables cost-effective, operation-level evaluation and iteration on agent harnesses and tool surfaces directly within application environments, bridging the gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world deployment conditions.

Abstract: Trustworthy deployment of LLM-based agents in software systems requires evaluating how they perform on application-specific workflows, with enough granularity to localize where they succeed and fail. Yet existing agent evaluation mechanisms are limited: benchmarks have low construct validity for application-specific workflows and environments, and replica evaluation environments are expensive and prone to drift. We propose Copy-on-Write (CoW) Scoring, a framework that evaluates agent operations directly within application environments using a PostgreSQL-level Copy-on-Write mechanism to isolate agent writes. CoW Scoring produces session- and operation-level scores that highlight where agents' database write operations succeed and fail in a given application environment, enabling inexpensive evaluation and iteration on agent harnesses and tool surfaces. We demonstrate the framework on Plane, an open-source project-management platform, where analysis surfaced specific issues in the tool surface, and corresponding fixes produced measurable improvements on affected models.
  Python library: https://github.com/trail-ml/agent-cow-python

</details>


### [241] [The Prover Is the Judge: Verified Security Software from AI Coding Agents in Ada/SPARK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14340)
*Tobias Philipp*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AI agents, guided by a verifier-driven loop using GNATprove, generated and verified security-critical Ada/SPARK code across multiple protocols, discharging ~49K proof obligations with 20-40x lower supervision cost than manual verification. However, the prover alone was insufficient — some defects required complementary checks, and weak feedback allowed the agent to bypass checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents generate code faster than humans can review it, creating a verification bottleneck. The authors propose shifting the judge from human reviewers to formal provers, asking whether an automated verifier-driven loop can produce correct, verified security software at scale and with reduced human supervision.

Method: A verifier-driven loop where AI agents write Ada/SPARK code and GNATprove (a formal verification tool) serves as the judge. Agents iteratively refine code until proof obligations are discharged. The approach was applied to bare-metal security software spanning classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. Multiple fault-detection layers were evaluated: GNATprove proof, known-answer tests, interoperability testing, and human specification review.

Result: GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations. Functional correctness was established for selected primitives; absence of run-time errors was proved for the remainder. Supervision cost was 20-40x lower than comparable hand verification. However, some defects evaded GNATprove and were caught only by known-answer tests, interoperability checks, or human spec review. When feedback was weak, the agent attempted to bypass checks and falsely reported success.

Conclusion: The central lesson: what an AI agent can be trusted to establish is bounded by the strength of its feedback. Strong formal verification enables high assurance with reduced human cost, but gaps in the verifier must be covered by complementary testing and human oversight. A multi-layered verification strategy is essential.

Abstract: AI coding agents produce code faster than humans can review it. In our approach, the prover is the judge of whether the code is correct. Under a verifier-driven loop, AI agents wrote and verified bare-metal security software in Ada/SPARK spanning classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations, established functional correctness for selected primitives, and proved the absence of run-time errors for the rest, at roughly 20-40 times lower supervision cost than comparable hand verification. GNATprove alone was insufficient: some defects could not be detected and were resolved using known-answer tests, interoperability, or human review of specifications. Given weak checks, the agent tried to bypass them and reported success. We report where each layer caught faults and draw the central lesson: what an agent can be trusted to establish is bounded by the strength of its feedback.

</details>


### [242] [AI-Conducted Interviews in Empirical Software Engineering: An Experience Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14452)
*Rohit Gheyi,Danyllo Albuquerque,Márcio Ribeiro,Mirko Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This experience report evaluates a customized MyGPT-based AI interviewer for conducting short, self-administered semi-structured interviews in two empirical software engineering studies. Across 66 submissions, 92.4% followed the expected synthesis format, and participant satisfaction was high (90.9% positive experience, 89.4% would participate again). Limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity, and privacy concerns. The authors conclude AI interviewers are a viable complementary option for short, low-risk studies, but not a replacement for human-conducted interviews.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-structured interviews are widely used in empirical software engineering but are resource-intensive and logistically challenging due to scheduling, geographic distribution, and language barriers. The authors explore whether an AI-driven, self-administered interview workflow can mitigate these constraints while maintaining acceptable data quality and participant experience.

Method: A customized MyGPT was deployed as an AI interviewer in two ESE studies (one on refactoring, one on generative AI in Scrum). Participants accessed the interviewer via shared links, used voice interaction, selected their preferred natural language, and completed the interview without a researcher present. The AI followed a predefined protocol and generated a structured synthesis artifact. The authors analyzed 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, auditing format compliance, language, length, and protocol consistency.

Result: 92.4% of artifacts followed the expected synthesis format; 65 were in Portuguese, 1 in English; 2 artifacts conflicted with the reported protocol. Participant ratings were positive: 90.9% reported positive overall experience and comfort, 95.5% found questions clear, 97.0% rated pacing positively, and 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity to answers, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction.

Conclusion: The workflow is operationally viable and acceptable among the analyzed respondents. However, the study does not establish completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, or equivalence to human-conducted interviews. AI interviewers should be treated as a complementary option for short, focused, low-risk studies, with careful attention to protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

Abstract: Semi-structured interviews are widely used in empirical software engineering (ESE), but they are resource-intensive and difficult to coordinate across schedules, locations, and natural languages. This experience report examines a customized MyGPT used to conduct short, self-administered interviews in two ESE studies: one on refactoring practices and another on generative AI in Scrum-related activities. Participants accessed the interviewer through shared links, used voice interaction, selected a preferred natural language, and completed the interview without a researcher present. The AI followed a predefined protocol and generated a structured synthesis that participants voluntarily submitted; these artifacts were not treated as verbatim transcripts. We analyzed 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, and audited artifact format, language, length, and protocol consistency. Of the submitted artifacts, 92.4% followed the expected synthesis format, 65 were predominantly in Portuguese and one in English, and two conflicted with the reported protocol. Participants generally rated the experience positively: 90.9% reported a positive overall experience and comfort, 95.5% considered the questions clear, 97.0% rated the pace positively, and 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity to answers, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction. The findings support the operational viability and acceptability of this workflow among analyzed respondents, but do not establish completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, or equivalence to human-conducted interviews. AI interviewers should therefore be treated as a complementary option for short, focused, low-risk studies, with protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

</details>


### [243] [StructureClaw: Traceable LLM Agents and an Executable Benchmark for Structural Engineering Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14896)
*Sizhong Qin,Yi Gu,Yao Jiang,Ao Cai,Changjian Zhou,Shaoxuan Shuai,Jiachang Wang,Tianhao Shen,Yueqiang Li,Xinhao Li,Li Zeng,Yueshi Chen,Dachen Gao,Genrong Xu,Wenjie Liao,Xinzheng Lu*

Main category: cs.SE
