TL;DR: StructureClaw introduces an artifact-centered workbench and benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on structural engineering workflows, requiring complete, verifiable chains of interdependent artifacts. The full automatic workflow achieves 88.6% success rate vs. 56.8% baseline, while exposing key challenges in invalid input handling and structural model reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations for structural engineering tasks focus narrowly on question answering or script generation, neglecting the full chain of interdependent artifacts (requirements, models, validation, solver outputs, code-checks, reports). This rewards fluent but internally inconsistent or non-executable outputs. A rigorous, executable, end-to-end evaluation framework is needed to assess workflow-level correctness.

Method: The authors present StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench where LLM agents operate via governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. They also introduce StructureClaw-Bench: 150 controlled scenarios across three categories — standard workflow execution (50 scenarios), interactive robustness, and multimodal structural-model reconstruction. A scenario is considered successful only when all artifact-level and execution-level assertions pass in a single run.

Result: Across ten agent-model configurations evaluated on 50 standard cases, the average Success Rate rises from 56.8% (generic-skill baseline) to 88.6% (full automatic workflow). The interactive and multimodal evaluations reveal two key remaining challenges: safe handling of invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models.

Conclusion: Artifact-centered evaluation exposes workflow-level failures invisible to final-response-only assessments, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents. Code and benchmark are publicly available.

Abstract: Addressing a structural-engineering request requires more than a single answer; it requires a chain of interdependent artifacts: interpreted requirements, a computable model, validation records, solver outputs, code-check records, and a final report. Evaluations centered on question answering or script generation rarely verify this complete evidence chain and may therefore reward fluent outputs even when the underlying engineering workflow is incomplete, internally inconsistent, or non-executable. To address this limitation, we present StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench in which LLM agents operate through governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. We also introduce StructureClaw-Bench, an executable benchmark of 150 controlled scenarios spanning standard workflow execution, interactive robustness, and multimodal structural-model reconstruction. A scenario succeeds only when all required artifact- and execution-level assertions pass in a single run. Across ten agent-model configurations, each evaluated on the same 50 standard cases, the average Success Rate rises from 56.8% with the generic-skill baseline to 88.6% with the full automatic workflow. The interactive and multimodal evaluations identify two prominent remaining challenges: safe handling of invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models. These findings show that artifact-centered evaluation can expose workflow-level failures that are difficult to identify from final responses alone, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents. The code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/structureclaw/structureclaw.

</details>


### [244] [Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14456)
*Harris Borman,Herman Wandabwa,Fusun Yu,Sandeepa Kannangara,Justin Liu,Anna Leontjeva,Ritchie Ng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether specialist software agents outperform generalist ones in transforming BPMN diagrams into executable agentic workflows. The specialist solution significantly exceeds generalist baselines (Roo, Cline) in tool-use exactness (+9–20pp), latency (2–4x better), error reduction (3x fewer), and token cost (95%+ lower), while eliminating repair iterations. Generalist agents produce inconsistent, unreliable code unsuitable for industrial use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software development agents are now widespread as IDE extensions, but are typically general-purpose. It is unclear whether building specialist agents—which require additional development effort—is justified. The paper examines this in the context of business process automation, specifically converting BPMN diagrams (with explicit control-flow semantics) into deterministic, executable agentic workflows where the process model and inputs uniquely determine the execution path.

Method: The authors design a specialist workflow agent tailored for BPMN-to-agentic-workflow transformation, exploiting the deterministic control-flow semantics of BPMN. They compare this specialist against generalist coding agents (Roo and Cline) on metrics including tool-use exactness, penalty-adjusted latency, tool-call errors, generation token cost, and number of repair iterations. The evaluation focuses on correctness, efficiency, consistency, and reliability.

Result: The specialist agent outperforms generalist baselines by approximately 9–20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, achieves 2–4x improvement in penalty-adjusted latency, makes 3x fewer tool-call errors, reduces generation token cost by over 95%, and completely eliminates repair iterations. Generalist agents also exhibit inconsistent code generation in both functionality and quality.

Conclusion: Specialist agents provide substantial, measurable advantages over generalist agents for well-defined, deterministic tasks like BPMN-to-workflow transformation, justifying their additional development effort. Generalist agents' inconsistency in code quality and functionality makes them poorly suited for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are critical.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated the adoption of software development agents, now widely available as Integrated Development Environment (IDE) extensions and standalone applications. While these agents are typically general-purpose, it remains unclear whether specialist agents justify their additional development effort. We investigate this question in the context of business process automation, focusing on the transformation of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams into executable agentic workflows. Since BPMN specifies explicit control-flow semantics, we focus on deterministic workflows in which a fixed process model and inputs uniquely determine the executed path. We introduce a specialist workflow for this task and compare it against generalist agents such as Roo and Cline. Our results show that the specialist solution produces agents that outperform generalist baselines by approximately 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in penalty-adjusted latency, and 3x fewer tool-call errors, while reducing generation token cost by over 95% and eliminating repair iterations. We also find that generalist agents generate code inconsistently in both functionality and quality, limiting their suitability for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are essential.

</details>


### [245] [Predicting Human Visual Attention on Words in Source Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14535)
*Chia-Yi Su,Collin McMillan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a neural network model that predicts programmer visual attention on source code by aligning artificial attention with human eye-tracking data via a novel similarity-based loss function, outperforming baselines across Java and C datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding where programmers look when reading source code reveals cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention can improve UI design and tooling. Existing models lack explicit alignment between machine attention and human gaze patterns.

Method: A computational model with a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention (from eye-tracking) and internal neural network attention. Evaluated against three eye-tracking datasets (two Java, one C) using Pearson correlation, normalized Levenshtein distance for scanpath prediction, and comparison against Claude and GPT-5 on reading and writing tasks.

Result: The model outperforms the SE baseline by 64%, 16%, and 467% (Pearson correlation) across the three datasets. It achieves statistically significant improvement over baselines on scanpath prediction (normalized Levenshtein distance) and outperforms Claude and GPT-5 on both reading and writing tasks.

Conclusion: Aligning artificial neural network attention with human visual attention via a tailored loss function yields substantial predictive gains. The model generalizes across programming languages and demonstrates superior capability in tasks requiring understanding of human thought processes during code comprehension.

Abstract: This paper presents a computational model to predict human visual attention over words in software source code. The visual attention of software engineers when reading source code has long been studied as a means to understand human cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention is important for perfecting user interface design and understanding what information human programmers need. We propose a model of programmer visual attention in which we design a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention measured during eye tracking experiments and the internal attention of the artificial neural network. We evaluate our model by comparing its outputs to actual eye tracking data from three separate datasets. Two are in the Java programming language and one is in the C programming language. Our model outperforms the baseline in software engineering by 64%, 16%, and 467% in each of these studies according to Pearson correlation. We used scanpath prediction as an example to demonstrate that our model is more capable of the task that requires the understanding of human thought process. Our model achieves a statistically significant improvement over the close baseline in the reading task according to normalized Levenshtein distance and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on both reading and writing tasks.

</details>


### [246] [A Deterministic Binary Fingerprinting Framework with Zero-Trained Feature Extraction for Sparse Count Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14596)
*Lei Zhao,Fujin Huang,Ling Kang,Quan Guo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MMTB introduces a deterministic, non-learned binary representation framework that transforms sparse count matrices into compact thermometer fingerprints via Min-Max normalization and fixed cutoffs. It achieves ~10× memory reduction over float32, yields NMI of 0.99 on coarse cell-line clustering, but underperforms continuous embeddings (e.g., Scanpy) on fine-grained tissue annotation (NMI 0.39 vs. 0.49 on PBMC), positioning it for resource-constrained coarse separation rather than subtype discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional analysis of sparse count matrices (scRNA-seq, k-mer profiles, document-term frequencies) relies on PCA-based dimensionality reduction, graph clustering, or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces — all of which are computationally expensive, require label supervision or gradient optimization, and produce dense float32 representations. There is a need for a lightweight, deterministic, non-learned binary encoding that reduces memory footprint, enables fast Hamming-distance indexing, and supports clustering without model fitting, particularly for resource-constrained or edge deployments.

Method: MMTB (Min-Max Thermometer Binarization) applies column-wise Min-Max normalization to sparse count matrices, then thresholds each normalized value against a fixed set of cutoffs to produce a thermometer-encoded binary fingerprint per sample. The encoding is deterministic, requires no gradient-based optimization or label supervision, and yields fixed-width binary codes. Clustering is performed via Hamming-distance nearest-neighbor graph construction followed by Leiden community detection. A label-free suitability score is proposed as a heuristic deployment guideline.

Result: On a three-cell-line mixture, a 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell. Hamming distances empirically correlate with normalized L1 distances (Pearson r ≈ 0.92 on scRNA-seq pairs). On PBMC data, MMTB yields NMI of 0.39 versus Scanpy's 0.49, indicating unsuitability for fine-grained subtype discovery. Memory reduction is approximately 10× versus dense float32, though PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR formats may be even smaller — no universal compression is claimed.

Conclusion: MMTB is a viable coarse-grained clustering tool for resource-constrained settings, offering deterministic binary codes with Hamming-indexability and ~10× memory savings. However, it is not a general replacement for continuous embeddings and trails behind methods like Scanpy on fine-grained annotation tasks. Its practical value lies in scenarios prioritizing simplicity, speed, and low memory over maximum discriminative resolution.

Abstract: Sparse count matrices from single-cell transcriptomes to k-mer profiles and document-term frequencies are conventionally analyzed via PCA-reduced graph clustering or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces. We introduce MMTB, a deterministic non-learned binary representation framework that requires no label supervision, model fitting, or gradient-based optimization. Column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs maps each sample to a thermometer fingerprint whose Hamming distances show empirical correspondence with normalized L1 distances, with Pearson correlation approximately 0.92 on single-cell RNA-seq pairs. In a favorable three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell. Under a fair Hamming nearest-neighbor graph plus Leiden readout, MMTB approaches PCA plus Leiden on this coarse task. On challenging tissue-like annotations, continuous pipelines often lead; PBMC Seurat NMI is 0.39 for MMTB versus 0.49 for Scanpy, underscoring that MMTB is suited for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments rather than fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings. Relative to dense float32 representations, MMTB fingerprints reduce memory by approximately 10-fold while providing fixed-width Hamming-indexable codes. PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR may be smaller; we do not claim universal compression. A label-free suitability score is provided as a deployment guideline, not a performance predictor.

</details>


### [247] [SYNAPSE: A Multi-LLM Orchestrated AI Tutor for Secure Software Development Education with Neurodivergent-First Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14601)
*Giusy Ferrara,Ashkan Sami*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SYNAPSE is an adaptive tutoring platform that uses multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) orchestrated via the Model Context Protocol with a Socratic hint policy to teach secure software development through a deliberately vulnerable web application, demonstrating comparable usability and cognitive load across neurodivergent and neurotypical learners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vulnerability detection and remediation skills are rarely taught directly in programming education—secure development is typically introduced only after programming fluency, and accessibility features are treated as an afterthought, systematically disadvantaging learners with ADHD and executive-function differences.

Method: SYNAPSE integrates three LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) coordinated via the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It provides 18 always-visible accessibility features and uses ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, to train learners in the detect-understand-remediate loop. A feasibility pilot evaluated the platform with 19 participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts.

Result: The pilot study (n=19) yielded a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 76.4, engagement rated at 4.2 out of 5, and comparable cognitive-load levels across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts.

Conclusion: SYNAPSE demonstrates that multi-LLM orchestration with deliberate accessibility design can effectively support secure software development training across diverse learner populations, with the platform publicly deployed and available for broader use.

Abstract: Developers who maintain real systems must continually recognise and remediate vulnerabilities in existing code, yet this skill is rarely trained directly: secure software development is commonly taught only after programming fluency is acquired, and accessibility support is treated as a secondary concern, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and related executive-function differences. This paper presents SYNAPSE, a publicly deployed adaptive tutoring platform for Java, Python for cybersecurity, and secure software development. SYNAPSE coordinates Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini through the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It exposes eighteen always-visible accessibility features and anchors practice in ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, on which learners practise the detect-understand-remediate loop characteristic of software maintenance. A feasibility pilot with nineteen participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts returned a System Usability Scale score of 76.4 and engagement of 4.2/5, with comparable cognitive-load levels across cohorts. SYNAPSE is available at https://synapse-course.com; a screencast is available at https://youtu.be/9R17KC47qQI.

</details>


### [248] [Rethinking Issue Resolution for AI/ML Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14657)
*Ahmed Adnan,Mushfiqur Rahman,Antu Saha,Oscar Chaparro*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A qualitative study of 100 issue reports/PRs from TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT reveals that AI/ML issue resolution involves unique characteristics—stochastic behavior, iterative experimentation, multi-artifact coordination—absent in traditional software maintenance. The authors propose a vision and research agenda for AI/ML-specific issue resolution frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing issue resolution frameworks are designed around traditional software maintenance and fail to account for AI/ML-specific traits: stochastic/nondeterministic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations) beyond source code. There is a need for frameworks explicitly tailored to these characteristics.

Method: The authors conducted a qualitative study of issue resolution workflows by analyzing 100 issue reports and pull requests from four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. They examined resolution activities, stages, artifact types, and challenges documented in these reports.

Result: Key findings: (1) issue resolution in AI/ML involves recurring AI/ML-specific activities spanning multiple stages; (2) iterative experimentation and adaptive verification are pervasive; (3) changes are coordinated across diverse artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations); (4) challenges include reproducibility issues, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination difficulties.

Conclusion: The findings motivate a vision for AI/ML-specific issue resolution frameworks. The authors outline research directions and tooling support needed, emphasizing that frameworks must accommodate experimentation loops, multi-artifact coordination, and the inherent stochasticity of AI/ML systems.

Abstract: We advocate for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks tailored to maintenance workflows and the nature of modern AI/ML systems. Existing issue resolution frameworks largely emerged for traditional software maintenance practices and do not explicitly account for characteristics common in AI/ML systems, such as stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts beyond source code. To identify the unique characteristics of issue resolution in AI/ML systems and motivate the need for tailored frameworks, we conducted a qualitative study of issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests across four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. Our findings suggest that issue resolution in AI/ML systems involves: recurring AI/ML-related activities that span multiple resolution stages; iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; and coordinated changes across artifacts such as datasets, prompts, and model configurations. We also observed challenges related to reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination. Building on these findings, we present a vision for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks and discuss research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

</details>


### [249] [LLM-Driven Approach to Modeling Tool Interoperability in Automotive Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14659)
*Nenad Petrovic,Jiajie Zhang,Vahid Zolfaghari,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability in MDE, focusing on mapping model instances to target metamodels and merging metamodels. Demonstrated with Ecore and SysML v2 transformations, automotive case studies show LLMs can significantly reduce manual effort while producing structurally valid cross-tool models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In Model-Driven Engineering, especially in the automotive domain, heterogeneous modeling tools with different languages and proprietary/open-source standards create significant interoperability challenges. Manual transformation between these tools is labor-intensive and error-prone, motivating the need for automated solutions.

Method: The authors propose an LLM-driven methodology addressing two aspects: (1) mapping model instances from a source metamodel to a target metamodel, and (2) merging disparate metamodels. The approach is demonstrated using Ecore and SysML v2 metamodel transformations, with structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models to ensure correctness.

Result: Automotive case studies demonstrate the feasibility of the approach, showing that LLMs can substantially reduce the manual effort required for model transformations while reliably generating structurally valid target models suitable for cross-tool interoperability.

Conclusion: LLM-driven automation presents a promising solution to the longstanding interoperability problem in MDE toolchains. The approach effectively bridges heterogeneous modeling environments with reduced manual overhead, though the paper implies further validation across broader domains may be needed.

Abstract: Interoperability between heterogeneous modeling tools remains a significant challenge in Model-Driven Engineering (MDE), particularly in the automotive domain where multiple modeling languages, as well as defacto standard proprietary and open-source tools coexist. This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability by considering two relevant aspects: 1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel 2) merging of metamodels. The proposed methodology is demonstrated through transformations involving Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodels and incorporates structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models. Automotive case studies illustrate the feasibility of the approach and show that large language models can significantly reduce manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid target models for cross-tool interoperability.

</details>


### [250] [Large Language Models for Code Generation from Multilingual Prompts: A Curated Benchmark and a Study on Code Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14816)
*Saima Afrin,Alessandro Midolo,Camilo Escobar-Velásquez,Mario Linares-Vásquez,Weiyuan Ding,Bowen Xu,Massimiliano Di Penta,Antonio Mastropaolo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how the natural language used in prompts (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Italian) affects code generation quality across three LLMs (GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, Claude) for Python and Java, finding that English does not consistently yield the best results and that prompt language significantly influences functional correctness, structural quality, and lexical characteristics of generated code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While language bias in LLMs is well-studied for general text generation, its specific impact on code generation quality and programming conventions remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically evaluating how non-English prompts affect generated source code across multiple dimensions.

Method: The authors curated a benchmark of 460 coding tasks (230 Python, 230 Java) with prompts translated from English into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian, manually verified for technical accuracy. They evaluated outputs from GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, and Claude along multiple dimensions: functional correctness (test pass rates), structural quality (established code metrics), static analysis issues, and lexical characteristics (identifier/comment language usage).

Result: Three key findings: (i) English prompts do not consistently produce the best functional correctness or code quality; (ii) the effect of prompt language depends on the interplay between the programming language and the specific LLM; (iii) generated code frequently mixes English with the prompt language in comments and string literals.

Conclusion: The paper contributes the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias specifically in code generation and provides actionable insights for building more robust, language-agnostic code generation systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform differently on identical programming tasks when prompted in different natural languages, a phenomenon known as language bias. While this behavior has been widely studied for general text generation, its impact on code generation quality and programming conventions remains largely unexplored. We investigate how the language used to describe programming tasks affects the source code generated by GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, and Claude. Our study comprises 460 coding tasks spanning Python (230) and Java (230). We translate and manually curate the original English prompts into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian while preserving their technical meaning. We evaluate the generated code using multiple dimensions, including functional correctness through test pass rates, structural quality using established code metrics, issues detected by static analysis tools, and lexical characteristics such as the language used in identifiers and comments. Our results show that (i) English prompts do not consistently produce the best functional correctness or code quality, (ii) the impact of prompt language depends on both the programming language and the LLM, and (iii) generated code frequently mixes English with the prompt language in comments and string literals. These findings provide the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias in code generation and offer insights for developing more robust multilingual code generation systems.

</details>


### [251] [AI Prototyper: A Figma Plugin for Decomposition-Based GUI Prototyping with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14830)
*Tawatchai Salangsingha,Sami Ashkan,Md Zia Ullah,Iain McGregor*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AI Prototyper is an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping from natural-language descriptions using a decomposition-and-retrieval-augmented-generation pipeline with a human-in-the-loop editing step, demonstrating superior speed and quality over manual prototyping across multiple languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI prototyping is time-consuming, requires design expertise, and involves non-code artifacts that evolve alongside requirements throughout the software development cycle. Automating prototype generation addresses a key software maintenance and evolution challenge by reducing manual effort and accelerating iteration.

Method: The system employs a decomposition and RAG pipeline: (1) natural-language descriptions are decomposed into discrete GUI features using Gemini 2.5 Flash; (2) matching components are retrieved from a custom 32-primitive library; (3) components are rendered as fully editable Figma layers with auto-layout. A key novelty is the human-in-the-loop editing step allowing users to review, modify, or extend the generated feature list before rendering. The backend runs on Node.js/Express, and the system supports multilingual input (Thai, English, Mandarin Chinese).

Result: In a preliminary evaluation, AI Prototyper users completed more prototypes within a fixed time window compared to manual prototyping. Expert practitioners rated the AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions.

Conclusion: AI Prototyper demonstrates that a decomposition-and-retrieval-augmented approach with human-in-the-loop oversight can effectively automate GUI prototyping, yielding faster completion and higher-quality outputs than manual methods, with practical multilingual support.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) prototyping remains a time-consuming activity that demands both design expertise and considerable manual effort. As GUI prototypes are non-code artifacts that evolve alongside requirements throughout the development cycle, automating their generation is directly relevant to software maintenance and evolution. We present AI Prototyper, an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping through a decomposition and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Given a natural-language description of a desired screen, such as a login page or a product detail card, the plugin decomposes the request into discrete GUI features, retrieves matching components from a custom 32-primitive library, and renders each component as a fully editable Figma layer with auto-layout. The pipeline uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as its LLM back-end and a Node.js/Express service. Unlike existing decomposition-based tools, AI Prototyper introduces a human-in-the-loop editing step that lets users review, modify, or extend the generated feature list before rendering, uses a different technology stack and LLM family, and supports multilingual input, producing correctly labelled interfaces in Thai, English, and Mandarin Chinese. In a preliminary evaluation, participants using AI Prototyper completed more prototypes in a fixed time window than those working manually, and expert practitioners rated the AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/pRoFAH7MQaE. The source code and component library are available at https://github.com/tongsalangsingha/AI-prototyper-tool

</details>


### [252] [FirmPilot: Evidence-Guided Multi-Agent Environment Recovery for IoT Firmware Rehosting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14903)
*Yanbing Shen,Fan Zhang,Haitao Xu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FirmPilot is an evidence-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates firmware rehosting as iterative environment reconstruction, using similarity-based retrieval and feedback-grounded coordination to resolve cross-layer dependencies across boot, persistent state, and networking. It significantly outperforms FirmAE on real-world firmware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing firmware rehosting pipelines are fragile across diverse real-world firmware images because reaching an externally observable execution state depends on tightly coupled artifacts spanning boot scripts, persistent configuration (NVRAM), and network setup. Template-driven frameworks fail on long-tail vendor conventions, while unconstrained LLM use risks unsupported modifications and irreproducible results.

Method: FirmPilot uses an evidence-guided multi-agent architecture: a search agent grounds decisions through similarity-based retrieval, a planner coordinates execution-accepted transitions, and specialized agents recover filesystem/init artifacts, persistent state, and network exposure. The system iteratively reconstructs the environment through repeated execution and evidence-grounded artifact deltas.

Result: On the LFwC corpus, FirmPilot improved web-service reachability over FirmAE from 25.49% to 52.39% and network reachability from 39.30% to 71.93%. The average number of detected services per firmware rose from 0.86 to 1.62, enabling downstream workflows like RouterSploit interaction and protocol-aware fuzzing.

Conclusion: Evidence- and feedback-grounded agent coordination significantly improves rehosting success, service recovery, and downstream utility in automated firmware rehosting for IoT devices.

Abstract: Firmware rehosting executes firmware images in emulated environments such as QEMU to enable scalable dynamic analysis of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In practice, rehosting pipelines remain fragile across diverse real-world firmware images, as reaching an externally observable execution state depends on tightly coupled artifacts spanning boot scripts, persistent configuration (e.g., NVRAM-like key-value state), and network setup. Template-driven frameworks often fail to accommodate long-tail vendor conventions, while unconstrained use of large language models (LLMs) risks unsupported modifications and irreproducible executions. We introduce FirmPilot, an evidence-guided multi-agent framework for environment recovery in firmware rehosting. FirmPilot reformulates rehosting as iterative environment reconstruction in which a search agent grounds decisions through similarity-based retrieval, a planner coordinates execution-accepted transitions, and specialized agents recover filesystem/init artifacts, persistent state, and network exposure. Through repeated execution and evidence-grounded artifact deltas, the system resolves cross-layer dependencies across boot, state, and networking that otherwise prevent firmware executions from reaching a stable, externally reachable state in emulation. Evaluated on the large-scale, real-world LFwC firmware corpus, FirmPilot improves web-service reachability over FirmAE from 25.49% to 52.39% and network reachability from 39.30% to 71.93%. The resulting rehosts raise the average number of detected services per firmware from 0.86 to 1.62 and support downstream analysis workflows, including RouterSploit interaction and protocol-aware fuzzing over recovered service surfaces. The evaluation shows that evidence- and feedback-grounded agent coordination improves rehosting success, service recovery, and downstream utility in automated firmware rehosting.

</details>


### [253] [Leaf: An Instrumentation-based Dynamic Analysis Framework for Rust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15025)
*Mohammad Omidvar Tehrani,Marco Gaboardi,Nick Sumner,Steven Y. Ko*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LEAF is an instrumentation-based dynamic analysis framework for Rust that exposes compiler-level semantic information (MIR) enriched with runtime data as an event stream, enabling diverse analyses like concolic execution, sanitization, and control-flow tracing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rust's ecosystem lacks a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework capable of supporting varied analysis tasks. Existing tooling does not fully leverage Rust's rich semantic information (ownership, types, memory model, MIR) at runtime, creating a gap LEAF aims to fill.

Method: LEAF captures Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR)-level semantic information at compile time, augments it with runtime facts, and delivers both to analyses via Dynamic MIR (DMIR) — an event-driven programming interface. This instrumentation-based approach makes compiler-internal semantics available as structured event streams for dynamic analysis consumption.

Result: The framework was validated through three substantial dynamic analyses: a concolic executor, a Rust-specific sanitizer, and a control-flow tracer. Evaluation shows the framework is practical and expressive, with compile-time and runtime overhead that is meaningful but manageable.

Conclusion: LEAF successfully demonstrates that a Rust-native, MIR-based dynamic analysis framework is both feasible and practical, enabling rich dynamic analyses by bridging compile-time semantic information with runtime behavior through an event-driven interface.

Abstract: This paper presents LEAF, an instrumentation-based dynamic analysis framework for Rust. Although Rust has grown rapidly in recent years, the landscape of program analysis tools for Rust is still in relatively early stages. One notable gap is the lack of a general-purpose dynamic analysis framework that can support different analysis tasks. LEAF aims to fill this gap by providing a Rust-native framework for analyzing Rust programs at runtime. Rust provides rich semantic information through its ownership model, type system, memory model, and compiler-level representation. Therefore, LEAF focuses on how to make this information available to dynamic analyses. In particular, LEAF captures MIR-level semantic information, augments it with runtime facts, and delivers it to analyses as an event stream through Dynamic MIR (DMIR), an event-driven programming interface. Through three substantial dynamic analyses -- a concolic executor, a Rust-specific sanitizer, and a control-flow tracer -- we demonstrate the practicality and expressiveness of LEAF. Our evaluation further shows that LEAF's compile-time and runtime overhead is meaningful but manageable.

</details>


### [254] [Capturing and Exploiting Design Pattern Variability in Mobile Application Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15099)
*Ramón Peralta,Jose-Miguel Horcas*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes using UVL (Universal Variability Language) to model variability in software design patterns (Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Factory Method) and integrating these models with Jinja templates to generate customizable, well-structured Swift mobile applications via SPL engineering principles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auto-generated mobile code often neglects design principles and architectural quality. The authors aim to embed design pattern variability into the code generation process to systematically produce maintainable and architecturally sound applications.

Method: The approach uses UVL to explicitly model structural and behavioral variation points of five common design patterns. These variability models are integrated with reusable Jinja templates to generate Swift code. The work applies SPL engineering principles, treating design patterns as configurable assets, and analyzes the configuration space to assess variability complexity.

Result: The paper presents formalized UVL models for five design patterns, demonstrates automated code generation in Swift via Jinja templates, and provides an analysis of the configuration space, revealing the variability complexity of each modeled pattern.

Conclusion: Formalizing design pattern variability and embedding it into model-driven generation bridges MDE with practical mobile development, promoting maintainable, reusable, and architecturally sound applications through automated, configurable design pattern synthesis.

Abstract: The increasing reliance on automatic code generation in mobile application development often leads to code that neglects fundamental design principles and architectural quality. In this work, we address this challenge by capturing and exploiting the inherent variability of software design patterns to systematically generate customizable and well-structured mobile applications. We propose the use of the Universal Variability Language (UVL) to explicitly model the structural and behavioral variation points of common design patterns, such as Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Adapter, and Factory Method. These models are integrated with reusable Jinja templates, enabling code generation in Swift. Our approach leverages Software Product Line (SPL) engineering principles, treating design patterns as configurable assets within a product line and supporting automated generation of custom design patterns. We also analyze the configuration space of the modeled patterns, offering insights into their variability complexity. By formalizing design pattern variability and embedding it into the generation process, our work bridges model-driven engineering with practical mobile development, promoting the production of maintainable, reusable, and architecturally sound applications.

</details>


### [255] [Navigating the Socio-Technical Complexity Challenge in Quantum Software Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15135)
*Ronja Heikkinen,Santiago Núñez-Corrales,Vlad Stirbu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a socio-technical evaluation framework for quantum computing environments, introducing three key constructs—gravity wells, their properties, and socio-technical desiderata—to help practitioners make deliberate, context-aware choices amidst a fragmented landscape.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum computing environments are heterogeneous, fragmented, and rapidly evolving, with practitioners lacking principled guidance for navigating technology choices across hardware, SDKs, and applications.

Method: Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, combined with insights from quantum software engineering literature and socio-technical/organizational research, to develop and demonstrate the framework through exemplary cases.

Result: Three analytical constructs: (1) gravity wells—how certain technologies exert increasing pull on surrounding choices; (2) properties of gravity wells; and (3) socio-technical desiderata—normative goals for evaluating those pulls. The framework is demonstrated and evaluated through exemplary cases.

Conclusion: The framework advances both the theory of quantum ecosystems and provides practical guidance for organizations navigating the evolving quantum computing field, enabling deliberate choices that preserve architectural flexibility and support evolutionary development.

Abstract: Quantum computing environments are composed of heterogeneous layers spanning hardware, software development kits, and applications. Practitioners curating these environments face a fragmented and rapidly evolving landscape with few principled guides for navigation. This paper presents a framework for evaluating quantum computing environment choices through a socio-technical lens, developed using Design Science Research methodology. Drawing on the quantum software engineering literature as well as organizational and socio-technical research, the framework introduces three analytical constructs: gravity wells and their properties, which characterize how certain technologies and structural conditions exert increasing pull on surrounding environment choices, and socio-technical desiderata, which articulate the normative goals against which those pulls can be evaluated. The framework supports practitioners in making deliberate, context-aware environment choices that preserve architectural flexibility and support the evolutionary development of the field. Demonstration and evaluation of the framework is conducted through exemplary cases. The contribution advances both the theory of quantum ecosystems and the practical guidance available to organizations and practitioners navigating the current, evolving field of quantum computing.

</details>


### [256] [MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15205)
*Shaoxiong Zhan,Shi Hu,Boyu Feng,Hai Lin,Andrew Gong,Zhengda Zhou,Jiaying Zhou,Yunyun Hou,Hao Su,Hai-Tao Zheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MM-IssueLoc is a controlled benchmark for evaluating repository-level issue localization using visual evidence (screenshots, error dialogs, UI states, logs). It contains 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages with image category/relevance annotations, and reveals that current LLM and retrieval systems perform poorly on multimodal localization, with text-only SWE benchmark results not transferring to multimodal settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Repository-level issue localization heavily relies on visual evidence like screenshots and error dialogs in practice, yet existing benchmarks evaluate it as a text-only task. Prior multimodal SE benchmarks confound localization with end-to-end repair (patch synthesis), making it impossible to determine whether visual inputs actually aid localization. A dedicated, controlled benchmark is needed to isolate and evaluate multimodal localization performance.

Method: The authors introduce MM-IssueLoc with 652 issue-PR instances across 23 programming languages. It provides: (1) annotations for 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels; (2) file-level and function-level gold labels; (3) paired text-only and with-image evaluation settings; and (4) VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. They evaluate LLM-based agents, retrieval-based systems, and introduce MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever for comparison.

Result: The strongest LLM agent achieves only 38.96% file Acc@5 and 22.45% function Acc@10. The best retriever reaches 33.86% function Acc@10. High localization scores from text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer to multimodal issue localization, revealing a significant performance gap and the inadequacy of current systems for multimodal repository-level localization.

Conclusion: MM-IssueLoc isolates visual evidence as an explicit evaluation variable, enabling future research to determine whether systems genuinely improve through visual input for localization rather than relying on text-only cues or downstream patch-generation effects. Current systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization.

Abstract: Real repository issues routinely include visual evidence such as screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI states, and logs, yet repository-level issue localization is evaluated mostly as a text-only task. Existing multimodal SE benchmarks evaluate end-to-end repair, entangling localization with patch synthesis and obscuring whether visual input helped, hurt, or was ignored. We introduce \textbf{MM-IssueLoc}, a controlled benchmark and evaluation protocol for repository-level localization with visual evidence. MM-IssueLoc contains 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages, with annotations for 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. It provides file-level and function-level gold labels, paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. We evaluate LLM-based and retrieval-based systems, including MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever. Results show that existing systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization: the strongest agent reaches 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10, while the strongest retriever reaches 33.86 function Acc@10. Cross-benchmark comparisons show that high localization scores on text-dominant SWE benchmarks do not transfer cleanly to multimodal issue localization. MM-IssueLoc turns visual evidence into an explicit evaluation variable, enabling future work to test whether systems improve by using visual evidence for localization, rather than by relying on text-only cues or downstream patch-generation effects.

</details>


### [257] [Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13070)
*Deepak Soni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents a methodology for falsifiable release gates in self-improving AI agent runtimes, implemented in the open-source Antahkarana runtime. Seven machine-verifiable acceptance gates enforce safety invariants via capability tokens from a control ring, exhaustive bounded model checking (~1M states), and a constrained self-modification loop where tightening changes auto-apply but loosening changes require human approval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes rely on self-grading — policy files, guardrails, or README promises — with no machine-verifiable, falsifiable mechanism to ensure that new capabilities preserve safety invariants before deployment. There is a need for objective, reproducible, and automated safety gates.

Method: The author proposes falsifiable release gates: each new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before shipping. The method is instantiated in the Antahkarana runtime across seven sequential gates covering observability to self-governance. Key mechanisms: (1) a control ring mints safety-critical property capability tokens required for any effector action; (2) exhaustive bounded model checking over ~1M reachable states; (3) counterexample generation from a purposely broken model to demonstrate the checker's efficacy; (4) a constrained self-enhancement loop where the write surface is limited to policy rules — tightening changes auto-apply, loosening changes require human merge, and proposals that mispredict their own effect are auto-closed.

Result: The paper publishes acceptance measured results for all seven gates. The scope is bounded to the coordination skeleton (not learned components). The runtime, command-line tools, and gate suite are released openly, enabling single-command reproducibility and cross-framework application. The purposely broken model produces the shortest counterexample, validating that the checker has genuine enforcement power.

Conclusion: Falsifiable, machine-verifiable release gates provide a rigorous alternative to self-graded safety claims, enabling reproducible safety enforcement for self-improving agent runtimes with clear scope boundaries and human-in-the-loop constraints on capability loosening.

Abstract: Safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are almost always self-graded: a policy file, a guardrail, or a README commitment. We describe falsifiable release gates, and a methodology to build and validate such systems, such that every new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before it ships, and a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved at each gate. I think we applied the method in the Antahkarana, an open runtime, via seven gates from basic observability into a self governing loop that suggests changes to its own policy. no action goes to an effector without a safety-critical property capability token minted by a control ring is exhaustively machine-checked over the one million recorded reachable state space of a bounded model and re-checked against execution traces. A purposely broken model gives the shortest counterexample, so the checker has teeth, is apparent. The self-enhancement loop is positively Constrained: the entire write surface is policy rules, tightening changes. may auto-apply loosening changes always require a human merge and a proposal autoclosed is one that mispredicts its own effect; We publish the acceptance measured results for all the seven gates, define precisely the scope of each claim (a bounded of the coordination skeleton (not the learned components) and free the runtime, either command line tools and the gate suite, so the results reproduce, and gates can run against other agent frameworks. Reviewers may repeat the single command central non-bypass in seconds.

</details>

### [258] [World-Model-Aware Responsibility Allocation in Heterogeneous Logistics Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14550)
*Artan Markaj,Niklas Jobs,Felix Gehlhoff*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: WMARF proposes dynamic authority assignment based on world-model quality to prevent deadlocks in mixed-autonomy logistics systems, demonstrating its effectiveness via VDA 5050-based simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In mixed-autonomy logistics, static authority assignment causes deadlocks when an ALE's local world model and the central system's global model diverge. Existing resource-based deadlock handling cannot explain or prevent these divergence-induced conflicts, necessitating a model-aware approach.

Method: The World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF) dynamically assigns decision authority by evaluating CS world-model quality and equipment automation level. It classifies deadlocks into three states — no authority, authority in transition, or divergent authority. Validation uses discrete-event simulation of two ALEs at a semi-automated transfer point, implemented over the VDA 5050 interface, with a proximity-triggered handoff mechanism.

Result: Under static control, a divergence deadlock occurs at the transfer point. The proximity-triggered handoff in WMARF prevents this deadlock by reassigning authority to the entity with the more current world model.

Conclusion: Because authority follows information quality rather than relying on a shared protocol, WMARF remains valid as equipment autonomy levels increase, offering a scalable solution for deadlock prevention in evolving logistics systems.

Abstract: Logistics systems increasingly mix \emph{autonomous logistic equipment} (ALE) with non-autonomous machinery under a central control system (CS), where the best decision-maker depends on who holds the most current world model, yet authority is fixed at design time. When an ALE's local model and the CS global model diverge, both act on incompatible beliefs and produce deadlocks that resource-based handling neither explains nor prevents. We propose the World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF), which assigns authority dynamically from CS world-model quality and equipment automation level, and classifies deadlocks by the state of authority -- none, in transition, or divergent. In a discrete-event simulation of two ALE converging on a semi-automated transfer point, reproduced over the VDA~5050 interface, a divergence deadlock under static control is prevented by a proximity-triggered handoff. Because authority follows information quality rather than a shared protocol, the scheme stays valid as autonomy grows.

</details>


### [259] [Multi-Scale Equilibrium under Variable Indicator Dimensionality: Faithful Reduction of Dynamic Attractors in Urban Mobility Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14815)
*Ali Ghoroghi,Yacine Rezgui,Afrouz Ghaemi,Cristina De Nardi,Andrei Hodorog*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper formally addresses the mismatch between the high-dimensional nature of urban mobility equilibrium analysis and the variable data availability across cities. It develops a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor model with fast performance and slow strategic layers, establishes mathematical conditions under which lower-dimensional indicator projections remain faithful to the full equilibrium structure, and demonstrates through simulation that as few as two observable channels can suffice for antifragility classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban mobility systems are inherently high-dimensional, yet the indicators available to city authorities vary dramatically across cities and during disruptions. There is no formal framework for determining when a reduced set of observable indicators can faithfully represent the full equilibrium dynamics, leaving authorities without principled guidance on which indicators are essential to monitor.

Method: The authors construct a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor comprising: (1) a fast performance layer that relaxes toward an indicator-dependent target, (2) a slow strategic layer yielding a joint fixed point across traffic assignment, modal choice, and learning dynamics, and (3) an antifragility classification via a statistical decision rule on post-to-baseline performance ratios. They then mathematically derive four conditions for faithful lower-dimensional projection: exact/approximate projectability with error bounds, preservation of the two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary, retained Fisher information under a measurement model, and a one-sided restoration-time bias. A simulation study on three stylized pilot-city configurations validates the theoretical results.

Result: Four key theoretical results are established: (i) conditions and explicit error bounds for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor; (ii) the coupled two-layer fixed point is preserved up to a contraction boundary; (iii) Fisher information and decision power are retained for any indicator support under the measurement model; (iv) reduced monitoring produces a one-sided bias that can only understate recovery duration. The simulation study confirms all results and demonstrates that two observable channels are sufficient for antifragility classification when the indicator catalogue permits.

Conclusion: The framework provides city authorities with a principled, mathematically rigorous basis for deciding which urban mobility indicators must be maintained during disruptions, showing that faithful lower-dimensional monitoring is achievable under explicit conditions, and that the primary risk of inadequate monitoring is systematic underestimation of recovery time.

Abstract: Equilibrium analysis of urban mobility systems is formulated in a high-dimensional indicator space, whilst data availability varies sharply across cities and disruption contexts. This paper gives a formal treatment of that mismatch. It presents a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor for disrupted urban mobility, in which a fast performance layer relaxes towards an indicator-dependent target, a slow strategic layer supplies a joint traffic, modal and learning fixed point, and antifragility is classified through a statistical decision rule on the post-to-baseline performance ratio. It then characterises when a lower-dimensional indicator projection is faithful to this equilibrium structure, establishing four results: conditions for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor with an explicit error bound; preservation of the coupled two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary; the retained Fisher information and decision power of any indicator support under a measurement model on observable urban indicators; and a one-sided restoration-time bias, whereby reduced monitoring can only understate recovery duration. A simulation study on three stylised pilot-city configurations verifies each result, and shows that two observable channels suffice for the candidate classification target where the indicator catalogue permits. The framework gives city authorities a principled basis for deciding which indicators must be maintained.

</details>


### [260] [Randomized routing strategies of fleets of CAVs may prove market efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14859)
*Grzegorz Jamróz,Łukasz Gorczyca,Rafał Kucharski*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper examines the market structure of competing CAV fleet operators in future cities where both human-driven vehicles (HDVs) and connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) coexist. It finds that when HDV drivers exhibit diverse attitudes toward CAVs, randomized CAV routing (causing unpredictable travel times for HDVs) outperforms routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium. The authors propose augmenting market-share objectives with mean systemwide travel time to discourage antisocial strategies and steer competition toward social welfare.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As cities transition toward mixed traffic environments with both HDVs and CAVs, competing fleet operators may emerge to manage CAV routing. The key question is what market structure would align these profit-motivated operators with broader city goals (social welfare). The authors seek to understand how market-share-based competition among CAV fleet operators affects overall traffic efficiency and how market design can prevent antisocial routing strategies.

Method: The authors define a market variant where fleet operator revenue is proportional to market share. They develop benchmark scenarios and propose multiple routing algorithms for comparison. Key analysis involves studying how randomized CAV routing (producing unpredictable travel times for HDVs) versus routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium performs under conditions where HDV drivers' attitudes toward CAVs are diverse. The paper evaluates market outcomes through simulation and algorithmic comparison.

Result: Randomized CAV routing, which generates unpredictable travel times for human-driven vehicles, proves more efficient than routing strategies aligned with system optimum or user equilibrium when human drivers display significant diversity in their attitudes toward CAVs. This suggests that complete predictability in CAV routing may not always be socially optimal in mixed-traffic environments.

Conclusion: To prevent fleet operators from adopting antisocial randomized strategies purely for market-share gain, the authors recommend redesigning the market mechanism by incorporating mean systemwide travel time into the objective function alongside market share. This hybrid objective would guide competition toward cooperative behavior that benefits social welfare.

Abstract: In future cities every driver may own a vehicle which could be either independently driven (HDV), or autonomously routed and piloted (CAV). The autonomous operations could be handled by a few competing companies. What is the market structure which would make this market aligned with city goals? In this paper we discuss a variant of the emerging market of collectively routed fleets of CAVs, where revenue for fleet operators is proportional to market share. We provide benchmark scenarios to compare the routing algorithms. We present several routing algorithms and demonstrate that, when the attitudes of human drivers towards CAVs exhibit significant diversity, randomised CAV routing, resulting in unpredictable travel times for HDVs, is more efficient than routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium. Based on this, we propose to improve the design of the market by augmenting the market-share objective with mean systemwide travel time in order to limit antisocial randomised strategies of fleet operators and drive the competition towards social welfare oriented cooperation.

</details>


### [261] [The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14865)
*Lucas Bergholdt Hansen,Federico Torrielli,Filippo Tonini,Lukas Galke Poech*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The Energy Society is a minimal multi-agent simulation where LLM-based agents must manage energy (spent via token generation, earned via jobs/donations) to survive. The study examines how competitive vs. cooperative incentives shape emergent behavior, finding that larger models are energy-inefficient, cooperation promotes altruistic donations and better job allocation, and architectural features like inter-agent recommendations and memory improve coordination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments, the incentives embedded in those environments can profoundly shape agent behavior. However, there is limited understanding of how inference costs—directly tied to model size and token generation—interact with competitive or cooperative pressures when survival is at stake. The authors introduce a controlled testbed to systematically study these dynamics.

Method: The authors built The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy simulation. Agents consume energy proportional to model size when generating tokens. They regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations and deactivate if energy hits zero. The experiment compares a competitive objective, a cooperative objective, a baseline, and several control variants. Ablations test the effects of inter-agent action recommendations and memory. Behavior is measured through energy consumption, donation patterns, job allocation, sabotage attempts, and survival outcomes.

Result: Larger models consistently consume the most energy and run net energy deficits, even when token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives lead agents to donate energy to reactivate others—sometimes sacrificing their own survival—and alter job allocation patterns. Inter-agent recommendations support coordination and ambitious job selection; memory helps agents calibrate risk from prior outcomes. Agents rarely engage in direct sabotage but exhibit subtle self-serving behavior under competition.

Conclusion: The Energy Society provides a compact, tractable testbed for studying how token-based inference costs and group incentives interact under survival pressure. The findings highlight that model size, incentive structure, and communication/memory capabilities all significantly influence emergent multi-agent behavior, with implications for designing safe and efficient multi-agent LLM systems.

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

</details>


### [262] [Stigmergic Graph Memory: An Environment-Aware Approach for Many-to-Many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15182)
*Aditya Dutta,Joon-Seok Kim*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: SGM introduces a decaying memory layer that records recent traffic on warehouse nodes/edges to inform endpoint selection (which agent, source, destination) before path planning, improving MAPD throughput by 20.5–36.7% over baselines across all tested conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-guidance methods only influence routing after goals are fixed, leaving the endpoint instantiation phase (agent, source, and destination selection) uninformed by recent traffic conditions. This gap degrades throughput in many-to-many MAPD where endpoints are not predetermined.

Method: Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM): a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges. These signals rank feasible endpoint choices (agent, source, destination) and route preferences without altering collision constraints or planner validity, thereby integrating traffic-aware memory into the goal-selection phase upstream of path planning.

Result: SGM outperformed two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines across all 15 map-load conditions (5 layouts × 3 load levels, 25 seeds each), yielding paired throughput gains of 20.5–36.7%.

Conclusion: Recent execution memory improves warehouse throughput by shaping which feasible goals enter the planner, not merely how agents navigate to already-fixed goals. This demonstrates the value of traffic-informed endpoint instantiation in many-to-many MAPD systems.

Abstract: Automated fulfillment warehouses must continuously assign and execute pickup-and-delivery work while avoiding congestion. In many-to-many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD), a request specifies a stock-keeping unit rather than fixed endpoints, requiring the controller to select an agent, source, and destination before path planning. Existing graph-guidance methods primarily influence routing after goals are fixed, leaving endpoint instantiation uninformed by recent traffic. We introduce Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM), a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges to rank feasible endpoints and route preferences without altering collision constraints or planner validity. Across paired request streams on five layouts, three load levels, and 25 seeds per condition, SGM outperforms two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines in all 15 map-load conditions, with paired throughput gains of 20.5-36.7%. These results show that recent execution memory can improve warehouse throughput by shaping which feasible goals enter the planner, not only how agents travel to already fixed goals.

</details>
