### [263] [Exploring Delay-based PUFs for Energy-Efficient Low-Overhead Security of Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14395)
*Venkata Prasanth Yanambaka,Uma Choppali,Saraju P. Mohanty*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hardware-assisted, energy-efficient security solution for wearable IoT devices using Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs). It compares two PUF architectures — Arbiter PUF and Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF — finding that HOA PUF consumes only 2.7 μW versus 25 μW for Arbiter PUF, offering robust security with minimal power overhead for resource-constrained IoT systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wearable IoT devices continuously collect and transmit sensitive personal data (location, heart rate, etc.), creating significant privacy and security threats. Given these devices' resource constraints and the growing market, there is a pressing need for security solutions that are both energy-efficient and low-overhead.

Method: The authors analyze and compare two Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) architectures — Arbiter PUF and Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF — for integration into IoT systems. Both are hardware-based security primitives evaluated for power consumption, overhead, and suitability for cryptographic key generation in wearable devices.

Result: Arbiter PUF consumes 25 μW for cryptographic key generation, while HOA PUF consumes only 2.7 μW — approximately a 9.3× improvement. Both architectures introduce minimal power overhead while providing robust security, making them well-suited for resource-constrained IoT ecosystems.

Conclusion: HOA PUF is the superior choice for wearable IoT devices due to its significantly lower power consumption (2.7 μW) while still delivering robust hardware-level security. PUF-based solutions offer a viable path to securing resource-constrained IoT ecosystems without compromising energy efficiency.

Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) was introduced almost two decades ago. In the past two decades, technology has seen huge advancements. Many devices have become powerful and have less power consumption. Many IoT architectures and environments were introduced to help make life easier, especially in wearable devices. The market for these wearable devices has constantly increased over the years and is expected to reach its maximum in the next couple of years. They also pose a threat to users' privacy and security because they constantly store and transmit personal information such as location, heart rate, and other sensitive data. Therefore, addressing the security vulnerabilities is a crucial aspect of this research. This paper presents a hardware-assisted, energy-efficient, low-overhead security solution for wearable devices. Specifically, two Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) architectures: Arbiter PUF and Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF are analyzed for integration in IoT systems. The result shows that Arbiter PUF consumes 25 $μ$W, whereas HOA PUF consumes only 2.7 $μ$W to generate keys for cryptographic purposes. These architectures introduce minimal power overhead while providing robust security, making them well suited for resource-constrained IoT ecosystems.

</details>


### [264] [Better Privacy Guarantees for Larger Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14406)
*JacK Fitzsimons*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper studies count-dependent zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) for histograms with disjoint groups. It shows that the optimal privacy budget dependence on group size is inverse-square, i.e., v(n) = Θ(n⁻²), under a repaired relative-error utility condition that handles the boundary at count zero. The leading constant is tightly bounded between π/(4e²) and 1/π.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pujol and Desfontaines posed the question: can a private histogram allocate more error (i.e., looser privacy) to larger counts, thereby protecting members of larger groups more strongly? The original strict relative-error condition fails at count zero, so the paper repairs this formulation to make the problem well-posed and then determines the optimal privacy budget as a function of group size.

Method: The authors formalize count-dependent zCDP, where the privacy budget v(n) depends on the affected count n and is nonincreasing. They repair the utility condition to E|hat{x}_i − x_i| < r·max{x_i, 1}, which introduces explicit boundary tolerance at zero. For the upper bound, they specialize a shifted-transformation framework to construct a shifted-log Gaussian mechanism achieving v(n) = O_r(n⁻²). The lower bound uses an information-theoretic argument to show any mechanism satisfying the utility condition must have v(n) = Ω_r(n⁻²). A many-count argument further bounds the leading coefficient.

Result: The main result establishes that the optimal count-dependent privacy budget is v(n) = Θ(n⁻²). The shifted-log Gaussian mechanism certifiably achieves this rate. The lower bound matches, proving optimality. The leading coefficient in the large-count, small-error limit lies between π/(4e²) and 1/π (a factor below three). At r=1, a data-independent release trivially satisfies the criterion with zero privacy loss.

Conclusion: The inverse-square rate is optimal for count-dependent zCDP under the repaired relative-error utility condition. The tight constant bounds (factor <3) leave little room for improvement. The repaired formulation successfully resolves the boundary issue at count zero while preserving the original requirement at positive counts.

Abstract: Pujol and Desfontaines asked whether a private histogram can allow more error on larger counts and use that slack to protect members of larger groups more strongly. We study this question for fixed disjoint groups under add-or-remove-one adjacency. The privacy budget $v(n)$ depends on the affected count, is nonincreasing, and must bound both Rényi-divergence directions at every order. This is the count-dependent form of zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) studied here. The original strict relative-error condition is impossible at count zero. We therefore make the boundary tolerance explicit by requiring $\mathbb{E}\lvert\widehat{x}_i-x_i\rvert < r\max\{x_i,1\}$, without changing the requirement at any positive count. Our main result determines the best dependence on group size. For the upper bound, we directly specialize an existing shifted-transformation framework. The resulting shifted-log Gaussian mechanism has a certified budget $v(n)=O_r(n^{-2})$. Conversely, for every fixed $0<r<1$, any mechanism satisfying the same positive-count utility requirement and count-dependent zCDP must have $v(n)=Ω_r(n^{-2})$. Thus the inverse-square rate is optimal under the repaired formulation. A many-count information argument further places the leading coefficient in the large-count-then-small-error limit between $π/(4e^2)$ and $1/π$, a factor below three. At $r=1$, a data-independent release meets the repaired criterion with zero privacy loss.

</details>


### [265] [A Measurement Study of AI-Environment Realism Gaps in Malware-Analysis Sandboxes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14434)
*Zhiyong Sui,Lamine Noureddine,Mst Eshita Khatun,Sideeq Bello,Babangida Bappah,Justin Woodring,Aisha Ali-Gombe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces AIprint, a framework that probes for AI-environment artifacts (configuration files, model caches, env vars, etc.) to distinguish real AI-capable systems from sandboxes. The authors extract 450 artifacts from 284 GitHub projects, find that 12 artifacts appear exclusively on real hosts and not on any evaluated sandbox, and demonstrate that convincingly spoofing AI environments is far more costly than detecting shallow spoofing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern malware employs environment-aware techniques to detect and evade sandbox analysis. While prior evasion research focused on virtualization artifacts, timing discrepancies, and system realism, the rise of AI-capable endpoints creates a new realism gap: sandboxes typically lack the artifacts of genuine AI software ecosystems. The authors investigate whether AI-environment artifacts constitute a measurable and exploitable sandbox-evasion surface.

Method: The authors developed AIprint, a probe framework that captures persistent artifacts from AI-capable software, including AI-assistant config directories, model caches, environment variables, local inference services, and package dependencies. They systematically extracted 450 unique artifacts from 284 open-source AI projects on GitHub, compiled them into unprivileged Windows probes, and evaluated them across seven commercial and open-source sandbox backends alongside three AI-capable reference hosts. A controlled 214-step installation experiment established causality between AI tool installation and artifact accumulation, and adaptive spoofing experiments assessed the cost asymmetry between reproducing convincing environments and detecting shallow spoofing.

Result: Traditional VM-detection baselines failed to reliably distinguish real AI-capable systems from modern sandboxes. However, 12 AI-environment artifacts appeared on all three reference hosts and on none of the seven evaluated sandbox backends. The 214-step installation experiment confirmed a causal relationship between AI tool/package installation and measurable artifact accumulation. The adaptive spoofing experiments revealed that reproducing convincing AI software environments is substantially more expensive than detecting shallow spoofing attempts.

Conclusion: AI-environment artifacts represent a novel and practical sandbox-evasion surface that current sandbox implementations fail to replicate. Addressing this gap requires sandbox operators to either incorporate genuine AI software stacks or develop more sophisticated environment spoofing, both of which incur nontrivial maintenance costs. The work underscores a fundamental operational asymmetry favoring the evader in AI-contextualized environments.

Abstract: Sandboxing remains a core technique for observing suspicious program behavior, yet environment-aware malware increasingly suppresses execution when analysis is suspected. Prior generations of sandbox evasion focused on virtualization artifacts, timing discrepancies, and wear-and-tear realism. In this paper, we present the first systematic measurement study of AI-environment artifacts as a new sandbox-evasion surface. We operationalize this realism gap through AIprint, a probe framework that captures persistent artifacts left behind by AI-capable software ecosystems, including AI-assistant configuration directories, model caches, environment variables, local inference services, and package dependencies.
  We systematically extract 450 unique artifacts from 284 open-source AI projects on GitHub, compile them into unprivileged Windows probes, and evaluate them across seven commercial and open-source sandbox backends together with three AI-capable reference hosts. Our results show that traditional VM-detection baselines fail to reliably distinguish real AI-capable systems from modern sandboxes, whereas twelve AI-environment artifacts appear on the reference hosts and on none of the evaluated backends. A controlled 214-step installation experiment establishes a causal relationship between AI tool and package installation and measurable AI-environment artifact accumulation, while adaptive spoofing experiments reveal a fundamental operational asymmetry: reproducing convincing AI software environments is substantially more expensive than detecting shallow spoofing.

</details>


### [266] [Disclosure Divergence: Measuring Privacy Policy and Data Safety Misalignment at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14442)
*Mst Eshita Khatun,Lamine Noureddine,Sideeq Bello,Aisha Ali-Gombe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A large-scale study of 6,051 Android apps reveals significant inconsistencies between privacy policies and Google Play Data Safety labels, particularly for sensitive data like personal info and device IDs, with sharing disclosures worse than collection disclosures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile app platforms provide two separate disclosure channels — privacy policies and Data Safety labels — which may present conflicting information about data practices, creating uncertainty for users and regulators about which source to trust.

Method: An LLM-based extraction framework was applied to 6,051 Android apps, using a unified schema covering 14 Google Play data categories and two operations (collection and sharing). Consistency was measured per-app and per-category, and a sensitivity-weighted risk score was introduced to emphasize high-risk data types.

Result: Misalignment disproportionately affects sensitive categories such as personal information and device identifiers. Sharing disclosures exhibit lower consistency than collection disclosures. Elevated privacy risk is concentrated in app categories associated with persistent monitoring and communication.

Conclusion: Current disclosure mechanisms have structural gaps that undermine transparency. Stronger verification and greater transparency in platform-level privacy reporting are needed to address these inconsistencies.

Abstract: With the rapid growth of mobile applications, user data privacy has become an increasing concern. While privacy policies describe how apps collect and share data, platforms such as Google Play provide Data Safety labels intended to summarize these practices. Because these disclosure channels are declared separately, they may present inconsistent representations of app data practices, creating uncertainty for users and regulators. In this work, we conducted a large-scale empirical study of disclosure consistency across 6,051 Android apps. Using an LLM-based extraction framework and a unified schema over 14 Google Play data categories and two operations (collection and sharing), we measure per-app and per-category consistency and introduce a sensitivity-weighted risk score that emphasizes high-risk data types. We find that misalignment disproportionately affects sensitive categories such as personal information and device identifiers, with sharing disclosures exhibiting lower consistency than collection disclosures. Elevated privac risk is concentrated in app categories associated with persistent monitoring and communication. Overall, our findings highlight structural gaps in current disclosure mechanisms and underscore the need for stronger verification and greater transparency in platform-level privacy reporting.

</details>


### [267] [Context Contamination in LLM Analysis of Network Security Logs: Poison with Passive Prompt Injection and Mitigation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14493)
*Rabimba Karanjai,Yang Lu,Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao,Lei Xu,Weidong Shi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Adversaries can embed prompt injection payloads in log entries that persist in storage and later execute when analysts query LLMs for security analysis. The paper presents LogInject, a benchmark of 12,847 log entries, evaluates three production LLMs across four attack objectives, finds up to 88.2% attack success, introduces a novel "Context Stitching" evasion technique (76.4% success), and evaluates layered defenses achieving 90.4% reduction but with 8.4% residual risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) for log analysis, ingesting untrusted logs from external-facing services. The architectural pattern where untrusted log data and trusted instructions share the same context window creates a fundamental security vulnerability — the "confused deputy" problem — that has not been systematically studied.

Method: The authors develop LogInject, a systematic evaluation framework with LogInject-1.0 dataset (12,847 log entries, 2,569 adversarial). They test three production LLMs against four attack objectives: activity concealment, false positive generation, information exfiltration, and output hijacking. They introduce Context Stitching, which fragments payloads across multiple log entries to evade stateless filters while exploiting long-context reasoning. They also evaluate layered defenses combining input filtering, prompt hardening, and output validation.

Result: Baseline passive prompt injection achieves up to 88.2% ASR (83.4% average). Context Stitching achieves 76.4% success rate. Layered defenses reduce attacks by 90.4%, but 8.4% residual vulnerability remains. All three models evaluated are vulnerable.

Conclusion: LLM-based log analysis creates an inherent confused deputy vulnerability where untrusted data and trusted instructions compete indistinguishably for model attention. Defense-in-depth architectures and continued human oversight remain necessary for security-critical SOC decisions.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in Security Operations Centers for log analysis tasks including summarization, alert triage, and threat investigation. These systems ingest logs from external-facing services and process network logs as natural language contexts to generate security insights. We demonstrate that this architectural pattern introduces a critical vulnerability: adversaries can embed prompt injection payloads in log-generating fields that persist in storage and are executed when analysts query the LLM, achieving what we term passive prompt injection. We present LogInject, a systematic framework for evaluating these threats. Using LogInject-1.0, a benchmark of 12,847 log entries including 2,569 adversarial samples, we evaluate three production LLMs across four attack objectives: activity concealment, false positive generation, information exfiltration, and output hijacking. Our findings reveal an up to 88.2% attack success rate (83.4% average across models) under the baseline conditions. We introduce Context Stitching, a novel technique that fragments payloads across multiple log entries to evade stateless filters while exploiting LLM long-context reasoning, achieving a 76.4% success rate. As mitigation, we evaluate layered defenses by combining input filtering, prompt hardening, and output validation, demonstrating a 90.4% attack reduction, although 8.4% residual vulnerability persists. Our results establish that LLM-based log analysis creates an inherent confused deputy vulnerability where untrusted data and trusted instructions compete indistinguishably for model attention, requiring defense in-depth architectures and continued human oversight for security-critical decisions.

</details>


### [268] [Fully Automated End-to-End Adversary Emulation from MITRE ATT\&CK Based Cyber Threat Intelligence Using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14566)
*Jueon Choi,Seojun Lee,Sanggwon Yun,Kwanghoon Choi,Gunjin Cha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A fully automated end-to-end framework that uses LLMs to generate, execute, and self-correct adversary emulation playbooks from CTI reports. It outperforms prior SOTA (AURORA) by incorporating a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism, achieving 84.22% execution success with Claude Sonnet 4.5.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior adversary emulation systems either rely on prewritten playbooks (limited scalability), require manual intervention during playbook generation (e.g., AURORA), or lack mechanisms to revise playbooks based on execution failures. There is no unified, fully automated pipeline spanning playbook generation, execution, and failure recovery.

Method: The framework consists of three integrated stages: (1) LLM-based generation of Caldera-compatible playbooks from MITRE ATT&CK-aligned CTI reports, (2) automated execution of those playbooks, and (3) a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism that classifies failure types and revises failed Abilities accordingly. Four LLMs were evaluated: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 4 Fast.

Result: Best results with Claude Sonnet 4.5: 27.3 Abilities per playbook, 84.22% post-revision execution success, CTI Precision/Recall/F1 of 73.95%/52.48%/60.50%. The failure recovery mechanism improved execution success by 14.59–17.23 percentage points across all models. On 10 CTI reports from AURORA's dataset, the framework surpassed AURORA's final execution success rate.

Conclusion: A fully automated LLM-driven adversary emulation pipeline with failure-type-aware recovery is feasible and significantly outperforms semi-automated baselines like AURORA. The recovery mechanism is the key differentiator, consistently boosting execution success across diverse LLMs.

Abstract: This paper presents a fully automated end-to-end framework for adversary emulation from MITRE ATT&CK-aligned CTI reports using LLMs. Unlike prior work, which either executes prewritten playbooks or partially automates playbook generation, our framework unifies playbook generation, execution, and failure recovery in a single workflow. In particular, although AURORA, the most recent prior study, generates playbooks from CTI reports, it still requires partial manual intervention and does not revise playbooks based on execution failures. Our framework generates Caldera playbooks from CTI reports, executes them automatically, and revises failed Abilities through a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism. Evaluated on 11 CTI reports with Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 4 Fast, the framework achieved its best results with Claude Sonnet 4.5: 27.3 Abilities per playbook, 84.22% execution success after revision, and CTI Precision, Recall, and F1 of 73.95%, 52.48%, and 60.50%, respectively. The failure recovery mechanism consistently improved execution success across all evaluated LLM models by 14.59%p to 17.23%p. On the 10 CTI reports selected from AURORA's dataset, this mechanism further increased the final execution success rate, surpassing that of AURORA, which represents the state-of-the-art adversary emulation system.

</details>


### [269] [Qubes OS Security in the Public Record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14587)
*Alfonso De Gregorio*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A longitudinal analysis of 109 Qubes Security Bulletins (2011–2025) reveals that ~80% of public advisories stem from upstream components (Xen, CPU/microarchitectural), not Qubes-core logic. Disclosure rates plateaued post-2018, with 2015Q1 as the dominant structural break. S-shaped vulnerability discovery models fit descriptively but offer no forecasting advantage over a rolling-mean baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Qubes OS's architecture makes component boundaries security-relevant, offering a unique lens for security measurement. The study aims to quantify the extent of upstream dependence in the public advisory record and assess whether disclosure trends have shifted over time, using the official QSB and XSA tracker as a measurable, protocol-driven dataset.

Method: Protocol-driven longitudinal analysis of 109 QSBs (2011–2025) and the Qubes-maintained XSA tracker. Methods include deterministic component attribution with audited codebook, change-point analysis for structural breaks, overdispersion diagnostics (Poisson vs. negative-binomial), severity-proxy weighting, censoring sensitivity checks, documentary latency lower bounds, and baseline-aware evaluation of S-shaped vulnerability discovery models against a rolling-mean baseline.

Result: 113 of 464 tracked XSAs affect Qubes; 87 of 109 QSBs (79.8%) are attributable to upstream components (Xen, CPU/microarchitectural, other) rather than Qubes-core logic, consistent under weighted views. 2015Q1 is the dominant change-point; post-2018 annual disclosure rates are statistically flat. Poisson inferences hold under dispersion diagnostics and negative-binomial sensitivity. The attribution codebook performs well in a stratified 30-QSB audit. S-shaped VDMs fit descriptively but do not significantly outperform a rolling-mean baseline in short-horizon forecasts.

Conclusion: The Qubes public advisory record is stable but not quiet: disclosure activity has plateaued at a level higher than the earliest years, with the burden concentrated in upstream trust anchors. This persistent upstream dependence underscores systemic challenges for security architectures that rely on strong component isolation.

Abstract: Qubes OS is a revealing case for security measurement because its architecture makes component boundaries security-relevant. We present a protocol-driven longitudinal analysis of 109 public Qubes Security Bulletins (QSBs, 2011--2025), the official Qubes-maintained Xen Security Advisory (XSA) tracker, and a secondary vulnerability-event sensitivity series. The study measures the public advisory record rather than latent vulnerability incidence or realized compromise. The methodology combines audited deterministic component attribution, change-point analysis, overdispersion checks, severity-proxy weighting, censoring sensitivity, documentary latency lower bounds, and baseline-aware evaluation of vulnerability discovery models (VDMs).
  The results show persistent upstream dependence in that public record. On the official tracker, 113 of 464 XSAs affect Qubes; under primary labeling, 87 of 109 QSBs (79.8\%) are attributable to Xen, CPU/microarchitectural, or other upstream components rather than Qubes-core logic, with similar results under weighted views. Change-point analyses identify 2015Q1 as the dominant break in the quarterly advisory series, while post-2018 annual disclosure rates are statistically flat. Poisson inferences are stable under dispersion diagnostics and negative-binomial sensitivity checks. The attribution codebook performs well in a stratified 30-QSB audit, and S-shaped VDMs fit descriptively but do not significantly outperform a rolling-mean baseline in short-horizon forecasts.
  Overall, the Qubes public advisory record appears stable, but not quiet: disclosure activity plateaus at a higher level than in the earliest years, while the observed burden remains concentrated in upstream trust anchors.

</details>


### [270] [Bad Memory: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risks from Memory in Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14611)
*Soham Gadgil,David Alexander,Sai Sunku,Franziska Roesner*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Agentic systems with persistent memory across sessions are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks where malicious payloads planted in memory files can influence behavior in current and future sessions, though overwriting memory via untrusted content is difficult. Attack success varies by system, model, and adversarial strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly retain state across sessions (memory files, preferences, knowledge bases), enabling self-improvement but introducing a new attack surface. The authors aim to systematically study how prompt injection attacks exploit persistent memory in these systems.

Method: The authors use a sandboxed synthetic workspace to evaluate prompt injection attacks on two agentic systems — Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex — across four models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5). They test payload overwriting from untrusted content and attack propagation from pre-planted malicious payloads across single and multi-session sequences.

Result: Overwriting an agent's own memory files using untrusted external content is difficult. However, payloads already embedded in memory files successfully compromise both current and future sessions. Attack success rates and payload persistence vary significantly across systems, models, adversarial goals, and multi-session attack sequences.

Conclusion: Persistent memory fundamentally alters the threat model for prompt injection. Defenses must focus on protecting memory update mechanisms while preserving the adaptive benefits of persistent agent state.

Abstract: A growing class of agentic systems maintain persistent state across sessions through memory files, behavioral preferences, and knowledge bases. While this makes agents more useful and self-improving, it also creates a new attack surface for prompt injections in which malicious instructions can be embedded within persistent files and influence future behavior. In this work, we study prompt injection attacks in memory-based agentic systems using a sandboxed synthetic workspace. We evaluate two agentic systems, Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, across four models: Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.5. Our results show that although it is difficult to make an agent overwrite its own memory files using untrusted external content, payloads already planted in those files can successfully attack current and future sessions. Attack success and payload persistence vary substantially across systems, models, adversarial goals, and multi-session attack sequences. These findings show that persistent memory changes the threat model for prompt injection and motivate defenses that protect memory updates without removing useful agent adaptation.

</details>


### [271] [MemPoison: Uncovering Persistent Memory Threats and Structural Blind Spots in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14651)
*Jifeng Gao,Kang Xia,Yi Zhang,Xiaobin Hong,Mingkai Lin,Xingshen Wei,Wenzhong Li,Sanglu Lu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MemPoison is a benchmark for evaluating adversarial attacks on persistent agent memory, introducing a three-tier attack taxonomy (direct, compositional, context-triggered) and demonstrating that write-time defenses fail against sophisticated multi-record and dormant corruption attacks, advocating for context-sensitive memory defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent external memory improves agent continuity but creates persistent security vulnerabilities where adversarial content injected through normal interaction channels can be retained across turns and distort future agent behavior. Existing write-time defenses are insufficient against sophisticated attack patterns.

Method: The authors construct MemPoison, a benchmark with 1,227 hand-validated cases spanning four attack types, three injection channels, and three memory substrates, evaluated on seven open-weight and three closed-weight models. They propose a three-tier taxonomy: L1 (direct single-record corruption), L2 (compositional multi-record corruption), and L3 (context-triggered dormant corruption). They also introduce mechanistic influence decomposition (MID) to analyze structural blind spots in write-time defenses.

Result: Write-time defenses like consistency checks substantially suppress L1 direct attacks but fail against L2 and L3 attacks. MID analysis reveals that seemingly benign records pass write-time filters and later become harmful through joint retrieval composition or trigger-conditioned activation, exposing fundamental structural blind spots in static filtering approaches.

Conclusion: The findings advocate shifting from static write-time filtering to adaptive, context-sensitive memory defense strategies that can detect and mitigate compositional and dormant attack patterns that unfold across multiple records and turns.

Abstract: Persistent external memory enhances agent continuity but introduces persistent security vulnerabilities: adversarial content can be injected via standard interaction channels, retained across turns, and later distort downstream behavior. To address this challenge, we propose MemPoison, a comprehensive benchmark and analysis framework featuring 1227 hand-validated cases across four attack types, three injection channels, and three representative memory substrates, evaluated on seven open-weight and three closed-weight model families. We introduce a three-tier taxonomy: (L1) direct single-record corruption, (L2) compositional multi-record corruption and (L3) context-triggered dormant corruption. Our evaluations reveal a distinct defense frontier: while baseline write-time defenses, such as consistency checks, substantially suppress direct L1 attacks, they fail to reliably suppress L2 and L3 attacks. Through mechanistic influence decomposition (MID), we demonstrate structural blind spots in write-time defenses, which admit seemingly benign records that later become harmful through joint retrieval composition or trigger-conditioned activation. Our findings advocate for shifting from static filtering to adaptive, context-sensitive memory defense strategies.

</details>


### [272] [Lattice-based extended withdrawability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14690)
*Ramses Fernandez-Valencia*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper constructs lattice-based extended withdrawable signatures by combining a claimable ring signature approach: a one-out-of-N anonymous signature (black-box) provides signer ambiguity, while the signer's claim is a binding signature with an opening of a hiding index commitment. No signer-derived values are published in the clear, ensuring anonymity-until-claim. Security is proven under MLWE, MSIS, and EUF-CMA assumptions in the (Q)ROM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on extended withdrawable signatures suffered from privacy leakage because a per-signer shift was transmitted in the clear, directly identifying the signer. The authors aim to eliminate this leakage by designing a lattice-based construction where signer identity remains fully hidden until the signer explicitly claims the signature, achieving anonymity-until-claim under post-quantum assumptions.

Method: The construction uses the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. It realizes extended withdrawable signatures as a claimable ring signature with two layers: (1) a one-out-of-N signature scheme (black-box) provides anonymity under full key exposure, and (2) confirmation is achieved via the signer's claim — a binding signature combined with the opening of a hiding index commitment bound into the transcript. Critically, no signer-derived value appears in the clear. The scheme is instantiated with a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style base signature and an established lattice-based one-out-of-many proof.

Result: The authors provide complete security proofs establishing: correctness, extended withdrawability (anonymity-until-claim), unforgeability under insider corruption, and claimability soundness. Security reduces to Decisional MLWE (commitment hiding), MSIS (commitment binding), the anonymity of the one-out-of-N scheme, and EUF-CMA security of the base signature — all in the (quantum) random-oracle model.

Conclusion: The paper successfully constructs the first lattice-based extended withdrawable signatures that avoid the privacy leakage of prior approaches. By embedding a hiding index commitment into the transcript and using the signer's claim as confirmation, the scheme achieves full anonymity-until-claim with post-quantum security guarantees grounded in standard lattice assumptions.

Abstract: We extend the extended withdrawable signatures of Liu, Susilo and Baek to lattice-based constructions built on the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. Departing from an earlier draft that transported a per-signer shift in the clear, which leaks the signer, we realise extended withdrawable signatures as a claimable ring signature: signer ambiguity is provided by a one-out-of-N signature used as a black box (anonymity under full key exposure), and confirmation is the signer's claim, a binding signature together with the opening of a hiding index commitment bound into the transcript. No signer-derived value is published in the clear. We give complete proofs of correctness, extended withdrawability (as anonymity-until-claim), unforgeability under insider corruption, and claimability soundness, reducing to decisional MLWE (commitment hiding), MSIS (commitment binding), the anonymity of the one-out-of-$N$ scheme, and the EUF-CMA security of the base signature, in the (quantum) random-oracle model. We instantiate the base signature with a no-hint, full-$t$ Dilithium-style scheme and the one-out-of-$N$ layer with an established lattice one-out-of-many proof.

</details>


### [273] [FlowGuard: From Signals to Evidence for MCP Security Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14754)
*Baichao An,Pei Chen,Geng Hong,Yueyue Chen,Mengying Wu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FlowGuard is an evidence-grounded security detection system for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that combines semantic analysis with runtime verification to identify both execution-related vulnerabilities (e.g., command injection, file system access) and semantic risks in tool metadata/returned content, achieving high F1 scores and 2.23x lower latency than existing scanners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MCP security scanners rely on suspicious semantic signals rather than actual execution behaviors, leading to unreliable risk assessment (e.g., credential-like placeholders flagged as leaks). A gap exists for systems that provide runtime evidence for execution-related risks while also performing careful semantic analysis for risks embedded in metadata or returned content.

Method: FlowGuard employs a five-stage pipeline: (1) semantic risk triage to classify and prioritize potential risks, (2) recon-guided payload narrowing to focus probing on relevant attack surfaces, (3) schema-valid probe generation to produce well-formed, context-aware test payloads, (4) evidence adjudication to confirm risks using runtime execution evidence, and (5) history-guided refinement to iteratively improve detection accuracy based on prior findings.

Result: On a benchmark of 1,880 MCP cases across five vulnerability categories, FlowGuard achieves F1 scores of 0.879 for Command Injection and 0.942 for File System Access. It reduces end-to-end latency by up to 2.23x compared to existing dynamic scanners. In real-world testing, FlowGuard reported 523 findings across 326 MCP servers.

Conclusion: Evidence-grounded detection that integrates runtime verification with semantic triage is effective for assessing both execution-related and semantic risks in MCP interactions, offering a more reliable and efficient alternative to purely signal-based MCP security scanning.

Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to interact with external tools through metadata exchange, tool invocation, and response consumption. Existing MCP security scanners primarily reason about suspicious semantic signals rather than real execution behaviors, which can lead to unreliable risk assessment. For example, credential-like strings may simply be placeholders rather than actual leakage. This gap requires runtime evidence for execution-related risks and careful semantic analysis for risks carried in metadata or returned content. We present FlowGuard, an evidence-grounded MCP security detection system. FlowGuard combines semantic risk triage, recon-guided payload narrowing, schema-valid probe generation, evidence adjudication, and history-guided refinement. It verifies execution-related risks through runtime evidence and detects semantic risks in tool metadata and returned content. We evaluate FlowGuard on an executable benchmark containing 1,880 MCP cases across five vulnerability categories. FlowGuard achieves F1 scores of 0.879 and 0.942 on the execution-related Command Injection and File System Access categories, respectively. Compared with existing dynamic scanners, FlowGuard reduces end-to-end latency by up to 2.23x. In the real-world evaluation, FlowGuard reports 523 findings across 326 servers. These results show that evidence-grounded detection can assess both execution-related and semantic risks in MCP interactions.

</details>


### [274] [Is External Database Protection Static in Retrieval-Augmented Generation? Rethinking Privacy Preservation under Dynamic Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14811)
*Gang Zhang,Mingyu Tian,Xukun Luan,Yuanchi Ma,Jinyan Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PA-HDP is a dynamic, query-aware differential privacy framework for RAG that assesses document sensitivity based on the user's query, then applies adaptive protection only to truly sensitive content, achieving a superior privacy-utility trade-off over static document-level methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing privacy protection for RAG assumes a static, document-level risk model where all retrieved documents are treated equally. This ignores the query-driven nature of RAG: a document's privacy risk depends on what the user asks. A dynamic, query-dependent approach is needed.

Method: PA-HDP operates in two stages: (1) Prompt-aware risk hierarchy — dynamically assesses privacy risk of retrieved documents conditioned on the query; (2) Differentiated protection — applies adaptive sensitive entity replacement and exponential mechanism-based text selection to inject differential privacy proportional to assessed risk, modifying only query-relevant sensitive content.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show PA-HDP significantly reduces privacy leakage while maintaining high retrieval quality, outperforming prior methods in the privacy-utility trade-off.

Conclusion: Dynamic, query-dependent privacy risk assessment is essential for RAG. By protecting only what is truly sensitive under a given query, PA-HDP achieves better privacy preservation with minimal semantic degradation, advancing the state of privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented generation.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models via external document retrieval, but retrieved contexts may leak sensitive information. Current privacy protection methods typically rely on a document-level static risk assumption, treating all retrieved documents as having the same privacy leakage risk. However, this assumption overlooks a fundamental characteristic of RAG: the privacy risk of a document is highly dependent on the user's query, making privacy leakage inherently query-driven and dynamic. To address this challenge, we propose a Prompt-Aware Dynamic Hierarchical Differential Privacy framework (PA-HDP) for privacy-preserving RAG. PA-HDP first performs a prompt-aware risk hierarchy to dynamically assess privacy risks under different queries. It then applies adaptive sensitive entity replacement and exponential mechanism-based text selection to provide differentiated privacy protection while preserving semantic utility. By protecting only the content that is truly sensitive under a given query, PA-HDP minimizes unnecessary modifications to the retrieval corpus. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PA-HDP significantly reduces privacy leakage while maintaining high retrieval quality, achieving a better privacy-utility trade-off than prior methods.

</details>


### [275] [The Distributed Open-Source Vulnerability Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14900)
*Peter Mandl,Paul Mandl*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents a conceptual framework analyzing why different vulnerability scanners produce inconsistent results for the same software. It traces vulnerability information through creation, standardization, enrichment, and interpretation, identifying heterogeneous sources, divergent identity/version models, temporal change, and context-dependent assessment as root causes of divergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite shared standards like CVE and CPE, vulnerability scanners consistently report divergent findings for identical software inventories. The paper argues these discrepancies are not merely implementation bugs but systemic issues rooted in the distributed, multi-stage nature of the open-source vulnerability ecosystem.

Method: The authors develop a conceptual framework that models vulnerability management as a distributed information exchange and transformation process. They trace vulnerability information across four stages: (1) creation and standardization, (2) enrichment, (3) context-dependent interpretation, and (4) scanner reporting. At each stage, they identify structural sources of inconsistency.

Result: The analysis identifies four major causes of inconsistent scanner findings: (1) heterogeneous information sources (e.g., NVD, OSV, vendor advisories), (2) divergent identity and version models for matching software to vulnerabilities, (3) temporal dynamics as vulnerability knowledge evolves, and (4) context-dependent assessment criteria that vary across scanners.

Conclusion: Inconsistent scanner results are an inherent property of the vulnerability ecosystem, not merely implementation flaws. The paper calls for (1) nuanced interpretation of scanner outputs, (2) reproducible evaluation methods that account for systemic divergence, and (3) practical strategies for handling the dynamic nature of vulnerability knowledge in software supply chain security.

Abstract: Identifying known software vulnerabilities is a central task in software supply chain security management. Although publicly available vulnerability information is based on shared standards, different vulnerability scanners often report divergent results for identical software inventories. These differences do not arise solely from individual data sources or scanner implementations. They can emerge at several stages of the open-source vulnerability ecosystem. This paper presents a conceptual framework that describes vulnerability management as a distributed process of information exchange and transformation. It traces vulnerability information from its creation and standardization through enrichment to context-dependent interpretation. The analysis identifies heterogeneous information sources, divergent identity and version models, temporal change, and context-dependent assessment as major causes of inconsistent scanner findings. It then discusses the implications for interpreting analysis results, designing reproducible evaluation methods, and handling dynamic vulnerability knowledge in practice.

</details>


### [276] [A Queueing-Stability Criterion for Causal IPD-QIM Network Flow Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14954)
*Jiuxiang Cai,Guang Cheng,Guangjie Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper provides a rigorous theoretical stability analysis of causal QIM (Quantization Index Modulation) watermarking on multi-hop encrypted links. It models the embedder as a reflected dwell queue, derives a stability criterion (buffer stable iff effective injection rate < 1), and validates the criterion via both simulation and real IPD traces, yielding a testable stable-embeddability condition and a quantization-step configuration baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On multi-hop encrypted links like Tor, packet lengths and protocol fields are flattened by tunneling, making inter-packet delay (IPD) the primary carrier for active flow attribution. Causal QIM watermarking injects only nonnegative delays (dwell), risking unbounded buffer growth, lattice misalignment, and unacceptable connection delays. Prior work left stable embeddability on bursty traffic to empirical tuning without formal analysis; this paper addresses that gap.

Method: The embedder is modeled as a reflected dwell queue under a fixed dual-lattice, equiprobable-bit rule with state-dependent injection. Using the substitution Y_i = δ_i - r_i, a Lindley-type algebraic identity is obtained. Stability is analyzed via busy-state drift at large dwell, where the effective interval collapses to zero and mean injection becomes Δ/4. The analysis covers i.i.d. backgrounds, stationary-ergodic traffic, and finite-state Markov-modulated traffic, deriving the condition that time-average intensity ρ̄ < 1 for stability. The exogenous decoding floor Δ ≥ cσ_ξ (c = 4Q⁻¹(ε/2)) yields an operating window Δ ∈ [cσ_ξ, 4μ̄_d).

Result: Simulations confirm a sharp stability transition at ρ = 1 governed solely by the mean. On four real IPD traces with single-flow simulated chains, the criterion correctly predicts stability direction under flow-local correlation and burstiness. Pooled cross-flow means are shown to overestimate the stability margin. The operating window Δ ∈ [cσ_ξ, 4μ̄_d) emerges as a practical configuration baseline.

Conclusion: The paper delivers a testable stable-embeddability criterion and a quantization-step configuration baseline for causal QIM network flow watermarking. The stability condition ρ̄ < 1 (equivalently Δ < 4μ̄_d) provides a principled alternative to empirical configuration, with practical implications for deploying flow attribution on Tor and cascaded VPNs.

Abstract: On multi-hop encrypted links such as Tor and cascaded VPNs, tunneling flattens packet lengths and protocol fields, leaving inter-packet delay (IPD) as the main carrier for active flow attribution. Causality lets the embedder delay packets but never advance them, so each quantization-index-modulation (QIM) alignment injects nonnegative dwell into a delay buffer; unbounded dwell breaks lattice alignment and delays the host connection unacceptably. Whether a causal QIM watermark embeds stably on bursty traffic has largely been left to empirical configuration rather than analysis. We model the embedder as a reflected dwell queue under the fixed dual-lattice, equiprobable-bit rule, where injection is state-dependent -- set by the current interval and bit -- rather than exogenous. The substitution $Y_i=δ_i-r_i$ gives only an algebraic Lindley-form identity; stability is governed by the busy-state drift at large dwell, where the effective interval collapses to zero and the mean injection becomes $Δ/4$. Away from the critical boundary, the buffer is stable iff $μ_d>Δ/4$ (i.e. $Δ<4μ_d$) for i.i.d. backgrounds, and, under stationary-ergodic and finite-state Markov-modulated traffic with instantaneous overload, iff the time-average intensity $\barρ<1$. With the exogenous decoding floor $Δ\ge cσ_ξ$ ($c=4Q^{-1}(ε/2)$), this yields the operating window $Δ\in[cσ_ξ,4\barμ_d)$. Simulations confirm a sharp transition at $ρ=1$ set only by the mean; on four real IPD traces, with each simulated chain confined to a single flow, the criterion gives the correct stability direction under flow-local correlation and burstiness, while pooled cross-flow means overestimate the margin. These results give a testable stable-embeddability criterion and a quantization-step configuration baseline for causal QIM network flow watermarking.

</details>


### [277] [NFSA: Non-Forward Secure Aggregation with One Server via Two Layer Secret Sharing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15052)
*Yufei Zhou*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A new two-layer secret sharing protocol for Federated Learning that eliminates direct user-to-user communication and server data forwarding, using Shamir's Secret Sharing combined with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing and PRF/KhPRF, achieving up to 100x communication efficiency improvement and significant computational reductions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing server-based secure aggregation protocols require the server to forward sensitive data between users, which increases communication overhead and introduces security risks. The authors aim to eliminate this intermediary forwarding and direct user-to-user communication while maintaining privacy guarantees in FL.

Method: The protocol combines Shamir's Secret Sharing with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing using a Pseudo-Random Function (PRF). It extends this with Key-homomorphic PRF (KhPRF) for high-dimensional data aggregation, enabling one-shot secure aggregation with a single server. A new Chinese Remainder Theorem-based encoding method is introduced for the almost KhPRF mask, reducing KhPRF calls and mitigating model update expansion after masking.

Result: At 100 users, the scheme improves communication efficiency by nearly 100x and reduces computational overhead by ~17% compared to existing methods. User computation time is reduced by 51–75% when input length is 2^18.

Conclusion: The proposed protocol significantly outperforms existing methods in auxiliary node overhead, achieving substantial gains in both communication efficiency and computational cost, making secure aggregation in FL more practical and scalable.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training while preserving privacy by keeping data local. However, the risk of sensitive data leakage through model updates necessitates the use of secure aggregation protocols. Existing server-based secure aggregation protocols typically require the server to forward sensitive data shared between users, which increases communication overhead and introduces potential security risks. In this work, we propose a novel secure aggregation protocol based on two-layer secret sharing to address these issues. By combining Shamir's Secret Sharing with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing using a Pseudo-Random Function (PRF), our protocol eliminates direct communication between users, thereby removing the need for the server to forward data. We further extend the protocol with Key-homomorphic PRF (KhPRF) to support high-dimensional data aggregation and apply it to FL, enabling one-shot secure aggregation with a single server and no intermediary data forwarding. To reduce user overhead, we design a new encoding method based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem for the almost KhPRF-based mask, reducing the number of KhPRF calls and mitigating the model update expansion issue after masking. Experimental results show that our scheme significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of auxiliary node overhead. For instance, when the number of users is 100, our scheme improves communication efficiency by nearly 100 times and reduces computational overhead by approximately 17\%. Moreover, user computation time can be reduced by 51\% to 75\% when the input length is $2^{18}$.

</details>


### [278] [Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised: Weaponizing Setup Instructions Against AI Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15143)
*Aadesh Bagmar,Pushkar Saraf*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AI coding agents blindly follow project documentation to install dependencies, making them vulnerable to supply-chain attacks embedded in READMEs, requirements files, or Makefiles. An attacker can redirect agents to malicious packages through typosquatting, separator confusion, registry redirection, or known-vulnerable versions. A systematic evaluation across frontier models and production harnesses reveals that security depends on the harness-model combination, not the model alone; source-based attacks are almost universally missed, while deterministic pre-install verification closes most of the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents increasingly automate software project setup by parsing documentation and installing dependencies, yet they lack verification of package names, sources, or known vulnerabilities. Existing supply-chain attack vectors — typosquatting, dependency confusion, registry poisoning — are well-documented, but no prior work has systematically evaluated how these attacks succeed when mediated through coding-agent harnesses that interpret project documentation. The authors aim to quantify this emerging threat surface where documentation itself becomes a vector for remote code execution.

Method: The authors conduct the first systematic evaluation of package-install-time supply-chain attacks delivered through project-setup documentation. They design twelve attack scenarios spanning five attack classes (typosquatting, separator confusion, registry redirection, known-vulnerable versions, and wrong-but-plausible names), all grounded in real-world documented incidents. These scenarios are tested across multiple production coding-agent harnesses (e.g., ChatGPT Code Interpreter, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot Workspace) using frontier large language models. Each harness-model combination is probed to determine whether the agent installs a malicious dependency or detects the attack, with results analyzed by ecosystem (npm, PyPI, Cargo) and by harness-model pairing.

Result: Key findings: (1) The same model catches an attack in one harness but installs it in another, demonstrating that install-time security is a property of the harness-model combination. (2) Agents reliably detect blatant typosquats, but separator-confusion names (e.g., azurecore vs. azure-core) frequently slip through, with success rates varying by harness-model pairing. (3) Source-based attacks like registry redirection are missed almost universally. (4) The source blind spot persists across npm and Cargo ecosystems, where nearly every model installs the untrusted dependency. (5) Security-oriented prompts partially recover detection gaps but only for explicitly named dimensions. (6) A deterministic pre-install check verifying names, sources, and versions before any code executes closes most of the vulnerability gap.

Conclusion: Documentation-driven dependency installation constitutes a practical and under-explored supply-chain attack surface against AI coding agents. Security cannot be achieved through model capabilities alone; harness-level deterministic verification of package identity, provenance, and version integrity before any installation code runs is essential. The authors advocate for pre-install guardrails as a necessary architectural countermeasure in agentic coding systems.

Abstract: AI coding agents set up projects by reading documentation and installing the dependencies it lists, without verifying their names, sources, or known vulnerabilities. By editing only a README, requirements file, or Makefile, an attacker can redirect the agent to an untrusted registry, a known-vulnerable version, or a wrong-but-plausible name: documentation becomes a vector for code execution. We present the first systematic evaluation of package-install-time supply-chain attacks delivered through ordinary project-setup documentation across production coding-agent harnesses, probing frontier models on twelve scenarios in five attack classes, grounded in documented incidents. The same model catches an attack through one harness and installs it through another: install-time security rests on the harness-model combination, not the model alone. Agents catch blatant typosquats reliably, but plausible separator-confusion names (azurecore for azure-core) slip through, and how often depends on the harness-model pairing. Source-based attacks like registry redirection are missed almost everywhere. The source blind spot recurs on npm and Cargo, where nearly every model installs the untrusted dependency; name detection carries over less consistently across ecosystems. Security-oriented prompts recover part of the gap but only for the dimension they name; a deterministic pre-install check that verifies names, sources, and versions before any code runs closes most of it.

</details>


### [279] [DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15081)
*Zefeng Wu,Weiwei Qi,Jielong Chen,Tianhang Zheng,Di Hong,Chaochao Lu,Liang He,Zhan Qin,Kui Ren*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DataShield is a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments by aligning them against consensus safe/unsafe subspaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs, enabling effective filtering and masking without target-model-specific computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for detecting safety-degrading fine-tuning data rely on a single mean vector from a specific model-tokenizer pair to represent the safety direction, which limits both their effectiveness in identifying risky data and their transferability across models.

Method: DataShield constructs a joint safety-critical semantic space from multiple safety-aligned LLMs using semantic spectral decomposition on safe/unsafe data representations. It extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces, then scores data samples or token segments by measuring their relative alignment (projection ratio) with these subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking.

Result: DataShield reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) by 14.6% using sample-level filtering and by 32.3% using segment-level masking compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving downstream utility.

Conclusion: Consensus subspace alignment across multiple safety-aligned LLMs provides a more effective and transferable approach to identifying safety-risky fine-tuning data than single-model safety direction methods.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs. Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

</details>


### [280] [Automated Template-free Synthesis of Instruction-Centric Leakage Contracts for Black-Box CPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15118)
*Elvira Moreno,Tiziano Marinaro,Ryan Williams,Marco Patrignani,Roberto Guanciale,Hamed Nemati,Marco Guarnieri*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: malcos automates the synthesis of ISA-level leakage contracts for black-box CPUs (x86 and ARM) using a template-free methodology, demonstrating that precise and sound leakage contract extraction from modern processors is feasible with minimal manual intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Side-channel attacks exploit microarchitectural discrepancies to leak information. Leakage contracts provide an ISA-level security abstraction for secure CPU programming, but crafting them manually for complex modern CPUs is prohibitively labor-intensive. Consequently, contemporary CPUs lack dedicated leakage contracts. This motivates an automated approach to extract contracts with minimal manual effort.

Method: The authors introduce a template-free methodology for extracting instruction-centric leakage contracts from black-box CPUs. They implement this in malcos, a tool that automatically synthesizes leakage contracts by observing CPU behavior during synthesis without relying on pre-defined templates or white-box knowledge of the microarchitecture.

Result: malcos was evaluated on x86 and ARM CPUs. The synthesized leakage contracts were shown to be precise and sound with respect to all leaks observed during the synthesis process, confirming the feasibility of learning leakage contracts from black-box CPUs.

Conclusion: Automated, template-free synthesis of leakage contracts for real-world CPUs is feasible. malcos demonstrates that precise and sound contracts can be learned from black-box observation, paving the way for practical deployment of leakage contracts as a security abstraction on modern processors.

Abstract: Side-channel attacks pose a significant security threat for modern computing platforms, because they exploit subtle discrepancies in CPU behaviors to leak sensitive information. To model the information leaked by a CPU via microarchitectural side-channels, recent work proposed leakage contracts: an ISA-level security abstraction that provides the foundations for secure CPU programming. Unfortunately, due to the complexity of current microarchitectures, devising a leakage contract for a CPU requires extensive manual effort and thus modern CPUs lack dedicated leakage contracts.
  We present a methodology to extract instruction-centric leakage contracts for major CPU architectures with minimal manual intervention. We implemented this technique in malcos, the first template-free tool that automates the synthesis of leakage contracts for black-box CPUs. We evaluate malcos on x86 and ARM CPUs, and show that the contracts it synthesizes are precise and sound with respect to all leaks observed during synthesis. Our results demonstrate that learning leakage contracts from black-box CPUs is feasible.

</details>


### [281] [Beyond Success Rate: Cost-Aware Evaluation of Offensive and Defensive Security Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15263)
*Paul Kassianik,Blaine Nelson,Yaron Singer*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper argues that security-agent evaluations should measure cost-efficiency alongside task success, showing that while offensive CTF performance scales with compute, defensive SOC investigation success depends more on disciplined tool use than raw reasoning budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing security-agent benchmarks focus on peak offensive capability under generous inference budgets, overlooking operational cost constraints. In real-world security operations, every reasoning step and tool call consumes budget, making cost-aware evaluation essential for assessing practical utility.

Method: The authors evaluate language-model security agents through a cost-success lens on two task types: offensive Cybench CTF challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigation challenges. They compare models at fixed cost levels, decomposing performance by inference spend and tool spend, rather than reporting only best-case success rates.

Result: Offensive CTF performance improves with additional test-time compute, and scaled open-weight models can approach frontier proprietary systems while remaining cost-competitive. Defensive SOC investigation does not scale similarly: success depends more on disciplined tool use, telemetry navigation, and selective enrichment than on raw reasoning budget alone.

Conclusion: Security-agent benchmarks should incorporate economic efficiency and operational fit alongside task success. Cost-aware, SOC-native evaluations provide a clearer picture of which models are practically useful and where defensive agents need improvement.

Abstract: Security-agent evaluations commonly measure peak offensive capability under generous inference budgets, emphasizing vulnerability discovery, exploit development, penetration testing, and CTF completion. Such measurements are useful but incomplete: in operational security, every reasoning step, tool call, telemetry query, and enrichment request consumes budget. We evaluate language-model security agents through this cost-success lens on offensive Cybench challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigation challenges. Instead of reporting only best-case success, we compare models at fixed cost levels and decompose performance by inference spend and tool spend. Our results show distinct scalingregimes for red- and blue-team tasks. Offensive CTF performance improves with additional test-time compute, and scaled open-weight models can approach frontier proprietary systems while remaining cost-competitive. Defensive SOC investigation does not scale in the same way: success depends more heavily on disciplined tool use, telemetry navigation, and selective enrichment than on raw reasoning budget alone. We argue that security-agent benchmarks should measure economic efficiency and operational fit alongside task success. Cost-aware, SOC-native evaluations provide a clearer picture of which models are practically useful today and where defensive agents still need to improve. We present an interactive website with our results https://evals.frontier.security.

</details>
