# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [282] ["Trust Junk" Leads to Unjustified Support for Highly Discriminatory Predictive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14152)
*Michael Correll,Lucy Havens,Mahsan Nourani*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Accurate but irrelevant data in visual explanations can induce unjustified trust in discriminatory AI models, revealing a persuasive dark side of data visualization in XAI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether accurate yet superfluous or irrelevant information presented in model explanations can mislead users into trusting and forming positive beliefs about a model that is demonstrably discriminatory and unfair.

Method: A crowdsourced study in which participants were shown explanations of a predictive model (which was explicitly discriminatory) that included accurate but extraneous data visualizations, and their trust and perceptions of the model were measured.

Result: Providing accurate but superfluous/irrelevant data in model explanations led to unjustified trust and positive beliefs about the model, even when the model was clearly discriminatory and unfair.

Conclusion: XAI designers and developers must critically examine the implicit and explicit rhetorics embedded in their visual explanations, as visualizations can inadvertently confer unearned trust upon flawed or unfair models.

Abstract: The persuasive power of data visualizations can go awry: for instance, in an explainable AI (XAI) context, visualizations can produce over-trust of predictive models. In this paper, we use a crowdsourced study to show that providing accurate (but superfluous or irrelevant) data in a model explanation can, in fact, result in unjustified trust and other positive beliefs about a model, even when the model is patently discriminatory and unfair. Our results suggest that XAI designers and developers need to consider the implicit or explicit rhetorics of their work, and beware of the potential of visualizations to imbue models with unearned trust.

</details>


### [283] [From Product-Centred Retrieval to Experience-Led Commerce:Twelve Candidate Design Principles for Fashion E-Commerce User Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14429)
*Nafiul I. Khan,Mansura Habiba,Rafflesia Khan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Proposes twelve candidate design principles for Experience-Led Commerce in high-constraint relational fashion e-commerce, surfaced through building the VogueDrop prototype, with prespecified hypotheses and planned empirical evaluation via critical-incident study and preregistered experiment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fashion e-commerce involves high-constraint, relational interactions — fit, composition, material, identity-sensitive preferences, seller fragmentation, visual correspondence, and delivery timing — where conventional transactional e-commerce design patterns break down. The authors use fashion as an intentionally bounded domain to surface observable interaction breakdowns and derive experience-led design principles.

Method: Design-led induction through building VogueDrop, a multi-vendor fashion e-commerce prototype. Twelve candidate design principles are surfaced, each paired with a prespecified hypothesis, primary behavioural outcome, and rejection condition. A formative critical-incident study and a preregistered matched-interface experiment are specified with separate user-experience and platform-facing outcome reporting.

Result: No empirical results are reported; the paper presents the twelve candidate principles and the experimental framework before studies are completed. The principles cover: multi-entry discovery, experience continuity, relational exploration, preference sovereignty, evidence-scoped correspondence, recommendation-time feasibility, customer-compatible commercial ranking, adaptive but stable workspaces, attributable transaction authority, outcome-linked learning, shared composition authoring, and accountable human-to-agent handoff.

Conclusion: The paper explicitly refrains from claiming empirical superiority or universal applicability, positioning the twelve principles as candidate propositions awaiting validation through the specified studies. The domain-bounded approach (fashion) is framed as a methodological strength rather than a limitation.

Abstract: This paper proposes twelve candidate Experience-Led Commerce design principles for high-constraint, relational fashion e-commerce, surfaced through design-led induction while building VogueDrop, a multi-vendor prototype. The principles address multi-entry discovery, experience continuity, relational exploration, preference sovereignty, evidence-scoped correspondence, recommendation-time feasibility, customer-compatible commercial ranking, adaptive but stable workspaces, attributable transaction authority, outcome-linked learning, shared composition authoring, and accountable human to agent handoff. The paper uses fashion as an intentionally bounded domain in which fit, composition, material, identity-sensitive preference, seller fragmentation, visual correspondence, and delivery timing make the interaction breakdown observable; it does not claim universal applicability across e-commerce. Each candidate principle is paired with a prespecified hypothesis, primary behavioural outcome, and rejection condition. A formative critical-incident study and a preregistered matched-interface experiment are specified, with user-experience and platform-facing outcomes reported separately. No empirical superiority is claimed before those studies are completed.

</details>


### [284] [Not Just Pockets: Understanding Phone-Carrying Behaviors of Wheelchair Users for Mobile Context-Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14437)
*Yunzhi Li,Patrick Carrington*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Wheelchair users exhibit distinct smartphone-carrying patterns — including wheelchair-mounted accessories and body placements — shaped by physical ability, wheelchair design, and social/activity contexts. These carrying locations can serve as context proxies to enable more inclusive context-aware applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile sensing for context-awareness (e.g., detecting accessibility barriers) depends heavily on where phones are carried and the resulting signal quality. While phone-carrying behaviors are well-documented for the general population, patterns specific to wheelchair users remain unexplored, limiting the accuracy and inclusivity of context-aware systems for this population.

Method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) a survey of 91 wheelchair users, and (2) semi-structured interviews with 15 wheelchair users, systematically investigating phone-carrying locations and the factors that influence them.

Result: Wheelchair users employ diverse carrying strategies beyond traditional pockets, notably wheelchair-mounted accessories (e.g., bags, mounts, pouches attached to the chair) and around-body placements. These choices are shaped by a complex interplay of physical ability, wheelchair design/configuration, and everyday contextual factors including social settings, activities, and device characteristics.

Conclusion: Phone-carrying location can serve as a proxy for inferring user context, enabling novel context-aware experiences. The authors propose design implications for building more inclusive and effective mobile context-aware applications that account for the unique carrying patterns of wheelchair users.

Abstract: Smartphone-based context-awareness holds significant promise for wheelchair users -- from detecting everyday accessibility barriers to enabling ability-based adaptations. Such capabilities often build on passive context inference through mobile sensing, yet their accuracy hinges on how and where phones are carried and the resulting signal quality. While prior work documents phone-carrying behaviors in the general population, patterns specific to wheelchair users remain underexplored. Through a mixed-methods approach combining a survey of 91 and interviews with 15 wheelchair users, we systematically investigate their phone-carrying locations and influencing factors. Our findings reveal distinct patterns extending beyond pocket storage to diverse wheelchair-mounted accessories and around-body placements, shaped by the interplay of physical ability, wheelchair design, and everyday contexts, including social, activity, and device factors. Grounded in these findings, we articulate how carrying location can serve as a proxy for user context to enable novel context-aware experiences, and discuss design implications for developing inclusive and effective mobile context-aware applications.

</details>


### [285] [Skeleton: Visual Authoring of Non-visual Data Experiences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14579)
*Frank Elavsky,Chieri Nnadozie,Lucas Nadolskis,Patrick Carrington,Dominik Moritz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Skeleton is a direct-manipulation authoring environment that makes accessible navigation structures visible and editable. It introduces an Inspector that renders navigation graphs as interactive node-link diagrams and a Dimensions API for expressing navigation via data dimensions. Through co-design and an in-situ study with 8 practitioners, the authors show that visualizing navigation structure shifts accessibility from a compliance task to a design problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sighted practitioners currently build accessible navigation structures for data visualizations entirely in code with no visual representation, preventing them from developing judgment about navigation quality. This lack of a feedback loop caps the quality of non-visual experiences.

Method: Longitudinal co-design with practitioners across cartography, design systems, and open-source visualization. Development of Skeleton, featuring: a dual-view editor (navigation model + spatial experience), a scaffolding engine for automated spatial node placement via visualization rendering pipelines, a live label-template editor with real-time screen-reader preview, and a visually trackable traversal testing mode.

Result: An in-situ study with 8 practitioners showed that making navigation structure visible led practitioners to reconsider their visualization architectures, attend to broader input modalities, and reframe accessible design as a design problem rather than a compliance task.

Conclusion: Providing visual representations of non-visual navigation structures enables practitioners to develop judgment and improve accessible visualization quality, fundamentally shifting the mindset around accessibility work.

Abstract: When sighted practitioners author accessible data visualizations, they build navigation structures (the nodes, edges, and input bindings that govern how assistive technologies traverse an interface) entirely in code, with no visual representation. Without a representation to react to, practitioners cannot develop judgment about what makes navigation good or bad, and the quality ceiling of non-visual experiences is set by the absence of a feedback loop. We address this problem through longitudinal co-design with practitioners across cartography, design systems, and open-source visualization, and make three contributions. First, we introduce an Inspector that renders navigation graphs as interactive node-link diagrams, and a Dimensions API that expresses navigation in terms of data dimensions rather than explicit graph construction. Second we present Skeleton, a direct-manipulation authoring environment in which the properties of an accessible navigation structure are translated into visual representations authors can observe and manipulate. Key techniques include a dual-view editor that simultaneously shows the system's navigation model and the end user's spatial experience, a scaffolding engine that automates spatial node placement by repurposing a visualization rendering pipeline, a live label-template editor with real-time screen-reader-output preview, and a testing mode that makes traversal sequence visually trackable. Third, we evaluate Skeleton through an in-situ study with 8 practitioners across visualization design, engineering, and research. Making navigation structure visible changed how practitioners engaged with accessible design: they reconsidered the architecture of their own visualizations, attended to a broader range of input modalities, and shifted from treating accessibility as a compliance task to treating it as a design problem. (abstract shortened for arxiv)

</details>


### [286] [Conversational Tactile Data Interfaces: Co-Designing Accessible Data Experiences with Blind Users Using Refreshable Tactile Displays and Conversational AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14588)
*Samuel Reinders,Munazza Zaib,Bongshin Lee,Ingrid Zukerman,Matthew Butler,Thien Autran,Sascha Cowley,Francois Jacobs,Lizhen Qu,Kim Marriott*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A co-design study with three BLV co-designers over eight months produced Graphy, a conversational tactile data interface combining refreshable tactile displays with LLM agents, yielding design recommendations including layered presentation, feedback grammar, and a sequential interaction pattern (select-confirm-ask-verify).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While combining refreshable tactile displays (RTDs) with conversational AI holds promise for accessible data visualization for BLV users, it is unclear how these modalities should be integrated to support meaningful data experiences.

Method: A co-design process with three BLV co-designers over eight months, involving four workshops. Building on a prior Wizard-of-Oz study, the team iteratively developed and refined Graphy, a CTDI combining an RTD with an LLM-powered conversational agent.

Result: Key findings include: (1) a layered presentation approach using progressive, interactive layers to scaffold chart exploration; (2) a feedback grammar distinguishing user-initiated vs. agent-initiated tactile feedback; (3) a sequential interaction pattern of select → confirm → ask → verify where each step grounds the next. Co-designers used touch for spatial understanding (shape, trends, relationships) and the conversational agent for calculation and analysis, using the RTD chart to verify agent responses.

Conclusion: The work contributes the Graphy system along with design knowledge and actionable recommendations for building conversational tactile data interfaces (CTDIs) that effectively blend tactile and conversational modalities for BLV users.

Abstract: Combining refreshable tactile displays (RTDs) with conversational AI offers a promising approach to accessible data visualization for people who are blind or have low vision (BLV). However, it remains an open question how these modalities should be integrated to support accessible data experiences. We address this through a co-design process with three BLV co-designers. Building on our prior Wizard-of-Oz study, we created a conversational tactile data interface (CTDI) that combines an RTD with an LLM-powered conversational agent, refined through four workshops over eight months. In addition to the resulting system, Graphy, we contribute design knowledge and recommendations for CTDIs. Co-designers used touch as the primary sensemaking channel for spatial understanding of the data's shape, trends, and relationships, reserved the agent for what touch could not resolve (e.g., calculation and analysis), and used the chart on the RTD to verify the agent's responses. Key findings include: a layered presentation that scaffolds chart exploration through progressive, interactive layers; a feedback grammar that distinguishes user- and agent-initiated tactile feedback; and a sequential interaction pattern -- select, confirm, ask, verify -- where each step grounds the last.

</details>


### [287] [Memory-Driven Self-Disclosure and Relational Turning Points: A Longitudinal Multimodal Study of Human-AI Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14593)
*Ryuichi Sumida,Mao Saeki,Masaki Eguchi,Sadahiro Yoshikawa,Koji Inoue,Tatsuya Kawahara,Yoichi Matsuyama*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A longitudinal multimodal study (24 participants × 10 sessions) reveals that human-AI relationships develop through two dynamics: slow accumulation (conversational quality drives momentary enjoyment; perceived memory is relationally conditioned and promotes future self-disclosure) and abrupt turning points (enjoyment crashes/surges), with surges being more behaviorally detectable and persistent than crashes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As conversational AI systems are designed for repeated, longitudinal use, there is an open question about how a series of discrete interactions transforms into a sustained human-AI relationship. The authors aim to uncover the temporal dynamics and relational constructs that underpin this process.

Method: A longitudinal multimodal study with 24 participants interacting with a memory-augmented conversational agent across 10 sessions. After each session, participants rated five relational constructs: familiarity, self-disclosure, perceived memory, conversational quality, and enjoyment. Multimodal behavioral signals (e.g., speech, language, facial expressions) were also captured to trace turning points.

Result: Two complementary dynamics were identified. (1) Slow accumulation: conversational quality strongly predicts within-session enjoyment but does not carry over across sessions; perceived memory is shaped by prior relational state (not just system memory capability) and indirectly boosts later enjoyment by fostering subsequent self-disclosure. (2) Turning points: enjoyment exhibits discrete crashes and surges; surges are more behaviorally detectable in real time than crashes; enjoyment surges persist more reliably than crashes recover; some crashes are better forecast from person-specific behavioral drift than detected post hoc.

Conclusion: Longitudinal human-AI relationships are jointly built through gradual relational accumulation and discrete, punctuated turning points. These findings offer practical implications for designing agents that can detect, forecast, and respond to critical relational moments.

Abstract: As conversational AI systems are designed for repeated use, a central question is how a series of interactions becomes a relationship. We present a longitudinal multimodal study of a memory-augmented conversational agent (24 participants x 10 sessions), in which participants rated five relational constructs -- familiarity, self-disclosure, perceived memory, conversational quality, and enjoyment -- after each session. Two complementary dynamics emerge. First, conversational quality strongly shapes how enjoyable a session feels in the moment but does not carry forward across sessions, whereas perceived memory is relationally conditioned -- predicted by prior relational state rather than reflecting system capability alone -- and it shapes later enjoyment indirectly, via subsequent self-disclosure. Second, relationships are punctuated by discrete turning points -- crashes and surges -- that are partially traceable in multimodal behavior and open different intervention windows: surges are more behaviorally detectable in the moment, enjoyment surges persist more reliably than enjoyment crashes recover, and some crashes are better forecast from person-specific behavioral drift than detected after they have already occurred. Together, the findings suggest that longitudinal human-AI relationships are built through both slow accumulation and abrupt turning points.

</details>


### [288] [Dendrite: A Real-Time Python Application for Online Brain-Computer Interface Research and Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14655)
*Niko Kroflic,Jan Babič*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Dendrite is an open-source Python application for real-time BCI research that integrates multimodal signal acquisition, online decoder training, and live inference into a single reproducible workflow, while keeping the experimental paradigm external and networked.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online BCI research currently lacks integrated software that simultaneously handles multimodal physiological data acquisition, online decoder training/updating, live inference, and full experimental provenance tracking within a modifiable, reproducible framework.

Method: Dendrite records multiple signal streams concurrently at native rates, runs parallel processing modes, supports mid-session decoder fitting without stopping the pipeline, tracks all recordings/decoders/training runs in a database with provenance linking, and accepts external experimental paradigms over network connections — all built as a single Python application.

Result: The system was validated end-to-end on both in-house and public BCI datasets, demonstrating successful online decoder training and updating while real-time processing continued uninterrupted.

Conclusion: Dendrite provides a reproducible, open-source biomedical-computing platform (GPL-3.0) that unifies the full BCI pipeline — acquisition, training, inference, and provenance — enabling robust development and evaluation of online BCI paradigms.

Abstract: Online brain-computer interface research requires software that can acquire multimodal physiological data, train and update decoders, run live inference, and preserve the full experimental provenance in a reproducible workflow. We present Dendrite, a real-time brain-computer interface application in Python that brings signal acquisition, decoder training, and live inference together in a single, ready-to-run application that stays modifiable. Dendrite records several signal streams at once, each at its native rate, and executes multiple processing modes concurrently against them. A decoder can start from a previously trained model or be fit mid-session while the pipeline keeps running, and the same recordings feed offline training in the same application. Each recording, decoder, and training run is tracked in a database, and every decoder records the configuration and the source recordings it was trained from, so a deployed decoder traces back to what produced it. The experimental paradigm stays external, an independent program in any language that reaches Dendrite over the network, rather than a module built inside the runtime. We validate the full system end-to-end on in-house and public BCI datasets, training and updating decoders online while the pipeline runs in real time. Dendrite is open-source under the GPL-3.0 license at https://github.com/dendrite-bci/dendrite. The result is a reproducible, open-source biomedical-computing system for developing and evaluating online BCI paradigms.

</details>


### [289] [Understanding of Task-specific and Subject-specific Components in Surface EMG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14744)
*Yangyang Yuan,Jionghui Liu,Xinyu Jiang,ChihHong Chou,Chenyun Dai,Jiahao Fan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A disentanglement model separates sEMG signals into task-specific (gesture-related) and subject-specific (identity-related) components, improving cross-subject generalization for both gesture recognition and user identification while revealing physiological insights about neuromuscular signal characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sEMG-based models for gesture recognition and user identification suffer from poor cross-subject generalization due to individual-specific neuromuscular characteristics, limiting practical deployment in human-machine interfaces.

Method: A disentanglement model that decomposes sEMG signals into two latent components: task-specific features capturing gesture-related activation patterns and subject-specific features encoding individual neuromuscular characteristics. These disentangled representations are then used for downstream gesture classification and user identification tasks.

Result: The disentangled components significantly improve both gesture classification and user identification accuracy across subjects and days, outperforming conventional methods. Task-specific components consistently capture gesture activation patterns across individuals, while subject-specific components show lower cross-day similarity, explaining the greater temporal degradation in user identification accuracy compared to gesture recognition.

Conclusion: The disentanglement approach enhances both classification performance and physiological interpretability of sEMG signals, with promising implications for robust real-world applications in rehabilitation and user authentication.

Abstract: Surface electromyogram (sEMG) signals are widely used in human-machine interfaces for gesture recognition and user identification, but existing models often struggle to generalize across individuals due to subject-specific neuromuscular characteristics. This study introduces a disentanglement model that separates task-specific and subject-specific components from sEMG signals, thereby improving the generalization and interpretability of gesture recognition and user identification systems. Experimental results demonstrate that the disentangled components significantly improve the accuracy of both gesture classification and user identification across subjects and days, outperforming conventional methods under the same experimental conditions. Further analysis reveals that the task-specific components capture consistent activation patterns associated with the same gestures across individuals. In contrast, the subject-specific components reflect unique neuromuscular characteristics that can be used for user identification. Notably, the subject-specific components show lower similarity across days than the task-specific components, contributing to a greater decrease in user identification accuracy than in gesture recognition accuracy. These findings suggest that the disentanglement approach not only improves classification performance but also provides deeper insights into the physiological mechanisms underlying sEMG signals. The model's ability to isolate and interpret different neuromuscular components holds promise for enhancing the robustness of sEMG-based applications in real-world settings, including rehabilitation and user authentication. Our code is available at https://github.com/Open-EXG/HandDisentanglement.

</details>


### [290] [Authoring Narrative Visualization in Motion: Visual Storytelling in Swimming Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14924)
*Junhao Zhao,Romain Vuillemot,Petra Isenberg,Lijie Yao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper explores supporting the authoring of narrative visualizations in motion within sports videos, using swimming races as a case study. It develops an automated data extraction pipeline, derives narrative constructs from sports broadcast analysis, and designs a technology probe evaluated with content creators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches focus on embedding visualizations into videos but lack support for authoring narratives that coordinate views, data, and temporal progression to explain unfolding races. Content creators increasingly need tools to present complex sports events to general audiences.

Method: The authors (1) build an automated pipeline extracting structured data from swimming videos; (2) conduct observational analysis of sports broadcasts to derive narrative constructs; (3) design a technology probe supporting narrative visualization authoring; and (4) evaluate the probe with experienced content creators and graphic designers.

Result: The evaluation examines benefits and challenges of authoring narrative visualizations in motion with experienced content creators and graphic designers. Supplemental materials are available on OSF.

Conclusion: The paper contributes a pipeline, narrative constructs, and a technology probe that together form a systematic approach to support authoring narrative visualizations in motion for sports videos, demonstrated through swimming races.

Abstract: We investigate how to support authoring narrative visualizations in motion in sports videos, drawing on automated data preparation, systematic analysis, technology probe design, and evaluation, using swimming races as a case study. Sports videos are widely broadcast and shared across social media, where content creators increasingly seek to present and explain complex events to general audiences. Visualization in motion has been explored as an efficient way to embed data into videos and to move with the data referents, providing additional information and helping audiences understand races. However, existing approaches primarily focus on embedding visualizations in videos, lacking exploration of how to support authoring narratives that coordinate views, data, and temporal progression to explain the unfolding races. To address this gap, we use swimming videos as an ideal case for exploration, as swimming is a sport with rich, dynamic data and visualizations in practice. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts structured data from videos, derive narrative constructs through observational analysis of sports broadcasts, and design a technology probe that supports authoring using data prepared by our pipeline and narrative constructs derived from our observations. We evaluate our approach with experienced content creators and/or graphic designers to examine the benefits and challenges of authoring narrative visualizations in motion. All supplemental materials are described in the Supplemental Material Pointers section and are on OSF: osf.io/bq47n/.

</details>


### [291] [When AI Blurs the Boundaries of Contribution: An Empirical Study of Authorship Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15006)
*Célina Treuillier,Denis Lalanne*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Users who rely heavily on AI tend to misjudge their own authorship in collaborative content creation, while infrequent AI users show more accurate self-awareness. This "authorship calibration" gap has implications for metacognition and learning outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The widespread adoption of Generative AI raises critical questions about how users perceive their own contribution versus the AI's contribution when co-creating content. Understanding this perception — termed authorship calibration — is essential for responsible AI integration, particularly in educational contexts where misjudging one's authorship could undermine metacognitive monitoring and learning strategies.

Method: The authors conducted an empirical analysis using the CoAuthor dataset, examining how authorship calibration (the accuracy of users' awareness of their actual authorship when collaborating with AI) varies across individuals and how it correlates with the frequency of AI usage.

Result: Results show high inter-user variability in authorship calibration. Heavy AI users systematically misjudge their authorship, whereas less frequent AI users demonstrate significantly more accurate authorship calibration. This suggests that AI interaction can obscure users' perception of their own creative or intellectual contribution.

Conclusion: AI systems can distort users' self-perception of authorship, which in learning environments may impair metacognitive monitoring, learning strategies, and ultimately learning outcomes. Fostering accurate authorship calibration is therefore critical for promoting responsible and educationally meaningful AI integration.

Abstract: The broad adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Generative AI, raises pressing questions about how users interact with these systems to produce new content. In this paper, we introduce the concept of authorship calibration, defined as users awareness of their actual authorship when interacting with AI. Using the CoAuthor dataset, we empirically examine how authorship calibration varies across users and how it relates to their frequency of AI use. Our results reveal high variability: users relying heavily on AI tend to misjudge their authorship, whereas those using AI less frequently exhibit more accurate authorship calibration. These findings suggest that AI can obscure users perception of their own authorship. In learning contexts, miscalibration can affect metacognitive monitoring and learning strategies, ultimately impacting learning outcomes. Fostering authorship calibration then appears essential for promoting responsible and educationally meaningful AI integration.

</details>
